stages.label: Absent
stages.desc: Nothing of the kind exists, and a dated source says so.

stages.label: Preparing
stages.desc: Announced, drafted, piloted: an intention with an instrument or a pilot behind it.

stages.label: Establishing
stages.desc: In service, but limited in scope, coverage or use.

stages.label: Operating
stages.desc: In service at scale: funded, regulated, used, maintained.

stages.label: Leading
stages.desc: Embedded: interoperable, measured, sustained; at or beyond the continental norm.

grey.label: No evidence
grey.desc: Not staged: nothing held, or evidence held that meets no rung.

gov.legislate--access-to-information-leg.label: Access to information legislation: access to information law

ladder.text: A source from the past three years says the country has no access to information law and no draft of one. A right of access written in the constitution alone is not a law.

A bill or draft exists: published, validated, out for consultation, before cabinet or parliament, or passed and not yet promulgated. A law that is only announced, planned or called for does not count.
An access to information law is in force, however old: an act, ordinance or decree with the force of law that gives a right to ask public bodies for information.
The law has been put to work: a decree, regulation or order made under it, or its information commission or commissioner set up, or an existing body it names taking up the oversight.

The law has been applied in the past three years: a decision, order or penalty by the oversight body or a court, published figures of requests or complaints, or a rule made under the law. Training, an awareness campaign or an oversight body merely existing does not reach this stage.

gov.legislate--ai-legislation-regulation.label: AI legislation / regulations: AI law or binding rule

ladder.text: A source from the past three years says the country has no law or regulation on AI and no draft of one.
A bill, draft decree or draft regulation on AI exists: published, out for consultation, or before cabinet or parliament. A law that is only announced or planned does not count.

A law, decree or regulation in force names AI and sets a rule for it, in one sector or for one use: AI in higher education, AI-generated content in the media or in elections. A strategy, ethics guidelines or a data protection law's general rule on automated decisions does not count.
A law on AI itself is in force and applies across sectors.
That law has been applied in the past three years: a regulation or order has been made under it, or the body it names has registered, licensed, decided or penalised.
A source from the past three years says the country has no national AI strategy and none is being written.

A national AI strategy, policy or roadmap is being written or is out for consultation, or the last one has run out with no successor adopted. A task force appointed to write it counts. AI named as a priority in a digital strategy does not.
A national AI strategy is adopted and still running: approved by cabinet, or launched or issued by the head of state, the minister or the agency responsible. No body is yet named to carry it out.
The government has named a body to carry out the strategy: a council, office, agency, committee or ministry unit set up or named for it.

Public money has gone into carrying out the strategy in the past three years: a dated source names money allocated to it, or an action in it started with its funding named. How good the strategy is, is not judged.
A source from the past three years says the country has no national broadband plan and none is being written.
A national broadband plan is being written or is out for consultation, or the last one has ended with no successor adopted.

A national broadband plan is adopted by the government or the minister and its period has not ended. It may be part of a larger digital strategy or development plan that states broadband targets. No money tied to it is on record in the past three years.
Money has been committed to the plan in the past three years: a budget line, a universal service fund allocation or a financed programme that the source ties to the plan.
The plan is funded, and the government has published figures against the plan's own targets in the past three years. Whether the targets are met is not judged.

gov.policy--data-storage-cloud-strategy-.label: Data storage / cloud strategy: hosting policy

ladder.text: A source from the past three years says the government has no hosting or cloud policy and none is being written.

A government hosting or cloud policy is being written or is out for consultation, or the last one has ended with no successor adopted. A data centre or government cloud with no policy behind it does not count.

A policy on where the state's data is hosted, or on how public bodies may use cloud, is adopted and in force. It may be a cloud-first policy, a circular, a hosting standard or part of a larger strategy or law. Where public bodies must host is not yet named.
The government has named where public bodies must host: a government cloud or data centre in service that the policy tells them to use, or a published list of approved providers.
Public bodies have moved onto the named hosting in the past three years: a dated source names or counts the ministries or agencies that have. How good the policy is, is not judged.

gov.legislate--cybersecurity-legislation.label: Cybersecurity legislation: cybercrime and cybersecurity law

ladder.text: A source from the past three years says the country has no cybercrime or cybersecurity law and no bill for one.
A cybercrime or cybersecurity bill is drafted, before parliament or passed. No law is known to be in force.
A cybercrime or cybersecurity law is in force, as an act of its own or as part of a penal or digital code. No use of it is on record in the past three years.
The law has been used in the past three years: a dated arrest, charge, prosecution or conviction, or a penalty from the body it sets up. Who it was used against is not judged.
The law is used, and a count of cases investigated, prosecuted or decided under it is published for a period ending within the past two years.

gov.policy--data-governance-policy-natio.label: Data governance policy: national data policy

ladder.text: A source from the past three years says the country has no national data policy and none is being written.

A national data policy, strategy or framework is being written or is out for consultation, or the last one has run out with no successor. A draft validated at a workshop is still a draft. A tender to hire the writer, or a stated intention, does not count.

The government has adopted the policy and it has not run out: approved by cabinet, or launched or issued by the head of state, the minister or the agency responsible. A policy on sharing or managing data across the whole government counts; a data protection law or an open data policy does not. No body is yet named to carry it out.

A body is named to carry out the policy: a council, office, agency, committee, chief data officer or ministry unit set up or named for it. The ministry that wrote the policy being responsible for it in general does not count.

A rule or standard the policy called for has been issued in the past three years: a law, regulation, standard or guideline, such as one on classifying data or on sharing it between public bodies. How good the policy is, and whether it follows the African Union's framework, is not judged.
A source from the past three years says the country has no rule that data must be kept in the country and none is being written.

A rule that data, or a named kind of data, must be stored or processed in the country is being written or is out for consultation, or the last one was repealed with no successor. A minister's stated intention with no drafting begun does not count, and nor does a data centre.

A rule is in force: a law, decree, regulation or regulator's directive that data, or a named kind of data, must be kept in the country. A rule on one kind of data counts; a condition on sending data abroad does not. No body is yet named to enforce it.
A body is named to enforce the rule: a regulator, agency or ministry unit that checks compliance or grants exemptions. A regulator that issued the rule for the bodies it licenses counts.

The rule has been applied in the past three years: a dated source names an organisation ordered to bring data into the country, penalised or exempted under it, or counts those that have moved data to comply. How wide the rule is, and whether the country should have one, is not judged.
A source from the past three years says the country has no data protection authority, and no law in force names one.
A law names a data protection authority. No source says its head or members have been appointed.
The authority's head or members are appointed, or an existing body given the job is doing it. No ruling against a named organisation is on record in the past three years.
The authority has ruled against a named organisation in the past three years: a decision, fine or order. A court's judgment does not count.
The authority publishes a count of its decisions, fines or complaints settled, for a period of a quarter or more ending within the past two years.
A dated source states that the country has no general data protection law, and none is on record as enacted or in preparation.
A data protection law is announced, being drafted, before parliament, or passed and not yet promulgated.
A data protection law is enacted or in force, whether it stands alone or is part of a larger law. No decision under it is on record in the past three years.

The law is in force and has been applied: a dated sanction, order, decision or court judgment on a controller within the past three years. Without a constituted supervisory authority the stage is capped at 3.
The law has regulations in force under it, and a count of decisions, sanctions or complaints settled is published for a period ending within the past two years.

gov.protect--national-data-protection-re.label: National data protection readiness: data protection system

ladder.text: No data protection law is in force: there is none, or it is still a bill or has not yet commenced.
A data protection law is in force. The country has not ratified the Malabo Convention and no authority is appointed.
A law is in force, and the country has ratified the Malabo Convention or appointed an authority. Nothing in the past three years shows the authority at work.
The law is being implemented: in the past three years an appointed authority has registered organisations, taken breach reports, issued guidance or inspected.
The authority is acting: in the past three years it has ruled against a named organisation, or it publishes a count of its rulings. A court's judgment does not count.

gov.regional--cross-border-data-transfer.label: Cross-border data transfers: rule on sending data abroad

ladder.text: A source from the past three years says the country has no rule on sending personal data abroad and none is being written.

A rule on sending personal data, or a named kind of data, out of the country is being written: a bill or a published draft that sets a condition for it. A law passed but not reported in effect counts here. A stated intention with no drafting begun does not.

A rule is in force: a law, regulation or directive that lets data leave only on a condition, such as the receiving country's protection judged good enough, the authority's permission, the person's consent or a contract. A data protection law alone does not count, and nor does a rule that data must stay in the country.

The authority has published the means of complying: a list of countries data may go to, model contract terms, a procedure for applying for permission, or guidance on transfers. A procedure in the rule's own text, or guidance on the whole law, does not count.

The rule has been applied in the past three years: a dated source names a country approved to receive data, or an organisation given or refused permission, ordered to comply or penalised for sending data abroad, or gives a count of permissions. How strict the rule is, is not judged.

gov.legislate--legislation-covering-digi.label: Legislation covering digital id: national identity law

ladder.text: A source from the past three years says the country has no national identity law and no bill for one.
A bill for a national identity law is drafted, before parliament or passed and not yet promulgated, or the identity system runs on a decree or order with no law behind it.

A national identity law is in force: a law, ordinance or decree-law that sets up the identity number, the register of persons or the identity card, however old. A data protection law, or a civil registration law that sets up no identity number or card, does not count.

The law in force provides for a digital identity: a biometric register, an identity number unique to each person, or an identity that can be checked electronically. A law for a paper card only does not reach this stage.

Rules have been made under that law in the past three years: a regulation or decree applying it, or a rule that banks, phone companies or public bodies must check identity against the system. Cards issued, people enrolled and changes to fees do not count.
A dated source states that the country has no national digital strategy, and none is on record as adopted, launched or in preparation.
A national digital strategy is announced, being drafted, or validated and awaiting adoption. Or one is adopted and its text is not public. Or its period has ended and a successor is in preparation.

A national digital strategy is adopted, its text is public, and its period has not ended. A text the government has published, and no source calls a draft, counts as adopted. A strategy with no stated period stops here.

The strategy has a delivery plan with dated actions or costs, and the government has published results against its own targets within the past three years. Without a mandated body and a domestic budget line the stage is capped at 3.
The delivery plan is costed, and results against the strategy's targets are published on every pillar within the past two years.

finance.budget--sustainable-domestic-fin.label: Sustainable domestic financing of digital transformation: state money for digital programmes
finance.budget--sustainable-domestic-fin.short_label: The state's own money for digital programmes

ladder.text: A source from the past three years says the state budget gives no money to digital programmes, or that they are paid for wholly by donors and lenders.
In the past three years the state budget gave money to a digital ministry, a digital agency or a named digital programme. A line paid wholly by a loan or grant does not count.
That money was higher in the latest budget than in the one before, in the country's own currency and not adjusted for inflation. Lower or the same holds a country at stage 2, whatever else it has.

In the past three years a fund, levy or tax assigned by law to digital programmes was created, collected money or paid for a project, or the government put state money to a digital programme it had said the country must pay for itself. A fund abolished, or held only in an old law, does not count.
A budget execution report, settlement law, audited accounts or the fund's own account gives what was actually spent, for a year from 2024.
A source from the past three years says the country has no law on electronic transactions or e-commerce and no draft of one.
A bill or draft exists: published, out for consultation, before cabinet or parliament, or passed and not yet promulgated. A law that is only announced or planned does not count.

A law is in force that gives electronic contracts, records or signatures legal effect, or sets rules for selling online, however old. A law on electronic signatures alone counts, as does the part of a digital code or consumer protection law that does this job.
A decree, regulation or order has been made under the law: on electronic signatures, on those who certify them, or on those who sell online.

The law has been applied in the past three years: a provider of electronic signatures accredited or licensed under it, online sellers registered or licensed, or an order or penalty made. A government office using electronic signatures does not reach this stage.

digital.rural--digitalisation-of-rural-h.label: Digitalisation of rural health clinics: HMIS

ladder.text: A dated source states that routine health reporting is not entered digitally at any level of the health system.

A digital reporting system is used by hospitals only or in some districts, or a national rollout is contracted or being prepared: staff trained, equipment delivered or an agreement signed. Primary clinics do not use it, beyond pilot sites.
A national system takes the clinics' reports, which are keyed in at district level from the clinics' paper forms. A minority of primary clinics enter their own reports, or no figure is published.
More than half of primary clinics enter their own reports at the facility. The figure is a published share, or a count given with its total.
At least 90 per cent of primary clinics enter their own reports at the facility, on a figure published within the past two years. Reporting completeness is published as well.

digital.rural--digitalisation-of-rural-h.label: Digitalisation of rural health clinics: EMR

ladder.text: A dated source states that patient records are kept on paper at every level of the health system.

Electronic patient records are in use in some hospitals or pilot facilities, or a national system is procured or being prepared: staff trained, equipment delivered or an agreement signed. Primary clinics do not use them, beyond pilot sites.

Electronic patient records are in use in most hospitals, or in primary clinics in some districts, but each record stays in the facility that made it. A minority of primary clinics use them, or no figure is published.
More than half of primary clinics keep electronic patient records, entered at the point of care. Each record is held under a unique patient identifier and can be retrieved at another facility.
At least 90 per cent of primary clinics keep such shared records, on a figure published within the past two years. A record can be retrieved anywhere in the public network.
A dated source states that the country has no ICT or telecommunications sector policy, none is on record as adopted or in preparation, and no national digital strategy is held.
A sector policy is announced, being drafted, or validated and awaiting adoption. Or one is adopted and its text is not public. Or its period has ended and a successor sector policy is in preparation.
A sector policy is adopted, its text is public, and its period has not ended. A policy with no stated period stops here. A national digital strategy is assessed on its own row and does not count.

The policy has a delivery plan with dated actions or costs, and the government has published results against the policy's own targets within the past three years. Without a mandated body and a domestic budget line the stage is capped at 3.
The delivery plan is costed, and results against the policy's targets are published on every objective within the past two years.

gov.standards--adoption-of-international.label: Adoption of international standards: international standards for information technology and data
gov.standards--adoption-of-international.short_label: International standards for information technology and data

ladder.text: A source from the past three years says the country belongs to no international standards organisation.

The country's standards body is a member of ISO, the International Organization for Standardization, or of IEC, its counterpart for electrical technology. Full, correspondent and subscriber members all count. Membership of the African or a regional standards organisation does not.

The country has adopted an international standard on information technology or data as a national standard: a named ISO, IEC or ITU standard on information technology, information security, software or data. A count of adopted standards that names none, a draft, and a standard in another field do not count.

Public bodies must meet a named international standard: a law, decree, regulation, directive or circular names an international standard on information technology or data and requires ministries, agencies or government systems to meet it. A rule for one sector, a text modelled on a standard, and a system built to one do not count.

The country has taken part in writing international standards on information technology in the past three years: a dated source names the standards body or a public body as a participating member, chair or secretariat of an ISO or IEC committee on information technology or data. An observer seat does not count.

gov.policy--data-interoperability-framew.label: Data interoperability framework / roadmap: government interoperability framework

ladder.text: A source from the past three years says the government has no interoperability framework and none is being written.

A framework, standard or regulation for how government systems exchange data is being written or is out for consultation, or the last one has ended with no successor adopted. An exchange platform with no framework behind it does not count, and nor does interoperability named only as an aim.

A framework for how government systems exchange data is adopted and published. It may be an interoperability framework, a standard, a decree or part of a larger law. No instrument yet makes it compulsory and names who enforces it.
Public bodies are required to follow the framework: a decree, law, regulation or circular makes it compulsory and names the body that enforces it.

Public bodies are following the framework in the past three years: a dated source names or counts the ministries, agencies or systems that exchange data under it or are certified as meeting it. How good the framework is, is not judged.

gov.legislate--legislation-enabling-data.label: Legislation enabling data interoperability: data sharing law

ladder.text: A source from the past three years says the country has no law or decree on public bodies sharing data with each other and no draft of one.

A bill, draft decree or draft regulation on public bodies sharing data is published, before parliament or cabinet, or passed and not yet in force. An executive order that legislation is to replace stops here.

A law, decree or regulation on public bodies sharing data is in force, however old. An interoperability framework counts where it is issued as a decree or regulation. A law for one sector, or a data protection law, does not count.

The law in force requires public bodies to share: to exchange data, to connect to the government's exchange platform, or not to ask a person for what another public body already holds. A law that only allows sharing does not reach this stage.
The law has been applied in the past three years: a regulation, decree or order has been made under it, or public bodies are named as exchanging data because it requires them to.

gov.standards--national-interoperability.label: National interoperability standards: technical standards for government systems

ladder.text: A source from the past three years says the government has no technical standards for its systems to exchange data and none are being written.

Standards are being written: a named set of technical standards for government systems to exchange data is being drafted or is out for consultation. An unapproved edition counts here. A mandate or a stated intention to write standards does not.

Standards are published: the government, the agency responsible or the standards body has issued the data formats, codes, interfaces or protocols its systems must use. An interoperability framework counts only where a source says it sets technical standards. Standards for one sector or one function do not count.

Public bodies are required to use the standards: a law, decree, regulation or circular makes them compulsory for the systems public bodies build or buy. A text that says of itself that it is compulsory does not count.

A system has been checked against the standards in the past three years: a dated source names a public body, system or product tested, audited or certified against them, or gives a count. How good the standards are is not judged.

digital.localgov--ict-infrastructure-for.label: ICT infrastructure for local government: office connection

ladder.text: A dated source states that local government offices have no connection of their own. Staff working on their own phones or modems does not change this.

A programme to connect local government offices is being prepared or piloted: equipment handed over, a contract signed or pilot offices connected. Or only the capital city or the regions above are connected.

Some local government offices outside the capital are connected, past any pilot, or work in a national system. They are a minority, or no share of local governments is published. A share equipped or covered by a programme, however high, places here.
More than half of local governments have a connection provided to the office by the state or the authority. The figure is a published share, or a count given with its total.

At least 90 per cent of local governments are connected and work in national systems over the connection, on a figure published within the past two years. The figure gives the share for rural local governments.

digital.localgov--digitalisation-of-loca.label: Digitalisation of local government records: revenue records

ladder.text: A dated source states that local governments keep their revenue records on paper, with no system in use.
A system is being prepared or piloted, or a one-off survey has built a register with no system to keep it. Or only the capital city or the regions above record digitally.

Some local governments outside the capital record payments in a system, past any pilot. They are a minority, or no share is published. Electronic receipts with no register of payers place here, and so does a share given a system or trained on it, however high.
More than half of local governments keep a digital register of their payers, with each bill and payment against it. The figure is a published share, or a count given with its total.
At least 90 per cent of local governments keep that register in a national or shared system, on a figure published within the past two years.

finance.new--mobilisation-of-non-state-f.label: Mobilisation of non-state finance: private money for digital businesses

ladder.text: A source from 2024 or later says no private money has gone into the country's digital businesses, or that investors have withdrawn.

From 2024 on, a named amount was lent to, invested in, guaranteed for or granted to a private digital business, fund or partnership in the country, or a company said what it was investing there itself. Money to the state, and memoranda and plans, do not count.
Such amounts were signed or started in two different years from 2024. Two in one year hold a country at stage 2, whatever else it has.

From 2024 on, a named amount came from a bank, pension fund, insurer, investor or company of the country itself, or was raised by a bond or share issue on the country's own market. The state's own funds do not count.

From 2024 on, the government signed a public-private partnership, concession or joint venture in which the private partner puts a named amount into a public digital project, or private investors paid into a state fund.

gov.policy--open-data-policy-national-op.label: Open data policy: national open data policy

ladder.text: A source from the past three years says the country has no open data policy and none is being written.

An open data policy, strategy, decree or law is being written or is out for consultation, or the last one has run out with no successor. A draft validated at a workshop is still a draft. A portal with no policy behind it, or a commitment in an open government action plan, does not count.

The government has adopted the policy and it has not run out: approved by cabinet, or launched or issued by the head of state, the minister or the agency responsible. The open data part of a wider data policy counts where a source says it sets the rule; an access to information law does not. No government portal is yet reported running under it.
A government open data portal is running under the policy. A statistics office's data portal, or one a donor or development bank runs for the country, does not count.

Public bodies have published data under the policy in the past three years: a source names a ministry or agency that has released data, or counts the datasets or the bodies publishing. How good the policy is, and how open the licence, is not judged.

gov.discourse--open-discussion-of-govern.label: Open discussion of government policy: freedom to discuss policy online and in the press
gov.discourse--open-discussion-of-govern.short_label: Freedom to discuss policy online and in the press
gov.discourse--open-discussion-of-govern.topic: Public debate and participation in policymaking

ladder.text: In the past twelve months the government, a regulator or the security forces cut the internet or blocked a social media service, messaging service or news site, anywhere in the country; or a source from the past three years says no independent newspaper, broadcaster or news site is allowed to work.
In the past three years a newspaper, broadcaster, party or group inside the country criticised a government policy in public, and no cut is on record in the past twelve months.

A source says the country went the past twelve months with no one arrested, charged or jailed, and no outlet suspended or closed, for what was said or published. One such arrest or closure in the twelve months holds a country at stage 2.
In the past three years parliament repealed, or a court of the country struck down, an offence of criminal defamation, false news, sedition or insulting the head of state.
In the past three years a law, a ruling of the country's own court that a cut was unlawful, or an undertaking given in court barred the government from cutting the internet.
A source from the past three years says the country has no payments law or e-money rules and no draft of either.
A payments bill or draft e-money rules are published, before parliament or passed and not yet in force, or mobile money runs on a central bank's letter with no rules behind it.

A payments law or central bank rules on e-money or payment services are in force, however old. A regional central bank's regulation counts for each member it binds. A law on crypto or virtual assets does not count.
Companies that are not banks can be licensed under the law or rules in force to offer payments or issue e-money: a source says so, or names one licensed.

A rule requires mobile money providers and banks to connect to each other or to a national or regional switch. A switch that providers may join by choice, or a rule that binds banks only, does not reach this stage.

digital.rural--digitalisation-of-rural-p.label: Digitalisation of rural police stations: station records

ladder.text: A dated source states that police stations record reports and cases on paper only. A fingerprint database, a crime statistics return or an online reporting portal does not change this.

A system for stations to record reports or cases is being prepared or piloted: staff trained, equipment delivered, an agreement signed or pilot stations using it. Or one runs at headquarters or in the capital only.

Reports or cases are entered digitally, past any pilot, in some stations outside the capital; they are a minority, or no share of stations is published. A share of stations equipped or connected, however high, places here.
More than half of stations enter reports or cases digitally at the station when they are taken, into the national system. The figure is a published share, or a count given with its total.
At least 90 per cent of stations do so, for both the first report and the case file, on a figure published within the past two years. The figure gives the share for rural stations.

gov.discourse--non-governmental-contribu.label: Non-governmental contribution to national policy: consultation on digital law and policy
gov.discourse--non-governmental-contribu.short_label: Consultation on digital law and policy
gov.discourse--non-governmental-contribu.topic: Public debate and participation in policymaking

ladder.text: A source from the past three years says a named digital law or policy was made without consulting people outside government, or that they were refused a part in it, and none says they were asked.

In the past three years the government, parliament or a regulator asked people outside government for their views on a named digital law or policy: a draft put out for comment, or a hearing, workshop or meeting they took part in. A national internet governance forum, a consultation on something that is not digital, and a workshop of officials, donors and consultants do not count.
In the past three years it published what it was told: a report of the consultation, the comments received, or its written answer to them.

In the past three years a consultation on a digital law or policy was held because a law, decree or published procedure required it. The rule alone, with no consultation held under it, does not count.
In the past three years a standing body with members from outside government gave its view on a named digital law or policy. A body that has only been set up or has only met does not count.

gov.standards--national-quality-standard.label: National quality standards: national standards for information technology and data
gov.standards--national-quality-standard.short_label: National standards for information technology and data

ladder.text: A source from the past three years says the country has no national standards body.
A national standards body exists: a body set up by a law or decree to write or adopt national standards. One announced and not yet created does not count.

The body has issued a national standard on information technology or data: a named standard on information technology, information security, software or data, issued or adopted as a national standard. A national quality policy, telecoms quality-of-service rules and quality management standards do not count.

An organisation can be certified against such a standard in the country: the standards body, or a certifier accredited in the country, offers certification against it or has certified an organisation. A certificate from a certifier abroad does not count.

A public body has been certified in the past three years: a dated source names a ministry, agency or state-owned body certified against such a standard by the standards body or a certifier accredited in the country. How good the standards are is not judged.

gov.regional--shared-regional-infrastruc.label: Shared regional infrastructure: digital links and facilities shared with other African countries
gov.regional--shared-regional-infrastruc.short_label: Digital links and facilities shared with other African countries

ladder.text: A source from the past three years says the country has no digital link with a neighbour, or stands outside the shared links of its region, and none is on record.

In the past three years the country has agreed to build or join a link or facility shared with another African country: a cross-border fibre link, a sea cable joining two African countries, a shared exchange point, data centre or satellite. Talks, a study or a bid to host do not count.
Building has started in the past three years: a contract awarded, works begun or cable being laid. A tender opened or money promised does not count.
A shared link or facility is in service: lit, commissioned or opened to traffic. A ceremony for the start of works, or a test, does not count.

It is reported carrying another country's traffic in the past three years: published figures of capacity sold or traffic carried across the border, a named user from the other country, or a fault that cut the other country's service.

gov.regional--regional-legal-harmonisati.label: Regional legal harmonisation: regional digital law taken into national law
gov.regional--regional-legal-harmonisati.short_label: Regional digital law taken into national law

ladder.text: A source from the past three years says the country has not signed, and no other shared African legal text on a digital matter is on record for it.

The country has signed an African legal text on a digital matter, such as the African Union's cyber security and data protection convention, or is bound by a named act or regulation of its regional community. It has not ratified.
The country has ratified or acceded to such a text, by a law or decree approving it or by depositing the instrument. A cabinet approval, a bill or a promise to ratify does not count.
A national law, decree or regulation has been passed or amended to give effect to a shared text. A draft, a consultation or a study does not count.

The shared law is reported applied across a border in the past three years: a licence or signature recognised, a request between authorities answered, a ruling, or the regional body's finding that the country complies.

gov.regional--regional-policy-collaborat.label: Regional policy collaboration: regional cooperation on digital policy

ladder.text: A source from the past three years says the country is suspended from, has left or stands outside the African bodies that make digital policy, and no agreement is on record.

The country belongs to an African body that makes digital policy, or takes part in its meetings, and nothing more is on record. Membership of the African Union or a regional community alone does not count.

In the past three years the country has signed a digital agreement or declaration with another African government or African body, hosted or chaired a meeting of such a body, or won a seat or office in one. Talks, visits and meetings attended do not count.

Something the country agreed has been put into effect: roaming charges cut with a neighbour, a joint body set up and meeting, a regional guideline adopted as a national rule, or a shared service opened.

What was put into effect is reported in use in the past three years: published figures of its use, a decision of the joint body, or a review of what the agreement delivered. A launch, a renewal or projects agreed do not reach this stage.

digital.rural--digitalisation-of-rural-r.label: Digitalisation of rural registry offices: civil registration

ladder.text: A dated source states that local civil registration offices register births and deaths on paper only. Scanning or keying old registers does not change this.
A system for local offices to register births digitally is being prepared or piloted, or one runs at the national office or in the capital only.

Births are entered digitally when they are registered, past any pilot, in some local offices; they are a minority, or no share of offices is published. A share of offices equipped or connected, however high, places here.
More than half of local offices enter births digitally at the office when they are registered, into the national register. The figure is a published share, or a count given with its total.
At least 90 per cent of local offices do so, for deaths as well as births, on a figure published within the past two years. The figure gives the share for rural offices.

digital.rural--digitalisation-of-rural-p.label: Digitalisation of rural primary schools: EMIS

ladder.text: A dated source states that primary schools keep their learners' records on paper only. An annual school census, however it is collected and whatever it is called, does not change this.
An EMIS for primary schools is being prepared or piloted: staff trained, equipment delivered, an agreement signed or pilot schools using it. Or one runs in secondary schools only.

An EMIS is past its pilot and in live use in some primary schools, which enter attendance or results during the year; they are a minority, or no figure is published. Or schools past the pilot fill a national learner register once a year.
More than half of primary schools enter attendance or results for each learner during the school year, at the school. The figure is a published share, or a count given with its total.
At least 90 per cent of primary schools do so, with attendance entered daily, on a figure published within the past two years. The figure gives the share for rural schools.
A source from the past three years says the country has no statistics law and no draft of one.

A bill or draft exists: published, validated, out for consultation, before cabinet or parliament, or passed and not yet promulgated. A law that is only announced or planned does not count. A statistics office set up by an ordinary decree, with no statistics law behind it, stops here.
A statistics law is in force, however old: an act, ordinance or decree with the force of law that governs official statistics or sets up the national statistics office.
A decree, regulation or order has been made under the law: on the statistics office, the statistics council or board, the approval of surveys or the confidentiality of data.

The law has been applied in the past three years: its council or board appointed or meeting, a standard, release calendar or survey approval issued under it, a rule made under it, or a penalty. A census or survey carried out, a strategy or a budget does not reach this stage.

AGO.short: Angola's 2002 law on access to administrative documents is in force; rules made under it and an oversight body are not known.
AGO.summary:
Law in force. Angola's law is Law no. 11/02 of 16 August 2002, the Law on Access to Administrative Documents. It gives a right to ask public bodies for the documents they hold and has stood since 2002, which makes it one of the oldest laws of its kind on the continent.

Law put to work and applied. The nearest held fact is the law itself, Law no. 11/02 of 2002. What would put it to work is a decree, regulation or order made under it, an information commission or commissioner appointed, or an existing body such as an ombudsman taking up its oversight. What would show it applied is a decision, order or penalty on a request for information, or figures of requests published by the body that oversees it. Neither is recorded for Angola.

Not held. No source held names rules made under the law or says its oversight body is set up.

BDI.short: Burundi's Senate adopted an access to public information bill on 29 September 2026; whether it has been promulgated is not known.
BDI.summary:
Law in force. Burundi has a bill and no law. The Council of Ministers adopted the draft law on access to public information on 10 June 2026, with the ministry describing a legal vacuum on the subject. The bill was on the programme of the National Assembly's session opened on 3 August 2026, and the Senate adopted it unanimously on 29 September 2026. Its promulgation is not recorded.

Law put to work and applied. The nearest held fact is the draft, the bill the Senate adopted on 29 September 2026. A bill makes no rules and sets up no oversight body until it is passed, promulgated and in force. Once it is, what would put it to work is a decree or regulation made under it, or an information commission or commissioner appointed, and what would show it applied is a decision or penalty on a request for information, or published figures of requests.

Not held. No source held says an access to information law is in force.

BEN.short: Benin was drafting an access to information law as of December 2022, with no adoption timetable; nothing held says it is in force or applied.
BEN.summary:
Law in force. The World Bank's December 2022 open data readiness assessment says the government, through the BAI presidential reform office, is drafting a new access to information law, an avant-projet with an Open Data section and a decree. The text had been under discussion in government for nearly two years, with no adoption timetable and no civil society involvement. The draft is titled Projet de loi d'accès à l'information, and its owner is the BAI (Bureau d'Analyse et d'Investigation) in the Presidency.

Law put to work and applied. The same assessment says the HAAC, the body named under Loi n° 2015-07, the Code de l'information et de la communication of 2015, does not appear to have undertaken any initiative to promote access to information. Civil society organisations found the right little known and little used, and their test letters to administrations were generally ignored.

Not held. Nothing held says an access to information law is in force, or that any rule or oversight body exists under one.

BFA.short: Burkina Faso's law on access to public information is in force but described in 2025 as forgotten; rules and an oversight body are not known.
BFA.summary:
Law in force. Burkina Faso has a law on access to public information and administrative documents. The Centre national de presse Norbert Zongo's digital rights report, published in February 2025, records no change to the law and says it has fallen into oblivion. The report names no repeal and no replacement, so the law stands.

Law put to work and applied. The nearest held fact is the law itself, the law the 2025 report describes as forgotten. What would put it to work is a decree, regulation or order made under it, an information commission or commissioner appointed, or an existing body such as an ombudsman taking up its oversight. What would show it applied is a decision, order or penalty on a request for information, or figures of requests published by the body that oversees it. Neither is recorded for Burkina Faso.

Not held. No source held names rules made under the law or says its oversight body is set up.

BWA.short: Botswana's Access to Information Act of 2024 is made and starts on a date set by notice; that date and any rules are not known.
BWA.summary:
Law in force. Botswana's law is the Access to Information Act, Act 16 of 2024, dated 26 July 2024, which creates a general right of access to information held by public authorities and starts on a date to be set by notice. The President's State of the Nation Address in November 2025 counted the Act among the laws Parliament had passed. The date it starts is not recorded.

Law put to work and applied. The nearest held fact is the law itself, the Access to Information Act of 2024. What would put it to work is a decree, regulation or order made under it, an information commission or commissioner appointed, or an existing body such as an ombudsman taking up its oversight. What would show it applied is a decision, order or penalty on a request for information, or figures of requests published by the body that oversees it. Neither is recorded for Botswana.

Not held. No source held names rules made under the law or says its oversight body is set up.

CAF.short: Nothing held says whether Central African Republic has an access to information law or a draft of one, so no stage is set.
CAF.summary: Not held. Nothing held names an access to information law or a draft of one, or says there is none.

CIV.short: Côte d'Ivoire's 2013 law is in force and its commission, set up in 2013, is at work; decisions on requests are not known.
CIV.summary:
Law in force. Côte d'Ivoire's law is Law no. 2013-867 of 23 December 2013 on access to information of public interest. The president of the commission that oversees it describes it as guaranteeing every citizen the right of access to public information.

Law put to work and applied. The law's oversight body is in place. The Commission d'Accès à l'Information d'intérêt public et aux Documents Publics, the CAIDP, was created in 2013. Its president presented a programme named ACCESS CAIDP on 25 July 2025, and in September 2026 the commission began a national register of public documents with about 200 information officers. A decision, order or penalty on a request for information, or figures of requests published by the oversight body, dated in the last three years, is not recorded.

Not held. No source held dates a decision, order or penalty on a request, published figures of requests, or a rule made under the law, in the last three years.

CMR.short: Cameroon's draft law on access to public information was validated by a workshop in November 2025; it has not reached parliament.
CMR.summary:
Law in force. Cameroon has a draft and no law. A draft law on the right of access to and use of public information and on the digital transformation of the administration was published on 22 May 2023. A national workshop at Ebolowa on 3 to 14 November 2025 gave the draft its technical validation, and the project behind it lists the text among those examined there.

Law put to work and applied. The nearest held fact is the draft, the draft validated at Ebolowa in November 2025. A bill makes no rules and sets up no oversight body until it is passed, promulgated and in force. Once it is, what would put it to work is a decree or regulation made under it, or an information commission or commissioner appointed, and what would show it applied is a decision or penalty on a request for information, or published figures of requests.

Not held. No source held says an access to information law is in force.

COD.short: DR Congo's National Assembly took up an access to information bill in March 2026; it is still a bill.
COD.summary:
Law in force. The Democratic Republic of the Congo has a bill and no law. On 27 March 2026 the National Assembly declared receivable a private member's bill on access to information and transparency of public life and sent it to a joint committee with ten days to report. The right of access written in the constitution has no law behind it until the bill passes.

Law put to work and applied. The nearest held fact is the draft, the bill declared receivable on 27 March 2026. A bill makes no rules and sets up no oversight body until it is passed, promulgated and in force. Once it is, what would put it to work is a decree or regulation made under it, or an information commission or commissioner appointed, and what would show it applied is a decision or penalty on a request for information, or published figures of requests.

Not held. No source held says an access to information law is in force.

COG.short: Congo has no access to information law and no draft, by a UNESCO assessment of 2025.
COG.summary:
Law in force. The Republic of the Congo has no access to information law and no draft of one. UNESCO's assessment of the country's internet development, dated 2025, recommends that the government draft and adopt a freedom of information law, and lists a commission on access to public information among the bodies still to be set up. The assessment names no bill in preparation.

Law put to work and applied. The nearest held fact is the statement that there is no law, UNESCO's 2025 assessment. With no law and no draft there are no rules, no information commission or commissioner and no decisions on requests to record. A bill published, put out for consultation or sent to cabinet or parliament would be the first step, and a law in force the second.

Not held. Nothing further: every question is answered.

COM.short: The Comoros has no access to information law and no draft, by a UNESCO statement of January 2026.
COM.summary:
Law in force. The Comoros has no access to information law and no draft of one. UNESCO's contribution to the country's Universal Periodic Review, published in January 2026, states that no access to information law has been adopted. The contribution names no bill in preparation, in cabinet or before the Assembly of the Union.

Law put to work and applied. The nearest held fact is the statement that there is no law, UNESCO's contribution of January 2026. With no law and no draft there are no rules, no information commission or commissioner and no decisions on requests to record. A bill published, put out for consultation or sent to cabinet or parliament would be the first step, and a law in force the second.

Not held. Nothing further: every question is answered.

CPV.short: Cabo Verde's 2022 law on access to administrative documents is in force; rules made under it and an oversight body are not known.
CPV.summary:
Law in force. Cabo Verde's law is Law no. 10/X/2022 on access to and reuse of administrative documents, approved on 8 April 2022, promulgated on 9 May 2022 and published on 16 May 2022. It gives everyone a right to consult and copy administrative documents and to be told what they contain.

Law put to work and applied. The nearest held fact is the law itself, Law no. 10/X/2022. What would put it to work is a decree, regulation or order made under it, an information commission or commissioner appointed, or an existing body such as an ombudsman taking up its oversight. What would show it applied is a decision, order or penalty on a request for information, or figures of requests published by the body that oversees it. Neither is recorded for Cape Verde.

Not held. No source held names rules made under the law or says its oversight body is set up.

DJI.short: Djibouti's Council of Ministers approved a draft Digital Code with a right of access to information in 2023; whether it passed is not known.
DJI.summary:
Law in force. The Council of Ministers, chaired by the head of state, examined and approved a draft law on the Digital Code in June 2023. Book VII of the draft provides a general right of access to administrative documents and public information, with rules on how it is exercised. The report was published on 1 June 2023, and the draft is titled Projet de loi portant Code du Numérique. Its owner is the Ministère délégué chargé de l'Économie numérique et de l'Innovation.

Law put to work and applied. The nearest held fact is the same Council of Ministers report, which concerns a draft only: the Code du Numérique, examined and approved by the Council of Ministers under the head of state in June 2023. Nothing held shows a rule made, an oversight body set up or a request decided under an access law.

Not held. Nothing held says the draft was passed, or that any access law is in force or applied.

DZA.short: Nothing held says whether Algeria has an access to information law or a draft of one, so no stage is set.
DZA.summary: Not held. Nothing held names an access to information law or a draft of one, or says there is none.

EGY.short: A freedom of information bill signed by 60 members was submitted to Egypt's parliament in August 2026; no law is in force.
EGY.summary:
Law in force. Egypt has a bill and no law. A freedom of information bill backed by the Journalists Syndicate was submitted to the House of Representatives on 9 August 2026 with the signatures of 60 members; it would create an Authority for the Protection of Freedom of Information. Its explanatory memorandum says the right in Article 68 of the constitution has had no law for years.

Law put to work and applied. The nearest held fact is the draft, the bill submitted on 9 August 2026. A bill makes no rules and sets up no oversight body until it is passed, promulgated and in force. Once it is, what would put it to work is a decree or regulation made under it, or an information commission or commissioner appointed, and what would show it applied is a decision or penalty on a request for information, or published figures of requests.

Not held. No source held says an access to information law is in force.

ERI.short: Eritrea has no freedom of information law and no draft, by a UNESCO statement of January 2026.
ERI.summary:
Law in force. Eritrea has no access to information law and no draft of one. UNESCO's contribution to the country's Universal Periodic Review, published in January 2026, states that no freedom of information law has been adopted and recommends that the government introduce one. The contribution names no bill in preparation.

Law put to work and applied. The nearest held fact is the statement that there is no law, UNESCO's contribution of January 2026. With no law and no draft there are no rules, no information commission or commissioner and no decisions on requests to record. A bill published, put out for consultation or sent to cabinet or parliament would be the first step, and a law in force the second.

Not held. Nothing further: every question is answered.

ETH.short: Ethiopia has had a mass media and access to information proclamation since 2008; its Ombudsman oversight is reported ineffective, and application is not known.
ETH.summary:
Law in force. Proclamation No. 590/2008 on Freedom of the Mass Media and Access to Information, dated 4 December 2008 and proclaimed under Article 55(1) of the Constitution, is published by the Ministry of Justice and affirms in its preamble individuals' right to access information held by public bodies and a duty on public officials to facilitate it. A June 2023 study lists it among Ethiopia's laws, and a draft Access to Information Proclamation prepared by a media law working group had not been passed as of March 2023.

Law put to work and applied. The same study says the Ethiopian Institution of the Ombudsman was designated the organ responsible for implementing freedom of information. The study is dated 1 June 2023. It reports studies finding the Ombudsman ineffective for lack of resources to evaluate public bodies, and it gives no date for that finding.

Not held. Nothing held names rules made under the proclamation, says its oversight body is set up as such, or shows requests or decisions under it.

GAB.short: Gabon has no access to information law and no draft, by a UNESCO statement of December 2025.
GAB.summary:
Law in force. Gabon has no access to information law and no draft of one. UNESCO's contribution to the country's Universal Periodic Review, published in December 2025, states that Gabon has no access to information law and encourages it to adopt one. The contribution names no bill in preparation, in cabinet or before parliament.

Law put to work and applied. The nearest held fact is the statement that there is no law, UNESCO's contribution of December 2025. With no law and no draft there are no rules, no information commission or commissioner and no decisions on requests to record. A bill published, put out for consultation or sent to cabinet or parliament would be the first step, and a law in force the second.

Not held. Nothing further: every question is answered.

GHA.short: Ghana's 2019 Right to Information Act is in force, and its commission fined 254 public institutions in August 2026 for missed reports.
GHA.summary:
Law in force. Ghana's law is the Right to Information Act, 2019 (Act 989). It puts the constitutional right to information to work and sets the procedure for asking public institutions for what they hold.

Law put to work and applied. The Right to Information Commission, with a board and chairman, oversees and enforces the Act, and the 2026 budget votes it GHS 20,413,271. On 5 August 2026 the Commission imposed penalties of GHS 20,000 each on 254 public institutions that had not filed their 2025 annual reports under the Act. A newspaper count puts the practice lower: 21 institutions failed to release information in 24 requests made between January 2025 and July 2026. The penalties are for missed reports; a published decision on a single request is not recorded.

Not held. Nothing on the four questions.

GIN.short: Guinea's 2020 law on access to public information is in force; whether its commission has been appointed is not known.
GIN.summary:
Law in force. Guinea's law is Law no. 2020/0027/AN on the right of access to public information, signed in Conakry on 19 December 2020, in effect from its promulgation. The law provides for an autonomous commission on access to public information; its members being appointed is not recorded.

Law put to work and applied. The nearest held fact is the law itself, Law no. 2020/0027/AN. What would put it to work is a decree, regulation or order made under it, an information commission or commissioner appointed, or an existing body such as an ombudsman taking up its oversight. What would show it applied is a decision, order or penalty on a request for information, or figures of requests published by the body that oversees it. Neither is recorded for Guinea.

GMB.short: The Gambia's 2021 Access to Information Act is in force and its Information Commission is at work; decisions on requests are not known.
GMB.summary:
Law in force. The Gambia's law is the Access to Information Act, 2021. The Personal Data Protection and Privacy Act of 2025 cites it as Act No. 10 of 2021, and the Gambia Press Union said in August 2026 that it had been in force for more than a year.

Law put to work and applied. The Act's oversight body is set up. The Information Commission, with a deputy chairperson, was implementing the Act in September 2026. The Press Union sits on technical committees with it, and a United Nations agency tendered in August 2026 for a communication strategy for the Commission. A decision, order or penalty on a request for information, or figures of requests published by the oversight body, dated in the last three years, is not recorded.

GNB.short: Guinea-Bissau's draft access to information law was validated in April 2024 and awaits the Ministry of Justice; no law is in force.
GNB.summary:
Law in force. Guinea-Bissau has a draft and no law. A drafting commission met on 17 to 23 April 2024 and all those taking part validated the draft law on access to information, by UNESCO's account. The next step it gives is submission to the Ministry of Justice for adoption. No law is in force.

Law put to work and applied. The nearest held fact is the draft, the draft validated in April 2024. A bill makes no rules and sets up no oversight body until it is passed, promulgated and in force. Once it is, what would put it to work is a decree or regulation made under it, or an information commission or commissioner appointed, and what would show it applied is a decision or penalty on a request for information, or published figures of requests.

GNQ.short: Equatorial Guinea's Senate passed a transparency and access to public information bill in May 2026; promulgation is not known.
GNQ.summary:
Law in force. Equatorial Guinea has a bill passed by parliament and not shown as promulgated. The Prime Minister presented the bill for a Code of Transparency, Access to Public Information and Good Governance in Public Finance Management to the Chamber of Deputies on 5 February 2026. The Senate approved it unanimously on 8 May 2026, which leaves promulgation by the Head of State.

Law put to work and applied. The nearest held fact is the draft, the bill the Senate approved on 8 May 2026. A bill makes no rules and sets up no oversight body until it is passed, promulgated and in force. Once it is, what would put it to work is a decree or regulation made under it, or an information commission or commissioner appointed, and what would show it applied is a decision or penalty on a request for information, or published figures of requests.

Not held. No source held says an access to information law is in force.

KEN.short: Kenya's 2016 Access to Information Act is in force, with regulations made under it in 2023; decisions on requests are not known.
KEN.summary:
Law in force. Kenya's law is the Access to Information Act, 2016. It gives effect to Article 35 of the Constitution, and the press describes it as the guarantee of the right to information. It has stood since 2016 with no repeal recorded.

Law put to work and applied. The Access to Information Regulations of 2023, made under the Act, define proactive disclosure and set what public bodies must publish. Regulations made in the last three years are counted as the law applied. A forum in September 2026 assessed how public institutions carry the Act out. A decision or penalty on a request, and published figures of requests, are not recorded. A separate bill of 2026 on classified information is noted and does not change the Act's standing.

Not held. Nothing on the four questions.

LBR.short: Liberia's 2010 Freedom of Information Act is in force and its commission ran a compliance campaign in 2026; decisions on requests are not known.
LBR.summary:
Law in force. Liberia's law is the Freedom of Information Act of 2010. The Press Union of Liberia cited it in August 2026 as law a government agency's staff confidentiality agreement must fit. The Act gives a right to ask public bodies for information and has stood since 2010.

Law put to work and applied. The Act's oversight body is set up. The Independent Information Commission, with an executive director and directors for outreach and compliance, ran a compliance campaign across public bodies from 11 August to 2 September 2026. A campaign is not a decision on a request. A decision, order or penalty on a request for information, or figures of requests published by the oversight body, dated in the last three years, is not recorded.

LBY.short: Libya's cabinet issued a draft bill in 2022 that would let citizens request information from public bodies; no law is in force.
LBY.summary:
Law in force. Libya has a draft and no law. A Council of Ministers draft bill on the national information system, issued on 8 October 2022 over the Prime Minister's signature, would give every citizen a right to request information from the information units of public bodies. Its passage is not recorded.

Law put to work and applied. The nearest held fact is the draft, the draft bill of October 2022. A bill makes no rules and sets up no oversight body until it is passed, promulgated and in force. Once it is, what would put it to work is a decree or regulation made under it, or an information commission or commissioner appointed, and what would show it applied is a decision or penalty on a request for information, or published figures of requests.

LSO.short: Lesotho's Access and Receipt of Information Bill of 2000 had not been passed by 2021; no law is in force.
LSO.summary:
Law in force. Lesotho has an old bill and no law. An assessment of September 2021 says the country has no real freedom of information law, and that the Access and Receipt of Information Bill of 2000, drafted by the Law Reform Commission, has not been passed by Parliament. Nothing later on the bill is recorded.

Law put to work and applied. The nearest held fact is the draft, the Access and Receipt of Information Bill of 2000. A bill makes no rules and sets up no oversight body until it is passed, promulgated and in force. Once it is, what would put it to work is a decree or regulation made under it, or an information commission or commissioner appointed, and what would show it applied is a decision or penalty on a request for information, or published figures of requests.
