In September 2026 the deputy minister said the redraft was at an advanced stage, with a final draft due to the minister by the end of November and then to Cabinet. The chair of the Information Regulator said that month that the country has no national AI policy.

Body named and action funded. The minister is committed to putting the draft policy before Cabinet by the end of the financial year. Because the strategy is not yet adopted, there is nothing for a body to carry out or for money to follow. No source held names a council, office, agency or ministry unit set up for it, or public money set aside for it. No implementation plan or budget for it is held.

Not held. No source held says a national AI strategy is adopted and still running.

ZMB.short: Zambia's national AI strategy runs to the end of 2026 and names a council and a coordinator; public money allocated to it is not known.
ZMB.summary:
Strategy adopted. Zambia has a National AI Strategy that runs to the end of 2026. In June 2026 the permanent secretary spoke of the country carrying out the strategy, and UNESCO said it expires at the end of 2026 and is to be reviewed and renewed. In July 2026 the head of the Presidential Delivery Unit said a national AI strategy was nearing completion.

Body named and action funded. The strategy sets up a National AI Council with sector working groups and makes the Smart Zambia Institute the coordinator of AI in government. A regional official said in August 2026 that Zambia is working on further frameworks to support the strategy. No source held from the last three years names public money allocated to the strategy, or an action in it started with its funding named. No budget line for the strategy is held.

Not held. No source from the last three years naming public money allocated to the strategy, or an action in it started with funding named, is held.

ZWE.short: Zimbabwe launched a national AI strategy for 2026 to 2030 in March 2026, with an implementation office and regulator-funded grants under it in 2026.
ZWE.summary:
Strategy adopted. Zimbabwe has a National AI Strategy for 2026 to 2030. The ICT minister presented it at the United Nations General Assembly in September 2026 as the country's strategy, and a media freedom organisation refers to it as in place. It was officially launched in March 2026, and Cabinet lists it among the frameworks the ICT sector works under.

Body named and action funded. An AI Strategy Implementation Office coordinates the strategy, with a national regulatory committee setting policy; in June 2026 the office was being set up inside the ICT ministry. The telecommunications regulator's challenge for 2026, which carries out an action in the strategy launched in March 2026, offers selected teams grants of up to USD 80,000, and the 16 winning teams are to be considered for its incubation programme.

Not held. Nothing on the four questions.

AGO.short: Angola adopted an ICT White Paper in 2024 resting on a national broadband strategy; its money and measurable targets are not known.
AGO.summary:
Plan adopted. Presidential Decree 272/24, published in the Diário da República on 5 December 2024, approved the ICT White Paper 2023-2027 after Council of Ministers review on 30 August 2024. The White Paper's stated objective is universal access to the broadband service for the whole population. It names the National Broadband Strategy and the National Broadband Network (RNBL) as its basis. The White Paper itself, published on the same date, says its measures follow from implementing that strategy.

Money and results. The White Paper describes the strategy as covering the modernisation and expansion of the primary electronic communications network, now called the National Broadband Network, as State-funded public-domain infrastructure. The decree text holds no numeric coverage, speed or price target for the 2023-2027 period, and no delivery figures are given there.

Not held. No budget line, universal service fund allocation or financed programme tied to the plan in the last three years is held.

BDI.short: Burundi has a Stratégie Large Bande 2025, reported in October 2025, but no targets, period dates, funding or results are known.
BDI.summary:
Plan adopted. Burundi's legal and regulatory framework includes the Stratégie Large Bande 2025, the broadband strategy 2025, according to the report on the national Africa-BB-Maps event held in October 2025 by the International Telecommunication Union. The same report lists a Universal Service Fund beside it, and names the telecommunications regulator ARCT and the ICT secretariat SETIC as the lead bodies. It names no successor to the strategy.

Money and results. Nothing is held on money or results. The nearest held fact is the October 2025 event report itself, which gives no period dates for the strategy and states no broadband targets. It sets out no delivery figures for the plan, and it attaches no budget to the Universal Service Fund beside it.

Not held. No budget line, universal service fund allocation or financed programme tied to the plan in the last three years is held.

BEN.short: A broadband deployment project in the 2021-2026 government action programme was running in 2024; whether money is committed or progress published is not known.
BEN.summary:
Plan adopted. The government's project sheet lists the high and very high speed internet deployment (phase 2) as a government project with status "En cours", and gives an execution period of 2022 to 2026. Its aim is to bring broadband to the whole national territory. On 21 November 2024 the minister of digital affairs said the government plans to connect 18 more communes to fibre by mid-2025, to reach all 77 communes, under the Programme d'action du gouvernement 2021-2026.

Money and results. Agence Ecofin reports the broadband deployment project of the Programme d'action du gouvernement 2021-2026 as costed at about 207 billion FCFA in November 2024. The project sheet names one expected result, a backbone capacity extension at 8 sites from 40 to 100 Gbps. It carries no date.

Not held. No budget line, universal service fund allocation or financed programme tied to the plan in the last three years is held, and no figures published against its targets.

BFA.short: Burkina Faso adopted its digital infrastructure plan in 2019 and a revision to 2030 is in draft; funding and results are not known.
BFA.summary:
Plan adopted. Burkina Faso's national plan is the Schéma directeur d'aménagement numérique (SDAN), the framework for digital infrastructure and services run by the Ministère de la Transition digitale, des Postes et des Communications électroniques. Sidwaya reports the minister saying on 24 October 2025, at the launch of the OAN platform, that the SDAN was adopted in 2019. Wearetech gives the same year and neither source states a period for the 2019 document or names a successor to it.

Money and results. Nothing is held on funding or results. The nearest held fact concerns the plan's targets: Wearetech reports that ministry and territorial-development representatives met on 6 to 12 September 2026 to consolidate a draft revised SDAN running to 2030, which goes next to the national commission for territorial planning (CNADDT).

Not held. No budget line, universal service fund allocation or financed programme tied to the plan in the last three years is held.

BWA.short: Botswana has a national broadband strategy published in June 2018; funding for it and progress against its targets are not known.
BWA.summary:
Plan adopted. The Ministry of Transport and Communications issued the National Broadband Strategy, in its final version of June 2018. The document states that the Government has developed the strategy, and it is the national plan for broadband in Botswana. It gives the Information Age Council the task of guiding implementation and monitoring progress. The June 2018 publication is the date held for the strategy, and no later plan or revision is held.

Money and results. No budget, financing or delivery report for the strategy is held. The nearest held fact is its targets. The strategy sets two coverage targets: 2 Mbps for 50% of citizens by the end of 2014, and 20 Mbps for 90% of the population by 2018. The same document says the Information Age Council is to monitor progress against them, but no progress figure is held.

Not held. No budget line, universal service fund allocation or financed programme tied to the plan in the last three years is held.

CAF.short: The government launched a USD 12.8bn programme in 2025 under its 2024-2028 development plan with a 3,000 km fibre target; funding and delivery are unknown.
CAF.summary:
Plan adopted. The government's press release of 4 September 2025 launches a USD 12.8bn investment programme built on its National Development Plan 2024-2028, a plan whose period, 2024 to 2028, had not ended at that date. Broadband is one part of that larger plan rather than a plan of its own, and the release sets a stated national target of 3,000 km of fibre-optic deployment by 2028.

Money and results. No spending or construction against that target is held. The nearest held fact is the same release, which gives the 3,000 km of fibre-optic deployment as a target for 2028, inside the USD 12.8bn investment programme, and reports no result delivered at the date of the release, which is the only held statement of the plan's delivery.

Not held. No budget line, universal service fund allocation or financed programme tied to the plan in the last three years is held.

CIV.short: Nothing held names a national broadband plan or says there is none, so no stage is set.
CIV.summary: Not held. Nothing held names a national broadband plan for the country, or says there is none.

CMR.short: Nothing held names a national broadband plan or says there is none, so no stage is set.
CMR.summary: Not held. Nothing held names a national broadband plan for the country, or says there is none.

COD.short: The Universal Service Development Fund unveiled a 2026-2035 connectivity strategy in August 2026; whether the government has adopted it is not known.
COD.summary:
Plan adopted. The Universal Service Development Fund (FDSU) unveiled a National Connectivity Strategy 2026-2035 in August 2026, with a 2030 target of 3,000 localities and 16 million people and further consultations with stakeholders planned. The FDSU's own site describes a national universal-connectivity strategy with a 40-site phase 0 and a phase 1 of about 300 sites in five zones, and a 14 August 2026 report says the fund is developing the national strategy to extend connectivity to underserved areas.

Money and results. The FDSU signed subsidy agreements with Airtel, Orange, Vodacom and Africell, covering 10 localities each, 40 localities and about 258,000 people in all, as the first step of the National Connectivity Strategy 2026-2035, reported by Developing Telecoms on 13 August 2026, with the first localities to be connected under those agreements.

Not held. No source held says a national broadband plan is adopted and still running.

COG.short: Nothing held names a national broadband plan or says there is none, so no stage is set.
COG.summary: Not held. Nothing held names a national broadband plan for the country, or says there is none.

COM.short: Nothing held names a national broadband plan or says there is none, so no stage is set.
COM.summary: Not held. Nothing held names a national broadband plan for the country, or says there is none.

CPV.short: Cabo Verde approved a national 5G strategy in February 2026, with targets for 2026 and 2030; its funding and results are not known.
CPV.summary:
Plan adopted. Cabo Verde's government presented the National Strategy for the Implementation of 5G on 11 February 2026, and Resolution No. 33/2026 of 20 February 2026 formally approved it, according to that report. The same report gives no plan period and names no successor. The strategy had been launched in public in September 2025, when the government presented it as a proposal. The government's own announcement of the strategy came a day earlier, on 10 September 2025.

Money and results. No budget, financing or delivery report for the strategy is held. The nearest held fact is its targets. When the government presented the proposed strategy on 10 September 2025, it set a goal of 90% internet penetration by 2026 and regional digital hub status by 2030.

Not held. No budget line, universal service fund allocation or financed programme tied to the plan in the last three years is held.

DJI.short: Djibouti unveiled a national broadband strategy in October 2024 with city-connection targets for 2027; funding and delivery are not known.
DJI.summary:
Plan adopted. Djibouti's national broadband plan is the Stratégie Nationale du Haut-Débit (SNHD). An editorial in La Nation published on 17 October 2024 says the strategy was recently unveiled. The same editorial describes the SNHD as aligned with Vision Djibouti 2035, so the strategy is tied to the country's own long-term vision for 2035 and not left as a stand-alone document. The editorial makes it part of its wider argument for digital inclusion.

Money and results. No budget or results are held. The nearest held fact concerns the plan's targets and delivery: the same La Nation editorial says the SNHD sets out two scenarios for connecting cities by 2027, one reaching ten cities and the other seven, the connection of those cities being the plan's stated aim for that year.

Not held. No budget line, universal service fund allocation or financed programme tied to the plan in the last three years is held. The plan's period is not stated either.

DZA.short: Algeria has had a national all-fibre strategy aiming at fibre nationwide by 2027, reported on in 2025; funding for it is not known.
DZA.summary:
Plan adopted. The Ministry of Post and Telecommunications calls its plan the "Tout Fibre" strategy and aims to generalise fibre by 2027 at the latest. In a 20 February 2026 message the minister said the government had adopted a comprehensive all-fibre communications strategy. A ministry communique of 30 September 2026 says the strategy aims to bring fibre to the whole territory by 2027, with the copper network phased out by the same date.

Money and results. The Ministry's page of 9 July 2025 sets a goal of 7 million households on fixed internet by the end of 2027, with fibre to the home as the core technology. It reports 6.6 million fixed internet subscribers in the first half of 2025, up from 3.5 million in early 2020, and says the intermediate objectives were reached.

Not held. Progress against the plan is published. No budget line, universal service fund allocation or financed programme tied to the plan in the last three years is held.

EGY.short: A national broadband plan was launched in 2011; whether it is still running, funded or reported on is not known.
EGY.summary:
Plan adopted. The Ministry of Communications and Information Technology, through the NTRA, launched the eMisr National Broadband Plan on 17 November 2011. It was a two-phase plan: the first phase was a Framework for Broadband Development, and the second a Broadband Action Plan. Egypt's own name for it is eMisr National Broadband Plan, and the Ministry of Communications and Information Technology and the NTRA are its named owners, with national scope.

Money and results. Nothing held shows money committed or progress published. The nearest held fact is that the second phase, the Broadband Action Plan, was due in the second quarter of 2012, after the Framework for Broadband Development that the Ministry of Communications and Information Technology and the NTRA launched on 17 November 2011 as the first phase.

Not held. No budget line, universal service fund allocation or financed programme tied to the plan in the last three years is held, and no figures published against its targets.

ERI.short: A 2019 listing shows no national broadband plan; nothing newer is known, so no stage is set.
ERI.summary: Not held. No plan or draft is on record, and no source dated in the last three years says the country has neither. A 2019 listing of countries with no broadband plan is too old to count.

ETH.short: Nothing held names a national broadband plan or says there is none, so no stage is set.
ETH.summary: Not held. Nothing held names a national broadband plan for the country, or says there is none.

GAB.short: In 2016 the ministry launched a broadband study to prepare a national strategy; whether one was ever adopted is not known.
GAB.summary:
Plan adopted. In July 2016 the digital economy ministry announced that it wants a national broadband promotion strategy and a costed operational plan in the coming months. The ministry had launched a broadband study to prepare them. No strategy had yet been adopted. The strategy is titled Stratégie nationale de promotion du Haut débit.

Money and results. Nothing held shows money committed or progress published. The nearest held fact is the 2016 announcement of a costed operational plan, which was still to be written. The digital economy ministry made that announcement in July 2016, on 4 July 2016. It names two documents: a national broadband promotion strategy, and an operational plan with costs. It says the ministry launched a broadband study to prepare both, and that no strategy was yet adopted.

Not held. No source held says a national broadband plan is adopted and still running.

GHA.short: The Ministry of Communications issued a national broadband policy in 2012 with targets to 2020; funding and progress figures are not known.
GHA.summary:
Plan adopted. The Ministry of Communications issued the National Broadband Policy and Implementation Strategy as Final Version 1.0 in October 2012. The strategy is the Ministry's national instrument, with targets of 40% household and 40% national broadband penetration by 2015, and of 90% by 2020.

Money and results. Nothing held shows money committed or progress published. The nearest held fact is the targets the 2012 document sets: 40% household and 40% national broadband penetration by 2015, and 90% by 2020. The Ministry of Communications issued that document in October 2012 as Final Version 1.0. The Ministry of Communications is the named owner of the strategy, which is a national plan. Its targets run to 2015 and 2020, and cover household penetration and national penetration. The first set of targets falls in 2015 and the final one in 2020, with the 90% target the highest of the three.

Not held. No budget line, universal service fund allocation or financed programme tied to the plan in the last three years is held, and no figures published against its targets.

GIN.short: Nothing held names a national broadband plan or says there is none, so no stage is set.
GIN.summary: Not held. Nothing held names a national broadband plan for the country, or says there is none.

GMB.short: A national broadband policy and strategy ran 2020 to 2024 with coverage targets; no successor is named and delivery against the targets is not known.
GMB.summary:
Plan adopted. The Ministry of Information and Communication Infrastructure issued the National Broadband Policy 2020-2024 in June 2020 for a five-year period ending in 2024. The same month it commissioned the National Broadband Strategy 2020-2024, which covers 2020 to 2024. Neither document names a successor plan, and the strategy's own text refers to a review for the next five-year cycle.

Money and results. The strategy sets targets of broadband coverage to more than 90% of the population by 2024, at least 75% of homes with affordable 5 Mbps download and upload speeds by 2022, and 4G coverage of at least 85% of the population by 2024 (strategy). The policy sets a 5 Mbps minimum for every user and near-100% of homes with affordable 5 Mbps by 2023 (policy).

Not held. Nothing held says a national broadband plan is adopted and still running, or reports its funding or results.

GNB.short: A draft universal-service plan with 2031 coverage targets was dated November 2025; whether a broadband plan is adopted and running is not known.
GNB.summary:
Plan adopted. Guinea-Bissau's Strategic Plan of the Access and Universal Service Fund (FASU) for 2026-2031 is a consultancy final report for the regulator ARN, dated 24 November 2025. The report states that it is still to be disseminated and validated in a public stakeholder consultation, and so it is a draft rather than a plan in force. ITU's 2019 table of broadband strategies, policies and plans answered no on whether a national broadband policy existed and named none.

Money and results. Nothing is held on funding, spending or results delivered under the plan. The nearest held fact is what the draft itself sets out, its coverage targets before 2031: 99% of the population for 2G, 98% for 3G and 96% for 4G broadband.

Not held. No source held says a national broadband plan is adopted and still running.

GNQ.short: Equatorial Guinea presented a draft telecommunications plan to the World Bank in December 2025; whether it is adopted, and any funding, is not known.
GNQ.summary:
Plan adopted. On 11 December 2025 the Ministry of Transport and Telecommunications presented to the World Bank a proposal for the Plan Nacional de Telecomunicaciones para la Transformación Digital. The plan includes a competitive network ensuring 100% coverage before 2030. The press article reporting it, published on 12 December 2025, describes the plan as still to be designed, with World Bank technical assistance. The Ministry of Transport and Telecommunications is the owner named for the plan.

Money and results. The nearest held fact is the same December 2025 proposal, which looks to World Bank technical assistance for the design of the plan. It states the 2030 coverage aim as a goal of the proposed plan, with no delivery figure against it. The Ministry of Transport, Telecommunications and Civil Aviation also issued a July-December 2026 half-year action plan, a national plan.

Not held. No source held says a national broadband plan is adopted and still running. Nothing held shows money committed to one.

KEN.short: Kenya has the Digital Superhighway 100,000km fibre plan, announced in 2022 and funded in 2026/27; progress against its targets is not known.
KEN.summary:
Plan adopted. President Ruto announced the Digital Superhighway's 100,000km national fibre target in November 2022, aiming at universal broadband availability across the country over five years. The deadline is 2027, which the Nation's 2 September 2026 report says is still ahead, and no successor plan is named.

Money and results. The programme is funded through the Universal Service Fund: the Communications Authority and the ICT Authority first signed a Sh5 billion agreement covering 19 counties, and Kenya Power had received Sh940.6 million by June 2025 for design, supply and installation of the fibre network. The FY2026/27 budget allocates Sh1.3 billion to maintain the national fibre backbone, Sh400 million for digital hubs and Sh382 million for digital superhighway cybersecurity, as part of the same agenda.

Not held. No review or report from the last three years giving figures against the plan's own targets is held.

LBR.short: Nothing held names a national broadband plan or says there is none, so no stage is set.
LBR.summary: Not held. Nothing held names a national broadband plan for the country, or says there is none.

LBY.short: Nothing held names a national broadband plan or says there is none, so no stage is set.
LBY.summary: Not held. Nothing held names a national broadband plan for the country, or says there is none.

LSO.short: Lesotho signed a Broadband Infrastructure Sharing Policy in June 2026, but no budget or delivery results are known, so the main unknown is funding.
LSO.summary:
Plan adopted. Lesotho's Minister of Information, Communications, Science, Technology and Innovation signed the Broadband Infrastructure Sharing Policy on 11 June 2026, according to Lesotho Times; no plan period is given. Before that, the ministry held a second draft of a Broadband and Shared Infrastructure Policy and Implementation Plan, dated 17 February 2025, and the Minister of Finance and Development Planning told Parliament on 19 February 2025 that a broadband policy was among those under development.

Money and results. No budget, fund allocation or delivery report is held. The nearest held fact is the second draft of the Broadband and Shared Infrastructure Policy and Implementation Plan of February 2025, which includes a monitoring and evaluation framework and states that formal broadband legislation is lacking.

Not held. No budget line, universal service fund allocation or financed programme tied to the plan in the last three years is held.

MAR.short: Morocco has a broadband plan, PNHD 2, listed in 2024, but no period, budget or financed programme for it is known.
MAR.summary:
Plan adopted. Morocco's Ministry of Digital Transition and Administration Reform lists a Plan National du Haut Debit 2 (PNHD 2) in its Digital Morocco 2030 institutional brochure of 18 September 2024, described as a programme to cover areas with little or no coverage (Digital Morocco 2030 brochure). A columnist writing in October 2026 refers to the same effort as the national high-speed plan, in Arabic al-mukhattat al-watani lil-sabib al-ali, and treats it as in force in late 2025 (Anfaspress, 5 October 2026). Neither source gives a period for the plan.

Money and results. No budget line or financed programme is held. The brochure states that PNHD 2 aims to cover 1,800 localities (Digital Morocco 2030 brochure). The columnist writes that more than 10,000 rural areas had been covered with 3G and 4G networks within the plan by late 2025 (Anfaspress).

Not held. No budget line, universal service fund allocation or financed programme tied to the plan in the last three years is held.

MDG.short: Nothing held names a national broadband plan or says there is none, so no stage is set.
MDG.summary: Not held. Nothing held names a national broadband plan for the country, or says there is none.

MLI.short: Mali's regulator launched a study for a national broadband plan in 2015; whether a plan was adopted, and any funding, is not known.
MLI.summary:
Plan adopted. In a 2015 article L'Essor reports that the regulator AMRTP held a launch workshop in Bamako for a study on the broadband implementation strategy. The study is to produce a short, medium and long-term broadband development plan, together with the introduction of 4G. The article reports a study under way, not a plan adopted by the government or the minister. The article carries no date, and its published field gives 2015. The study is titled Etude sur la stratégie de mise en œuvre du large bande au Mali.

Money and results. The nearest held fact is the same 2015 report of the launch workshop. It concerns the study that is to write the plan, so it names no budget line, fund allocation or financed programme tied to a plan, and no figures against targets. The report names the regulator AMRTP as the body that held the workshop, in Bamako, and says nothing of who would fund the study or the plan.

Not held. No source held says a national broadband plan is adopted and still running. Nothing held shows money committed to one.

MOZ.short: Mozambique launched an Internet for All plan to 2030 in 2024 or 2025; whether it is formally adopted and still running is not known.
MOZ.summary:
Plan adopted. In December 2024 the government launched the Internet for All project, which aims to raise internet access in Mozambique from under 25% of the population to 100% by 2030, according to the U.S. International Trade Administration. The Wearetech.africa report of 23 July 2026 also describes an Internet Para Todos programme, with a period running to 2030, which had not ended when it was published in July 2026. Both sources give 2030 as the end of the plan period.

Money and results. No funding or delivery figures are held. The nearest held fact is the targets: Wearetech.africa reports that the Internet Para Todos programme aims for 80% mobile penetration, 95% territorial coverage and 99% network availability by 2030. All three targets fall on a date that had not arrived when it was published in July 2026, so no result against them is held.

Not held. Nothing held says a national broadband plan has been adopted and is still running, or reports its funding or results.

MRT.short: A 2019-2025 broadband plan was proposed by the ministry in February 2019; whether the government adopted it is not known.
MRT.summary:
Plan adopted. The ministry's final study of February 2019 proposes a Stratégie Nationale Haut Débit / Plan National du Haut Débit for 2019-2025, with objectives dated 2020 and 2025. It sets coverage of all Moughataas as the short-term aim and the whole country as the medium-term aim. The study states no adoption by the government or a minister. The same study is titled "Stratégie de promotion du Haut Débit et d'accès Universel" by its authors, and the ministry's January 2019 action plan carries the name Stratégie Nationale de Promotion du Haut Débit.

Money and results. The February 2019 study puts the investment at 623 million US dollars over 25 years, as an estimate. The January 2019 action plan lists actions by theme with phasing and a preliminary calendar, with one action to launch in September 2019. It leaves the action sheets to a follow-up committee and states no broadband coverage, speed or price target.

Not held. No source held says a national broadband plan is adopted and still running. Nothing held reports funding committed or results delivered.

MUS.short: Mauritius issued a National Broadband Policy for 2012-2020 and none is held since, so whether a current plan is running is not known.
MUS.summary:
Plan adopted. The Ministry of Information and Communication Technology issued the National Broadband Policy 2012-2020 (NBP2012) in January 2012, as the national policy for broadband in Mauritius. Its stated period ran from 2012 to 2020, so the plan's own dates have passed. The document names no successor policy, and it is the only national broadband plan held for Mauritius from any year, including after 2020.

Money and results. No budget line, universal service fund allocation or financed programme tied to the plan is held, and no figures published against its targets are held either. The nearest held fact is the policy document itself, which fixes the period to 2020 and says nothing of a later plan or of delivery after that year.

Not held. No source held says a national broadband plan is adopted and still running.

MWI.short: Malawi's National Broadband Strategy ran 2019-2023 and no successor is on record as of 2025; whether a new plan is adopted is not known.
MWI.summary:
Plan adopted. Malawi's National Broadband Strategy ran from 2019 to 2023. It aimed to raise broadband penetration from 4.5% to 35% and average speeds from 256 Kbps to 5 Mbps, Ecofin Agency reported in October 2025. The report names no plan that follows it.

Money and results. The regulator, MACRA, launched a national broadband mapping system on 7 October 2025, with support from the International Telecommunication Union and the European Union, to find and fill coverage gaps between 2025 and 2028. Its own figures put 4G coverage at 75.1% by the third quarter of 2024 and mobile broadband subscriptions at 9.4 million, a penetration rate of 47%. Only 18% of Malawians used the internet in 2023. The government licensed Starlink, which began commercial service in July 2023.

Not held. No source held says a national broadband plan is adopted and still running.

NAM.short: Namibia has had a National Broadband Policy since 2020 and a National Digital Strategy since 2025; money committed and results published are not known.
NAM.summary:
Plan adopted. The Minister of Information and Communication Technology, Dr P. Mushelenga, signed the National Broadband Policy on 27 July 2020 and issued it to the Communications Regulatory Authority of Namibia as policy guidelines under section 7 of the Communications Act 2009. Government Notice No. 189 in Government Gazette No. 7308 published it on 14 August 2020. The National Digital Strategy, launched in 2025 with the Sixth National Development Plan, charts digital infrastructure for 2025/26 to 2029/30.

Money and results. The nearest held fact is the National Digital Strategy's target, stated in February 2026, of raising internet use from 53% to 90% by 2030, within a plan period that runs from 2025/26 to 2029/30 and had not ended when it was reported.

Not held. No budget line, universal service fund allocation or financed programme tied to the plan in the last three years is held.

NER.short: Nothing held names a national broadband plan or says there is none, so no stage is set.
NER.summary: Not held. Nothing held names a national broadband plan, or says there is none.

NGA.short: Nigeria's National Broadband Plan 2020-2025 has ended, with 51.97 percent penetration in December 2025 against a 70 percent target; any successor is not known.
NGA.summary:
Plan adopted. A committee led by Funke Opeke of MainOne, with Bashir Gwandu as co-chair, was inaugurated in December 2019 to develop a five-year broadband strategy through 2025, which produced the National Broadband Plan 2020-2025. In September 2020 BusinessDay NG referred to the recently updated Nigerian Broadband Plan, and the Nigerian Communications Commission (NCC) said a grant was in line with it. By September 2026 BusinessDay NG said the plan had ended, with no successor plan named.

Money and results. Citing NCC data, BusinessDay NG reports broadband penetration of 51.97 percent in December 2025 against the plan's 70 percent target, and 4G at 52.95 percent of mobile subscriptions against a 70 percent goal set for 2023. The only funding held is foreign: a US Trade and Development Agency grant to ipNX, signed on 17 September 2020, to expand fibre to more than 200,000 residences in Lagos, Abuja and Port Harcourt. Its amount is not stated.

Not held. No source held says a national broadband plan is adopted and still running. The money behind the plan is not stated.

RWA.short: Rwanda updated its National Broadband Policy and Strategy in 2022; whether money is committed to it or results are published is not known.
RWA.summary:
Plan adopted. The government updated its National Broadband Policy and Strategy in 2022, Telecom Review Africa reported in October 2025. The update ended the commitment to a single wholesale network. It introduced technology neutrality, so that mobile operators can reuse spectrum bands for several technologies at once, 4G and 5G among them.

Money and results. To support the change, more spectrum was allocated in the 700 MHz, 900 MHz, 1800 MHz and 2100 MHz bands, opening the way for more than one operator to build advanced networks. The same report estimates 4G coverage reaching 100% by the end of 2025, with 3G coverage at 99.71%. It sets neither figure against a target of the policy, and it names no money committed to it.

Not held. No budget line, universal service fund allocation or financed programme tied to the plan in the last three years is held.

SDN.short: Nothing held names a national broadband plan or says there is none, so no stage is set.
SDN.summary: Not held. Nothing held names a national broadband plan for the country, or says there is none.

SEN.short: Senegal's ministry presented guidelines for a national broadband plan in 2017; whether it was adopted, and any funding, is not known.
SEN.summary:
Plan adopted. A ministry slide deck of 2017 presents the guidelines of the Plan national haut/très haut débit, tied to Sénégal Numérique 2025. It sets out objectives, a diagnosis of the infrastructure and proposed investments. The deck presents guidelines and does not state that the plan was adopted. The deck is hosted by the ITU, carries no date of its own, and its published field gives 2017.

Money and results. The nearest held fact is the same 2017 deck, whose proposed investments are put forward as part of the guidelines. It names no budget line, fund allocation or financed programme, and no figures against the plan's targets. The deck links the plan to Sénégal Numérique 2025 and gives a diagnosis of the infrastructure beside the proposed investments, with no statement of who funds them.

Not held. No source held says a national broadband plan is adopted and still running. Nothing held shows money committed to one.

SLE.short: Sierra Leone has a National Broadband Strategy for 2023-2028, reported adopted in January 2025; what money or results sit behind it is not known.
SLE.summary:
Plan adopted. Sierra Leone has a National Broadband Strategy for 2023 to 2028. ITEdgeNews reported on 31 January 2025 that a government agreement to connect universities by satellite is in line with it.

Money and results. Under that agreement the Ministry of Communication, Technology and Innovation and the Ministry of Technical and Higher Education signed with ELCOME SL to bring Starlink internet to 12 public and private universities, with vocational schools to follow in a second phase. The minister said three local companies were by then providing Starlink services and that its arrival had spurred competition among providers. The report gives no cost for the agreement and no budget line or fund allocation behind the strategy, and it sets no figures against the strategy's targets.

Not held. No budget line, universal service fund allocation or financed programme tied to the plan in the last three years is held.

SOM.short: Nothing held names a national broadband plan or says there is none, so no stage is set.
SOM.summary: Not held. Nothing held names a national broadband plan for the country, or says there is none.

SSD.short: South Sudan launched a National Broadband Roadmap, reported in 2025; no money or results against it are known.
SSD.summary:
Plan adopted. South Sudan's National Communication Authority, as reported by Eye Radio on 3 July 2025, cited the launch of the National Broadband Roadmap among the developments behind the country's rise in internet users. The Authority names the plan as the National Broadband Roadmap and presents its launch as a development already behind the country, not one still to come. The same report places the roadmap alongside the Authority's own account of how internet use in South Sudan grew between 2024 and 2025.

Money and results. The nearest held fact is the Authority's count of internet users, which Eye Radio reported rose from 1.3 million in 2024 to 1.9 million in 2025. The Authority tied the launch of the National Broadband Roadmap to that rise, and the report gives it as a result of the wider set of developments, not as a figure measured against a target of the plan.

Not held. No budget line, universal service fund allocation or financed programme tied to the plan in the last three years is held.

TCD.short: Chad adopted Tchad Connexion 2030 in 2025, with an 80 percent coverage target, but money committed or results against it are not known.
TCD.summary:
Plan adopted. Chad's government launched Tchad Connexion 2030, which TechAfrica News reported on 18 July 2025 as a national digital strategy running to 2030, aimed at giving most Chadians quality internet access and extending digital coverage across the country. Biometric Update, on 16 March 2026, reports that the government is implementing it, with targets of at least 80 percent national internet coverage and about 80 percent mobile penetration.

Money and results. The held facts state planned investment and works, not figures against the targets. Ecofin, on 10 December 2025, gives US$1.5bn of planned digital investment. TechAfrica News lists fibre loops, a 509 km fibre link from N'Djamena to the Niger border and satellite coverage as the components of the launch programme.

Not held. No budget line, universal service fund allocation or financed programme tied to the plan in the last three years is held.

TGO.short: Nothing held names a national broadband plan or says there is none, so no stage is set.
TGO.summary: Not held. Nothing held names a national broadband plan for the country, or says there is none.

TUN.short: Tunisia has a national very high speed broadband strategy dated 2013; whether money was committed to it or results published is not known.
TUN.summary:
Plan adopted. The communication technologies ministry's fibre optic page names a national strategy for very high speed broadband, the Stratégie Nationale pour le Développement du très haut débit, which dates from 2013. The page sits under the digital infrastructure axis of Tunisie Digitale 2020. It gives no period for the strategy and names nothing that replaces it.

Money and results. Under the strategy the ministry publishes terms of reference for fibre to the home: for network studies, for civil works, for cabling the access network and for cabling buildings, with common annexes. They are meant to set one technical standard for laying fibre in Tunisia and for the studies and works of telecommunications projects. The page states no budget and no figures against the strategy.

Not held. No budget line, universal service fund allocation or financed programme tied to the plan in the last three years is held.

TZA.short: Tanzania has a national high-speed internet strategy whose steering committee first met in June 2026, but its period, funding and results are not known.
TZA.summary:
Plan adopted. Tanzania's Ministry of Communication and Information Technology reported on 26 June 2026 that the Steering Committee overseeing the National High-Speed Internet Communication Strategy (Mkakati wa Taifa wa Mawasiliano ya Intaneti ya Kasi) held its first meeting on 25 June 2026 in Dodoma. The Ministry's Permanent Secretary chaired the meeting. The same ministry report gives no period for the strategy, so the dates it covers are not stated.

Money and results. The nearest held fact on the plan's delivery is that first meeting of the steering committee, held in Dodoma on 25 June 2026 under the Permanent Secretary of the Ministry of Communication and Information Technology. It concerns the oversight of the strategy and says nothing of its targets, funding or results.

Not held. No budget line, universal service fund allocation or financed programme tied to the plan in the last three years is held.

UGA.short: Uganda has the National Broadband Policy 2018, reviewed in January 2026; money tied to it and figures against its targets are not known.
UGA.summary:
Plan adopted. Uganda's National Broadband Policy 2018 is the broadband plan the Ministry of ICT and National Guidance and the ITU describe as under implementation, in a review of it published on 12 January 2026. The review gives no end date for the policy and names no replacement. It is the policy the ministry and the ITU reviewed, and no other broadband plan appears beside it.

Money and results. The review of the 2018 National Broadband Policy's implementation, published on 12 January 2026 by the Ministry of ICT and National Guidance and the ITU, sets out a matrix covering each of the policy's objectives and strategies. For each it lists the activities undertaken, the outcomes, the level of implementation reported by stakeholders, the challenges met and the measures proposed to mitigate them.

Not held. No figures against the plan's targets are held. No budget line, universal service fund allocation or financed programme tied to the plan in the last three years is held.

ZAF.short: South Africa's SA Connect broadband policy, adopted in 2013, is cited as current in 2026; whether any money is committed to it is not known.
ZAF.summary:
Plan adopted. South Africa's national broadband plan is SA Connect, a policy dating from 2013 that sets "broadband for all". The government gazette page on the IMT Roadmap 2026 names that policy and states no end date or successor for it. In July 2026 the regulator ICASA named the SA Connect Broadband Policy as the existing national policy that its draft IMT Roadmap 2026 supports. A 28 July 2026 report on the same roadmap says ICASA cites the policy for broadband access.

Money and results. The government's SA Connect target, as an August 2026 article puts it, is universal broadband access with an average user experience of 100Mbps by 2030. The article says telecoms licensees' spectrum obligations align with that target, and it gives no figure for delivery against it.

Not held. No budget line, universal service fund allocation or financed programme tied to the plan in the last three years is held.

ZMB.short: A December 2025 working group found Zambia lacks a national broadband policy; whether other plans set broadband targets is not known.
ZMB.summary:
Plan adopted. Zambia has no national broadband policy. The policy working group at the Africa Broadband Maps national event, held in Lusaka with the regulator ZICTA on 9 to 11 December 2025, concluded so and recommended that one be written. The event was part of a project in eleven African countries, run with the International Telecommunication Union and paid for by the European Union.

Money and results. The project is to build a national broadband mapping system in four yearly phases from 2025 to 2028, owned by the government with ZICTA as its custodian, and to train staff in mapping, data management and policy. The report says it is meant to complement the country's digital transformation work and its existing mapping of ICT infrastructure. It states no broadband targets and no budget.

Not held. Whether broadband targets sit inside other government plans is not known.

ZWE.short: Zimbabwe has a National Broadband Plan, reported by its ICT minister in 2023; whether money has been committed or results published is not known.
ZWE.summary:
Plan adopted. Zimbabwe has a National Broadband Plan, which the ICT minister, Dr Tatenda Mavetera, said the government "came up with", as the Herald reported on 12 October 2023. The plan is a national one, and the Ministry of ICT, Postal and Courier Services is its owner, as the same report names it. The minister added that Potraz had been in sync with Government in implementing it, and that the plan covers access for government, business, households and individuals.

Money and results. The nearest held fact on delivery is the minister's statement of October 2023 that Potraz was implementing the plan alongside Government. The plan's stated aim, as the same report gives it, is to provide broadband access at four levels: government, business, household and individual.

Not held. No budget line, universal service fund allocation or financed programme tied to the plan in the last three years is held. No figures against the plan's own targets are held either.

AGO.short: Angola has a hosting policy being written and none in force, so where public bodies must host is not known.
AGO.summary:
Policy adopted. Angola has no hosting policy in force. In March 2026 the Instituto de Modernização Administrativa issued terms of reference for a five-month consultancy to draft a national policy on the management and hosting of public data, with its implementing regulation. The policy is to set hosting rules by category of data, covering on-premises systems, a government or sovereign cloud, hybrid arrangements and the conditions for using public cloud, together with rules on where data must reside.

Named hosting and moves. A report of November 2025 has the government saying that all government services must migrate to the national data centre within 30 days of its inauguration. The data centre is being developed alongside a unified government cloud, at a combined cost of about USD 90 million.

Not held. No source held says a government hosting or cloud policy is adopted and in force.

BDI.summary: Not held. Nothing held names a government hosting or cloud policy, or says there is none.

BEN.summary: Not held. Nothing held names a government hosting or cloud policy, or says there is none.

BFA.short: Burkina Faso tells public bodies to host nationally and opened two government cloud data centres in 2026; which bodies have moved is not known.
BFA.summary:
Policy adopted. The government's "Zéro donnée à l'extérieur" programme, one of twelve digital-transformation programmes to 2030, aims to host platforms and data on national territory; the Prime Minister's half-year evaluation of 25 July 2026 reported it as under way. It was first set out in a roadmap of 12 digital projects at a government seminar on 25 August 2025. A Prime Minister's circular tells public bodies to give priority to national hosting, and requests to operate a platform are screened for where the data is hosted, the director general of digital transformation said in March 2026.

Named hosting and moves. The two government-cloud data centres the Prime Minister inaugurated on 23 January 2026 are to host all public data. The state ICT agency's board set the repatriation of administrations' data to them as its course for 2026. By July 2026 the ministry had inventoried 120 public platforms for hosting in the country, with repatriation begun and due to finish before the end of 2026.

Not held. No source from the last three years naming or counting public bodies that have moved onto the named hosting is held.

BWA.short: Nothing held says Botswana has a government hosting or cloud policy, or says it has none, so no stage is set.
BWA.summary: Not held. Nothing held names a government hosting or cloud policy, or says there is none.

CAF.short: A 2023 World Bank record shows no government cloud policy in Central African Republic; nothing newer is held, so no stage is set.
CAF.summary: Not held. No policy or draft is on record, and no source dated in the last three years says the government has neither.

CIV.short: A cloud hosting procedure for ministries and institutions was approved in June 2021; where public bodies must host is not known.
CIV.summary:
Policy adopted. The ANSUT document Politique d'hébergement des données dans le cloud, version 1.0 dated 14 June 2021, was approved on 17 June 2021 by ANSUT's Directeur de l'Exploitation. It sets the procedure for ministries and institutions to host applications in the cloud. No end or replacement is stated. The document is version 1.0, dated 14 June 2021 and approved three days later, and ANSUT and the Ministry of Digital Transition are its listed owners.

Named hosting and moves. The 2021 document is a procedure for ministries and institutions hosting applications in the cloud, issued by ANSUT, the national digital agency under the Ministry of Digital Transition. It names a Microsoft Azure public cloud, bought through the eGOUV licence contract, and the Datacenter eGOUV, both run by ANSUT for national use across ministries, institutions and public administration. The document is the only source for both.

Not held. No source held says the government has named where public bodies must host, whether a government cloud or data centre the policy tells them to use, or a list of approved providers.

CMR.short: Nothing held says Cameroon has a government hosting or cloud policy, or says it has none, so no stage is set.
CMR.summary: Not held. Nothing held names a government hosting or cloud policy, or says there is none.

COD.short: A national data hosting strategy was being developed in March 2026, and no adopted policy is known; where public bodies must host is not known.
COD.summary:
Policy adopted. The Digital Transformation Project terms of reference of March 2026 say the government, helped by UNECA and GIZ, is developing a national data hosting strategy, under way mainly at central level. They seek consultants to define the hosting approach, for example cloud-first or cloud-appropriate, and to propose hosting and cloud decrees and directives. CIO Mag, 8 November 2023, reports that the Council of Ministers had adopted a draft decree on the management of national datacenters a year earlier. The article does not say the decree was later issued.

Named hosting and moves. The same March 2026 terms of reference say public-sector data hosting is fragmented, heterogeneous and insufficiently pooled, with no coherent national framework for classification, governance and pooling. They add that norms on sovereign hosting remain embryonic or inoperative.

Not held. No source held says a government hosting or cloud policy is adopted and in force.

EGY.short: Egypt adopted a Cloud First Policy in 2024, in force since August 2024; where public bodies must host under it is not known.
EGY.summary:
Policy adopted. The Supreme Council of Digital Society adopted the Cloud First Policy on 13 March 2024; it requires data classified top secret or secret to be hosted only within Egypt. The policy, with that requirement, entered into force on 22 August 2024. The Cabinet's spokesperson said the council, at its first meeting after being reconstituted under the Prime Minister, approved and launched the cloud computing policy in line with the Digital Egypt strategy.

Named hosting and moves. The ICT ministry is preparing a national data-centre strategy with other ministries and bodies, to expand data centres and their capacity inside Egypt, the minister told a cabinet meeting on 20 September 2026. He said on 8 September that it covers storage and compute needs, investment, regulation, standards, skills and digital sovereignty, and in July called it a core component of digital sovereignty.

Not held. No source held says the government has named where public bodies must host: a government cloud or data centre the policy tells them to use, or a list of approved providers.

GHA.short: Ghana held a validation workshop on a cloud and data centre framework in 2024; whether the framework has been adopted is not known.
GHA.summary:
Policy adopted. Ghana has a framework in preparation. On 26 June 2024 Smart Africa and the National Information Technology Agency held a validation workshop in Accra to gather stakeholders' input for an enhanced regulatory framework for cloud and data centres, the Ministry of Communications reported. The minister said the framework would help make Ghana the preferred place to host African data.

Named hosting and moves. After the workshop the minister said the government is working to have all its data held in other countries hosted in Ghana. Data produced in the country must be stored there, she said, and the large cloud operators are welcome to build data centres in Ghana; paying to host data abroad, to have it managed and to retrieve it means paying twice. She said local data centres would also create jobs.

Not held. No source held says a government hosting or cloud policy is adopted and in force.

GIN.short: Nothing held says Guinea has a government hosting or cloud policy, or says it has none, so no stage is set.
GIN.summary: Not held. Nothing held names a government hosting or cloud policy, or says there is none.

GMB.short: The Gambia has a government cloud policy and strategy dated 2023; where public bodies must host under it is not known.
GMB.summary:
Policy adopted. The Gambia has a Government Cloud Policy, with a strategy and an implementation plan, dated 2023. The Ministry of Communications and Digital Economy lists it among the country's policies, strategies and legal frameworks, beside the e-government strategy for 2021 to 2024 and the Digital Economy Masterplan for 2024 to 2034. The list also holds an open data strategy for 2024 to 2027 and a data protection and privacy bill.

Named hosting and moves. The ministry says the Government Cloud Strategy for 2023 to 2027 builds on the cloud policy and aims to modernise government service delivery through cloud adoption. The strategy sets goals, objectives and expected outcomes, and addresses the difficulties of adopting cloud. The same presentation lists underdeveloped data centres and limited cloud infrastructure among the bottlenecks to the country's digital transformation.

Not held. No source held says the government has named where public bodies must host: a government cloud or data centre the policy tells them to use, or a list of approved providers.

GNB.short: Nothing held says Guinea-Bissau has a government hosting or cloud policy, or says it has none, so no stage is set.

GNQ.summary: Not held. Nothing held names a government hosting or cloud policy, or says there is none.

KEN.short: Kenya's Cloud Policy took effect in May 2025 and gives State bodies 24 months to migrate; the list of approved providers is not yet published.
KEN.summary:
Policy adopted. The Kenya Cloud Policy, 2025 was signed on 7 April 2025 and took effect on 2 May 2025 on publication in the Kenya Gazette. It requires government data classified as sensitive, top secret, secret or restricted to be stored within Kenya. Implementation guidelines published by the Ministry of ICT and the Digital Economy bar public entities from hosting systems and data in their own server rooms without the authorisation of a Cloud Adoption Committee, and give all State organs 24 months to migrate systems that are not exempted.

Named hosting and moves. As reported on 6 August 2026, applications for accreditation as a government cloud service provider are open, to a Cloud Adoption Committee that is yet to be established. One provider is to be chosen from the accredited list to host all State data, and the list of eligible providers is yet to be published.

Not held. No source held says the government has named where public bodies must host: a government cloud or data centre the policy tells them to use, or a list of approved providers.

LBR.short: Nothing held says Liberia has a government hosting or cloud policy, or says it has none, so no stage is set.
LBR.summary: Not held. Nothing held names a government hosting or cloud policy, or says there is none.

LBY.short: Libya had a national cloud computing policy out for consultation in 2026; whether it has been adopted is not known.
LBY.summary:
Policy adopted. Libya has a policy in draft. The General Information Authority held a consultative meeting with ESCWA, ministries and representatives of the private sector and civil society to review the proposed National Cloud Computing Policy, reported in January 2026. The policy is described as a unified framework for hosting government data and services, and the meeting agreed to incorporate the feedback into its final version.

Named hosting and moves. The proposed policy aims to set one national framework for hosting government data and services, as part of the authority's work on digital infrastructure and the security of national data. The meeting heard a presentation on fitting cloud technology to the needs of Libyan institutions, and ESCWA, the United Nations commission that attended, acts as the authority's consulting partner on the policy.

Not held. No source held says a government hosting or cloud policy is adopted and in force.

LSO.short: Nothing held says Lesotho has a government hosting or cloud policy, or says it has none, so no stage is set.
LSO.summary: Not held. Nothing held names a government hosting or cloud policy, or says there is none.

MAR.short: Morocco made cloud the mandatory default for public-administration technology spending in 2025; where public bodies must host is not known.
MAR.summary:
Policy adopted. Morocco has a Cloud First Policy under Digital Morocco 2030, which makes cloud the mandatory default for all public-administration technology investments, the ministry's director of cloud infrastructure said in 2025. In a white paper of November 2025 the delegate minister for digital transition said her ministry carries a cloud roadmap for 2025 to 2030, with six objectives and 21 domains, and is putting a public-sector Cloud First policy in place.

Named hosting and moves. The same white paper, published by AUSIM, describes the cloud roadmap for 2025 to 2030 as not yet published. It says a national reference architecture is still to be defined, from 2026. The director of cloud infrastructure's account is that cloud is now the default for every technology investment by the public administration.

Not held. No source held says the government has named where public bodies must host: a government cloud or data centre the policy tells them to use, or a list of approved providers.

MDG.short: Nothing held says Madagascar has a government hosting or cloud policy, or says it has none, so no stage is set.
MDG.summary: Not held. Nothing held names a government hosting or cloud policy, or says there is none.

MLI.short: Nothing held says Mali has a government hosting or cloud policy, or says it has none, so no stage is set.
MLI.summary: Not held. Nothing held names a government hosting or cloud policy, or says there is none.

MOZ.short: Mozambique said in 2025 it is drafting a new framework for cloud adoption; whether one has been adopted for public bodies is not known.
MOZ.summary:
Policy adopted. Mozambique has a framework being drafted. In December 2025 the Minister of Communications and Digital Transformation said the government is drafting an updated regulatory framework for cloud adoption, to replace current legal restrictions. He said cloud adoption should be treated as a national priority reaching well beyond the financial industry. A Cloud Computing Regulation approved by Decree No. 72/2025 of 31 December 2025 licenses cloud providers.

Named hosting and moves. Alongside the framework the minister said the government plans over five years to establish domestic data centres able to host cloud services securely for banks and other institutions. He was speaking at a bank's anniversary event in Maputo. The law firm's account of the December 2025 decree describes the licensing of providers and no rule on where public bodies host.

Not held. No source held says a government hosting or cloud policy is adopted and in force.

MRT.short: Mauritania's data-protection authority has required its authorisation for cloud services abroad since 2025; where public bodies must host is not known.
MRT.summary:
Policy adopted. On 30 July 2025 Mauritania's data-protection authority issued deliberation 005/2025 on the minimum conditions for using cloud services abroad. It requires public and private data controllers to obtain the authority's authorisation before processing personal data on foreign cloud services, and to write set clauses into the provider contract: compliance with law 2017-020, transfer abroad, retrieval of the data and its permanent deletion. The authority's meeting of 29 April 2026 had amendments to some of the deliberation's articles on its agenda.

Named hosting and moves. The amended text of the deliberation was published on 30 April 2026. It governs the use of cloud services located abroad, by prior authorisation from the authority, and covers the return of data when a contract expires. It binds public bodies and private firms alike.

Not held. No source held says the government has named where public bodies must host: a government cloud or data centre the policy tells them to use, or a list of approved providers.

MUS.short: Nothing held says Mauritius has a government hosting or cloud policy, or says it has none, so no stage is set.
MUS.summary: Not held. Nothing held names a government hosting or cloud policy, or says there is none.

MWI.short: Malawi had no cloud policy enacted as at June 2025, the World Bank records; whether one is being written is not known.
MWI.summary:
Policy adopted. Malawi has no cloud policy in force. A World Bank status report on the Digital Malawi Acceleration Project records zero government data governance frameworks, data classification and cloud policies included, enacted and mandated for use as at 30 June 2025. The count is one of the measures under the project's first component, affordable broadband and secure data hosting.

Named hosting and moves. The same status report sets a target of three such frameworks enacted and mandated for use by October 2030. It records the national data centre in Lilongwe as complete, paid for under an earlier project, with the first few clients migrated to it. The report rates the project's progress as satisfactory and says 19 percent of its money had been disbursed.

Not held.

NAM.short: Nothing held says Namibia has a government hosting or cloud policy, or says it has none, so no stage is set.
NAM.summary: Not held. Nothing held names a government hosting or cloud policy, or says there is none.

NER.short: Nothing held says Niger has a government hosting or cloud policy, or says it has none, so no stage is set.
NER.summary: Not held. Nothing held names a government hosting or cloud policy, or says there is none.

NGA.short: Nigeria released a National Digital Cloud Policy in August 2026, replacing its 2019 policy; a government cloud in service is not yet named.
NGA.summary:
Policy adopted. On 17 August 2026 the Federal Ministry of Communications, Innovation and Digital Economy released the National Digital Cloud Policy, which supersedes the Nigeria Cloud Computing Policy 2019, the policy that first introduced Cloud First. The state IT agency NITDA signed the National Cloud Computing Guideline, a technical guideline and an assurance framework earlier that month. The new policy targets US$750 million in private cloud and data-centre investment.

Named hosting and moves. Under the policy the state-owned Galaxy Backbone will aggregate government cloud demand from registered providers and negotiate framework agreements, with buying through a National Digital Marketplace on which NITDA registers providers. A 24-month roadmap plans the migration of priority ministries in months six to twelve. NITDA's director-general said in August 2026 that the Cloud First policy remains in force.

Not held. No source held says the government has named where public bodies must host: a government cloud or data centre the policy tells them to use, or a list of approved providers.

RWA.short: Rwanda has required critical government systems to be hosted in the National Data Center since 2012; which bodies have moved recently is not known.
RWA.summary:
Policy adopted. Rwanda's rule is Ministerial Instructions N° 001/2012, issued by the Minister in the Office of the President in Charge of ICT and in force from their signature on 12 March 2012. They include a rule on hosting critical government data and systems, and state no end date and no replacement.

Named hosting and moves. Article 17 of the instructions requires all government IT systems and applications that process, store or provide critical government data to be hosted in the National Data Center, website, email and shared applications included. Article 18 requires institutions that keep data centres of their own to arrange disaster recovery from the National Data Center. The instructions name the centre as the one place for critical systems, and both articles have stood since 2012.

Not held. No source from the last three years naming or counting public bodies that have moved onto the named hosting is held.

SDN.short: Nothing held says Sudan has a government hosting or cloud policy, or says it has none, so no stage is set.
SDN.summary: Not held. Nothing held names a government hosting or cloud policy, or says there is none.

SEN.short: Senegal's president instructed in 2021 that all state data move to the Diamniadio national data centre; which bodies have moved is not known.
SEN.summary:
Policy adopted. Commissioning the Diamniadio National Datacenter in June 2021, President Macky Sall instructed the government to migrate all state data and platforms to it and to repatriate national data hosted outside the country. State-owned businesses such as the electricity company Senelec are to move their data too, he said. A later account says Senegal then required all servers to be housed within its borders.

Named hosting and moves. The instruction names one place: the Diamniadio National Datacenter, built with Huawei on a Chinese loan at a cost given as $18.2 million. It is managed by the state IT agency ADIE, and all government data and applications are to be migrated to it and hosted there. The 2021 report gave its hosting capacity as 500 square metres and said its first phase would open in about six months.

Not held. No source from the last three years naming or counting public bodies that have moved onto the named hosting is held.

SLE.short: Nothing held says Sierra Leone has a government hosting or cloud policy, or says it has none, so no stage is set.
SLE.summary: Not held. Nothing held names a government hosting or cloud policy, or says there is none.

SOM.short: Nothing held says Somalia has a government hosting or cloud policy, or says it has none, so no stage is set.
SOM.summary: Not held. Nothing held names a government hosting or cloud policy, or says there is none.

SSD.short: Nothing held says South Sudan has a government hosting or cloud policy, or says it has none, so no stage is set.
SSD.summary: Not held. Nothing held names a government hosting or cloud policy, or says there is none.

STP.short: Nothing held says Sao Tome and Principe has a government hosting or cloud policy, or says it has none, so no stage is set.
STP.summary: Not held. Nothing held names a government hosting or cloud policy, or says there is none.

SWZ.short: Nothing held says Eswatini has a government hosting or cloud policy, or says it has none, so no stage is set.
SWZ.summary: Not held. Nothing held names a government hosting or cloud policy, or says there is none.

SYC.short: Nothing held says Seychelles has a government hosting or cloud policy, or says it has none, so no stage is set.
SYC.summary: Not held. Nothing held names a government hosting or cloud policy, or says there is none.

TCD.short: Nothing held says Chad has a government hosting or cloud policy, or says it has none, so no stage is set.
TCD.summary: Not held. Nothing held names a government hosting or cloud policy, or says there is none.

TGO.short: Nothing held says Togo has a government hosting or cloud policy, or says it has none, so no stage is set.
TGO.summary: Not held. Nothing held names a government hosting or cloud policy, or says there is none.

TUN.short: Tunisia's 2024 Cloud First circular sets hosting tiers and a list of labelled providers was published in 2026; which bodies have moved is not known.
TUN.summary:
Policy adopted. A ministerial order of 13 September 2023 requires public bodies' software, platforms and infrastructure to be hosted in-house or with cloud providers according to four tiers, any other arrangement needing the cybersecurity agency's approval. Circulaire n° 16 of 22 July 2024, from the Head of Government to ministers, governors and heads of public bodies, generalises cloud adoption under the "TN Government Cloud First Policy". A circular of 2 September 2026 tightens the hosting requirements.

Named hosting and moves. The 2024 circular sends sensitive internal systems to a private cloud or to national or sectoral government cloud centres, shared government systems to government cloud centres, and public e-services to the body's private cloud, government cloud centres or providers holding the N-Cloud label. The cybersecurity agency published its list of labelled providers on 17 September 2026, with six N-Cloud entries.

Not held. No source from the last three years naming or counting public bodies that have moved onto the named hosting is held.

TZA.short: Tanzania approved hosting standards for public institutions in February 2026; the approved hosting environments are not named.
TZA.summary:
Policy adopted. The e-Government Authority's Data Center Standards and Guidelines for Public Institutions, version 2.0, was approved by its board chairperson on 18 February 2026. It is issued under section 49 of the e-Government Act No. 10 of 2019, which requires the authority to issue technical standards on storing and processing electronic data.

Named hosting and moves. The standard rests on section 25 of the Act, which requires a public institution to host its systems in a government-approved hosting environment. The authority says it wrote the standard to guide public institutions in deciding where to host government ICT applications, and to stop them setting up new data centres. It will also serve as the minimum requirements for judging whether an existing data centre can be an approved hosting environment.

Not held. No source held says the government has named where public bodies must host: a government cloud or data centre the policy tells them to use, or a list of approved providers.

UGA.short: Cloud-first guidelines from October 2018 require ministries and agencies to host classified information in the government data centre; how many have moved is not known.
UGA.summary:
Policy adopted. NITA-U issued the National Guidelines on Cloud Computing for Government, Ministries, Departments and Agencies in October 2018, requiring all ministries, departments, agencies and local governments to adhere to Cloud First for IT-enabled services. The document gives no end date. It is version CPG1 of the guidelines and applies to the government bodies it lists.

Named hosting and moves. The same guidelines require those bodies to host information assets classed Official, Secret and Top Secret in the Government Cloud, the National Data Center run by NITA-U. They must also use it when procuring new ICT, and migrate existing classified services to it at contract expiry or refresh. NITA-U can approve offshore exceptions. The Government Cloud serves ministries, departments, agencies and local governments. NITA-U's 2023 statistical abstract lists the National Data Centre as serving 95 government entities in FY2022/23.

Not held. No source from the last three years naming or counting public bodies that have moved onto the named hosting is held.

ZAF.short: South Africa gazetted its National Policy on Data and Cloud in May 2024; no government cloud or list of providers is named.
ZAF.summary:
Policy adopted. The Department of Communications and Digital Technologies published the National Policy on Data and Cloud as Notice 2533 of 2024 in Government Gazette 50741 on 31 May 2024. It covers national and provincial government and organs of state. It was published under section 3(1) of the Electronic Communications Act, 2005, and the department listed the drafting of a Data and Cloud Strategy among its work in October 2024.

Named hosting and moves. The policy says government data shall be stored in unified, cloud-enabled data centres in designated locations, names the State Information Technology Agency as the authority to source data infrastructure and cloud services for government, and makes cloud the first option for new ICT procurement. A law firm's reading of June 2024 is that it requires government data-centre infrastructure to be in the country and still needs implementing with the agency and departments.

Not held. No source held says the government has named where public bodies must host: a government cloud or data centre the policy tells them to use, or a list of approved providers.

ZMB.short: A 2023 regulation requires public bodies to store personal data in Zambia; which hosting they must use is not known.
ZMB.summary:
Policy adopted. Statutory Instrument No. 43 of 2023, the Electronic Government (General) Regulations, gazetted on 6 October 2023 under the Electronic Government Act 2021, requires every public body to store the personal data it processes on infrastructure domiciled in Zambia, under regulation 8 of the regulations, which cite the Act as their authority. Storage abroad needs authorisation from the Electronic Government Division and the Data Protection Commissioner.

Named hosting and moves. The regulations require all public bodies to integrate their services with the Government Service Bus, run by the Electronic Government Division, and refer to the Government Wide Area Network for e-government services where applicable. They set the rule for where personal data is stored, not which hosting to use. Authorisation for storage abroad rests with two bodies, the Electronic Government Division and the Data Protection Commissioner.

Not held. No source held says the government has named where public bodies must host, whether a government cloud or data centre the policy tells them to use, or a list of approved providers.

ZWE.short: Nothing held says Zimbabwe has a government hosting or cloud policy, or says it has none, so no stage is set.
ZWE.summary: Not held. Nothing held names a government hosting or cloud policy, or says there is none.

AGO.short: Law 7/17 of 2017 is in force and a new bill passed parliament in August 2026; no use of either is known.
AGO.summary:
Law in force. A UNITA deputy, quoted by Novo Jornal on 23 January 2026, says Law 7/17 of 16 February, on the protection of computer networks and systems, is part of the current legal order and that the new bill would repeal it. The Council of Ministers considered the Cybersecurity Bill on 27 October 2025 for sending to the National Assembly. The Assembly approved it in general terms on 23 January 2026, with 105 votes for and 75 UNITA abstentions, and adopted the cybersecurity law on 12 August 2026, with MPLA votes carrying it.

Use of the law. The law adopted on 12 August 2026 sets fines of 7 to 4,000 national minimum wages, by gravity, according to ANGOP. The National Assembly's specialised committees approved the proposed law before the final vote, as Telecompaper reported on 10 August 2026. PTI reports that the final vote of 12 August 2026 was taken globally, with 104 in favour.

Not held. No arrest, charge, prosecution, conviction or penalty under the law in the last three years is held.

BDI.short: A 2022 cybercrime law is in force and was cited as applied in 2026; no use against anyone is known.
BDI.summary:
Law in force. Burundi's cybercrime law is Law No. 1/10 of 16 March 2022 on the prevention and repression of cybercrime. At a workshop in Bujumbura in February 2026, a government delegate cited it as adopted and in application. A speaker at the same workshop said the president signed it in 2022. The law is named in the article as the country's cybercrime law, and the Malabo Convention was the standard against which the workshop measured it.

Use of the law. The nearest held fact on use is the same February 2026 workshop in Bujumbura, where experts and participants discussed the law's enforcement and its gaps against the Malabo Convention. The government delegate presented the law at that workshop as being in application. The article gives that discussion and the 2022 date of signature, and the law is the Burundian text on cybercrime prevention and repression adopted in March 2022.

Not held. No arrest, charge, prosecution, conviction or penalty under the law in the last three years is held.

BEN.short: The 2018 Code du numérique is in force; in 2025 about 1,500 online-fraud suspects were arrested.
BEN.summary:
Law in force. Loi n° 2017-20 of 20 April 2018, the Code du numérique, was adopted by the National Assembly and promulgated by the President. Its Livre VI defines illegal access to and penetration of an information system. The code carries the date 20 April 2018, and its Livre VI treats unauthorised entry into computer systems as an offence, in two forms: illegal access and penetration.

Use of the law. Benin's Centre national d'investigations numériques reported over 6,500 digital-offence complaints in 2025, against about 4,000 the year before, and about 1,500 arrests of online-fraud suspects.
