Authority appointed. Cenfri says that the Data Protection Commission under Lesotho's Data Protection Act has remained unappointed, in its document published on 23 March 2026.

Implementing and acting. The law firm Z. Mayet and Associates states that the Act establishes a Data Protection Commission, but that the Commission and its Commissioner have not been appointed, in a document published on 31 October 2025.

Not held. No source dated in the last three years shows an appointed authority registering organisations, taking breach reports, issuing guidance or inspecting.

MAR.short: Law 09-08 is in force and the CNDP authority is working, issuing guidance in 2026; no ruling against an organisation is known.
MAR.summary:
Law in force. The president of the CNDP, interviewed on 4 August 2026, speaks of Law 09-08 as in force for more than fifteen years, with its paradigms still applicable.

Malabo Convention. The African Union status list of 2 February 2026 records no signature and no ratification of the Malabo Convention by Morocco.

Authority appointed. The CNDP, Morocco's national commission for the control of personal data protection, validated five new deliberations on 28 November 2025, acting as the supervisory body.

Implementing and acting. In a communiqué dated 28 August 2026, the CNDP gave guidance on Law 09-08 to political parties and voters for the 23 September 2026 elections, and opened a 3020 information line. It published a national register of notified processing operations in January 2023.

Not held. No ruling of the authority against a named organisation in the last three years is held.

MDG.short: A 2015 law is in force and its authority was sworn in during August 2025; no ruling against an organisation is known.
MDG.summary:
Law in force. Loi n° 2014-038 on the protection of personal data was promulgated on 9 January 2015, and the procedures manual of the data protection commission, dated December 2025, treats it as the operative legal basis for its work.

Malabo Convention. The African Union status list of 2 February 2026 records that Madagascar ratified the Malabo Convention on 17 July 2025 and deposited its instrument on 15 September 2025.

Authority appointed. Seven members of the Commission Malagasy de l'Informatique et des Libertés (CMIL) were sworn in at the Cour suprême on 4 August 2025. Its bureau was elected on 14 August 2025, and in March 2026 the Unité de Gouvernance Digitale announced the CMIL is now effectively in place.

Implementing and acting. The CMIL's annual report of January 2026 says no processing declaration has been registered yet, that citizens' complaints went untreated for ten years, and that the commission has no premises or staff, with 104 posts targeted in the 2026 Finance Law.

Not held. No source dated in the last three years shows the authority registering organisations, taking breach reports, issuing guidance or inspecting.

MLI.short: Law 2013-015 is in force and its authority works; it fined a Bamako clinic and a company in 2025.
MLI.summary:
Law in force. Law no. 2013-015 of 21 May 2013, as amended, is the basis the authority's president cited for its sanctions when opening its session on 3 August 2026. A decree of 14 May 2024 is made under it.

Malabo Convention. The African Union status list of 2 February 2026 records no signature and no ratification of the Malabo Convention by Mali.

Authority appointed. The Autorité de Protection des Données à Caractère Personnel (APDP) held its second ordinary session on 3 August 2026 under president Pr Mamoudou Samassekou with all commissioners present. It opened regional offices at Kayes, Sikasso, Segou and Mopti and a Ségou antenna on 4 December 2025.

Implementing and acting. In 2025 the APDP fined a Bamako clinic 5 million FCFA for obstructing a verification mission and fined Société Aminata Konaté SARL 5 million F CFA for refusing one. Sahel Tribune, summarising the 2025 annual report, reports fines totalling 22 million FCFA.

Not held. Nothing further on the four questions is held.

MOZ.short: No law is in force and no authority is appointed; a draft law is on parliament's October 2026 agenda. No ruling is known.
MOZ.summary:
Law in force. DLA Piper states, in a guide last modified on 17 February 2026, that Mozambique has no specific data protection legislation. The World Bank says the Data Protection Act had not been approved by Cabinet or submitted to Parliament as of October 2025, and on 1 October 2026 the Assembly's Standing Commission placed a draft law on the agenda of the session opening 28 October.

Malabo Convention. The African Union status list of 2 February 2026 records that Mozambique ratified the Malabo Convention on 2 December 2019 and deposited its instrument on 21 January 2020.

Authority appointed. A June 2025 inception report states that Mozambique has no data regulatory authority. A review of the draft law says it designates the existing Regulatory Authority for ICT as the National Authority for the Protection of Personal Data.

Implementing and acting. The World Bank's October 2025 paper says the Data Protection Office is not yet established, which prevents its operationalisation, and that the project envelope for it was cut from US$18m to US$11m.

Not held. A law in force, an appointed authority and any ruling are not held.

MRT.short: A 2017 law is in force and its authority met monthly and took decisions in 2026; no ruling against an organisation is known.
MRT.summary:
Law in force. Law 2017-020 of 22 July 2017 on personal data protection is applied in the authority's deliberation 002/2026 of 24 March 2026. Deliberation 005/2025 of 30 July 2025 is issued under it and requires controllers using foreign cloud services to seek authorisation.

Malabo Convention. The African Union status list of 2 February 2026 records that Mauritania ratified the Malabo Convention on 19 April 2023 and deposited its instrument on 9 May 2023.

Authority appointed. The Autorité de Protection des Données à Caractère Personnel (APD) held its ordinary monthly session on 30 June 2026 under its president, with its members and the Government Commissioner present. Its site lists monthly meetings of 25 March, 29 April and 6 May 2026, and its president was sworn in for a second term on 7 October 2026.

Implementing and acting. On 24 March 2026 the APD gave a favourable opinion, conditional on its remarks, on the joint decision authorising Maaden Mauritanie's Maadeni system. At its 29 April 2026 meeting it approved amendments to its transfer and cloud deliberations, and on 19 November 2025 it examined complaints 004-2025, 006-2025 and 007-2025.

Not held. No ruling of the authority against a named organisation in the last three years is held.

MUS.short: A law is in force and the authority is working; in 2024 it reported rejecting 12 cross-border transfers and closing 39 complaints.
MUS.summary:
Law in force. The Data Protection Office reports on its enforcement in 2024 of the Data Protection Act 2017, citing its sections on complaints, transfers, registration, certification and appeals. Commissioner Madhub describes the 2017 regime as the country's current law, after a first law in 2004 partly implemented in 2009. The office also submitted a draft Data Protection Bill to the ministry to amend the Act for European Commission adequacy.

Malabo Convention. Mauritius ratified the Malabo Convention on 6 March 2018 and deposited its instrument on 14 March 2018, according to the African Union's status list of 2 February 2026.

Authority appointed. Drudeisha Madhub is named as Data Protection Commissioner, and the Data Protection Office has been operational since 16 February 2009. In January 2026 the Office co-led the launch of the National Data Strategy 2025-2029 with the ministry, and a June 2026 set of regulations give it roles in receiving data protection officer notifications within 14 days and certifying officers.

Implementing and acting. For January to December 2024 the Office reports 179 new complaints, 39 closed, 105 personal data breaches notified, 112 cross-border transfers authorised and 12 rejected, and four compliance inspections. It issued guidelines for the insurance sector and 3,076 registration certificates in 2024.

Not held. Nothing further on the four questions.

MWI.short: A law is in force and an authority is working; no ruling against an organisation is known as of 2026.
MWI.summary:
Law in force. The Data Protection Act, 2024 (Act No. 3 of 2024) was assented to on 31 January 2024 and published on 2 February 2024. The Authority's compliance guideline says it applies at once to non-Malawi controllers and to Malawi controllers of significant importance, and that other Malawi controllers and processors must comply from 3 June 2026.

Malabo Convention. The African Union's status list of 2 February 2026 records no signature and no ratification of the Malabo Convention by Malawi.

Authority appointed. The guidelines state that the Malawi Communications Regulatory Authority, MACRA, is the designated Data Protection Authority under the Act. Nyasa Times reports it convened a stakeholder consultation on draft regulations in Lilongwe in July 2026, with Daniel Chiwoni as Head of Data Protection. The World Bank said in November 2025 that MACRA had appointed an acting Data Protection Commissioner.

Implementing and acting. In October 2025 the Authority published guidelines on personal data breach notifications, with a 72-hour notice to the Authority and to data subjects, and a compliance guideline and checklist covering the Act's duties, data subject rights and cross-border transfers. GIZ ran a training-of-trainers programme with the Authority in September 2026.

Not held. No ruling of the authority against a named organisation in the last three years is held.

NAM.short: Namibia has no law in force and no authority appointed, so none has ruled against an organisation; a bill is being finalised in 2026.
NAM.summary:
Law in force. Minister Theofelus said in July 2026 that Namibia is finalising the Data Protection Bill. In January 2026 she said the bill had been through consultation and drafting and was ready for resubmission to the Cabinet Committee on Legislation for onward processing by Parliament. An opposition MP told the Windhoek Observer in August 2026 that Namibia has no data protection statute.

Malabo Convention. Namibia ratified the Malabo Convention on 25 January 2019 and deposited its instrument on 1 February 2019, according to the African Union's status list of 2 February 2026.

Authority appointed. The ministry's revised draft Data Protection Bill of 2022 provides in its long title for establishing a Data Protection Supervisory Authority and its powers, duties and functions. Section 25 of the 2020 draft establishes the Data Protection Supervisory Authority of Namibia, with Part VII running to section 37.

Implementing and acting. Minister Theofelus said on 14 August 2025 that the ministry would table a Data Protection Bill in September 2025. In 2018 the Minister of ICT told Parliament that Namibia had embarked on developing Personal Data Protection and Cyber Security Bills.

Not held. No law in force, no appointed authority and no activity by one are held.

NER.short: A law is in force, but its authority was abolished by decree in 2026; no ruling against an organisation is known.
NER.summary:
Law in force. The president of the High Authority for the Protection of Personal Data, HAPDP, said in an interview published on 28 July 2025 that law no. 2022-59 of 16 December 2022 repealed and replaced the 2017 law as amended in 2019. The authority's consolidated text of April 2026 presents the law as the operative general law, amended by Law 2023-31 of 4 July 2023.

Malabo Convention. Niger ratified the Malabo Convention on 22 February 2022 and deposited its instrument on 16 March 2022, according to the African Union's status list of 2 February 2026.

Authority appointed. Africa Data Protection reports that the government has by decree abolished the HAPDP and split its powers between the Ministry of Justice and the Ministry of the Interior, in a report published on 13 June 2026. In July 2025 the HAPDP president said the authority had ten members and that its president took office on 18 September 2024.

Implementing and acting. The HAPDP president said in July 2025 that the authority processed 139 compliance files since September 2024, covering declarations, video-surveillance declarations, and processing and transfer authorisations, and ran four control missions in 2025 on mobile operators.

Not held. No authority appointed after the decree is held, and none registering organisations, taking breach reports, issuing guidance or inspecting.

NGA.short: A data protection law is in force and the authority is working; it fined Multichoice Nigeria in 2025.
NGA.summary:
Law in force. The Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023 was signed by President Tinubu on 12 June 2023. In July 2026 the Federal High Court treated the Act as operative in a case against the Commission, and a federal circular dated 27 July 2026 directed all federal ministries, departments and agencies to comply with it.

Malabo Convention. Nigeria signed the Malabo Convention on 23 January 2024 and had not ratified it at the African Union's status list of 2 February 2026.

Authority appointed. The Nigeria Data Protection Commission is a full data protection authority under the Act, according to its National Commissioner on 14 September 2026, when its new Abuja headquarters was commissioned. Voice of Nigeria names Vincent Olatunji as National Commissioner and CEO.

Implementing and acting. The Commission fined Multichoice Nigeria N766,242,500 in 2025 for violating the Act. Premium Times reports its Final Order against Meta imposed a $32.8 million fine, later set aside when the Federal High Court adopted a settlement. In August 2026 it opened an investigation into the University of Lagos, Lotus Bank and Hackerbella Ltd.

Not held. Nothing on the four questions is outstanding.

RWA.short: A data protection law has applied since 2023 and an authority registers controllers (2026); a ruling against an organisation is not known.
RWA.summary:
Law in force. Rwanda's Data Protection Act was introduced on 15 October 2021, and its two-year grace period ended on 15 October 2023, marking the transition to enforcement and accountability, according to a legal adviser writing in The New Times.

Malabo Convention. Rwanda ratified the Malabo Convention on 14 November 2019 and deposited its instrument on 21 November 2019, according to the African Union's status list of 2 February 2026.

Authority appointed. The National Cyber Security Authority acts as the supervisory authority for personal data protection and privacy under the Data Protection Act, as Rwanda observed Data Privacy Week in January 2026. In July 2026 CIPESA stated that Rwanda's AI policy positions the Authority to oversee data protection compliance relevant to AI systems.

Implementing and acting. The New Times reported in January 2026 that over the last four years the Authority has registered data controllers and processors with registration certificates, trained over 100 public sector data protection officers, and run sector workshops for pharmacists and local government entities.

Not held. No ruling of the authority against a named organisation in the last three years is held.

SDN.short: Sudan has no data protection law in force in 2026; two authorities set up by decree in 2025 have issued no binding rules.
SDN.summary:
Law in force. On 6 August 2026 the Council of Ministers discussed a draft data and artificial intelligence bill and directed further study before approval by the interim parliament. On 11 August 2026 the Justice Ministry's under-secretary said the ministry is preparing a 2026 Law on Regulating Data and Artificial Intelligence with the digital transformation ministry. The Sudanese Center for Policy Studies says Sudan has no privacy law governing personal data and that a 2018 draft bill was never enacted.

Malabo Convention. Sudan signed the Malabo Convention on 15 March 2023 and had not ratified it at the African Union's status list of 2 February 2026.

Authority appointed. The Sudanese Center for Policy Studies says the Sudanese Data and Artificial Intelligence Authority and the Sudanese Cybersecurity Authority were both established by a November 2025 decree.

Implementing and acting. According to the same Center, citing the AI Regulation Tracker, neither of those two authorities had issued binding rules as of mid-2026.

Not held. Any ruling by an authority against an organisation, and the content of the draft bill.

SEN.short: A 2008 data protection law is in force and the authority is working; it ordered a company to remove a camera in March 2026.
SEN.summary:
Law in force. A reference summary states that Law No. 2008-12 on the protection of personal data was enacted on 25 January 2008 and has been in force since 2014. In April to June 2026 the Commission issued receipts, authorisations and a rejection under that law. An expert told APS in March 2026 that a bill to replace it is reportedly in the circuit.

Malabo Convention. Senegal ratified the Malabo Convention on 3 August 2016 and deposited its instrument on 16 August 2016, according to the African Union's status list of 2 February 2026.

Authority appointed. The Commission de protection des données personnelles (CDP) is an independent administrative authority set up by Law No. 2008-12. It held two plenary sessions in April to June 2026, and its president signed a partnership convention with Benin's authority in April 2026.

Implementing and acting. On 12 March 2026 the CDP, after a complaint, inspected Digicommunication International unannounced and ordered the meeting-room camera uninstalled. For April to June 2026 it reported 195 files handled, 39 authorisations issued and one processing rejected. In 2024 it served a formal notice on SOLID SA, operator of the Kay Voter platform.

Not held. Nothing on the four questions is outstanding.

SLE.short: In 2026 the data protection law is still a draft bill and no authority is appointed; no ruling against an organisation is known.
SLE.summary:
Law in force. Sierra Leone has a Data Protection and Right to Access Information Bill, which the Information Minister said in November 2025 had finished its final national validation, with Cabinet and Parliament still to come. In April 2026 Cabinet approved a National Data Protection Policy and authorised a new Data Protection and Right to Access Information Act.

Malabo Convention. Sierra Leone signed the Malabo Convention on 29 January 2016, and the African Union status list of 2 February 2026 records that it had not ratified it.

Authority appointed. The 2025 Bill would establish for the first time a single independent authority for both data protection and access to information, and that authority is not yet constituted because the Bill is unenacted.

Implementing and acting. Cabinet's April 2026 decision left the Ministry of Information and Civic Education and the Attorney-General's office to finalise the Bill and table it in Parliament.

Not held. Whether any authority is constituted or acting is not held, and neither is any ruling against an organisation.

SOM.short: Somalia's data protection law is in force and an authority is appointed and taking registrations since 2026; no ruling against an organisation is known.
SOM.summary:
Law in force. Somalia's Data Protection Act, Law No. 005 of 2023, was enacted on 23 March 2023 and became effective immediately, according to TechHive Advisory. In June 2026 the Authority's notice required registration under Article 32 of the Act from all entities that collect, store, process or share personal data in Somalia.

Malabo Convention. The African Union status list of 2 February 2026 records no signature and no ratification of the Malabo Convention by Somalia.

Authority appointed. Somalia inaugurated its Data Protection Authority on 24 February 2024. Its own service page of 2 June 2026 lists the registration forms it issues, and its January 2026 Registration Guidelines set fees and a 30-day approval timeline.

Implementing and acting. On 2 June 2026 the Authority began accepting registration applications from controllers and processors and said it will issue certificates only to those meeting the conditions. In February 2024 it published guidelines for implementing the law.

Not held. No ruling of the authority against a named organisation in the last three years is held.

SSD.short: In 2026 South Sudan's data protection law is still a draft bill; no authority is appointed and no ruling against an organisation is known.
SSD.summary:
Law in force. A two-day workshop of over 30 stakeholders, convened by Digital Rights Frontlines with the NCA, reviewed the Data Protection Bill, 2025 in a post dated 5 May 2026. The ICT Minister said in December 2025 the government will introduce its first Data Protection Bill in 2026. The World Bank's 2026 diagnostic states there is no national data protection or privacy law.

Malabo Convention. The African Union status list of 2 February 2026 records no signature and no ratification of the Malabo Convention by South Sudan.

Authority appointed. Digital Rights Frontlines states in February 2026 that the country lacks a fully operational, independent Data Protection Authority. Radio Tamazuj reports the draft bill, once passed, will establish a Data Protection Commission.

Implementing and acting. In October 2025 Paradigm Initiative and Koneta Hub held a two-day Juba convening of lawmakers, civil society and officials to seek parliamentary commitment to table the draft Bill.

Not held. No enacted data protection law, no operating authority and no ruling against an organisation is held.

STP.short: The 2016 data protection law is in force; the authority, appointed, signed a cooperation agreement in 2026; no ruling against an organisation is known.
STP.summary:
Law in force. The IBA chapter of 2024 names the Personal Data Guarantee and Protection Law, Law 03/2016, as the primary instrument, covering processing by controllers headquartered or established in the country. Lei n.º 03/2016 was published in the Diário da República of 10 May 2016.

Malabo Convention. The African Union status list of 2 February 2026 records that São Tomé and Príncipe ratified or acceded on 25 September 2023 and deposited its instrument on 15 February 2024.

Authority appointed. The Agência Nacional de Protecção de Dados Pessoais has a president, José Manuel Costa Alegre. In April 2026 he met the National Assembly president to plan oversight of personal data in the electoral roll, and on 1 June 2026 the agency signed a cooperation memorandum with Macau.

Implementing and acting. The IBA chapter describes the fines and criminal sanctions the law provides and says the agency imposes fines and ancillary measures. In January 2025 its president described working with Facebook on fake profiles.

Not held. No source dated in the last three years shows the authority registering organisations, taking breach reports, issuing guidance or inspecting. No ruling against an organisation is held.

SWZ.short: A data protection law is in force and the authority is working; it has ruled against named organisations, most recently in 2025.
SWZ.summary:
Law in force. The Data Protection Act, 2022 was gazetted on 4 March 2022. The Ministry of ICT referred to its implementation and enforcement as current in August 2026, and enforcement notices under section 41 of the Act run to March 2025.

Malabo Convention. The African Union's status list of 2 February 2026 records no signature and no ratification of the Malabo Convention by Eswatini. In July 2026 the Minister of ICT presented to a Senators' workshop on the importance of ratifying it.

Authority appointed. The notice of 2024 states the Act designates the Eswatini Communications Commission as the Eswatini Data Protection Authority. The Ministry of ICT vests oversight of compliance in it, and it has powers to investigate breaches, resolve complaints and impose sanctions. In September 2026 it was led by an acting chief executive.

Implementing and acting. The Authority issued enforcement notices under section 41 in June 2024 to MTN Eswatini and Liberty Life Swaziland Limited and in March 2025 to the Royal Science Technology Park. Registration of controllers and processors became mandatory on 1 March 2024. In June 2026 it opened a formal investigation into the Ministry of Home Affairs.

Not held. Nothing further is held on the four questions.

SYC.short: A data protection law is in force and the authority is working, handling 14 cases in 2025; no ruling against an organisation is known.
SYC.summary:
Law in force. The Data Protection Act, 2023 was assented to on 19 December 2023 and bears the operative date 22 December 2023. The Commission's page states the Act came into effect, and Appleby reports an 18-month transition for controllers and processors from that date.

Malabo Convention. The African Union's status list of 2 February 2026 records no signature and no ratification of the Malabo Convention by Seychelles.

Authority appointed. The Information Commission is named in section 5 as the competent authority, with powers to investigate, audit, issue enforcement notices and impose administrative fines up to SCR200,000. In 2025 it had a Chief Information Commissioner, two Information Commissioners and a CEO in post, and it took on the mandate at the end of December 2023.

Implementing and acting. The Commission handled 14 cases under the Act in 2025: 6 on data transfers, 5 breaches, 2 refused deletion requests and 1 consultation. In 2024 it received four data protection cases, mostly from the non-banking financial sector. In 2026 it marked Data Protection Day with guidance to organisations and the public.

Not held. No ruling of the authority against a named organisation in the last three years is held.

TCD.short: A digital law covering data protection was still being finalised in March 2026; no authority or ruling is known.
TCD.summary:
Law in force. A digital law covering data protection is still being finalised. Minister Boukar Michel announced on 9 December 2025 that authorities are finalizing a digital law incorporating international standards on cybersecurity, data protection and internet governance. Ecofin reports the Digital Code has been under development since December 2025 and incorporates international standards on cybersecurity and data protection.

Malabo Convention. The African Union's status list of 2 February 2026 records that Chad signed the Malabo Convention on 14 June 2015 and had not ratified it.

Authority appointed. Ecofin reports that Chad's Digital Code, under development since December 2025, incorporates international standards on cybersecurity and data protection.

Implementing and acting. The Minister's announcement of 9 December 2025 concerned a digital law still being finalised, with data protection among the standards it incorporates. Ecofin's report of 16 March 2026 still describes the Code as under development.

Not held. The evidence does not show a data protection law in force, an authority appointed or any ruling.

TGO.short: A data protection law is in force and the authority is working in 2026; no ruling against an organisation is known.
TGO.summary:
Law in force. Loi n° 2019-014 of 29 October 2019 on personal data protection was adopted by the National Assembly and promulgated. In September 2026 the IPDCP briefed ministry cabinet directors and secretaries-general on their obligations as data controllers under it, and in June 2026 it said 35 data protection correspondents had been designated under the law.

Malabo Convention. The African Union's status list of 2 February 2026 records that Togo ratified or acceded to the Malabo Convention on 30 September 2021 and deposited its instrument on 19 October 2021.

Authority appointed. The IPDCP became operational in 2024 and, per its head, holds powers of control, injunction and sanction. It officially launched its activities in Lomé on 28 March 2025, and in 2026 it ran the June correspondent training and signed a cooperation agreement with Mali's APDP on 23 September.

Implementing and acting. The IPDCP ran a three-day training for 35 data protection correspondents from 22 to 24 June 2026 and opened its first evaluation and certification session for correspondents in Atakpamé on 30 September 2026, with 32 professionals. On 15 September 2026 it convened a compliance meeting for public administrations. It launched a public-awareness campaign in March 2025.

Not held. No ruling of the authority against a named organisation in the last three years is held.

TUN.short: A 2004 law is in force; an authority appointed in 2021 is reported at a standstill in 2026, with no ruling against an organisation known.
TUN.summary:
Law in force. Organic law no. 2004-63 of 27 July 2004 sets the general processing, consent and rights regime, and a Forum Chawki Gaddes statement of 3 October 2026 cites it as the law guaranteeing personal data protection. A replacement bill, no. 095/2025, was deposited before the Assembly on 14 July 2025. It would repeal the 2004 law six months after publication.

Malabo Convention. The African Union status list of 2 February 2026 records that Tunisia signed on 23 April 2019 and had not ratified.

Authority appointed. Government decree no. 2021-230 of 16 April 2021 appointed twelve named members to the national personal data protection authority for three years. Decree no. 2020-312 of 15 May 2020 puts the citizen-ID register under its control.

Implementing and acting. The Forum Chawki Gaddes says in a statement of 3 October 2026 that the activities of the authority, INPDP, are at a standstill and calls for its reactivation.

Not held. No source dated in the last three years shows the authority registering organisations, taking breach reports, issuing guidance or inspecting. No ruling against an organisation is held.

TZA.short: A data protection law has been in force since 2023, the Commission is working, and it ruled against a company in 2025.
TZA.summary:
Law in force. The Personal Data Protection Act, Chapter 44, commenced on 1 May 2023 and applies to Mainland Tanzania and, for union matters, Zanzibar. The Citizen reported on 28 August 2026 that the Commission will inspect compliance with the Act from 31 August 2026.

Malabo Convention. The African Union status list of 2 February 2026 records no signature and no ratification of the Malabo Convention by Tanzania.

Authority appointed. Section 6 of the Act establishes the Personal Data Protection Commission as a body corporate. Director General Dr Emmanuel Mkilia announced on-site inspections in Dodoma on 28 August 2026. The Commission ran the eighth phase of its DPO training in Morogoro on 7-8 October 2026.

Implementing and acting. PDPC figures cited in October 2026 show 15,146 institutions registered and 445 complaints received by August 2026. A ruling reported in August 2025 awarded TZS 20,000,000 against Mi Casa Company Limited and ordered deletion of personal data. FB Attorneys reports a ruling of 19 August 2025 with TZS 20 million damages, a TZS 5 million fine and deletion of a newborn's photos within 14 days.

Not held. No sanction is named in the 2026 registration and inspection reports.

UGA.short: A data protection law is in force, the Personal Data Protection Office is working, and it ruled against Google in 2025.
UGA.summary:
Law in force. The Data Protection and Privacy Act, Cap 97, was applied by the Personal Data Protection Office in its decision of 18 July 2025 as law in operation, including its reach over foreign entities handling Ugandans' personal data. The PDPO director says the Act requires registration of data collectors and processors and makes failure to register a criminal offence.

Malabo Convention. The African Union status list of 2 February 2026 records no signature and no ratification of the Malabo Convention by Uganda. Police forensic-services director Andrew Mubiru said on 12 August 2026 that Uganda has not ratified it and needs to domesticate it.

Authority appointed. The Personal Data Protection Office is headed by director Baker Birikujja, who addressed an ISACA Kampala breakfast on 18 August 2026. It briefed government IT officers on data protection on 13 August 2026.

Implementing and acting. The PDPO's decision of 20 February 2026 partly upheld a complaint against WhatsApp LLC and Meta Platforms and issued corrective orders; on 17 July 2026 it confirmed WhatsApp had implemented them. On 18 July 2025 it found Google in breach and ordered it to register within 30 days.

Not held. The director names no case taken to court.

ZAF.short: A data protection law has been in force since 2021; the Information Regulator is working and issued an enforcement notice to a college in 2026.
ZAF.summary:
Law in force. ITWeb reports that the Protection of Personal Information Act came into force on 1 July 2021 after a year-long grace period, with fines up to R10 million and up to 10 years' imprisonment.

Malabo Convention. The African Union status list of 2 February 2026 records South Africa as having signed on 16 February 2023, with no ratification or accession date.

Authority appointed. The Information Regulator was established on 1 December 2016 and its chairperson Pansy Tlakula spoke for it in September 2026. Parliament's Justice Committee published candidate names for vacant positions on 11 September 2026. National Treasury appropriated R135.7m for 2025/26 to the Regulator.

Implementing and acting. The Regulator received over 8,000 security-compromise reports to date, 1,220 of them since April 2026. It issued the South African Bureau of Standards an enforcement notice in August 2026 giving it 90 days to revise policies and implement security measures. Its first fine, R5 million, was imposed on the Department of Justice and Constitutional Development in July 2023.

Not held. The Regulator's work with the justice department to amend POPIA for artificial intelligence has no bill or draft described.

ZMB.short: A data protection law is in force and an authority is appointed and working; no ruling against an organisation is known in 2026.
ZMB.summary:
Law in force. The Data Protection Act No. 3 of 2021 is the law a World Bank tender notice of 10 August 2026 treats as being implemented. A July 2026 report describes it as part of the operating legal framework beside the Cyber Security Act and Cyber Crimes Act.

Malabo Convention. The African Union's status list of 2 February 2026 records Zambia as having ratified the Malabo Convention on 15 December 2020 and deposited its instrument on 24 March 2021.

Authority appointed. The first Data Protection Commissioner was appointed in June 2023. In September 2025 the Commissioner and a Deputy Commissioner took part in a review of a draft health data statutory instrument.

Implementing and acting. The Commissioner's office opened online registration for controllers and processors, with a 30 April 2025 deadline. UNDP lists training staff in over 145 offices across 10 provinces on the Act as a requirement of the digital ID rollout.

Not held. No ruling of the authority against a named organisation in the last three years is held.

ZWE.short: A data protection law is in force and an authority is appointed and working; no ruling against an organisation is known in 2026.
ZWE.summary:
Law in force. The Cyber and Data Protection Act [Chapter 12:07] is applied through SI 155 of 2024, which took effect in September 2024 and made a Data Controller Licence mandatory. Business Times states the Act provides criminal sanctions for accountable officers.

Malabo Convention. The African Union's status list of 2 February 2026 records no signature and no ratification of the Malabo Convention by Zimbabwe.

Authority appointed. POTRAZ states it is the designated Data Protection Authority under section 5 of the Act and is acting as such. Section 6(2) says it is not subject to the direction or control of any person in exercising its functions.

Implementing and acting. POTRAZ handed over the first Data Controller Licences to 570 companies in June 2025. In December 2025 it reported 831 organisations recognised as compliant. Its Regulatory Notice 2 of 2026 announces mandatory compliance inspections from 1 September 2026.

Not held. No ruling of the authority against a named organisation in the last three years is held.

AGO.short: Angola's 2011 law requires notice or the regulator's authorisation to send data abroad; a firm was fined in 2026; guidance is not known.
AGO.summary:
Rule in force. Angola's Law 22/11 on personal data protection came into force on publication, 17 June 2011. Articles 33 and 34 make sending personal data abroad to a country with adequate protection subject to notification to the data protection agency (APD), and to a country without it subject to APD authorisation on stated grounds such as the data subject's written consent. Hunton reported in 2011 that the APD must approve transfers to countries without adequate protection. The APD's fee regulation, Presidential Decree 60/21 of 10 March 2021, lists an act of authorisation for international data transfer at Kz 350,450.

Means of complying published and rule applied. The APD fined Crescer Tech US$505,000 in 2026 for failing to notify it and obtain authorisation for the international transfer of personal data to a cloud located abroad. Valor Económico reported on 26 June 2026 a fine of about USD 505,000 (c. 549 million kwanzas) on the company for no notification or prior authorisation and an unauthorised international transfer to foreign cloud servers.

Not held. No published list of approved countries, model contract terms, application form or guidance on transfers is held. The dates of the deliberations behind the fines are not given.

BDI.short: Nothing held names a rule on sending personal data abroad or says there is none, so no stage is set.
BDI.summary: Not held. Nothing held names a rule on sending personal data abroad, or says there is none.

BEN.short: Nothing held names a rule on sending personal data abroad or says there is none, so no stage is set.
BEN.summary: Not held. Nothing held names a rule on sending personal data abroad, or says there is none.

BFA.short: Nothing held names a rule on sending personal data abroad or says there is none, so no stage is set.
BFA.summary: Not held. Nothing held names a rule on sending personal data abroad, or says there is none.

BWA.short: Botswana's Data Protection Act, in force since January 2025, allows data abroad only to approved countries; how it has been applied is not known.
BWA.summary:
Rule in force. The Data Protection Act has been in effect since January 2025. Mmegi reported on 25 November 2025 that it allows data transfers abroad only to approved countries. The Act was published in the Extraordinary Gazette of 29 October 2024 as the Data Protection Act, 2024.

Means of complying published and rule applied. Botswana keeps a list of countries that data may go to. A DIAL expert comment published on 15 June 2026 says the list held only two African countries. Under the rule Mmegi reported in November 2025, data may go to the countries on that list and to no others. A country that is not on the list cannot receive data sent from Botswana under the Act.

Not held. No source from the last three years names a country approved to receive data. None names an organisation given or refused permission, ordered to comply or penalised for sending data abroad.

CAF.short: Nothing held names a rule on sending personal data abroad or says there is none, so no stage is set.
CAF.summary: Not held. Nothing held names a rule on sending personal data abroad, or says there is none.

CIV.short: Decree 2015-79 of 2015 requires the telecoms regulator's prior authorisation to send personal data abroad; whether any transfer has been authorised is not known.
CIV.summary:
Rule in force. Côte d'Ivoire has a rule in force on sending personal data abroad. Decree 2015-79 of 4 February 2015, issued under law 2013-450, requires prior authorisation from the telecoms regulator ARTCI before personal data is transferred to a third country. The receiving country must give protection equal to or higher than that of Côte d'Ivoire, and the requirement is set out in article 6 of the decree. The regulator publishes the decree on its own website, and the decree is the only instrument held on this point.

Means of complying published and rule applied. The nearest held fact is the same decree, which sets sanctions for non-compliance with the transfer rule in article 8. Its title states that it fixes how declarations are filed, how requests are presented, and how authorisations are granted and withdrawn for the processing of personal data, so the decree itself is the one published procedure held. Nothing held shows the rule being applied to a particular transfer.

Not held. No source held says the authority has published a list of countries, model contract terms, a permission procedure or guidance on sending data abroad.

CMR.short: Nothing held names a rule on sending personal data abroad or says there is none, so no stage is set.
CMR.summary: Not held. Nothing held names a rule on sending personal data abroad, or says there is none.

COD.short: Transfers abroad need the data protection authority's approval under the digital code, exercised by ARPTIC since 2024; any published procedure is not known.
COD.summary:
Rule in force. The Code du numérique, in articles 262 to 270, creates a data protection authority whose duties include authorising or refusing cross-border transfers of personal data to third states. The authority itself is not yet set up, so since 17 August 2024 a ministerial order has given those duties to ARPTIC, the regulator for posts and telecommunications. The source is dated to 2025.

Means of complying published and rule applied. The nearest fact held is that the decision on any transfer of personal data to a third state sits, for now, with ARPTIC rather than with a separate data protection authority. That is the whole of what is held on how an exporter would comply, and on how the rule is applied in practice.

Not held. No source held says the authority has published a list of countries, model contract terms, a permission procedure or guidance on sending data abroad.

COG.short: Nothing held names a rule on sending personal data abroad or says there is none, so no stage is set.
COG.summary: Not held. Nothing held names a rule on sending personal data abroad, or says there is none.

COM.short: The 2021 data protection law governs sending personal data abroad on a risk-based model, and it is not known whether the rule has been applied.
COM.summary:
Rule in force. The Protection of Personal Data Law, enacted on 29 June 2021, governs international transfers of personal data, according to TechHive Advisory's review of the Comoros data protection law, published on 23 July 2025. The review describes a risk-based model for sending data abroad. Under it, a transfer can rest on an adequacy finding about the receiving country, on appropriate safeguards, or on one of the derogations the law provides.

Means of complying published and rule applied. The nearest fact held is the model itself: the 2021 law sets three routes for an international transfer, which are adequacy of the receiving country, appropriate safeguards and derogations. The 2025 review sets out these three routes as the law's way of governing transfers, and it dates the law to 29 June 2021, the day of its enactment. That date is the latest one held for the rule on sending data abroad.

Not held. Nothing held says the authority has published a list of countries, model contract terms, a permission procedure or guidance on sending data abroad, or has applied the rule to a transfer.

CPV.short: Cape Verde law since 2013 lets personal data go abroad only to countries judged adequate or on listed grounds; its application is not known.
CPV.summary:
Rule in force. Cape Verde's Data Protection Law (Law 133/V/2001, amended by Law 41/VIII/2013 and Law 121/IX/2021) permits international transfer of personal data, as published in January 2025, only to a country with an adequate level of protection, or otherwise with the data subject's consent or in listed situations such as contract necessity or vital interests. Law 41/VIII/2013, published on 17 September 2013, made article 19 allow transfer abroad only to a country assuring an adequate level of protection, with the national data protection commission (CNPD) deciding which foreign states do.

Means of complying published and rule applied. The same 2013 amendment lets the CNPD permit a transfer to any other country on consent, contract necessity, public interest, vital interests or a public register. Article 20 also lets the CNPD authorise a transfer where the controller gives sufficient guarantees, such as adequate contractual clauses.

Not held. No source held says the authority has published a list of countries, model contract terms, a permission procedure or guidance on sending data abroad.

DJI.short: Djibouti's digital code, published in September 2025, bars sending personal data abroad without equivalent protection; whether the authority has published means of complying is unknown.
DJI.summary:
Rule in force. Djibouti's Code Numérique, Loi n° 019/AN/23/9ème L, was published in the Journal Officiel on 18 September 2025. Under article 99, a controller or processor may not transfer personal data to a third country or an international organisation unless it ensures an equivalent and sufficient level of protection. Article 102 sets exceptions: the person's consent, a contract, public interest, legal claims or vital interests, or authorisation by the Commission nationale de protection des données.

Means of complying published and rule applied. The nearest held fact is the same law: the Code Numérique of 18 September 2025 sets the conditions in articles 99 to 103 and gives the Commission nationale de protection des données the power to authorise a transfer.

Not held. No source held says the authority has published a list of countries, model contract terms, a permission procedure or guidance on sending data abroad.

DZA.short: Algeria's 2025 amendment requires an adequacy assessment before data go abroad for criminal-justice purposes; whether any list, contract terms or procedure exists is not known.
DZA.summary:
Rule in force. Law 25-11 of 24 July 2025, published in the Journal Officiel that day, amends Law 18-07 with a new article 45 bis 13. Before data are transferred to a foreign State or international organisation, the competent authority assesses whether it gives an adequate level of protection. This applies to transfers for criminal-justice purposes. Transfer on insufficient safeguards is allowed only in listed cases: vital interests, a threat to public security, and individual criminal cases. The Authority's Délibération n° 04 of 15 July 2026 extends the law's rules to images published on social platforms and treats publication on foreign-run platforms as a transfer abroad.

Means of complying published and rule applied. The nearest fact held is the Authority's Délibération n° 04 of 15 July 2026, which applies the transfer rule to images published on foreign-run platforms. It is a ruling on one kind of transfer, and the law's article 45 bis 13 is the assessment it rests on.

Not held. No source held says the authority has published a list of countries, model contract terms, a permission procedure or guidance on sending data abroad.

EGY.short: Nothing held names a rule on sending personal data abroad or says there is none, so no stage is set.
EGY.summary: Not held. Nothing held names a rule on sending personal data abroad, or says there is none.

ERI.short: Eritrea had no rule on sending data abroad as of 2026, and whether any draft or sector rule exists is not known.
ERI.summary:
Rule in force. The UNECA digital trade profile, published on 1 January 2022, states that no legal regime in Eritrea deals with the general flow of data and that no conditions are made for the flow of data. Levellers, in a legal-status page last reviewed on 8 June 2026, states that Eritrea has no data protection legislation and no restriction on cross-border transfer of data in its law.

Means of complying published and rule applied. Eritrea's law places no restriction on cross-border transfer of data, according to Levellers on 8 June 2026, and the UNECA profile of 2022 records no conditions on the flow of data. Those are the nearest held facts to a means of complying or a rule applied: in neither source is a sender asked to meet any condition before sending data abroad.

Not held. Whether any draft rule on sending data abroad exists, and whether any sector rule applies, is not known. No published means of complying and no case of a rule applied is held.

ETH.short: Ethiopia's 2024 data protection law conditions sending data abroad, and about 10 requests were approved in 2025; published means of complying are not known.
ETH.summary:
Rule in force. Techhive Advisory reports that Ethiopia's Personal Data Protection Proclamation was published in the Federal Negarit Gazette on 24 July 2024, bringing it into effect. Articles 18-21 make international transfers depend on an adequacy decision by the Authority, the data subject's explicit consent, necessity, or public registry purposes, and transfers of sensitive data need the Authority's prior authorisation.

Means of complying published and rule applied. In November 2025 the Ethiopian Communications Authority's Director General told Shega the Authority had received about 10 requests to transfer data abroad and had approved them as a temporary measure; the article records no sanction and no published count of decisions. Officials previewed a forthcoming registration portal for data controllers and processors at a workshop co-hosted with Huawei.

Not held. The evidence does not show a published list of countries data may go to, model contract terms or guidance on transfers. It gives no count of decisions and no refusal or penalty tied to sending data abroad.

GAB.short: Nothing held names a rule on sending personal data abroad or says there is none, so no stage is set.
GAB.summary: Not held. Nothing held names a rule on sending personal data abroad, or says there is none.

GHA.short: Ghana's 2012 law was being amended in 2025 to add transfer rules; whether any rule on sending data abroad is in force is not known.
GHA.summary:
Rule in force. A roundup of data protection in Africa, published in January 2026, says amendments to the Data Protection Act 2012 are in process. It says they would add rules on international transfers, alongside rules on children's and sensitive data, retention limits, impact assessments and privacy by design. The same roundup says a draft Data Protection Act, 2025 was published, with no month given for the draft.

Means of complying published and rule applied. The nearest held fact is the same roundup's account, dated 2025, of the draft Data Protection Act, 2025 and of the amendments to the 2012 Act that would add rules on international transfers. Both are described as a draft and as amendments in process, and the roundup is the only source held that speaks to Ghana's rule on sending data abroad.

Not held. No source says a rule on sending personal data abroad is in force. Nothing says what the authority has published to help organisations comply, or that the rule has been applied.

GIN.short: A 2016 law gives the data protection authority a transfer approval function; whether any procedure or guidance on sending data abroad exists is not known.
GIN.summary:
Rule in force. Guinea's law on cybersecurity and the protection of personal data, published in July 2016, defines a data protection authority, the Autorité de Protection. It gives that authority functions covering declarations and authorisations, transfer approval, investigation and guidelines. Article 5 sends processing declarations to the competent authority "designated by regulation". The law lists transfer approval as one of the authority's own functions, alongside investigation and guidelines.

Means of complying published and rule applied. The nearest held fact is the same 2016 law, which lists authorisations, transfer approval and guidelines among the authority's functions. The law names no constituted body or appointed members, and it leaves the designation of the competent authority to regulation, so the body that would approve transfers is not identified in the law itself.

Not held. No source held says the authority has published a list of countries, model contract terms, a permission procedure or guidance on sending data abroad.

GMB.short: The Gambia's 2025 data protection Act lets its Commission set conditions on sending data abroad; whether guidance or permissions exist is not known.
GMB.summary:
Rule in force. The Gambia has the Personal Data Protection and Privacy Act, 2025 (Act No. 11 of 2025), and a February 2026 legal commentary on its key features describes the Act as setting up a data protection authority, called the Commission. The commentary says the Commission assesses cross-border transfers of personal data and may impose conditions on them. The full text of the Act is published as Act No. 11 of 2025.

Means of complying published and rule applied. The nearest held fact is the Commission's role in transfers. As described in the February 2026 commentary, the Commission is the body that assesses transfers of personal data out of the country and decides whether to attach conditions. That is a power the Act gives it, and it is the closest the held material comes to the way the rule is carried out in practice.

Not held. No source held says the Commission has published a list of countries, model contract terms, a permission procedure or guidance on sending data abroad. No source held names an approval, refusal or penalty under the rule.

GNB.short: Nothing held names a rule on sending personal data abroad or says there is none, so no stage is set.
GNB.summary: Not held. Nothing held names a rule on sending personal data abroad, or says there is none.

GNQ.short: Nothing held names a rule on sending personal data abroad or says there is none, so no stage is set.
GNQ.summary: Not held. Nothing held names a rule on sending personal data abroad, or says there is none.

KEN.short: Kenya's 2019 Data Protection Act governs sending personal data abroad, with authority guidance published in 2026; whether it has been applied is not known.
KEN.summary:
Rule in force. ITWeb Africa reported on 9 September 2026 that the Data Protection Act (2019), the Constitution and the Kenya Cloud Policy (2025) govern the cross-border transfer of personal data in Kenya. The same report says the guidance of the Office of the Data Protection Commissioner (ODPC) sets out the legal obligations and conditions for lawful transfer abroad. The conditions therefore rest on a statute, the Constitution and a cloud policy, with the ODPC guidance stating the conditions for sending personal data out of the country, as reported in September 2026.

Means of complying published and rule applied. The same ITWeb Africa report of 9 September 2026 says the ODPC, through Data Commissioner Immaculate Kassait, has issued guidance on cross-border data transfers. That guidance covers the conditions for lawful transfer, the safeguards required and the mechanisms for adequate protection. A controller or processor in Kenya therefore has published guidance from the data protection authority on how to meet the rule before sending personal data abroad, and the report presents it as the authority's own statement of the safeguards expected.

Not held. No source from the last three years names a country approved to receive data, or an organisation given or refused permission, ordered to comply or penalised for sending data abroad.

LBR.short: Nothing held names a rule on sending personal data abroad or says there is none, so no stage is set.
LBR.summary: Not held. Nothing held names a rule on sending personal data abroad, or says there is none.

LBY.short: Nothing held names a rule on sending personal data abroad or says there is none, so no stage is set.
LBY.summary: Not held. Nothing held names a rule on sending personal data abroad, or says there is none.

LSO.short: Lesotho's 2012 Data Protection Act sets rules on sending data abroad, in force as of 2025; whether any authority applies them is not known.
LSO.summary:
Rule in force. Z. Mayet and Associates says that Lesotho's Data Protection Act (Act No. 5 of 2012) is the law in force, in a piece published on 31 October 2025. It says the Act carries rules on cross-border data transfers inspired by the SADC model, and that those rules need modern adequacy tools. The piece is the firm's own commentary on what should change next in the Act.

Means of complying published and rule applied. As at 31 October 2025, the same firm says the Data Protection Commission and Commissioner have not been appointed, so no authority exists to approve cross-border mechanisms or issue guidance. It adds that standard contractual clauses and binding corporate rules are not yet in place.

Not held. No source held says the authority has published a list of countries, model contract terms, a permission procedure or guidance on sending data abroad.

MAR.short: Morocco's law sets a condition on sending personal data abroad, as stated in 2012, with a 2015 country list; recent application is not known.
MAR.summary:
Rule in force. Morocco's Act 09-08, named in Morocco as Loi n° 09-08 and overseen by the supervisory authority CNPD, lays down protection of transfers of personal data to foreign countries, according to the Council of Europe Consultative Committee in a document of 18 October 2012. Its articles 43 and 44 apply that protection in particular where the receiving country does not provide an adequate level of protection, the same document states.

Means of complying published and rule applied. A DIAL expert comment states that Morocco's 2015 adequacy list, a list of countries personal data may be sent to, did not recognise a single African country. The year is the only date the comment gives for the list, so a published list of receiving countries is the means of complying that the evidence dates.

Not held. No source from the last three years names a country approved to receive data, or an organisation given or refused permission, ordered to comply or penalised for sending data abroad.

MDG.short: Nothing held names a rule on sending personal data abroad or says there is none, so no stage is set.
MDG.summary: Not held. Nothing held names a rule on sending personal data abroad, or says there is none.

MLI.short: Mali's 2013 data protection law sets the rule on sending data abroad; whether the authority has published lists, model terms or guidance is not known.
MLI.summary:
Rule in force. Law no. 2013-015 of 21 May 2013 on the protection of personal data was adopted by the National Assembly on 9 May 2013 and promulgated. Article 11 lets a data controller transfer personal data to a foreign state when the data protection authority finds the receiving state's protection sufficient. The law as held gives no repeal, so it is the rule on sending data abroad that the 2013 law sets today.

Means of complying published and rule applied. The nearest held fact is in the same law. Article 11 also covers a transfer made under contract clauses or internal rules, and for that case the authority's decision is what allows the transfer. The law names these two routes, a finding of sufficient protection and a decision on clauses or rules, and places both with the data protection authority.

Not held. No source held says the authority has published a list of countries, model contract terms, a permission procedure or guidance on sending data abroad.

MOZ.short: A bill approved in March 2026 would let personal data leave only where protection is equivalent; whether any rule is in force is not known.
MOZ.summary:
Rule in force. On 3 March 2026 the Council of Ministers approved the Personal Data Protection Bill, the Proposta de Lei que estabelece o Regime Jurídico de Protecção de Dados Pessoais, for submission to the Assembly of the Republic, according to INTIC. INTIC published its report on 5 March 2026 under the headline that the bill goes to the Assembly for debate. The bill sets strict rules for international transfers of personal data, allowed only where equivalent protection is assured.

Means of complying published and rule applied. The nearest held fact is the same bill. As INTIC reported on 5 March 2026, once before the Assembly it would allow transfers of personal data abroad only where equivalent protection is assured, and the rule is the bill's, dated 3 March 2026.

Not held. No source held says a rule on sending personal data abroad is in force, or that the authority has published the means of complying with one or applied one.

MRT.short: Mauritania has barred sending personal data abroad without adequate protection since 2017 and published a country list in 2025; no case applied is known.
MRT.summary:
Rule in force. Articles 20 to 25 of Law 2017-020, of 22 July 2017, bar a controller from sending personal data to a third country unless it ensures a sufficient level of protection, with authorisation by the data protection authority (APD) on guarantees such as contract clauses. Deliberation 004/2025, adopted by the APD on 14 July 2025, sets the conditions, rules and procedures for sending personal data abroad. Deliberation 005/2025, adopted on 30 July 2025, requires controllers using cloud services abroad to obtain prior APD authorisation.

Means of complying published and rule applied. Deliberation 005/2025 refers to a list of countries, published in deliberation 004/2025, that determines which host countries offer adequate protection. Where the host country is not on that list, a separate foreign-transfer authorisation request is required, in the text amended and published on 30 April 2026. The APD's monthly meeting of 29 April 2026 listed amending both deliberations on its agenda.

Not held. No source from the last three years names a country approved to receive data, or an organisation given or refused permission, ordered to comply or penalised for sending data abroad.

MUS.short: Mauritius's Data Protection Act 2017 governs sending data abroad, and in 2024 the regulator authorised 112 transfers and rejected 12; wider framework not known.
MUS.summary:
Rule in force. Mauritius enforces the Data Protection Act 2017. The Data Protection Office's annual report for 2024 sets out that enforcement for the year, and cites the Act's sections on complaints, transfers, registration, certification and appeals. Transfers abroad are therefore one of the duties the Office reports on within the Act, alongside its other functions such as registration and certification.

Means of complying published and rule applied. For January to December 2024 the Data Protection Office reports 112 cross-border transfers authorised and 12 rejected under section 36 of the Act. In the same year it reports 179 new complaints, 158 of them on CCTV, and 39 complaints closed. It also reports 105 personal data breaches notified, 10 impact assessments received and four compliance inspections during 2024.

Not held. Nothing further is held on the rule beyond the Office's 2024 report, so the wider framework for sending data abroad is not described here.

MWI.short: Malawi's Data Protection Act, in force since 2024, restricts sending personal data abroad; any approved country list or permission procedure is not known.
MWI.summary:
Rule in force. The Data Protection Act came into force on 3 June 2024, and sections 38 to 40 restrict transfers of personal data outside Malawi unless the receiving country has adequate data protection laws or a mechanism such as binding corporate rules is in place. The Act, No. 3 of 2024, assented on 31 January 2024, bars a controller or processor from transferring personal data unless the recipient is under a law, binding corporate rule, contractual clause, code of conduct or certification affording adequate protection, or consent or a contract condition applies.

Means of complying published and rule applied. On 17 October 2025 the Authority published a compliance guideline and checklist covering the Act's duties, data subject rights, breach notice and cross-border transfers, and a registration requirement for controllers of significant importance. No decision or sanction is reported.

Not held. No source held says the authority has published a list of countries, model contract terms, a permission procedure or guidance on sending data abroad.

NAM.short: Namibia had no rule on sending data abroad in August 2026, according to an opposition MP; whether a draft would set one is not known.
NAM.summary:
Rule in force. In an article published on 4 August 2026, Rodney Cloete, the opposition IPC's shadow minister of international relations and trade, told the Windhoek Observer that Namibia has no data protection statute, and so no rules govern cross-border transfers of data. This is the stated position of a named opposition member of parliament, not a statement from the government. He made it while raising concerns about data control of a smart-city grant from China.

Means of complying published and rule applied. The nearest fact held is the same one: the August 2026 statement by the opposition shadow minister that no rules govern cross-border transfers of data. With no rule stated to be in force, there is no published means of complying and no application of a rule to describe.

Not held. Whether any law or draft sets a rule on sending data abroad is not shown by what is held. Nor is how any such rule would be applied.

NER.short: Nothing held names a rule on sending personal data abroad or says there is none, so no stage is set.
NER.summary: Not held. Nothing held names a rule on sending personal data abroad, or says there is none.

NGA.short: Nigeria's 2023 data protection law sets rules on sending personal data abroad; whether the authority has published lists, contract terms or guidance is not known.
NGA.summary:
Rule in force. The Nigeria Data Protection Act, 2023, signed on 12 June 2023, has a Part VIII on cross-border transfers of personal data, in sections 41 to 43: the basis for transfer, the adequacy of protection, and other bases for transfer outside Nigeria. Vanguard reports the National Commissioner of the Nigeria Data Protection Commission saying that the Act, enacted in June 2023, mandates the Commission to decide the adequacy of other countries' data protection as a basis for cross-border transfer of personal data.

Means of complying published and rule applied. According to the National Commissioner, in Vanguard's report of 30 April 2025, the Commission approves binding corporate rules, codes and certification mechanisms as means of transferring personal data across borders under the Act. The Act's Part VIII on cross-border transfers is listed in the Official Gazette text as covering other bases for transfer outside Nigeria.

Not held. Whether the Commission has published a list of countries, model contract terms, a permission procedure or guidance on sending data abroad is not known, and nothing held shows how the rule has been applied.

RWA.short: Nothing held names a rule on sending personal data abroad or says there is none, so no stage is set.
RWA.summary: Not held. Nothing held names a rule on sending personal data abroad, or says there is none.

SDN.short: A July 2026 source says Sudan has no statutory rule on sending data abroad; whether any draft law or guidance exists is not known.
SDN.summary:
Rule in force. The Sudanese Center for Policy Studies, in July 2026, says mobile banking data in Sudan transits infrastructure the country neither owns nor regulates. It says no statutory requirement governs data localization or cross-border transfer, and it proposes localisation only as a first legislative tranche. The piece introduces a series on Sudan's privacy gap and the balance between digital transformation and data laws.

Means of complying published and rule applied. The nearest held fact is the same July 2026 statement that no statutory requirement governs cross-border transfer of data in Sudan. With no rule stated, nothing is held on published means of complying or on a rule being applied, and that statement is the only source held that speaks to the country's rule on sending data abroad.

Not held. No source states a rule on sending personal data out of Sudan, or a data protection law that covers it. Nothing says what guidance exists on complying or that any rule has been applied.

SEN.short: Senegal's 2008 data protection law bars sending data abroad unless the receiving country protects it enough, reported in 2018; the authority's practice is not known.
SEN.summary:
Rule in force. Senegal's Data Protection Act, Law 2008-12 of 25 January 2008, sets the rule in Article 9. As a law-firm note of 11 May 2018 reports, a data owner cannot transfer data to another country unless the receiving country gives sufficient protection. The condition falls on the data owner, and it sits in the country's general data protection law rather than in a separate transfer instrument.

Means of complying published and rule applied. The nearest fact held is the same note of 11 May 2018 on Article 9: the data protection authority, the CDP, must be informed before any transfer, and its authorisation must be sought. That places the authority at the centre of every transfer, as the route a data owner has to follow before sending data out of Senegal.

Not held. No source held says the authority has published a list of countries, model contract terms, a permission procedure or guidance on sending data abroad.

SLE.short: Since 2020, telecom regulations bar sending subscribers' registration information abroad without the regulator's approval; how approval is sought or granted is not known.
SLE.summary:
Rule in force. Regulation 22(3) of the Telecommunications (Subscribers Identification and Registration) Regulations 2020, Statutory Instrument No. 35 of the Gazette of 6 November 2020, says subscribers' registration information shall not be transferred outside Sierra Leone without prior approval by the National Telecommunications Commission. The document is dated 6 November 2020 and gives no commencement date or later repeal. The rule is set in telecommunications regulations and applies to subscribers' registration information, not to personal data generally.

Means of complying published and rule applied. The same regulation 22(4) requires any request to the Commission for approval to justify the purpose of the transfer. Beyond that requirement in the 2020 text, the sources held state nothing on how approval is sought, what the Commission decides, or whether any approval has been given.

Not held. No source held says the authority has published a list of countries, model contract terms, a permission procedure or guidance on sending data abroad.

SOM.short: Somalia's 2023 data protection law bars sending personal data abroad without adequate protection or a stated exception; published guidance and enforcement are not known.
SOM.summary:
Rule in force. Somalia's Data Protection Act, Law No. 005 of 2023, is dated 22 March 2023, the presidential signature date. Articles 30 and 31 bar a data controller from transferring personal data outside Somalia unless the recipient country, organisation or sector gives adequate protection, or a stated exception such as the person's consent or a contract applies. The law takes effect on adoption by Parliament, promulgation by the President and publication in the Official Bulletin.

Means of complying published and rule applied. The nearest fact held is in the same Articles 30 and 31 of the 2023 Act, which accept a recipient bound by a law, binding corporate rules or contractual clauses that give adequate protection as a way to send data abroad. They set out the means in law; they do not show a list or model terms published by the authority.

Not held. No source held says the authority has published a list of countries, model contract terms, a permission procedure or guidance on sending data abroad. No application of the rule to a transfer is known.

SSD.short: Nothing held names a rule on sending personal data abroad or says there is none, so no stage is set.
SSD.summary: Not held. Nothing held names a rule on sending personal data abroad, or says there is none.

STP.short: A 2016 law limits sending personal data abroad to places with adequate protection, in force as of 2022; published ways to comply are not known.
STP.summary:
Rule in force. Law No. 03/2016, called Lei n.º 03/2016 in the country, was passed on 15 February 2016 and promulgated on 18 March 2016. It allows personal data to leave the national territory only where the receiving legal system ensures an adequate level of protection, with the National Data Protection Agency (ANPDP) deciding adequacy under Article 19. Article 20 sets exceptions: notification to the ANPDP for unequivocal consent or contractual necessity, and ANPDP authorisation backed by contractual clauses. Breaching Articles 19 and 20 carries fines of 45 to 90 million dobras. A factsheet dated 24 June 2022 lists the law as in place, with the authority operational.

Means of complying published and rule applied. The nearest held fact is that the ANPDP decides adequacy and grants authorisation backed by contractual clauses, under Articles 19 and 20 of the law. The authority is listed as operational as of 24 June 2022.

Not held. No source held says the authority has published a list of countries, model contract terms, a permission procedure or guidance on sending data abroad.

SWZ.short: Nothing held names a rule on sending personal data abroad or says there is none, so no stage is set.
SWZ.summary: Not held. Nothing held names a rule on sending personal data abroad, or says there is none.

SYC.short: Seychelles has had a rule on sending personal data abroad in force since December 2023; whether means of complying are published is not known.
SYC.summary:
Rule in force. The Data Protection Act, 2023 (Act 24 of 2023) came into force on 22 December 2023. DLA Piper states, in its summary of the country's data protection law that it permits transfer of personal data outside Seychelles provided the transfer ensures an adequate level of protection, with appropriate safeguards or legal mechanisms.

Means of complying published and rule applied. The nearest held fact, dated 2025, is in the Information Commission's annual report for 2025: it received and handled 14 cases under the Act in 2025, 6 of them data transfers, 5 breaches, 2 refused deletion requests and 1 a consultation. The report describes the handling as guidance, assessment and corrective advice, with no decision or sanction on a named controller and no count of cases settled.

Not held. No source held says the authority has published a list of countries, model contract terms, a permission procedure or guidance on sending data abroad.

TCD.short: Nothing held names a rule on sending personal data abroad or says there is none, so no stage is set.
TCD.summary: Not held. Nothing held names a rule on sending personal data abroad, or says there is none.

TGO.short: Nothing held names a rule on sending personal data abroad or says there is none, so no stage is set.
TGO.summary: Not held. Nothing held names a rule on sending personal data abroad, or says there is none.

TUN.short: Tunisia's 2004 law bars sending personal data abroad without the authority's prior permission; whether any transfer has been approved, refused or penalised is not known.
TUN.summary:
Rule in force. Tunisia's Organic Law 2004-63 of 27 July 2004, in articles 50 to 52, bars sending personal data abroad where it would harm public security or Tunisia's vital interests. It allows a transfer only to a country with an adequate level of protection. In every case it requires the prior authorisation of the data protection authority, the INPDP, which must decide within one month. The source notes that no replacement law had been adopted when it was retrieved in 2026.

Means of complying published and rule applied. The published means of complying is a list of countries judged adequate. A DIAL article of 15 June 2026 says Tunisia's 2018 adequacy list of countries for data transfers identified only five African countries. The 2004 law leaves the authorisation of each transfer to the INPDP, the authority it names as owner of the rule.

Not held. No source from the last three years names a country approved to receive data, an organisation given or refused permission, or an order or penalty for sending data abroad.

TZA.short: Tanzania's 2023 data protection law sets rules for sending personal data abroad; whether the authority has published guidance or country lists is not known.
TZA.summary:
Rule in force. The Personal Data Protection Act, Chapter 44, published in the Gazette on 13 June 2023, has a Part V on transborder data flow: section 31 covers transfer to a state with adequate data protection and section 32 transfer to a state without it. A journal study of August 2026 cites the Act as Cap. 44 R.E. 2023 alongside the Data Protection (Collection and Processing Personal Data) Regulations, GN No. 349 of 2023.

Means of complying published and rule applied. The Personal Data Protection Commission reported in August 2026 that its preliminary assessments found unlawful data transfers abroad, and listed rectification directives, warning letters and fines as remedies. The 24 August 2026 study finds the framework on cross-border transfers progressive on paper, with gaps in institutional capacity and enforcement.

Not held. No source held says the authority has published a list of countries, model contract terms, a permission procedure or guidance on sending data abroad.

UGA.short: Uganda's 2019 Act sets safeguards for sending data abroad and the regulator applied them in 2025 and 2026; published guidance for complying is not known.
UGA.summary:
Rule in force. Uganda's Data Protection and Privacy Act, 2019 carries safeguards governing international transfers of personal data. The Personal Data Protection Office (PDPO) applies Regulation 30 on cross-border transfers, and Regulation 48 sets a fine of up to three currency points a day or six months' imprisonment for offences.

Means of complying published and rule applied. In a decision of 20 February 2026 the PDPO partly upheld a complaint against WhatsApp LLC and Meta Platforms, Inc. and ordered, within 90 days, a Regulation 30 adequacy assessment and an intra-group data protection impact assessment. On the same day it directed both companies to ensure lawful safeguards for transfers of Ugandan users' personal data. On 18 July 2025 it found Google in breach for transferring data abroad without adequate safeguards, and gave it 30 days to register and submit transfer-compliance evidence.

Not held. No published list of approved countries, model contract terms, application form or guidance on transfers is held.

ZAF.short: Since July 2020 the law bars sending personal data abroad without adequate protection or consent, but no approved country list or guidance is known.
