A commitment to pay at home, and the act that follows it. A named analyst writes that the fund is fed by a legal levy of 1% to 2% of operators' turnover and collected today, with delays and arrears. AGEFAU collected 23.18 billion CFA francs in the first half of 2026 and is financing network extension, access centres, school computer rooms and training for 1,000 young people. On 22 July 2026 it signed conventions with the education and employment ministries.

Not held. Nothing: all four questions are answered.

MOZ.short: Digital lines in the 2026 budget rose 20.8 per cent and a 1% operator levy funds universal access; nothing is unknown.
MOZ.summary:
Money in the state budget, its direction and what was spent. The state budget documents publish 1,819,266,720 meticais as actually spent on digital lines for 2025. The digital lines held for both years total 1,075,518,250 meticais for 2026 against 890,407,150 for 2025, up 20.8 per cent; the 2026 budget gives 1,759,755,310 meticais to 31 digital lines.

A commitment to pay at home, and the act that follows it. The communications regulator INCM's 2024 report says each licensed operator pays 1% of its prior-year gross revenue into the Fundo de Serviço de Acesso Universal, which in 2024 financed digital squares, school computer rooms and rural mobile network expansion. Decree 11/2025 of 16 May 2025 approved a new regulation for the fund, keeping the 1% levy and assigning 60% of fines under it to the fund.

Not held. Nothing: all four questions are answered.

MRT.short: The digital ministry's 2026 budget is reported up 104.6%, but the universal access fund was repealed in 2026 and its replacement is not known.
MRT.summary:
Money in the state budget, its direction and what was spent. Ecofin Agency states the Ministry of Digital Transformation's 2026 budget of 24.2 million US dollars is up 104.6% on 2025. The budget law publishes 1,157,168,883 ouguiya as actually spent on digital lines for 2024, and the 2026 budget gives 1,676,040,009 ouguiya to 96 digital lines.

A commitment to pay at home, and the act that follows it. On 29 July 2026 the Council of Ministers approved a draft decree repealing and replacing the 2020 decree on the Universal Access Fund for Services, citing shortcomings in how its resources are mobilised and assigned. Emergence's headline says the fund's resources are centralised in the Treasury, and the text gives no replacement terms.

Not held. The fund that paid for digital programmes is repealed and its resources moved to the Treasury, and nothing held replaces it.

MUS.short: Digital lines in the 2026/27 budget rose 10.0 per cent, but no fund, levy or assigned tax for digital programmes is known.
MUS.summary:
Money in the state budget, its direction and what was spent. The digital lines held for both years total 2,713,445,000 rupees for 2026/27 against 2,465,710,000 for 2025/26, up 10.0 per cent across 59 lines; the 2026/27 budget document gives 4,534,960,000 rupees in all to 117 digital lines. The Treasury annual report publishes 2,625,753,182 rupees as actually spent on digital lines for 2024/25.

A commitment to pay at home, and the act that follows it. The nearest held fact is a budget line, not a fund: the 2026-2027 Budget, as L'Express reports it, allocates 25 million rupees to create a National AI Learning Platform with a certification and start-up incubation programme. The budget document gives 4,534,960,000 rupees to digital lines for 2026/27.

Not held. No fund, levy or assigned tax for digital programmes is shown created, collecting or paying, and no source has the government both saying it must pay from its own resources and acting on it.

MWI.short: Malawi's 2026/27 budget raised its comparable digital lines by 5.7 per cent; whether any fund pays for digital programmes is not known.
MWI.summary:
Money in the state budget, its direction and what was spent. The digital lines held for both years total 71,039,592,349 kwacha for 2026/27 against 67,220,261,503 for 2025/26, a rise of 5.7 per cent across the 131 lines held in both years, and the 2026/27 budget gives 80,831,355,150 kwacha to 178 digital lines in all. No figure published as spent on digital lines is held for any year, so the budget figures above are what the state plans to give, not what it paid out.

A commitment to pay at home, and the act that follows it. No fund, levy or assigned tax paying for digital programmes is held with a date, and no statement that the state will pay for digital transformation itself is held with an act that followed it. The nearest held fact is the budget itself: 178 digital lines in the 2026/27 budget.

Not held. No source from the last three years shows the government saying digital transformation must be paid for from its own resources and acting on it. No fund, levy or assigned tax is shown created, collecting or paying.

NAM.short: Namibia's comparable digital budget fell 10.1 per cent for 2026/27, while the Universal Service Fund paid subsidies from 2025; levy income is not known.
NAM.summary:
Money in the state budget, its direction and what was spent. The digital lines held for both years total 931,625,000 Namibian dollars for 2026/27 against 1,035,870,355 for 2025/26, a fall of 10.1 per cent; 35 digital lines in the 2026/27 budget carry 989,443,000. The Ministry of Information and Communication Technology has 639.2 million Namibian dollars for 2026/27. 776,683,722 Namibian dollars is published as spent on digital lines for 2024/25.

A commitment to pay at home, and the act that follows it. Regulations of 27 September 2024 impose a universal service levy of up to 0.5 per cent of annual turnover on every licensee, payable into the Universal Service Fund. The Fund was launched on 19 March 2025 with three-year seed money from the Ministry, and its first bidding round allocated almost 31 million Namibian dollars of subsidies to MTC for nine sites. On 9 April 2026 Telecom Namibia and the regulator CRAN signed a Phase 2 subsidy of 9,796,650 Namibian dollars for rural network sites.

Not held. Money for digital programmes in the budget was lower in 2026/27 than the year before. What the levy has collected is not stated.

NER.short: Niger's 2026 budget raised its comparable digital lines by 60.7 per cent; whether any fund pays for digital programmes is not known.
NER.summary:
Money in the state budget, its direction and what was spent. The digital lines held for both years total 841,593,044 CFA francs for 2026 against 523,743,522 for 2025, a rise of 60.7 per cent across the 8 lines held in both years, and the 2026 budget gives 11,615,369,252 CFA francs to 100 digital lines in all. No figure published as spent on digital lines is held for any year, so the budget figures above are what the state plans to give, not what it paid out.

A commitment to pay at home, and the act that follows it. No fund, levy or assigned tax paying for digital programmes is held with a collection or a payment, and no statement that the state will pay for digital transformation itself is held with an act that followed it. The nearest held fact is the budget itself: 100 digital lines in the 2026 budget.

Not held. No source from the last three years shows the government saying digital transformation must be paid for from its own resources and acting on it. No fund, levy or assigned tax is shown created, collecting or paying.

NGA.short: Nigeria's comparable digital budget fell 14.5 per cent for 2026, and a levy-funded rural fund operates; the amounts it collects and pays are not known.
NGA.summary:
Money in the state budget, its direction and what was spent. The digital lines held for both years total 296,213,962,208 naira for 2026 against 346,601,399,254 for 2025, a fall of 14.5 per cent across the 947 lines held in both years; 1,209 digital lines in the 2026 budget carry 361,965,613,224 naira. No figure published as spent on digital lines is held for any year, so the budget figures above are what the state plans to give, not what it paid out.

A commitment to pay at home, and the act that follows it. BusinessDay says the Universal Service Provision Fund is funded mainly by a one per cent levy on telecom operators revenues and subsidises rural projects such as base stations, Rural Broadband Initiatives and community resource centres, in an article of 17 June 2026. No amount collected or paid is held.

Not held. Money for digital programmes in the budget was lower in 2026 than the year before. No amount the fund collected or paid for a project is held.

RWA.short: The 2026/27 budget gives digital lines 4.1 per cent more; spending is published for 2024/25 only, and no fund acting now is known.
RWA.summary:
Money in the state budget, its direction and what was spent. For 2026/27, the 34 digital lines held in both years total 90,624,439,159 Rwandan francs against 87,083,989,612 for 2025/26, a rise of 4.1 per cent on the year before. The budget for 2026/27 gives 92,074,979,130 francs to 38 digital lines in all. The latest published spending is for an earlier year, 2024/25: 8,945,757,344 francs spent on digital lines in 2024/25.

A commitment to pay at home, and the act that follows it. The nearest held fact is the budget itself, which is the latest budget held and sets the year's money for digital work: for 2026/27 it gives 92,074,979,130 Rwandan francs to 38 digital lines, 34 of them also held for 2025/26.

Not held. No fund, levy or assigned tax for digital programmes is shown created, collecting or paying in the last three years, and no government statement that digital transformation must be paid for at home.

SDN.short: Nothing held says whether the state budget funds digital programmes or whether a fund or levy pays for them, so no stage is set.
SDN.summary: Not held. Nothing held says whether the state budget gives money to digital programmes, or that a fund or levy pays for them.

SEN.short: Senegal's digital sector budget rose from 16.1 to 31.1 billion CFA francs in 2025; 2025 spending is published; the universal fund's payments are not known.
SEN.summary:
Money in the state budget, its direction and what was spent. The digital sector's budget rose 93.2 per cent, from 16.1 billion CFA francs in 2024 to 31.1 billion in 2025. For 2026, the Digital Ministry budget is 81.06 billion CFA francs, 58.2 billion of it for investment, and the state budget gives 31,915,316,171 CFA francs to 25 digital lines. The latest published spending is for 2025, the year before: 8,600,000,000 CFA francs spent on digital lines.

A commitment to pay at home, and the act that follows it. The nearest held fact is the budget itself: for 2026 it gives 31,915,316,171 CFA francs to 25 digital lines, and the Digital Ministry's 2026 budget of 81.06 billion CFA francs, 58.2 billion of it for investment.

Not held. No fund, levy or assigned tax for digital programmes is shown created, collecting or paying in the last three years, and no government statement that digital transformation must be paid for at home.

SLE.short: Sierra Leone's FY2026 budget gives digital lines 55.5 per cent more than FY2025; no fund acting now is known.
SLE.summary:
Money in the state budget, its direction and what was spent. For FY2026, the 40 digital lines held in both years total 1,064,019,424 new leones against 684,090,124 for FY2025, a rise of 55.5 per cent. The budget gives 1,074,150,124 new leones to 45 digital lines in all, and the tabled estimate for the Ministry of Communication, Technology and Innovation is 46,808,900 new leones. Published spending is for FY2025: 612,544,000 new leones spent on digital lines.

A commitment to pay at home, and the act that follows it. The nearest held fact is the budget itself, the latest held and the one that sets the year's money for digital work: for FY2026 it gives 1,074,150,124 new leones to 45 digital lines, 40 of them also held for FY2025.

Not held. No fund, levy or assigned tax for digital programmes is shown created, collecting or paying in the last three years, and no government statement that digital transformation must be paid for at home.

SOM.short: Somalia's 2026 budget gives the digital lines held in both years 5.7 per cent more than 2025; no fund is known.
SOM.summary:
Money in the state budget, its direction and what was spent. For 2026, the Data Protection Authority's proposed recurrent budget is 170,880 US dollars against 162,060 for 2025. The 2 digital lines held in both years total 2,312,240 US dollars against 2,187,720 for 2025, a rise of 5.7 per cent, and 13 lines are held for 2026, totalling 6,247,842 US dollars. Published spending is for 2025: 5,179,597 US dollars spent on digital lines.

A commitment to pay at home, and the act that follows it. The nearest held fact is the budget itself, the latest held and the one that sets the year's money for digital work: for 2026 it gives 6,247,842 US dollars to 13 digital lines, 2 of them also held for 2025.

Not held. No fund, levy or assigned tax for digital programmes is shown created, collecting or paying in the last three years, and no government statement that digital transformation must be paid for at home.

SSD.short: The 2025/26 budget gives 291,958,444,904 South Sudanese pounds to digital lines; whether it rose, and what was spent, are not known.
SSD.summary:
Money in the state budget, its direction and what was spent. The budget for FY 2025/26 gives 291,958,444,904 South Sudanese pounds to 15 digital lines, the total of the digital lines held for that year, dated 1 November 2025. No other year's figure is held.

A commitment to pay at home, and the act that follows it. The National Communication Act, 2012 (Act No. 24) sets out in Chapter XIII, sections 73 to 83, a Universal Service and Access Fund, with a board of trustees, its financial resources and uses, and its annual budget, accounts and audit. The budget document linked above names no fund, levy or assigned tax for digital programmes, and nothing held says the fund collected or paid for anything.

Not held. The budget for digital transformation is held for one year only, so whether it rose or fell is not known, and nothing held says what was spent.

STP.short: The 2024 budget gives 33,599,219 dobras to digital lines, but the year before and what was spent are not known.
STP.summary:
Money in the state budget, its direction and what was spent. The state budget for 2024 gives 33,599,219 dobras to 24 digital lines, the total of the digital lines held for that year, in the approved general expenditure tables dated 14 February 2024. No figure for the year before is held, so no direction is stated, and the same document gives no figure published as spent on those lines for any year.

A commitment to pay at home, and the act that follows it. The budget document linked names no fund, levy or assigned tax for digital programmes. The nearest held fact is the same approved 2024 budget with its 24 digital lines and their total of 33,599,219 dobras, dated 14 February 2024.

Not held. The budget for digital transformation is held for one year only, so whether it rose is not known. Nothing held names a fund or says what was spent.

SWZ.short: Eswatini raised its digital budget by 14.8 per cent for 2026/27 and a universal service fund paid for a project in 2023.
SWZ.summary:
Money in the state budget, its direction and what was spent. The budget for 2026/27 gives 416,824,106 emalangeni to 14 digital lines. The digital lines held for both years total 408,074,106 emalangeni for 2026/27 against 355,552,868 for 2025/26, a rise of 14.8 per cent. The Budget Estimates for 2024/25 publish 200,945,813 emalangeni as actually spent on digital lines for that year.

A commitment to pay at home, and the act that follows it. The Universal Access and Service Fund paid for a backbone redundancy project with EPTC, procuring equipment to connect to the MOTRACO powerline fibre route to Maputo, on the fund's page of 3 October 2023. ESCCOM's 2018 strategy says the fund holds money accumulated over eight years from licensee contributions made under licence conditions, first paid to EPTC and then to ESCCOM.

Not held. Nothing is missing on the four questions: the budget, its direction, what was spent and the fund's payments are all stated above.

SYC.short: Seychelles cut its digital budget by 8.9 per cent for 2026 and its universal service fund is not shown collecting or paying.
SYC.summary:
Money in the state budget, its direction and what was spent. The budget for 2026 gives 239,570,000 rupees to 25 digital lines. The 12 digital lines held in both years total 84,802,000 rupees for 2026 against 93,076,000 for 2025, a fall of 8.9 per cent. The 2024 Budget Estimates publish 137,339,919 rupees as actually spent on digital lines for 2024.

A commitment to pay at home, and the act that follows it. The Communications Act 2023, assented on 13 April 2023, sets up a universal access and universal service fund in Part XII with contributions under section 100. The Act commences on a date the Minister appoints by Gazette notice, and no collection or payment by the fund is held, and no abolition of it.

Not held. The money for digital programmes was lower in the latest budget than in the one before, so no rise is stated. Nothing held shows the fund collecting or paying.

TCD.short: The 2026 budget's digital lines held for both years fell 27.8 per cent from 2025; whether any fund pays for digital programmes is not known.
TCD.summary:
Money in the state budget, its direction and what was spent. The 2026 budget gives 3,645,150,873 CFA francs to nine digital lines, in the budget document dated 26 December 2025. Six of the nine are held for 2025 as well, and those six total 2,422,606,681 CFA francs for 2026 against 3,355,272,681 for 2025, 27.8 per cent lower. No figure for money actually spent on the lines is published for any year from 2024.

A commitment to pay at home, and the act that follows it. The 2026 budget document is the one source held on how Chad pays for digital programmes. It names no fund, levy or tax assigned to them. No law, decree or dated report from the three years to September 2026 shows such a fund created, collecting money or paying for a digital project, and none has the head of state or a minister saying digital transformation must be paid for from the country's own resources.

Not held. The money for digital transformation was lower in the latest budget than in the one before. No fund, levy or assigned tax for digital programmes is held.

TGO.short: The 2026 budget gives 28.2 billion CFA francs to 47 digital lines; the previous year's figure is not known.
TGO.summary:
Money in the state budget, its direction and what was spent. The 2026 budget gives 28,214,736,000 CFA francs to 47 digital lines, in the finance ministry's budget document of 15 January 2026. None of the 47 is held for 2025 as well, so the two years are not set side by side here, and no figure for money actually spent on the lines is published for any year from 2024.

A commitment to pay at home, and the act that follows it. The 2026 budget document is the one source held on how Togo pays for digital programmes. It names no fund, levy or tax assigned to them. No law, decree or dated report from the three years to September 2026 shows such a fund created, collecting money or paying for a digital project, and none has the head of state or a minister saying digital transformation must be paid for from the country's own resources.

Not held. Nothing held gives the money for digital transformation in two budget years running, so whether it rose is not known. No fund, levy or assigned tax for digital programmes is held.

TUN.short: The 2026 budget gives 102 million dinars to two digital lines; the previous year's figure is not known.
TUN.summary:
Money in the state budget, its direction and what was spent. The 2026 budget gives 102,130,000 dinars to two digital lines, in the finance ministry's budget document of 12 December 2025. Neither line is held for 2025 as well, so the two years are not set side by side here, and no figure for money actually spent on the lines is published for any year from 2024.

A commitment to pay at home, and the act that follows it. The 2026 budget document is the one source held on how Tunisia pays for digital programmes. It names no fund, levy or tax assigned to them. No law, decree or dated report from the three years to September 2026 shows such a fund created, collecting money or paying for a digital project, and none has the head of state or a minister saying digital transformation must be paid for from the country's own resources.

Not held. Nothing held gives the money for digital transformation in two budget years running, so whether it rose is not known. No fund, levy or assigned tax for digital programmes is held.

TZA.short: The ministry's 2026/27 budget fell 23.6 per cent though digital lines overall rose 7.9, and the service fund built towers; 2026/27 spending is not known.
TZA.summary:
Money in the state budget, its direction and what was spent. The Prime Minister said the government allocated more than 132 billion shillings in 2026/27 to the National Identification Authority for development projects. The Ministry of Communication and Information Technology's 2026/27 proposal of 222,589,451,000 shillings is 23.6 per cent below the 291,533,139,000 approved for 2025/26, with domestic development money unchanged at 98,480,905,000. The digital lines held for both years total 429,376,230,416 shillings for 2026/27 against 398,020,452,091 for 2025/26, 7.9 per cent higher. 545,314,926,071 shillings is published as spent on digital lines for 2024/25.

A commitment to pay at home, and the act that follows it. The Universal Communications Service Access Fund paid 71 billion of the 126 billion shillings cost of the 758-tower rural project. Its chief executive said on 5 October 2026 that it will build 250 school computer laboratories this financial year and has paid for 2,166 towers.

Not held. The ministry's own budget was lower in the latest year than the one before; nothing held shows it rose.

UGA.short: In 2026/27 the ICT ministry's budget rises to 144.7 billion shillings and a levy-funded universal access fund pays out; nothing further is unknown.
UGA.summary:
Money in the state budget, its direction and what was spent. Uganda's budget tables publish 669.9 billion Ugandan shillings as spent on digital lines for 2024/25. The Ministry of ICT and National Guidance budgets 144.696 billion for 2026/27 against 105.963 billion approved for 2025/26, a rise. The digital lines held for both years total 752.4 billion for 2026/27 against 862.0 billion for 2025/26.

A commitment to pay at home, and the act that follows it. The Uganda Communications Universal Service and Access Fund is paid by a levy of 2% of operators' gross annual revenue. In 2026 ATC Uganda paid 20.9 billion shillings into it, half of which goes to the Consolidated Fund and half is kept for the fund. On 29 September 2026 the Uganda Communications Commission sought a partner to run Phase III of the National e-Booster Programme through the fund for 2026/27.

Not held. Nothing: all four questions are answered.

ZAF.short: The digital and postal access budget rises for 2026/27 and the universal service fund spent 1.09 billion rand in 2025/26; nothing further is unknown.
ZAF.summary:
Money in the state budget, its direction and what was spent. The fund's own figures, given in a ministerial reply, show 1,087.9 million rand spent in 2025/26. The 2026 Estimates of National Expenditure raise the digital and postal access subprogramme of Vote 30 from 742.9 million rand in 2025/26 to 767.2 million for 2026/27. The digital lines held for both years total 8,082.2 million rand for 2026/27 against 7,685.6 million for 2025/26.

A commitment to pay at home, and the act that follows it. The Universal Service and Access Fund is paid for by operators' mandatory contributions. ICASA collected 281.2 million rand for it in 2025/26, and its administrator spent 1,087.9 million rand that year, leaving about 652.1 million unspent. The fund collected 1.2 billion rand over the five years to 2025/26. It has not been abolished. The 2026 Estimates put 146.0 million rand of 2026/27 towards the universal service and access bodies.

Not held. Nothing: all four questions are answered.

ZMB.short: The digital lines in Zambia's 2026 budget total more than in 2025, with 843.4 million kwacha spent in 2025; no fund or levy is known.
ZMB.summary:
Money in the state budget, its direction and what was spent. Zambia's budget tables publish 843.4 million kwacha as spent on digital lines for 2025. The digital lines held for both years total 1,792.9 million kwacha for 2026 against 1,594.5 million for 2025, a rise. The Appropriation Act, 2025 authorises 1.15 billion kwacha for Smart Zambia e-government for 2026, with 566.8 million kwacha for ICT development. The Supplementary Appropriation Act of 2025 added 162 million kwacha for Smart Zambia e-government and 194.3 million for ICT development for 2025. In May 2026 the minister announced approval of 255 million kwacha to upgrade digital infrastructure, mainly in rural areas.

A commitment to pay at home, and the act that follows it. The budget document linked names no fund, levy or assigned tax for digital programmes. The nearest budget fact is that the budget for 2026 gives 1,942.9 million kwacha to 45 digital lines.

Not held. Whether the government has said digital transformation must be paid for from its own resources and acted on it: no fund, levy or assigned tax is shown created, collecting or paying.

ZWE.short: Zimbabwe's ICT ministry budget rises about 3 per cent to 763.5 million Zimbabwe Gold for 2026; spending and any fund are not known.
ZWE.summary:
Money in the state budget, its direction and what was spent. The Budget Statement gives the ICT ministry's Vote 23 budget as 763.5 million Zimbabwe Gold for 2026 against 741 million for 2025, a rise of about 3 per cent. The digital lines held for both years total 4,503.5 million Zimbabwe dollars for 2026 against 5,703.9 million for 2025, 21.0 per cent lower. The Appropriation Act gives 258.3 million Zimbabwe Gold to the ministry's policy and administration programme and 505.2 million to ICT development and promotion for 2026. No figure for what was spent is held.

A commitment to pay at home, and the act that follows it. The budget document linked names no fund, levy or assigned tax for digital programmes. The nearest budget fact is that the 2026 budget gives 4,675.6 million Zimbabwe dollars to 31 digital lines.

Not held. What was actually spent on digital programmes, and whether the government has said they must be paid for from its own resources and acted on it: no fund, levy or assigned tax is shown created, collecting or paying.

AGO.short: Angola's 2011 presidential decree on information society services covers e-signatures and contracts; no rules made under it are known, and a 2026 regime awaits enactment.
AGO.summary:
Law in force. Angola's Presidential Decree 202/11, published in the Diário da República I Série no. 139 on 22 July 2011, approves the Regulamento das Tecnologias e dos Serviços da Sociedade da Informação. It covers information society services, electronic documents and legal acts, with qualified electronic signature, certification and electronic contracts, and electronic advertising. It enters into force 30 days after publication.

Rules made under the law and the law applied. The nearest held fact concerns a further e-signature regime. On 30 July 2026 the Assembleia Nacional unanimously approved, with 166 votes in favour, a bill authorising the President to legislate the Regime Jurídico da Assinatura Electrónica e da Certificação Digital, valid for 90 days after publication. Angop reports that the regime would set e-signature validity, evidential value and the Infra-Estrutura de Chaves Públicas de Angola. The regime itself is not yet enacted.

Not held. No decree, regulation or order made under the 2011 decree is held, and the new e-signature regime is not yet in force.

BDI.short: Burundi's 2024 communications code governs e-commerce, and the regulator issued guidelines and a conformity call in 2026; no licence or penalty is known.
BDI.summary:
Law in force. Burundi's Loi N°1/22 of 22 August 2024, the code des communications électroniques et postales, was promulgated. The regulator ARCT states that e-commerce activity on Burundi's territory is subject to a prior conformity obligation, applying the provisions of that code. The obligation was set out in an ARCT communiqué of 26 June 2026, which applies to e-commerce platforms and merchant sites.

Rules made under the law and the law applied. On 29 May 2026 ARCT published national e-commerce ecosystem guidelines, drawn from the regulation in force, which set technical, operational and organisational standards for interoperability, transaction security and consumer protection. On 26 June 2026 it issued a communiqué calling e-commerce platforms and merchant sites to declare their conformity, with a procedures manual, a conformity checklist and a declaration form annexed.

Not held. No accreditation, licence, registration or penalty under the code is held for the last three years, and no declaration of conformity is shown to have been received.

BEN.short: Benin's 2018 digital code is in force and sets duties for trust service providers; no decree or rules made under it are known.
BEN.summary:
Law in force. Benin's Loi n° 2017-20, the Code du numérique, was promulgated by the President on 20 April 2018 after adoption by the National Assembly and review by the Constitutional Court. The code is Benin's main digital law and includes a title on the obligations of trust service providers. The text is published by the Secrétariat général du gouvernement.

Rules made under the law and the law applied. The nearest held fact is that title itself. Articles 305 and 306 of the Code du numérique set out the freedom of establishment of trust service providers and their duty of declaration, which is the part of the code that bears on electronic signatures and certification. A trust service provider may therefore establish itself in Benin freely, and must declare itself once established.

Not held. No decree, regulation or order made under the code is held.

BFA.short: Burkina Faso's 2009 law on electronic services and transactions recognises e-signatures and is in force; no rules made under it are known.
BFA.summary:
Law in force. Burkina Faso's Law n°045-2009/AN regulates electronic services and transactions, covering electronic signatures, electronic formalities, e-commerce contracts and trust service providers. The National Assembly adopted it on 10 November 2009 and it was promulgated by Decree n°2009-824/PRES on 4 December 2009. No repeal is given in the document held.

Rules made under the law and the law applied. The nearest held fact is what the law says of signatures. Wearetech reports that law no. 045-2009 recognises the electronic signature in all matters and presumes reliable a secure signature based on a qualified certificate. The same report, on the public administration moving to electronic signature, was published on 14 September 2026, the day before a platform launch scheduled for 15 September.

Not held. No decree, regulation or order made under the law is held.

BWA.short: Botswana's 2014 electronic communications and transactions act has been in force since 2016 and covers contracts, signatures and online buyers; no rules are known.
BWA.summary:
Law in force. Botswana's law is the Electronic Communications and Transactions Act, 2014 (Act No. 14), which Parliament enacted and which was assented to on 14 May 2014. The Act gives electronic communications, contracts and signatures legal effect, and it covers the protection of consumers who buy online. It did not start on assent: commencement was by an Order of the minister published in the Gazette, and the regulator BOCRA records the Act as in force since 1 April 2016.

Rules made under the law and the law applied. The one instrument held that was made under the Act is the ministerial Order that brought it into force, which the Act itself provides for. No regulation on electronic signatures, on those who certify them or on those who sell online is named in the text held, and no accreditation, licence or penalty under the Act is recorded.

Not held. No regulation or order made under the Act, other than the commencement Order, is held.

CAF.short: The Central African Republic's regulator lists a 2022 electronic transactions law among the country's laws; no rules made under it are known.
CAF.summary:
Law in force. The Central African Republic has a law on electronic transactions. The regulator ARCEP lists Loi 22.002 of 11 January 2022, regulating electronic transactions in the country, among the laws on its official index of laws and ordinances. The index page was published on 21 February 2024, two years after the date the law carries, and it presents the law as one of the country's laws and not as a bill or a draft.

Rules made under the law and the law applied. The regulator's index names the law and gives its date, and it shows no decree, regulation or order made under it. No rule on electronic signatures, on those who certify them or on those who sell online is named there, and no accreditation, licence, registration or penalty under the law is recorded in the index.

Not held. No decree, regulation or order made under the law is held, and the text of the law is not held.

CIV.short: A 2013 electronic transactions law is in force with 2014 and 2016 decrees, but no use of it is dated in the last three years.
CIV.summary:
Law in force. Côte d'Ivoire's Loi n°2013-546 of 30 July 2013 on electronic transactions is the law that a decree of 12 March 2014 states it implements. APA reports that the ANSSI CI national public key infrastructure launched in July 2026 rests on this law, which it says gives electronic signatures legal value. AIP, citing an ANSSI-CI communiqué, reports the same, in an article of 25 July 2026.

Rules made under the law and the law applied. Decree 2014-106, signed by the President on 12 March 2014, sets rules on secure electronic signatures, qualified electronic certificates and the approval of certification service providers by ARTCI. Biometric Update reports further decrees of 2014 and 2016 that accompany the law and cover cryptology, electronic signatures and digital archiving.

Not held. No accreditation, licence, registration or penalty under the law in the last three years is dated in the sources held.

CMR.short: A 2010 e-commerce law is in force with a 2011 application decree, but no use of it is dated in the last three years.
CMR.summary:
Law in force. Law No. 2010/021 of 21 December 2010, adopted by the National Assembly and promulgated by the President, governs electronic commerce in Cameroon. It defines electronic signatures, certificates and certification authorities. The Prime Minister's decree of 15 June 2011 describes it as a made law and fixes its application rules.

Rules made under the law and the law applied. Decree no. 2011/1521/PM of 15 June 2011 fixes the modalities of application of law no. 2010/021 on electronic commerce. It defines the scope of e-commerce activity under the law. The decree was issued by the Prime Minister and is published on the Ministry of Commerce website, where the law is also published. It follows the law of 21 December 2010 that it implements, by about six months, and is the rule-making instrument for e-commerce in Cameroon.

Not held. No accreditation, licence, registration or penalty under the law in the last three years is dated in the sources held.

COD.short: A 2023 digital code governs e-signatures, with a March 2026 order on authorisation, but no licence under it is dated in the last three years.
COD.summary:
Law in force. Ordonnance-loi n° 23/010 of 13 March 2023, the Code du Numérique, governs electronic writings, electronic signatures, trust service providers and digital services. Under article 108, a qualified signature has the evidential force of a handwritten one. ACP reports that a ministerial order of March 2026 is made to implement the Code, which the order treats as the operative law for digital services.

Rules made under the law and the law applied. The ministerial order of 11 March 2026 sets an authorisation regime for qualified trust-service providers, marketplaces and e-commerce platforms, and enters into force on signature, with full application from 1 July 2026. ACP reports it was published on 17 March 2026, with a transition to 30 June 2026.

Not held. No accreditation, licence, registration or penalty under the law in the last three years is dated in the sources held.

COG.short: A 2019 electronic transactions law is treated as in force in 2026, but no rule made under it is known.
COG.summary:
Law in force. Loi n° 37-2019 of 12 December 2019 on electronic transactions is treated as an existing law by the four arrêtés of 9 July 2026, which cite it as a legal basis. Décret n° 2026-101 of 31 March 2026 cites the same law as a legal basis, again treating it as existing. Both instruments concern the certified electronic invoicing system and appeared in the Journal officiel in 2026.

Rules made under the law and the law applied. The four arrêtés of 9 July 2026 and Décret n° 2026-101 of 31 March 2026 are the nearest held instruments. Each names the 2019 law on electronic transactions among its legal bases, and each treats it as already in force. The law is dated 12 December 2019, while the decree and the arrêtés citing it are dated March and July 2026.

Not held. No decree, regulation or order made under the law is named in the sources held.

COM.short: A 2021 law on cyber security gives electronic signatures legal effect; nothing is known of rules made under it or of its use.
COM.summary:
Law in force. The UNECA Digital Trade Regulatory Integration profile, published in 2024, states that the 2021 law on cyber security and the fight against cybercrime, Law No. 21-012/AU, fills gaps in electronic transactions, notably by giving electronic signatures the same legal effect as handwritten ones. The same profile states that the Comoros has no stand-alone law on electronic transactions, no consumer protection framework and no UNCITRAL-based legislation for online transactions.

Rules made under the law and the law applied. The nearest held fact is the profile's account of that law, which names no decree, regulation or order made under it and no provider accredited under it. Before the law, the national digital strategy drawn up in December 2018 stated that the telecommunications-centred legal framework leaves a legal vacuum on digital transactions and electronic signature. In March 2021 ANADEN's legal affairs officer listed a law on e-commerce among legislation still to be drafted, to be part of a digital code targeted for 2024.

Not held. No decree, regulation or order made under the 2021 law, and no use of it in the last three years.

CPV.short: Cape Verde was said in 2025 to have a law on digital transactions, but no rule made under it is known.
CPV.summary:
Law in force. The Secretary of State for the Digital Economy, Pedro Lopes, cited Cape Verde's modern laws on data protection and digital transactions among its regulatory progress, in a report published on 31 July 2025. The article is about the country's digital start-up ecosystem, and the law on digital transactions is one of the regulatory advances it lists.

Rules made under the law and the law applied. The nearest held fact is the same statement: the Secretary of State for the Digital Economy cited Cape Verde's laws on data protection and digital transactions as regulatory progress in July 2025. It is the only statement held on the law on digital transactions. The statement dates from 31 July 2025 and comes from the Secretary of State, who presents the laws as part of the regulatory progress the country has made.

Not held. No decree, regulation or order made under the law is named in the sources held.

DJI.short: Djibouti's National Assembly passed a Digital Code covering e-commerce in June 2025; whether it is in force or has implementing rules is not known.
DJI.summary:
Law in force. Djibouti's National Assembly adopted the Digital Code unanimously on 30 June 2025, a text of nearly 800 articles that covers the regulation of online commerce among other areas. TechAfrica News describes it as the country's first Digital Code, in eight books including Book IV on e-commerce and Book V on consumer rights, announced by the Ministry of Digital Economy and Innovation. Jones Day reports that the law was still to be promulgated by the President and published in the Journal Officiel.

Rules made under the law and the law applied. Jones Day reports that the Digital Code, which covers e-commerce, cryptology service providers, data protection and cybersecurity in eight volumes, is to be supplemented by regulatory decrees. The Code passed the National Assembly on 30 June 2025, and the decrees are the rules that are to follow it.

Not held. Whether the Digital Code has been promulgated, is in force or has regulatory decrees is not held.

DZA.short: Algeria's e-commerce Law 18-05 is in force in 2026, and a 2025 trust-services bill is before parliament; rules under the e-commerce law are not known.
DZA.summary:
Law in force. Algeria's Law No. 18-05 on e-commerce is in force: in August 2026 the head of the national consumer-guidance organisation for e-commerce said most online sellers operate without the obligations it lays down. The Minister of Post and Telecommunications described Law 15-04 of 1 February 2015 on electronic signature and certification as the text in force in December 2025, covering certification and electronic signatures only. A draft law on trust services was approved by the Council of Ministers on 2 November 2025 and would update that legislation.

Rules made under the law and the law applied. The draft law on trust services for electronic transactions and electronic identification was presented to the National People's Assembly in December 2025. It would replace law 15-04, recognise electronic contracts and electronic documents as equal to paper, create the ANCE authority and set sanctions. For the e-commerce law, the consumer-guidance organisation describes sellers operating without its obligations.

Not held. No decree, regulation or order made under the law is named.

EGY.short: Egypt's Law 15/2004 on e-signatures is in force and has executive regulations, per 2025 legal guides; no dated licence or penalty is known.
EGY.summary:
Law in force. Egypt's Law No. 15/2004 regulating e-signatures establishes ITIDA, and its confidentiality duties bind licensed certification authorities, as an ICLG chapter written by a law firm lists it in July 2025. A Chambers guide of March 2025 also cites the law as part of Egypt's framework and states what it requires of applicants for e-signature services. Biometric Update states that digitally signed contracts are legally binding in Egypt.

Rules made under the law and the law applied. The law has executive regulations. The ICLG chapter states that they require applicants for e-signature services to implement systems securing the confidentiality of information, and the Chambers guide states that applicants must keep a secure system preserving the confidentiality of customers' data. Both statements date from 2025.

Not held. No accreditation, licence, registration or penalty under the law dated in the last three years is held.

ERI.short: A 2022 UN Africa commission profile said Eritrea had no e-commerce or e-signature law; nothing newer is held, so no stage is set.
ERI.summary: Not held. No law or draft is on record, and no source dated in the last three years says the country has none.

ETH.short: Ethiopia's e-signature Proclamation 1072/2017 is in force and its regulation was approved by the Council of Ministers in 2025; publication and use are not known.
ETH.summary:
Law in force. Ethiopia's electronic signature law is Proclamation No. 1072/2017 and its amendment, as the Ethiopian News Agency described it in November 2025. The agency reported that a regulation under the proclamation was a step toward fully operationalizing the law. The proclamation is the existing legal basis for electronic signatures in the country, and the regulation is the step the agency named toward putting it fully into operation.

Rules made under the law and the law applied. The Council of Ministers unanimously approved the Electronic Signature regulation under Proclamation No. 1072/2017 in November 2025. The regulation is to take effect on publication in the Federal Negarit Gazette. It is the rule made under the proclamation that the Ethiopian News Agency reported as the means of putting the law into operation.

Not held. No accreditation, licence, registration or penalty under the law dated in the last three years is held.

GAB.short: Gabon's Law 025/2021 regulates electronic transactions, and in September 2026 ministers adopted a draft trust-services decree; use of the rules is not known.
GAB.summary:
Law in force. Gabon's Law No. 025/2021 of 28 December 2021 regulates electronic transactions and was published in Journal Officiel no. 145 of 1 January 2022. It gives electronic acts, writings, signatures and invoices the same probative force as paper, and sets rules for e-commerce, distance contracts and consumer withdrawal.

Rules made under the law and the law applied. On 18 September 2026 the Council of Ministers adopted a draft decree setting how the qualified electronic signature certificate and other trust services are issued. It covers electronic signature and seal, website authentication, electronic invoice, and the approval conditions and duties of providers, to secure the legal value of electronic transactions. The decree sits alongside the 2021 law, whose rules on e-commerce, distance contracts and consumer withdrawal are in force.

Not held. No accreditation, licence, registration or penalty under the law dated in the last three years is held.

GHA.short: Ghana's 2008 Electronic Transactions Act is in force; a November 2023 notice required e-commerce platforms to register, and later enforcement is not known.
GHA.summary:
Law in force. Ghana's 2008 Electronic Transactions Act is in force. The US Country Commercial Guide, published 20 September 2024, calls it the baseline for e-commerce and e-signature in the country. Digital Policy Alert describes it as setting fair business practice requirements for suppliers, consumer rights and liability protections for intermediaries.

Rules made under the law and the law applied. The Act has been put to work. In November 2023 the Ministry of Communications and Digitalisation issued an enforcement notice under the Electronic Transactions Act, requiring all e-commerce platforms and digital delivery companies to register by January 2024, as Digital Policy Alert reports. The notice set a registration duty for every platform of those two kinds, with a deadline about two months after it was issued.

Not held. No source held shows a licence, penalty or court case under the Act after the 2023 notice, or lists further rules made under it.

GIN.short: Guinea has a 2016 transactions law, a 2021 decree and a 2026 e-signature decree; how far they are applied is not known.
GIN.summary:
Law in force. Guinea has two layers of law. Law L/2016/035/AN of 26 July 2016 on electronic transactions applies to all electronic transactions including online commerce, and covers electronic signature, digital archiving, system certification, consumer information duties, fines and prison terms, according to ANSSI's summary. A presidential decree signed on 19 August 2026 also gives an electronic signature the same probative force as a paper writing, covering public, private and person-to-person acts.

Rules made under the law and the law applied. Decree D/2021/092/PRG/SGG, signed on 25 March 2021, sets rules for electronic transactions including e-commerce, names the ARPT as regulator with sanction powers, and provides fines and penalties. The August 2026 decree requires every electronic-certification service provider to be approved by the competent authority, names the national digital agency ANDE as that authority for approval, control and audit, and refers technical standards to a joint order of the telecommunications and justice ministries.

Not held. No source held dates an accreditation, licence, registration or penalty under the law in the last three years.

GMB.short: The Gambia's Communications Bill 2025 covering electronic transactions passed second reading in March 2026; no law in force is known.
GMB.summary:
Law in force. The Gambia has a bill and no law in force that is held. The National Assembly approved the Communications Bill 2025 at second reading on 2 March 2026, after a first reading on 19 November 2025, and sent it to a committee. The Minister said the bill will create a legal framework for electronic transactions, recognising electronic signatures and contracts, and will cover electronic commerce services.

Rules made under the law and the law applied. No rules made under an e-commerce law are held, because the bill is still before the National Assembly. The Minister described the bill as the framework for electronic signatures, contracts and electronic commerce services, so any rules under it would follow its passage. No application of such a law is held.

Not held. No source held says a law on electronic transactions or e-commerce is in force.

GNB.short: Guinea-Bissau put a draft Electronic Transactions Law to consultation until 28 May 2026; no law in force is known.
GNB.summary:
Law in force. Guinea-Bissau has a draft law and no law in force that is held. In May 2026 the national regulator ARN-TIC put the draft Electronic Transactions Law out for public consultation, with responses due by 28 May 2026; it covers electronic communications and transactions, trust services and e-government. The 112-article text would give data messages, electronic records, contracts and electronic signatures legal effect, license trust-service providers and set e-commerce consumer rules.

Rules made under the law and the law applied. No rules are held, because the draft has not been enacted. The text enters into force only on a date the Minister designates, so any rules under it would follow later. The regulator ARN-TIC ran the consultation and is the body named in the notice.

Not held. No source held says a law on electronic transactions or e-commerce is in force.

GNQ.short: Equatorial Guinea enacted a law on electronic signature and documents on 10 January 2017; no rules made under it or application are known.
GNQ.summary:
Law in force. Equatorial Guinea has a law on electronic signature and documents. The official gazette compilation, published 10 January 2017, lists Ley Núm. 2/2.017, of 10 January 2017, on Firma y Documentos Electrónicos, a law of the country. The passages held give its title and date, so what the law requires is not described here. The entry names it as the country's law on electronic signature and documents, and it is the only fact held on the law.

Rules made under the law and the law applied. No decree, regulation or order made under the law is held. The compilation of electronic laws, published 10 January 2017, lists the 2017 law, and nothing held shows the law being applied. The nearest held fact is the law's own listing, which carries a title and a date and no text.

Not held. No source held names a decree, regulation or order made under the law.

KEN.short: Kenya gave electronic signatures legal effect and made certification rules by 2020; nothing is known of licences or penalties in the last three years.
KEN.summary:
Law in force. The Business Laws (Amendment) Act, 2020 came into force on 18 March 2020 and allows advanced electronic signatures in place of wet-ink signatures in nearly all legal documents, amending among others the Law of Contract Act. Under the Kenya Communications Act 1998 as amended in 2009, an advanced electronic signature has the same legal effect as a handwritten one.

Rules made under the law and the law applied. The Kenya Communications (Electronic Transactions) Regulations, 2009 set licensing, operating and liability rules for certification service providers. Valid advanced electronic signatures are issued by providers licensed under the Kenya Information and Communications (Electronic Certification and Domain Name Administration) Regulations 2020. On 1 September 2020 the Communications Authority required all foreign electronic certification providers to apply for recognition within 30 days. As at October 2020 only two certification service providers were licensed, and neither had yet started issuing advanced electronic signatures.

Not held. No accreditation, licence, registration or penalty under the law dated in the last three years.

LBR.short: Liberia's 2002 Electronic Transactions Law gives electronic contracts and signatures legal effect, but no regulation under it is known.
LBR.summary:
Law in force. Liberia's Electronic Transactions Law, Chapter 13 of Title 14 of the General Business Law, was approved on 8 January 2002 and published on 19 June 2002. It took effect on publication in handbills. The law gives electronic records, contracts and signatures legal effect, so a contract concluded electronically is recognised in Liberian law. It is a chapter of the General Business Law rather than a stand-alone act, and it dates from 2002.

Rules made under the law and the law applied. The law applies at once to matters under Titles 5 and 21 of the General Business Law. Anywhere else it applies only as regulations of the Minister of Foreign Affairs bring it into effect. That makes the Minister's regulations the route by which the law reaches the rest of the commercial code, and the nearest held fact on rules made under it is this delegation, not a regulation itself.

Not held. No source held names a decree, regulation or order made under the law.

LBY.short: Libya's 2022 electronic transactions law is in force and covers online sellers, but no rules made under it are known.
LBY.summary:
Law in force. Libya's Law No. 6 of 2022 on Electronic Transactions was issued by the House of Representatives on 4 October 2022. It gives electronic signatures, records and contracts legal effect. The repository that holds it lists it as in force, and its Article 87 makes it effective from the date of issue. The law is not limited to signatures: it also sets pre-contract disclosure and return rules for online sellers, so it reaches the sale of goods and services over the internet as well as the validity of electronic documents.

Rules made under the law and the law applied. The nearest held fact is Article 87, which makes the law effective from issue, so it applied from the date of issue. The same text sets the return rules that online sellers must follow. No regulation, order or decision made under the law is named in the evidence, and none is described as applying its rules to a particular seller or platform.

Not held. No source held names a decree, regulation or order made under the law.

LSO.short: Lesotho had no electronic transactions law in 2026 and a revised bill was in draft, so when it will pass is not known.
LSO.summary:
Law in force. The ministry responsible says Lesotho lacks a legal and regulatory framework for electronic transactions, which leaves government, businesses and consumers uncertain over electronic contracts, signatures, records, online services and digital commerce. A bill is in draft: the Electronic Transactions and Communications Bill, 2026 revises a 2022 bill of the same name. The government opened a two-day validation workshop in Maseru on 28 September 2026 to gather stakeholder views.

Rules made under the law and the law applied. No rules exist yet, because there is no law to make them under. The nearest held fact is the bill's progress: after the workshop, which was held with the United Nations Development Programme, the draft goes to the Office of the Parliamentary Counsel for refinement. The FinMark Trust said in June 2026 that Lesotho, with the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Zimbabwe, lacks comprehensive legislation on electronic transactions.

Not held. No source held says a law on electronic transactions or e-commerce is in force.

MAR.short: Morocco's 2020 trust services law is in force, with a 2023 decree and three approved qualified providers listed in September 2026.
MAR.summary:
Law in force. Morocco's Law 43-20 on trust services for electronic transactions sets the rules for trust services, cryptology means and services, and trust service providers and certificate holders. It also sets the powers of the national trust services authority. The law covers trust services, meaning signatures and certificates, rather than online selling. The DGSSI applies it, and its register of regulated services cites the law's Articles 8, 17, 46, 52 and 53 as the basis for what it regulates.

Rules made under the law and the law applied. Decree 2-22-687 was made to apply the law. It sets transitional periods running from 13 July 2023, including six months for non-qualified trust service providers under its Article 33. Under Article 53 the DGSSI publishes a list of approved trust service providers, which as of September 2026 names three at the qualified level: EURAFRIC INFORMATION, Barid Al Maghrib and DamaneSign. It also lists the conformity certificates it has issued for qualified signature and seal creation devices, six of them current, the latest dated 18 March 2026.

Not held. Nothing on the four questions.

MDG.short: Madagascar has had electronic transactions and signature laws since 2014, and a 2025 draft decree on electronic signature is not known to be adopted.
MDG.summary:
Law in force. Madagascar has a law on electronic transactions and a law on electronic signature, both dated 10 December 2014 and cited by a presidential decree as the legal basis it is made under. The transactions law, Loi no. 2014-024, has 35 articles in four parts, defines electronic signature and regulates e-commerce. Newsmada describes the signature law as the legal equivalent of the handwritten signature. Decree 2024-1911, published on 13 November 2024, gives documents signed through a certified electronic signature device the same recognition as paper.

Rules made under the law and the law applied. The 2024 decree is the nearest rule held that is made under the laws, and its Article 10 on certified electronic signatures is the part that applies them. In September 2025 Newsmada reported that a draft decree on electronic signature and interoperability was in preparation, and that the ministry held a validation workshop on the regulatory framework on 13 September 2025. The evidence does not say the draft decree has since been adopted.

Not held. No source held names a decree, regulation or order made under the law, other than the 2024 decree, and none says the draft decree has been adopted.

MLI.short: Mali's 2016 law on electronic transactions regulates e-commerce and is cited by the state in 2025, but rules made under it are not known.
MLI.summary:
Law in force. Mali's Law no. 2016-012 of 6 May 2016 on electronic transactions, exchanges and services regulates electronic commerce. It gives legal effect to electronic writings, electronic signatures, electronic certificates and electronic archiving, and it was published in the Journal officiel of 27 May 2016. A second text, consumer protection law no. 2015-036 of 16 July 2015, sets rules for distance sales including by electronic means and bans email advertising without consent. It covers online selling only in part, and it states that an electronic contract is validly concluded under the law on electronic exchange of legal data.

Rules made under the law and the law applied. The nearest held fact on application is a statement from the state. In November 2025 the Director General of Taxes cited the law on electronic transactions as part of a solid legal framework for digitalising public payments. The evidence names no decree, regulation or order made under the 2016 law, and no case of its provisions being applied to a particular seller or platform.

Not held. No source held names a decree, regulation or order made under the law.

MOZ.short: In 2026 Mozambique's electronic transactions law is applied through 19 operator licences, with about 170 companies under evaluation; wider enforcement is not known.
MOZ.summary:
Law in force. Mozambique's Electronic Transactions Law, Law no. 3/2017 of 9 January, is listed among its laws in force and sets rules on electronic marketing consent, intermediary service providers and personal data, with fines for breach. Licences to digital operators began under it on 8 June 2026. Decree No. 40/2026 of the Council of Ministers gives the electronic signature the same legal standing as a handwritten one.

Rules made under the law and the law applied. Decree no. 59/2023 of 27 October, amended by Decree no. 44/2025 of 28 November, requires intermediary electronic service providers and digital platform operators to register and be licensed with INTIC. A Digital Certification Regulation operates with the law for the Digital Certification System. On 8 June 2026 INTIC's board president said 19 licences had been issued, with about 170 registered companies under evaluation.

Not held. No further rule or enforcement figure is held beyond the above.

MRT.short: A 2006 ordinance covers e-commerce operations and a 2018 bill on electronic transactions passed the Assembly; whether the bill became law is not known.
MRT.summary:
Law in force. Ordinance No. 2006-031 of 23 August 2006 on payment instruments and e-commerce operations is, per the minister's account to the National Assembly reported by AMI on 30 January 2018, the law covering banking operations and some aspects of e-commerce. On 30 January 2018 the National Assembly adopted a 102-article bill on electronic transactions, covering electronic writing equal to paper, e-commerce provider liability and a national certification authority.

Rules made under the law and the law applied. The nearest held fact is the minister's statement to the Assembly that the ordinance operates with implementing texts, none of which is named. AMI's report of the adoption of the bill, also dated 30 January 2018, gives the bill's subject as electronic transactions and its length as 102 articles, and names no promulgation date.

Not held. Whether the 2018 bill was promulgated, any decree, regulation or order made under the ordinance, and any use of it in the last three years.

MUS.short: In 2026 Mauritius enacted an electronic transactions amendment act, to start on a date set by Proclamation; rules made under it are not known.
MUS.summary:
Law in force. Act No. 5 of 2026, the Electronic Transactions (Amendment) Act, was passed by the National Assembly on 19 May 2026 and assented to by the President on 25 May 2026, six days later. On 29 July 2026 the ICT minister referred to amendments to the Electronic Transactions Act 2006 meant to modernise digital commerce frameworks and strengthen consumer protection. That was ten weeks after the Act was passed.

Rules made under the law and the law applied. The 2026 Act comes into operation on a date to be fixed by Proclamation, and different sections may be brought into operation on different dates. The same minister's July 2026 statement treats the 2006 Act as existing law and gives no date for its entry into force.

Not held. No decree, regulation or order made under the law is held, and nothing shows the law applied in practice.

MWI.short: Malawi's electronic transactions act has been in force since June 2017; rules made under it and how it is applied are not known.
MWI.summary:
Law in force. The Electronic Transactions and Cyber Security Act (Act 33 of 2016, Chapter 74:02) was published in the Gazette on 4 November 2016 and commenced on 1 June 2017, seven months after Gazette publication. Part III of the Act gives legal recognition to electronic writing, electronic signatures and digital signature certificates, and the Act defines electronic commerce and distance contracts.

Rules made under the law and the law applied. The Act is held in the MalawiLII version, which includes amendments published up to 31 October 2021. That version is the nearest held statement on how the Act has been changed or applied since it commenced in June 2017, and it names no regulation made under the Act. In that version the Act sits as Chapter 74:02.

Not held. No decree, regulation or order made under the law is held, and nothing shows the law applied in practice.

NAM.short: Namibia's 2019 e-transactions law was applied in 2026, with a first certification provider accredited in September; the consumer protection chapter is not yet in force.
NAM.summary:
Law in force. Namibia's Electronic Transactions Act 4 of 2019 was promulgated in Government Gazette 7068 on 29 November 2019, covering legal recognition of data messages, electronic signatures, contracts, consumer protection and accreditation of security services. It was brought into force on 16 March 2020 by GN 75/2020, except section 20 (electronic signatures), Chapter 4 (consumer protection) and Chapter 5 (accreditation). Section 20 and Chapter 5 came into force on 15 June 2026 by GN 182/2026; Chapter 4 is annotated as not yet in force.

Rules made under the law and the law applied. Government Notice 335 records the Electronic Signature Regulations under section 20, signed 27 November 2025. CRAN also made regulations on accreditation of security products and services and certification service providers, published 17 December 2025. In the week of 3 September 2026 CRAN accredited the Ministry of Home Affairs as Namibia's first Certification Service Provider under the Act, for four years. DigiNam, the national public key infrastructure, was launched on 31 August 2026 under the Act, with CRAN as Root Certification Authority.

Not held. No count of accredited providers beyond the first, and no date for Chapter 4.

NER.short: Niger's 2019 electronic transactions law is presented by the ministry as governing; rules made under it and its application are not known.
NER.summary:
Law in force. The ministry's page presents Loi 2019-03 of 30 April 2019 on electronic transactions in Niger as governing electronic transactions. The law covers electronic signatures, contracts and payments, data retention and sanctions, so one text carries both the rules for electronic dealings and the penalties for breaching them. It dates from April 2019 and is presented on the page as the current text.

Rules made under the law and the law applied. The same ministry page is the nearest statement on rules made under the law: it presents Loi 2019-03 as the governing text for electronic transactions in Niger No decree, regulation or order made under it is named, and no figure for how the law is applied is given.

Not held. No decree, regulation or order made under the law is held, and no date of entry into force is held.

NGA.short: Nigeria's electronic-signature rules are in a bill the House approved by May 2026 and the Senate had not passed; the rules are not known.
NGA.summary:
Law in force. Nigeria has a bill, not yet a law. TechCabal reports that the National Digital Economy and E-Governance Bill, introduced in July 2024, gives qualifying electronic signatures the same validity as handwritten ones. By May 2026 the House of Representatives had approved the bill, and it was waiting for the Senate.

Rules made under the law and the law applied. Because the bill has not passed, no rules are yet made under it and nothing is applied. The nearest held fact is its design: as TechCabal describes it, the bill empowers the National Information Technology Development Agency (NITDA) to accredit certification authorities, the bodies that vouch for electronic signatures. That power sits in a bill that was still before the Senate in May 2026.

Not held. No source held says a law on electronic transactions or e-commerce is in force.

RWA.short: Rwanda's consumer law has had an e-commerce chapter in force since 4 March 2026; rules made under it are not known.
RWA.summary:
Law in force. Rwanda regulates e-commerce through its consumer law. Law 011/2026 of 26 February 2026 on competition and consumer protection carries a chapter on e-commerce, from Article 41 onward, setting obligations for an e-commerce enterprise and for an online intermediary. It came into force on its publication in the Official Gazette on 4 March 2026.

Rules made under the law and the law applied. The nearest held fact is the content of the law itself. Its e-commerce chapter, set out in the Official Gazette of 4 March 2026, places duties on two kinds of party, the e-commerce enterprise and the online intermediary, and has applied from that date. No decree, regulation or order made under the law is held, so the duties are stated at the level of the law.

Not held. No source held names a decree, regulation or order made under the law.

SDN.short: Sudan's Electronic Transactions Act of 2007 is the law cited in the May 2026 SudaPass terms; rules made under it are not known.
SDN.summary:
Law in force. Sudan's Electronic Transactions Act of 2007, with its amendments, is the law the national digital identity service relies on. The SudaPass terms of use, published on 21 May 2026, treat it as the governing law. They state that a digital signature meeting its requirements is equivalent to a handwritten signature (Article 8).

Rules made under the law and the law applied. The same SudaPass terms show the Act applied in a government service: they cite its Article 28 for punishing forgery and its Article 8 for the standing of digital signatures. This is the only application held, dated 21 May 2026. No decree, regulation or order made under the Act is held, so the rules are stated at the level of the Act itself.

Not held. No source held names a decree, regulation or order made under the law.

SEN.short: Senegal's 2008 law on electronic transactions and its 2008 implementing decree are in force; any use of them since 2023 is not known.
SEN.summary:
Law in force. Law no. 2008-08 of 25 January 2008 on electronic transactions gives electronic records and signatures equivalence with paper and sets rules for electronic commerce. The National Assembly adopted it on 30 November 2007. It is the law that gives electronic contracts and signatures their legal effect in Senegal, and the decree below is made to apply it.

Rules made under the law and the law applied. Decree no. 2008-718 of 30 June 2008 on electronic commerce was made to apply law no. 2008-08. It sets supplier information duties on what sellers must tell buyers, contractual liability, electronic advertising and electronic contract rules. The nearest held fact on application is that the decree was made in 2008; nothing held dates an application of the rules since.

Not held. No accreditation, licence, registration or penalty under the law in the last three years is held.

SLE.short: Sierra Leone's Electronic Transactions Act has been in force since 2019, but in July 2026 its enforcement was not fully set up.
SLE.summary:
Law in force. Sierra Leone's Electronic Transactions Act, Act 89 of 2019, is in force. The SierraLII record gives assent and commencement on 5 December 2019 and promulgation on 14 January 2020. Sierra Loaded reports that it gives legal recognition to electronic signatures, consumer protection and digital communications in courts. The UNECA digital trade profile lists it among the country's frameworks, with intermediary safe-harbour and consumer-protection provisions.

Rules made under the law and the law applied. Sierra Loaded reports that at a government dialogue on implementing the Act on 27 and 28 July 2026, its enforcement structures were not yet fully established. These include digital certification authorities, electronic evidence procedures, dispute resolution and penalties. The law is in force, but the machinery for applying it was still being set up in July 2026.

Not held. No source held names a decree, regulation or order made under the law.

SOM.short: Somalia's E-Transactions Law was described in August 2026 as moving through the legislative process; no law is known to be in force.
SOM.summary:
Law in force. Somalia has a draft, not a law in force. A Ministry of Information adviser, writing in a personal capacity in an article published on 19 August 2026, says an E-Transactions Law is moving through the legislative process, alongside a Data Protection Act and a Cybersecurity Bill. No date is given for the stage it has reached.

Rules made under the law and the law applied. Because the E-Transactions Law is still moving through the legislative process, as the adviser writes, no rules are made under it and nothing is applied. The same article names the Data Protection Act and the Cybersecurity Bill as companion measures in the same process, which places the law among three pieces of digital legislation under way in August 2026.

Not held. No source held says a law on electronic transactions or e-commerce is in force.

SSD.short: No law on electronic transactions or e-commerce, or draft of one, is known for South Sudan as at 2026, so no stage is set.
SSD.summary: Not held. Nothing held names a law on electronic transactions or e-commerce or a draft of one, or says there is none.

STP.short: São Tomé and Príncipe passed an e-signature law, reported in 2025; no rules made under it or use of it are known.
STP.summary:
Law in force. São Tomé and Príncipe has an E-Signature Law, the name the project report gives it. The World Bank's April 2025 implementation status and results report for the Digital Sao Tome and Principe project states that the law was passed. The report was published on 11 April 2025 and gives no date of passage or of entry into force, so that publication date is the latest date at which the law is stated to exist.

Rules made under the law and the law applied. The nearest held fact is the passing of the E-Signature Law, which the World Bank's implementation status and results report for the Digital Sao Tome and Principe project records in a report published on 11 April 2025. It states that the law was passed, and the page for the country stops at that statement.

Not held. No decree, regulation or order made under the law is held.

SWZ.short: Eswatini has an Electronic Communications Transactions Act of 2022, listed in 2024 as overseen by the regulator; no rules made under it are known.
SWZ.summary:
Law in force. Eswatini has the Electronic Communications Transactions Act of 2022. APC, in an article published on 22 July 2024, lists the Act among the ICT laws that the regulator ESCCOM oversees. The same article says that the four 2022 ICT Acts were tabled in Parliament under certificates of urgency, a procedure used to move the bills through quickly.

Rules made under the law and the law applied. The nearest held fact is the Act itself, which APC's article of 22 July 2024 lists among the ICT laws overseen by ESCCOM, the regulator named there. The article places the Act in the group of four 2022 ICT Acts and the article, published in July 2024, is the held statement of the Act's place among the laws of the sector.

Not held. No decree, regulation or order made under the law is held.

SYC.short: Seychelles has had an electronic transactions act in force since 2001, recognising electronic records and digital signatures; rules made under it are not known.
SYC.summary:
Law in force. The Electronic Transactions Act, 2001 (Act 8 of 2001) commenced on 20 December 2001 and gives legal recognition to electronic records and digital signatures. The consolidation published by SeyLII shows the Act as amended and current to 29 March 2018. The Act is the law that governs electronic dealings in Seychelles, and it has been in force since 2001.

Rules made under the law and the law applied. The consolidated text lists one further amendment as outstanding, Statutory Instrument 12 of 2024, which is not yet worked into it. It names no regulation on electronic signatures, on those who certify them or on those who sell online, and it records no accreditation, licence, registration or penalty under the Act.

Not held. No decree, regulation or order made under the law on signatures, certifiers or online sellers is held, and the 2024 amendment is not held.

TCD.short: Chad has a 2015 law on electronic transactions, and electronic signatures count in finance ministry correspondence from 2026; rules under the law are not known.
TCD.summary:
Law in force. Chad has Law No. 008/PR/2015 on electronic transactions, which the regulator ARCEP's register of laws lists among the country's laws; the register gives the law's year, 2015, and no other date. A second provision gives electronic signatures force: Article 53 of Law No. 008/AN/SENAT/2025, the finance law for 2026, makes electronic signature compulsory for administrative correspondence in the finance ministry from 1 January 2026 and states that it has the same legal value as a handwritten signature.

Rules made under the law and the law applied. The nearest held fact is Article 53 of the 2026 finance law, which sets the electronic signature in the finance ministry's administrative correspondence from 1 January 2026, and it states that this signature has the same legal value as a handwritten one.

Not held. No decree, regulation or order made under the law is held.

TGO.short: Togo's 2017 electronic transactions law, amended in 2023, and its 2018 decree on sellers, signatures and trust providers are in force.
TGO.summary:
Law in force. Decree 2018-062/PR of 21 March 2018 is made in application of Law 2017-007 of 22 June 2017 on electronic transactions, which it cites as the law governing electronic contracts, written records, electronic signatures and online selling. Law 2023-012 of 19 July 2023, published in Journal officiel no. 55 bis, amends the 2017 law. It redefines its terms and adds rules on electronic seals, digital safes and 20-year retention of electronic copies and signatures, and a penalty for usurping the status of trust service provider.

Rules made under the law and the law applied. The same Decree 2018-062/PR, adopted by the Council of Ministers on 21 March 2018, has 105 articles. It regulates electronic transactions and services under the 2017 law: formalities for e-commerce sellers in Article 6, electronic signatures and qualified certificates, trust service providers and the accreditation procedure.

Not held. No accreditation, licence, registration or penalty under the law in the last three years is held.

TUN.short: Tunisia has had an electronic exchanges and commerce law since 2000, reinforced in 2020, and no implementing rule is known.
TUN.summary:
Law in force. Law no. 2000-83 of 9 August 2000 on electronic exchanges and commerce was published in the Journal Officiel no. 64 of 11 August 2000 and gives electronic documents and signatures legal effect. Decree-law 2020-31 of 10 June 2020 (JORT no. 54) took effect on publication. It gives a reliable electronic signature the same evidentiary force as a handwritten one, and electronic documents the same force as paper.

Rules made under the law and the law applied. Law 2000-83 creates the national electronic certification agency (ANCE) and licenses certification providers.
