Managers interviewed for a study published in March 2026 said the ministry has developed an e-Health Strategy, cited as the National eHealth Strategy 2021-2025, to guide a digital platform for capturing patient data. The minister's budget speech of 6 May 2025 asked N$62.5 million for health data and policy support, with expanding the e-Health network among its priorities, and Namibia launched a National Digital Health Policy for 2026 to 2036 in February 2026.

Tiers in use. IHCIMS, launched for every facility, was fully deployed only at Windhoek Central Hospital and Oshakati State Hospital, on the study of September 2025.

Where data is digitised. Practitioners reach a patient's record only through the paper health passport and manual records, and there is no unique patient identifier, the same study states. The minister said in March 2026 that the system still faces paper-based records.

Last twelve months. The managers said in the study of March 2026 that the platform was starting with a billing module on pilot at Katutura and Windhoek Central hospitals.

Primary clinics doing the digital input. The health minister said on 6 May 2025 that five health centres and 18 clinics had the e-Health system's network in operation. The study of September 2025 states that the ministry still relies on paper records in most hospitals and clinics.

Not held. No count or share of primary clinics keeping an electronic record is held: the five health centres and 18 clinics of May 2025 are sites with the network in place. No budget line names the record system itself.

NER.short: Computerised patient records were set up in health centres and district hospitals in three districts (November 2024); how many centres is not known.
NER.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The mid-term evaluation for Enabel, of November 2024, states that the Enabel project PASS Sutura started the digitalisation with recruited consultancy firms, with the Ministry of Health's digital health directorate involved. PASS Sutura is a Belgian bilateral project with EUR 14.5 million for health over 2022-2026, and a Netherlands co-financing of EUR 3.2 million to 31 March 2025 puts particular emphasis on digitalisation. On 8 July 2026 the health minister opened the workshop validating the costed roadmap of the Schéma Directeur National de la e-Santé 2025-2029.

Tiers in use. By November 2024 the project had set up digitalisation, including computerised medical records and billing, in the integrated health centres (CSI) and district hospitals of Dioundiou, Gothèye and Gaya.

Where data is digitised. Enabel states that a hospital information system built around a computerised medical record was put in place at the district hospitals of Gaya and Gothèye after field missions in February and April 2024.

Last twelve months. At the workshop of 8 July 2026 the Directorate of e-Santé presented OpenClinic, its project for a hospital information system and computerised patient record, as already under way.

Primary clinics doing the digital input. The evaluation of November 2024 places the digitalised health centres in the project's three target health districts only. In September 2018 the ministry's strategy reported electronic patient record activity in two health districts, Gaya and Gothèye, of 72.

Not held. No count of health centres using the computerised record is held, and no denominator. Nothing held says whether the record is made at the point of care or keyed afterwards, and no sites or counts are given for OpenClinic.

NGA.short: 100 of Lagos State's 326 primary clinics record care electronically as it happens (May 2025); there is no national figure.
NGA.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The Federal Ministry of Health and Social Welfare's Nigeria Digital Health Architecture of December 2025 sets interoperable electronic health record systems across all levels of care as its first pillar. In the memorandum signed with the United States on 19 December 2025, Nigeria commits to roll digital medical records out in 20% of facilities by 2026 and 100% by 2030, and the United States plans approximately US$28 million for an enhanced electronic medical record system over 2026-2030.

Tiers in use. The Minister of State for Health told the National Council on Health on 20 November 2025 that over 200 hospitals are integrated with electronic medical records systems. In Lagos State an EMR was in use in primary health care centres in May 2025.

Where data is digitised. In May 2025 the Lagos State Primary Health Care Board described its EMR as working "at the point of care". The federal architecture of December 2025 states that health data systems remain largely siloed and paper based, especially in public facilities.

Last twelve months. On 16 September 2026 the minister of state for health said the electronic medical record systems deployed in health facilities are fragmented and that minimum standards would be set and enforced.

Primary clinics doing the digital input. The Lagos State Ministry of Health reported on 22 May 2025 the EMR platform deployed in 100 of the state's 326 primary health care facilities.

Not held. No national share or count of primary clinics using an EMR is held; the figure is Lagos State's alone, and the over 200 hospitals have no denominator or tier. No shared record on a unique identifier is evidenced, and Nigeria's own commitment to data systems is not broken down to the EHR.

RWA.short: All 42 district hospitals used electronic patient records in 2023, and the national system reached most public facilities by 2026; shared records are not shown.
RWA.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. Rwanda Biomedical Centre slides of April 2026 present eBuzima as the national system for all public health facilities, served from the Ministry of Health's own domain. In a memorandum signed on 5 December 2025 and running from April 2026 to December 2030, the government commits to expand national EMR systems across all health facilities. The United States plans to allocate US$6,806,292 over 2026 and 2027 to the e-Buzima rollout, and Rwanda commits to pay the ongoing licensing, cloud and hardware costs the United States does not.

Tiers in use. A survey of April and May 2023 found all 42 district hospitals using an electronic medical record system, 35 of them OpenMRS. King Faisal Hospital Rwanda, a referral hospital in Kigali, runs an Integrated Health Management Information System that gives each patient a single record, the Tony Blair Institute reported in July 2026.

Where data is digitised. The April 2026 slides describe eBuzima as centralised, web-based and synchronising records across public facilities.

Last twelve months. By 8 April 2026 eBuzima had been rolled out to the majority of public health facilities, with its HIV key-population and PrEP modules running in one Kigali pilot site.

Primary clinics doing the digital input. Tom Frieden wrote in a piece published in September 2026 that eBuzima is in more than two thirds of health centres. The 2023 survey found 71 of 215 randomly sampled public health centres (33.0%) using an electronic medical record system.

Not held. No unique patient identifier and no record retrieved at another facility is established. No count of facilities using eBuzima is held, nor who enters the record at the health centres or where it is keyed.

SDN.short: A hospital system with electronic medical records was launched at two hospital sites on 11 May 2026; routine use is not yet shown.
SDN.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The Ministry of Health and the Ministry of Digital Transformation and Communications launched the hospital management system (HMS) on 11 May 2026 as their own programme, on the Sudan News Agency's report. ICTworks' directory, as of July 2026, lists the Sudan eHealth Strategy of the WHO Global Observatory's 2014 cycle as the operative digital health instrument and states that no replacement has been promulgated.

Tiers in use. Phase one of the HMS started on 11 May 2026 at two hospital sites, Al-Nao hospital in Khartoum state and the diagnostic centre of Gedaref hospital, ahead of gradual expansion to health institutions in other states.

Where data is digitised. An MSc thesis at Sudan University of Science and Technology, of March 2021, states that hospitals in Sudan had no electronic medical records and kept patients' health records on paper.

Last twelve months. A directive published on 30 March 2026 has the Prime Minister ordering hospital systems digitised within two weeks through a first pilot phase at Soba teaching hospital and Gedaref hospital. The HMS launched on 11 May 2026 includes an electronic patient record and an electronic medical record.

Primary clinics doing the digital input. The first phase directed in March 2026 covers two hospitals only, with wider expansion left to a later phased plan. The thesis of March 2021 states that government clinics had no electronic medical record and depended wholly on paper records.

Not held. Whether the two sites are in routine use, the hospitals' level and where the record is entered are not established. No funding source is named for any system, and no sites or counts are held for SudaHealth, the Khartoum State platform.

SEN.short: The patient record runs only at pilot sites, in 1% of the 102 health centres (October 2025); health posts are not counted.
SEN.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The World Bank, in a paper of January 2026, names the Ministry of Health and Public Hygiene as lead agency, deploying the electronic medical record. The ministry's sector policy letter of 25 March 2025 sets the generalisation of the computerised patient record under its Health System Digitalisation Programme 2023-2029. The record is a core activity of the US$46 million health component of the IDA-financed Senegal Digital Economy Acceleration Project.

Tiers in use. The health ministry states that the record, which it calls the Dossier Patient Informatisé, has been in use since November 2024 at the Thierno Birahim Ndao regional hospital in Kaffrine. We Are Tech Africa reported on 30 April 2025 a completed pilot at two hospitals, the Khadim Rassoul health centre and the HLM Fass health post.

Where data is digitised. At the Kaffrine hospital the patient is created in the system at registration and the doctor enters observations directly into it after the consultation, on the ministry's account, since November 2024.

Last twelve months. The World Bank records that a pilot of the record across 51 health centres had not started as of December 2025, delayed by disagreement between the health and digital ministries.

Primary clinics doing the digital input. The World Bank's results framework gives 1 per cent of the 102 district-level health centres as using electronic medical records at 31 October 2025. An electronic record was available for 200,000 primary care patients at the same date.

Not held. Retrieval of a patient's record at another facility is not stated, and the 1 per cent counts health centres only, with health posts outside it. Nothing held says whether the 51-centre pilot began in 2026.

SLE.short: Electronic records run at one government hospital and one clinic (2026); a national system is not known to have been bought.
SLE.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. OpenMRS's case study of April 2026 describes the PIH EMR as Partners In Health's own OpenMRS distribution. The National Health Compact of 6 December 2025 commits the Government to roll out Electronic Medical Records to all medical facilities by 2030 and names a Ministry of Health directorate as lead. The Ministry's request for expressions of interest of 18 December 2025 states that a donor grant finances the initial phase.

Tiers in use. The case study states that Koidu Government Hospital, a referral centre, uses the PIH EMR and that the EMR has run at Wellbody Clinic since 2015. The Ministry reported on 11 October 2023 that it and Smart Systems Sierra Leone Ltd had launched an EMR pilot at Connaught Hospital in Freetown.

Where data is digitised. The case study states that the EMR at the Maternal Center of Excellence in Koidu is entered at the point of care, with retrospective entry also possible.

Last twelve months. The Maternal Center of Excellence opened on 14 February 2026 with the EMR covering all its inpatient wards. On 18 December 2025 the Ministry's project unit asked firms to express interest in deploying an OpenMRS-based EMR across 300 health facilities.

Primary clinics doing the digital input. The case study of April 2026 names one clinic using the PIH EMR, Wellbody Clinic. The Compact of 6 December 2025 gives a baseline of 5 health facilities implementing the system, in a network it puts at about 1,463 public facilities.

Not held. What share of primary clinics keep patient records electronically is not held, nor the present state of the pilots at other primary facilities. The Compact's baseline of 5 facilities is undated, and the Ministry's national EMR is not shown procured.

SOM.short: Two electronic record systems run in over 40 facilities (April 2026) and 111 primary facilities (2025); their share of all clinics is unknown.
SOM.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. By its own account the Ministry of Health developed RAAD as a national electronic health record for primary healthcare, implemented between 2023 and 2025. Its bulletin for July to September 2023 says the pilot was supported by the Government of Sweden through SPIDER. The Caafimaad+ Digitalized Data System (C+ DDS) is run by the CaafimaadPlus consortium of ten NGOs, in partnership with the Federal Ministry of Health, and funded by EU Humanitarian Aid, as the consortium stated in April 2026.

Tiers in use. The ministry's case study places RAAD in public primary healthcare facilities only, between 2023 and 2025.

Where data is digitised. RAAD captures clinical data as routine care documentation, in place of an average of 15 paper forms, on the ministry's case study of 2023 to 2025. The consortium said in April 2026 that C+ DDS replaces manual reports with real-time entry and makes a family's record available at any facility on the system.

Last twelve months. The consortium reports growth from a five-facility pilot in mid-2024 to over 40 facilities by April 2026.

Primary clinics doing the digital input. In April 2026 the consortium reported C+ DDS operational in over 40 facilities across 9 regions and more than 25 districts of South-Central Somalia. The ministry's case study reports RAAD deployed in 111 public primary healthcare facilities across six states between 2023 and 2025.

Not held. No count of all primary clinics is held to set either figure against, and the two systems' facilities are not shown to be separate. No plan naming an electronic medical record, no unique patient identifier and no tier for the C+ DDS facilities is held.

SSD.short: An electronic record tried at two hospitals in 2019 never reached routine use; nothing else shows patient records, so no stage is set.
SSD.summary: Not held. No electronic medical record in routine use is held, and no dated statement that patient records are on paper at every tier. An electronic medical record deployed at two hospitals in 2019 did not reach routine clinical use, and the 22.4% of health facilities that the February 2025 assessment records with facility-wide electronic systems comes with no system named.

STP.short: A patient record was piloted at the central hospital and in one health area in 2022; whether it was extended is not known.
STP.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The National Health Development Plan 2023-2032, dated September 2022, sets a strategic axis on expanding what it calls the single clinical process to the whole national health system. The Joint SDG Fund programme's final report of 26 July 2022 states that the Single Process module for patient files was developed inside DHIS2, the Ministry of Health's main information software, and that rolling it out beyond the pilot will be done with funding from other donors.

Tiers in use. In September 2022 the plan placed the record in a pilot phase at the Ayres de Menezes central hospital and the Água Grande Health Area.

Where data is digitised. The report of July 2022 states that patient data is entered from reception through the nurses and doctors, each patient's file reached by a bar code sticker and scanner.

Last twelve months. The plan of September 2022 states that the pilot is to be evaluated before expansion to the whole national health system.

Primary clinics doing the digital input. At 26 July 2022 the Single Process had not been rolled out to other districts and still needed consolidating in the first pilot district, Água Grande. The plan states that computerised clinical records are to be introduced gradually through a pilot model of health centres and the central hospital.

Not held. Nothing is dated after September 2022: whether the pilot was evaluated, consolidated or extended beyond Água Grande is not established. The health area's facilities are not named and no count of facilities using the record is given.

SWZ.short: A shared electronic record runs in 73% of all health facilities (2026); it stays at stage 3 because no current plan or budget was found.
SWZ.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. Data.FI described the Client Management Information System (CMIS) in April 2026 as an open-source, government-owned electronic medical record. The Ministry of Health's HMIS unit describes itself as custodian of the digital health systems, with its own in-country developers working on CMIS. Data.FI, a PEPFAR-funded USAID agreement, reported for the period ending March 2024 that it funds and carries out CMIS system development, security assessment and facility network support.

Tiers in use. Data.FI described CMIS in April 2026 as in use in the outpatient department of Piggs Peak Government Hospital and at local health clinics.

Where data is digitised. Data.FI said in April 2026 that clinicians open a client's full record on a unique ID number at their point of service, and that the record is available to clinicians at another clinic if the patient moves district.

Last twelve months. The HMIS unit reported in June 2026 that the integration of CMIS with eLMIS runs for ART medicines only and is ready for a facility-level pilot. In the first quarter of 2026 its developers completed training that produced automated, FHIR-aligned data flows from CMIS to DHIS2.

Primary clinics doing the digital input. Data.FI said in April 2026 that CMIS is used in 73% of the country's health facilities, with 233 live sites. For the period ending March 2024 it reported CMIS in use at 75% (247 of 327) of healthcare facilities.

Not held. No current plan naming CMIS and no domestic budget line for it is held. The 73% is a share of all health facilities with no denominator given, and no count of primary clinics alone is held.

SYC.short: A ministry system with electronic medical records has run since the end of 2021; whether clinics record on it or on paper is not known.
SYC.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. Seychelles Nation reports the health minister saying on 17 October 2023 that the Ministry of Health is investing in an Electronic Health Information System encompassing Electronic Medical Records, the ministry's name for it. The National Health Strategic Plan 2022-2026 sets specific objective 6.8, "Implement eHIS", and names the Health Care Agency as lead entity, with the Ministry of Health and the Public Health Authority contributing. Seychelles News Agency reports that the software is funded through a line of credit from the Indian government of around USD 4 million, under a contract of December 2019.

Tiers in use. The minister said in October 2023 that the system is to be accessible to all health professionals throughout the health system.

Where data is digitised. The Health Care Agency's chief executive said in June 2023 that some doctors still use handwritten notes. At its digital health visioning meeting of 22 January 2024 the ministry said it was trying to link the system with laboratories and X-ray so that doctors get results on their computers.

Last twelve months. A ministry press release carried by Seychelles Nation in January 2024 states that the system has been operational since the end of 2021.

Primary clinics doing the digital input. The Health Care Agency said in June 2023 that it was training doctors to use the electronic medical records clinic by clinic.

Not held. Sources do not agree on whether records in the clinics are entered electronically or on paper, so the tiers using the system and where the record is entered are not established. No count or share of clinics is published, and nothing dated inside the last twelve months is held.

TCD.short: The ministry signed a partnership for electronic medical records in its hospitals (reported August 2026); no facility is yet shown using one.
TCD.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The Ministry of Public Health and Prevention leads the electronic medical record initiative, with HISP Rwanda as technical assistant, HISP Rwanda states. Guinéenews reports that Kouma Academy supplies its Visa Medical record under a model in which the company invests its own funds in the equipment and infrastructure of public hospitals, and has an agreement with the ministry.

Tiers in use. The partnership Guinéenews reported on 13 August 2026 is for the national digitalisation of the country's hospitals with the Visa Medical digital medical record.

Where data is digitised. HISP Rwanda describes the record whose implementation it supports as a patient-centred Dossier Médical Électronique.

Last twelve months. On 15 April 2026 the ministry's Secretary-General chaired a high-level meeting devoted to modernising the patient medical record, and by 13 August 2026 Kouma Academy had signed its partnership with the ministry.

Primary clinics doing the digital input. Guinéenews describes the partnership as covering the country's hospitals.

Not held. No electronic medical record is held in use at any facility: no tier, no place of digitisation and no clinic figure. Neither the partnership nor the ministry's initiative carries a deployment, a pilot site, a budget or a timetable.

TGO.short: The World Bank reported in December 2025 that no electronic health record system was in place.
TGO.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The World Bank's additional-financing paper of 24 December 2025 states that since October 2025 the health ministry has been responsible for the health and insurance systems layer, including the electronic health record (EHR). The financing pays EUR 866,112.50 on establishment of the system and EUR 173,223 for every 10 contracted facilities with an EHR.

Tiers in use. The paper records "No" at December 2025 for the establishment of an electronic health record system.

Where data is digitised. The Togo Digital 2025 strategy of April 2021 plans a digital and centralised medical record, as something to be developed.

Last twelve months. On 24 December 2025 the World Bank put forward additional financing, a EUR 60.6 million credit and US$11 million in grants, with new conditions for establishing an EHR in facilities contracted under the national health insurance scheme, starting with a pilot.

Primary clinics doing the digital input. The paper's results framework gives a baseline of 0 facilities contracted with the national health insurance scheme holding an EHR at December 2025, out of about 335 contracted facilities.

Not held. No source states in terms that patient records are on paper at every tier, and the baseline does not cover facilities outside the insurance scheme. Where records are digitised is not held.

TUN.short: Electronic records are fully used in 50% of university hospitals and 32% of regional hospitals (2025), with pilot sites in one region's primary care.
TUN.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. WHO Tunisia stated in April 2024 that the Ministry of Health's Information Technology Centre develops and implements the hospital information management system, with a focus on electronic medical records. The draft National Health Policy of 2019 calls for the generalisation of a single, digitised medical record. The first-line record, which the programme calls the DMI, was developed under Essaha Aziza, a Ministry of Health and European Union programme.

Tiers in use. The World Bank's project document of 2 April 2025 gives the record as fully installed and used in 50 per cent of university hospitals and partially used in the other 50 per cent, and as fully operational in 32 per cent of regional hospitals, partially used in 52 per cent and absent from 16 per cent. In district hospitals it is neither installed nor used.

Where data is digitised. Of primary health care, the same document states that the health system remains largely paper-based and that the DMI pilot faces connectivity and functionality issues.

Last twelve months. The Ministry of Health confirmed on 21 July 2026 that the Sahetna.tn portal, through which citizens are to reach their medical records, had completed technical validation and a cybersecurity audit; it was not yet in service.

Primary clinics doing the digital input. Essaha Aziza states that it monitored the DMI's deployment on pilot sites in Nabeul. DH Arab, on the ministry's account at 25 September 2026, has 99 healthcare facilities at various stages of implementing electronic medical records.

Not held. No count of hospitals or of primary clinics using the record is held; the 99 facilities carry no tier and the Nabeul pilot sites no number. The plan is an uncosted draft of 2019, and no domestic budget line for the record is named.

TZA.short: A government system runs in 23.25% of all health facilities (2023 survey); records are not shown to be shared between facilities.
TZA.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The mid-term review of the Health Sector Strategic Plan V, published in March 2025, states that the Ministry of Health developed and launched Afya eHMS for all regional hospitals and plans to phase out the vendor-dependent Medipro and E-Medical used in zonal and specialised hospitals. It records that the Digital Health Strategy 2019-2024 had run out and its 2025-2030 successor was still being developed.

Tiers in use. The Citizen reported on 1 September 2026 that electronic medical record coverage had reached 100 percent of national, specialised, zonal and regional referral hospitals, and that adoption had expanded across district hospitals, health centres and dispensaries. The mid-term review of March 2025 states that all 28 regional hospitals use Afya eHMS.

Where data is digitised. The ministry's guidelines of May 2019 state that most confidential health data is held in health facilities in paper-based registers.

Last twelve months. The Permanent Secretary of the Ministry of Health said on 1 October 2025 that the country has an integrated electronic medical records system linking a patient's information from community level through health centres and district hospitals to national level.

Primary clinics doing the digital input. The mid-term review, citing the SARA survey of 2023, gives 23.25% of all health facilities using GOT-HoMIS, the government's facility system, against 44.9% of health centres and 10.63% of dispensaries. In March 2025 it states that more than 3,000 primary health care facilities use it as their electronic medical record system.

Not held. Nothing held establishes where the patient record is digitised or whether it can be retrieved at another facility. No financing is stated, no dated event falls in the last twelve months, and no community system is shown exchanging with the EMR.

UGA.short: The ministry's electronic record ran in referral and general hospitals and seven health centres in 2025; records are not shown to be shared.
UGA.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The Ministry of Health's guidelines of 18 September 2024 name the ministry as owner of the Electronic Medical Records System. The US-Uganda memorandum signed on 10 December 2025 names eAfya and ClinicMaster as the Government of Uganda's electronic medical records and sets a functional EMR in all facilities down to Health Centre III by 2028. Under it the United States plans US$113,102,289 for data systems over 2026-2030.

Tiers in use. The ministry says that as of 2025 the EMR is in referral and general hospitals and in some health centres. In Kiryandongo district it was in use in September 2026 at the general hospital, Nyakadoti Health Centre III and Mpumwe and Apodorwa Health Centre IIs.

Where data is digitised. The in-charge of Nyakadoti Health Centre III said on 19 September 2026 that patient data must be captured in the EMR at every stage of the visit. A census of all 265 government Health Centre IVs and hospitals, published in October 2025, found 94.3% keeping both paper and digital patient records.

Last twelve months. On 31 March 2026 Makerere University's METS programme handed the UgandaEMR repositories to the Ministry of Health. Health workers told a baraza on 19 September 2026 that the EMR was slowing care in Kiryandongo facilities because of poor connectivity, unstable power and too few computers.

Primary clinics doing the digital input. The ministry counts 5 Health Centre IVs and 2 Health Centre IIIs using the EMR as of 2025.

Not held. Nothing held shows a record retrievable at another facility, or what share of primary clinics use the EMR; hospital coverage is disputed between the ministry and a census of government facilities. No domestic budget line for the EMR is held.

ZAF.short: Hospital systems run in five provinces and 308 Western Cape primary facilities use electronic records (August 2025); there is no national count.
ZAF.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The Minister of Health told Parliament on 1 August 2025 that the National Department of Health is developing a single common Electronic Medical Record for primary health care facilities. The department's bid document of March 2026 says it developed the EMR itself and that its Digital Health Unit directs implementation.

Tiers in use. The same reply counts Clinicom in 53 Western Cape hospitals, the eHealth system in 42 KwaZulu-Natal public hospitals and HMS2 in 16 Free State hospitals. It states that Mpumalanga, North West, Limpopo and Northern Cape are not implementing such systems at hospitals.

Where data is digitised. The department describes its EMR, in March 2026, as capturing clinical information at the point of care, verified against the patient's identifier in the Health Patient Registration System.

Last twelve months. In March 2026 the department invited bids to scale up its EMR to all fixed primary health care facilities in eight provinces within 18 months. The Free State Department of Health won the Public Sector Digital Innovator Award for deploying its primary health care EMR, SAnews reported in May 2026.

Primary clinics doing the digital input. The Minister's reply states that the National EMR beta ran in 36 primary health care facilities between 22 October 2024 and 13 February 2025 and that Western Cape's Primary Health Care Information System is implemented in 308. It counts 3,333 primary health care facilities reporting to the 2024/25 Ideal Clinic Assessment.

Not held. No count of primary facilities using the national EMR in 2026 is held, and no total of hospitals against which the provincial counts can be set. Nothing held shows a record retrieved at another facility, and no funding source is named.

ZMB.short: An electronic record system was in use at 877 of 3,540 health facilities of all kinds (April 2025); the share of primary clinics is unknown.
ZMB.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The Global Fund's case study of April 2025 states that the Ministry of Health developed SmartCare and describes it as co-financed by the Global Fund. SMART Zambia's national coordinator said on 7 July 2026 that government aims at full national coverage of SmartCare Pro.

Tiers in use. SmartCare 2.0 Hospital Edition went live as a pilot at Ndola Teaching Hospital on 27 April 2026. Interviews of May and June 2019 found some larger health centres and hospitals collecting data in the electronic health record, in select districts.

Where data is digitised. The programme managers' presentation of March 2025 describes SmartCare Pro as capturing the patient encounter at facility level, on a central server that identifies each client uniquely and tracks patients between facilities. The implementers described in January 2026 a nurse at a rural clinic in Kafulafuta identifying a patient by fingerprint to reach his record.

Last twelve months. ITWeb Africa reported on 16 July 2026 that SmartCare Pro and SmartCare 2.0 will be migrated to the government-owned GovLink network, with three Copperbelt hospitals connected first.

Primary clinics doing the digital input. The Global Fund states that SmartCare Pro is in use at 877 health facilities, against 3,540 health facilities in Zambia, at April 2025. The March 2025 presentation puts SmartCare Legacy and SmartCare Plus together in approximately 1,800 healthcare facilities. SMART Zambia's national coordinator said on 7 July 2026 that SmartCare Pro has been deployed in approximately 80% of health facilities nationwide.

Not held. No count or share of primary clinics using SmartCare is held: every figure counts health facilities of all kinds, and the 80% is of deployment, with no numerator or denominator. Use at the primary tier rests on 2019 interviews and one rural clinic, and nothing held shows a record retrieved at a second facility in practice.

ZWE.short: An electronic record system ran in 1,254 health facilities of all types in August 2025, out of 1,900 planned; shared records are not shown.
ZWE.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The Global Fund said in August 2025 that the Government of Zimbabwe has been developing a national EMR system since February 2015, culminating in Impilo, for use in public health facilities. The ministry's National Health Strategy 2021-2025 commits to supporting the deployment of what it calls the electronic health record (Impilo) system. The Global Fund has put over US$43.1 million into digital health in Zimbabwe since 2014, US$9.85 million of it in the 2024-2026 grant cycle.

Tiers in use. The Permanent Secretary for Health and Child Care told The Sunday Mail on 17 November 2024 that the facilities with Impilo are spread across provinces and districts and include clinics, hospitals and other health centres.

Where data is digitised. A 2025 abstract on the DHIS2 community site states that Impilo captures real-time clinical and administrative data for services including HIV testing, antiretroviral therapy and maternal and child health, stored in centralised repositories and a national data warehouse.

Last twelve months. The Herald on 23 September 2026 described Impilo as the Ministry of Health's own electronic health records platform.

Primary clinics doing the digital input. The Global Fund reports 1,254 health facilities implementing Impilo as of August 2025, with deployment planned for all 1,900 health facilities. The Permanent Secretary put deployment at 1,178 health facilities on 17 November 2024. The Matabeleland South provincial health team reported 110 of the province's 153 health facilities (71.9%) with Impilo fully functional in May 2025.

Not held. Nothing held says an Impilo record can be retrieved at another facility. The counts are of facilities of every type where Impilo is deployed, not of primary clinics entering records, and no strategy current at 30 September 2026 is held.

AGO.short: Angola adopted its ICT white paper for 2023-2027 by presidential decree in December 2024; whether its text is public is not known.
AGO.summary:
Governance and finance. The telecommunications ministry, MINTTICS, put the proposed Livro Branco das TIC 2023-2027 to public consultation in 2024, and its minister writes that the policy aligns the sector with the National Development Plan 2023-2027.

Standing. The Livro Branco das TIC 2023-2027 was approved by Presidential Decree 272/24 of 5 December 2024, repealing the Livro Branco das TIC 2019-2022.

Text. The ministry's site carries Presidential Order 129/19 of 22 July 2019, which approved the Livro Branco das TIC 2019-2022, with a download link.

Period. The policy runs from 2023 to 2027, with five objectives targeted by 2027.

Delivery plan. A later decree describes the policy as setting policy measures and strategic actions for the ICT sector on six axes.

Reporting. In October 2025 the ministry reported that the president's State of the Nation message credited the Livro Branco das TIC and its instruments with moving the sector from reform to development.

Last twelve months. A March 2026 article cites the policy as setting plans for a space studies centre, expert training and communications, navigation and meteorology infrastructure.

Not held. Whether the text of the Livro Branco das TIC 2023-2027 is public is not known. Nothing is held on a mandated body, finance, a delivery plan or reporting against the policy, and no dated change to it falls in the twelve months to 30 September 2026.

BDI.short: The national ICT development policy adopted in 2011 ran to 2025; whether a successor is being prepared is not known, so no stage is set.
BDI.summary: Not held. The Politique nationale de développement des TIC (PNDTIC) 2010-2025 reached the end of its period in 2025, and no successor sector policy is held as announced, in drafting or validated. No delivery plan, report against the policy's targets or event in the last twelve months is held, and the newest facts on the responsible ministry and on finance date from 2021 and 2022.

BEN.short: A digital economy sector policy declaration adopted in 2016 ran to 2021; whether a successor exists is not known, so no stage is set.
BEN.summary: Not held. The Déclaration de politique sectorielle de l'économie numérique ran to 2021, and no successor sector policy is held as adopted or in preparation. No mandated body, finance, report against the policy's targets or event in the twelve months to 30 September 2026 is held.

BFA.short: The sector policy published in 2015 ran to 2020; whether a successor is in preparation is not known, so no stage is set.
BFA.summary: Not held. The newest sector policy on record is the Politique sectorielle de l'Economie numérique et des Postes 2016-2020, which the ministry published in September 2015 and whose period ended in 2020. Whether a successor sector policy has been announced, drafted, validated or adopted is not known, and nothing is held on a delivery plan, reporting or finance for the 2016-2020 policy.

BWA.short: Botswana has a national ICT policy approved by its National Assembly in 2007; its period, delivery plan and reporting are not known.
BWA.summary:
Governance and finance. The contents of the National ICT Policy (Maitlamo) of 2007 list a governance structure of an Information Age Council, an ICT Legal Reform Taskforce, an enhanced Department of Information Technology and an e-Governance Structure.

Standing. The National Assembly approved the policy in August 2007, as Government Paper No 3 of 2007, and a report published in December 2025 refers to it as Botswana's existing policy.

Text. The Ministry of Communications, Science and Technology published the full text in August 2007.

Period. The World Bank's 2022 diagnostic says the policy was launched in 2007.

Delivery plan. The same diagnostic says the policy was launched to guide the development of the sector.

Reporting. The December 2025 report gives the policy's aim as faster, cheaper and more transparent government services in support of socioeconomic development.

Last twelve months. The policy of 2007 was still the one named for Botswana in the report of December 2025.

Not held. Nothing held gives the policy an end year, a delivery plan, a report against its targets or a source of finance. Its governance bodies are known only from the 2007 text, and no dated event falls in the last twelve months.

CAF.short: A national digital strategy is held but no ICT sector policy is named; whether one exists is not known, so no stage is set.
CAF.summary: Not held. No ICT or telecommunications sector policy is named for the country. Whether one has been adopted, is in preparation or does not exist is not known.

CIV.short: Côte d'Ivoire has a national digital strategy for 2021 to 2025; whether it has an ICT sector policy is unknown, so no stage is set.
CIV.summary: Not held. No ICT sector policy is on record for Côte d'Ivoire, whether adopted, in preparation or expired. The only instrument held is the national digital strategy.

CMR.short: A posts, telecommunications and ICT sector strategy was finalised in 2005 with targets to 2015; its adoption is not known, so no stage is set.
CMR.summary: Not held. No source states that the Stratégie sectorielle des postes, télécommunications et TIC 2005 was adopted by decree or by the minister: it is held as finalised at a seminar in September 2005, and its targets ended in 2015. No successor sector policy is on record as adopted or in preparation, and no text, report against it, responsible body, budget line or activity in the last twelve months is held.

COD.short: DR Congo's 2009 telecommunications and ICT sector policy lapsed in 2014; whether a successor is being prepared is not known, so no stage is set.
COD.summary: Not held. The Document de politique sectorielle 2009 ran out in 2014 without its review, and no sector policy is held in preparation to succeed it. Its text, the cost of its targets for 2015, reporting, governance and finance, and any movement in the last twelve months are not held.

COG.short: A national ICT policy was drawn up in 2008-2009; whether its text was ever published is not known.
COG.summary:
Governance and finance. A project coordination unit in the Ministry of Posts and Telecommunications in charge of ICT was to monitor implementation of the National ICT Policy, as a project appraisal document of May 2011 set out.

Standing. The government drew up its national ICT development policy in 2008-2009, the minister told the Council of Ministers on 6 March 2019. An appraisal document of 4 May 2011 treats the National ICT Policy as existing.

Text. The 2011 appraisal document does not describe the policy's scope.

Period. The Council of Ministers communique of 6 March 2019 gives no date of adoption for the policy.

Delivery plan. In 2011 a project steering committee was to check project activities against the National ICT Policy.

Reporting. The coordination unit was to monitor the policy's implementation together with the government's ICT strategy, under the 2011 appraisal document.

Last twelve months. The latest dated fact is of 6 March 2019, when the minister said the electronic transactions bill follows the national ICT development policy.

Not held. Whether the policy's text was published, when and by what act it was adopted, the period it covers, and whether it has a delivery plan or any reporting. Nothing dated in the last three years says who runs or funds it.

COM.short: A telecommunications and digital sector policy, which the minister said in 2022 was being implemented; its text and adoption date are not known.
COM.summary:
Governance and finance. The minister for posts, telecommunications and the digital economy said in September 2022 that the country was implementing its sectoral policy.

Standing. The Politique sectorielle des télécommunications et du numérique is adopted: the minister told the ITU's plenipotentiary conference in September 2022 that Comoros was in the process of implementing it. The ministry's mission page, dated to 2016, refers to a "new sector policy" without saying that it was adopted.

Text. The ministry's mission page names the new sector policy beside the Comores numérique strategy.

Period. The ministry's page, dated to 2016, calls the sector policy new, and the minister described it as being implemented in September 2022.

Delivery plan. The ministry's page places the government's action within the new sector policy and the Comores numérique strategy.

Reporting. The minister's statement to the ITU conference says the sectoral policy is being implemented.

Last twelve months. The minister's statement that the policy is being implemented dates from September 2022.

Not held. No text of the policy is held, and nothing gives its adoption date, its period, a delivery plan, a report against it, a mandated body or a budget line. Nothing on the policy is dated after September 2022.

CPV.short: No ICT or telecommunications sector policy is on record as of 2026; whether one exists is not known, so no stage is set.
CPV.summary: Not held. No ICT or telecommunications sector policy is on record as adopted, in preparation or absent. A national digital strategy is held instead and is assessed on its own row.

DJI.short: Djibouti's sector policy, adopted in 2014, ran to 2024; whether a successor is adopted or being prepared is not known, so no stage is set.
DJI.summary: Not held. The Schéma stratégique intégré (SSI) 2014-2024, approved by a law published in February 2015, ended in 2024, and no successor sector policy is on record as adopted or in preparation; no text, dated action plan, report or finance is held for it. The Politique nationale de développement des TIC, which the minister named in July 2025, has no adoption date, period or text on record.

DZA.short: Algeria has a post and telecommunications ministry action plan, reported in 2023; whether a sector policy exists is not known, so no stage is set.
DZA.summary: Not held. No ICT or telecommunications sector policy is on record as adopted or in preparation, and no dated statement that the country has none is held. The one sector instrument on record is a ministry's action plan.

EGY.short: The 2013 national ICT strategy ran to 2017; whether the strategy to 2030 was adopted is not known, so no stage is set.
EGY.summary: Not held. The National ICT Strategy 2013-2017 reached the end of its period in 2017, and no sector policy is held as adopted or in preparation after it. The ministry's web page gives the ICT 2030 Strategy a period, to 2030, and nothing else: whether it was adopted, is being drafted or was only announced is not known, and neither are its text, governance, delivery plan or reporting.

ERI.short: Eritrea had no national ICT policy or development plan in 2009, UNECA said; whether one has been adopted since is not known.
ERI.summary:
Governance and finance. A UNECA paper on Eastern Africa, published in April 2009, states that Eritrea has no National ICT Development Agency.

Standing. The UNECA paper of April 2009 states that Eritrea has no national ICT policy defining the government's orientation and strategies for development, and its table of 13 states enters "No ICT Policy" against the country.

Text. UNECA, in April 2009, states that Eritrea has no national ICT policy.

Period. UNECA, in April 2009, states that Eritrea has no national ICT policy.

Delivery plan. The same UNECA paper states that no National ICT Development Plan exists for Eritrea.

Reporting. UNECA, in April 2009, states that Eritrea has neither a national ICT policy nor a National ICT Development Plan.

Last twelve months. The UNECA statement that Eritrea has no national ICT policy dates from April 2009.

Not held. The only statement that Eritrea has no ICT sector policy is UNECA's of April 2009, and nothing later confirms or contradicts it. Nothing is held on governance, finance or the last twelve months.

ETH.short: Ethiopia adopted a national ICT policy and strategy in 2016, endorsed by ministers in 2017; whether its text is published is not known.
ETH.summary:
Governance and finance. The Ministry of Innovation and Technology is mandated under the Communication Services Proclamation of 2019 to develop policy instruments, mobilise resources and guide and monitor the telecom sector. It was formed in October 2018 by merging the Ministry of Communication and Information Technology with the Ministry of Science and Technology. The policy's 2017 revision had financial support from the World Bank.

Standing. The National ICT Policy and Strategy was developed in 2016 and endorsed by the Council of Ministers in 2017.

Text. UNCTAD cites the policy as a 2016 document of the federal government.

Period. The policy revises one first drafted and submitted to the Council of Ministers in 2002.

Delivery plan. UNCTAD lists the interventions through which the policy is implemented.

Reporting. UNCTAD said in September 2021 that implementation was fragmented across projects and sectors.

Last twelve months. In September 2021 the policy was still being implemented.

Not held. Whether the policy's text is published, the period it covers, a delivery plan with dates or costs, and any report against its targets. No domestic budget line is stated, and nothing dated in the last twelve months is held.

GAB.short: Gabon had formulated a national ICT policy by 2022, a JICA study says; its adoption date, text and period are not known.
GAB.summary:
Governance and finance. A JICA baseline study of public service digitalisation in African countries, published in March 2022, states that Gabon has formulated a national ICT policy, the Politique nationale des TIC.

Standing. The JICA study of March 2022 states that Gabon has formulated a national ICT policy consistent with the PSGE Vision 2025, and gives no date of adoption.

Text. JICA, in March 2022, states that the national ICT policy has been formulated.

Period. The JICA study states that the policy is consistent with the PSGE Vision 2025.

Delivery plan. JICA, in March 2022, states that Gabon has formulated a national ICT policy.

Reporting. The same JICA study states that the policy has been formulated, consistent with the PSGE Vision 2025.

Last twelve months. The JICA statement that Gabon has formulated a national ICT policy dates from March 2022.

Not held. The only statement of the policy is JICA's of March 2022, which gives no adoption date. The policy's text, period, delivery plan, reporting, mandated body and finance are not held, and nothing is dated since.

GHA.short: Ghana's telecommunications policy of 2005 is in force with no end date; whether it reports against its targets is not known.
GHA.summary:
Governance and finance. The National Telecommunications Policy of 2005 makes the Ministry of Communications responsible for defining and reviewing telecommunications policy and the National Communications Authority responsible for implementing it. A guide published on 20 September 2024 says the Ministry of Communications and Digitalization directs communications-sector policy.

Standing. The Ministry of Communications released the National Telecommunications Policy as final on 10 January 2005. A report published on 8 October 2025 recommends updating it and the ICT for Accelerated Development Policy of 2003, and calls both outdated.

Text. The full 33-page text is on the National Communications Authority's website.

Period. The policy states no end date for itself and provides for the ministry to review and amend it.

Delivery plan. The policy sets dated actions and targets with no costs, among them 25% penetration and universal access by 2010.

Reporting. The policy gives the Ministry of Communications the monitoring of progress.

Last twelve months. The report of 8 October 2025 still names the 2005 policy as Ghana's.

Not held. No report against the policy's targets, no cost for its actions and no source of finance is held. No sector policy is held as adopted or in preparation to succeed it, and no dated event falls in the twelve months to 30 September 2026.

GIN.short: A digital sector policy letter was announced in a national strategy published in 2024; whether drafting has begun is not known.
GIN.summary:
Governance and finance. The national digitalisation strategy, published in June 2024, puts the drafting of the Lettre de politique sectorielle du numérique under the ministry it calls MPTEN, with the executive, and costs it at USD 50 thousand.

Standing. The letter is announced as initiative 1.1.8 of that strategy, to be drafted. The government adopted the Politique et stratégie nationales de développement des TIC in 2010.

Text. The strategy lists the letter as a document still to be drafted.

Period. The strategy allows six months for the drafting and gives it no date. An earlier national information and communication infrastructure plan covered 2001 to 2004.

Delivery plan. The 2010 policy set six aims and proposed one computer for each secondary pupil, higher-education student and teacher, with no cost or dates stated.

Reporting. UNESCO's profile of 2023 reports later initiatives launched in line with the 2010 policy.

Last twelve months. The latest dated fact on the letter is its listing in the strategy published on 11 June 2024.

Not held. Whether drafting of the sector policy letter has begun, and any text, period, delivery plan or report for it. The text of the 2010 policy is not held, and nothing on the letter is dated in the twelve months to 30 September 2026.

GMB.short: The Gambia has an ICT for development policy statement adopted for 2018 to 2028; whether its text is public is not known.
GMB.summary:
Governance and finance. The ICT4D Policy Statement 2018-2028 appears in a 2025 presentation by the Ministry of Communications and Digital Economy on data governance in The Gambia.

Standing. The ministry's presentation lists the statement among the country's existing policies, strategies and legal frameworks, and a Principal Assistant Secretary at the ministry named it in October 2026 among The Gambia's ICT policies.

Text. The presentation sets out the statement's nine priority areas.

Period. The statement runs from 2018 to 2028, as the ministry's presentation titles it.

Delivery plan. The presentation gives the statement's priority areas beside the ministry's other policies and strategies.

Reporting. The head of the Gambian delegation said in October 2026 that the country had already built gender considerations into the statement.

Last twelve months. The statement was on the ministry's list of policies in 2025.

Not held. No source holds, links or quotes the statement's text, and none says it is unpublished. Nothing is held on a delivery plan, reporting against targets, a mandated body or finance, and no dated event falls in the twelve months to 30 September 2026.

GNB.short: An ICT strategy was in preparation in 2021, when the regulator produced a preliminary report; whether it was adopted is not known.
GNB.summary:
Governance and finance. The regulator, ARN, produced the preliminary report on an ICT strategy in December 2021.

Standing. An ICT strategy was in preparation in Guinea-Bissau in December 2021, when the regulator issued a preliminary report on it.

Text. The strategy appears as a preliminary report of December 2021, cited for its data in the Guinea-Bissau Digital Economy Diagnostic.

Period. The same diagnostic also cites a "Preliminary ICT strategy report 2022" alongside the December 2021 report.

Delivery plan. By December 2021 the work on the strategy had reached a preliminary report, which the regulator ARN produced.

Reporting. The Guinea-Bissau Digital Economy Diagnostic, published in 2022, takes data from the regulator's preliminary ICT strategy report.

Last twelve months. The regulator's preliminary report dates from December 2021, and the diagnostic citing it from 2022.

Not held. The one source cites the regulator's preliminary report without giving the strategy's scope or saying it was adopted, and nothing dated since shows whether drafting continued. No text, period, delivery plan, reporting, responsible body or finance is held.

GNQ.short: No ICT or telecommunications sector policy is held; whether one is adopted or in preparation is not known, so no stage is set.
GNQ.summary: Not held. No ICT or telecommunications sector policy is held as adopted or in preparation, and no dated statement that the country has none is held. No mandated body, finance, delivery plan, report or event in the twelve months to 30 September 2026 is held.

KEN.short: Kenya has a national ICT policy adopted in 2019 and gazetted in 2020; its period, delivery plan and reporting are not known.
KEN.summary:
Governance and finance. Research ICT Africa's report of September 2026 says the Ministry of Information, Communications and the Digital Economy is responsible for policy formulation and sector coordination, with the Communications Authority as regulator.

Standing. The ICT Sector Policy Guidelines 2006 were reviewed and updated to a National ICT Policy in 2019, and the policy was gazetted in 2020 as Gazette Notice No. 5472.

Text. The policy was published in a special issue of the Kenya Gazette, and the September 2026 report cites it to a page on the ministry's website.

Period. The draft artificial intelligence policy of July 2026 lists the National ICT Policy 2019 among the instruments in place.

Delivery plan. The Communications Authority's consultation of September 2026 says the policy directs government agencies to promote and license private investment in carrier-neutral data centres.

Reporting. A 2022 review of the Digital Literacy Programme says the policy sets objectives for scaling up ICT in education.

Last twelve months. An analysis published in July 2026 names the ICT policy among Kenya's existing instruments.

Not held. Nothing held gives the policy an end year, a delivery plan, a report against its targets or a domestic budget line. Sources give both 2019 and 2020 as its year, and no dated event falls in the last twelve months.

LBR.short: Liberia's ICT policy, adopted in 2019, ran out in 2025 and a 2025-2030 successor is in draft; when it will be adopted is not known.
LBR.summary:
Governance and finance. The National ICT Policy 2019-2024 gives the Ministry of Posts and Telecommunications overall coordination, implementation, review and oversight, and the national digital strategy published in February 2026 says its governing board, chief information officer and council of chief information officers were put in place. On money, the policy says the Executive ensures resources are available to the ministries concerned.

Standing. The government adopted the policy in 2019, and the President signed it that year.

Text. The full text is on the ministry's website.

Period. The policy set itself five years, 2019 to 2024, and was extended to 2025. The ministry's draft of its successor, the National ICT Policy 2025-2030, dated 7 January 2025, lists it as expired.

Delivery plan. The policy carries a summary of measurable targets with timelines of one to five years after adoption.

Reporting. An appendix to the national digital strategy reviews the policy's initiatives and says its targets have not been met, among them internet access at 50% of clinics and hospitals.

Last twelve months. The national digital strategy, published on 3 February 2026, says the successor policy has been drafted and is in consultation, with approval targeted for the last quarter of 2025. A press release of 8 September 2026 lists a draft National ICT Policy.

Not held. No adoption of the National ICT Policy 2025-2030 is on record. A budget line for the 2019-2024 policy is not held.

LBY.short: Libya has a telecommunications and informatics strategy for 2023 to 2027, in use in 2025; whether its text is published is not known.
LBY.summary:
Governance and finance. The General Authority for Communications and Informatics (GACI) is the authority competent to regulate and develop the telecommunications and information technology sector, and it is the body that announces work done under the strategy.

Standing. In October 2025 GACI announced root servers in Tripoli and Benghazi as implementing the National Telecommunications and Informatics Strategy 2023-2027.

Text. The Ministry of Telecommunications and Informatics says the strategy aims to develop digital infrastructure and the sector's efficiency.

Period. The strategy covers 2023 to 2027, and the ministry gave the same years in October 2026.

Delivery plan. At a GACI workshop in February 2026, officials stated the aim of drafting legislation and a guidance manual for data centres and cloud computing.

Reporting. GACI presented the root-server launch of October 2025 as the strategy being carried out.

Last twelve months. Root servers entered service in data centres in Tripoli and Benghazi in October 2025. On 15 February 2026 GACI held a workshop in Tripoli on regulating data centres and cloud computing, within the national communications strategy.

Not held. No text of the strategy is held, and no source says whether it is published. No adopting act or date, delivery plan, budget line or report against the strategy's own targets is held.

LSO.short: Lesotho has a communications policy adopted in 2008 with no end year; its delivery plan and reporting are not known.
LSO.summary:
Governance and finance. The Lesotho Communications Policy 2008 makes the Lesotho Communications Authority the regulator for telecommunications, broadcasting and postal services, with the Minister setting basic policy. A 2025 tender notice says the ministry will review the policy with the authority.

Standing. The government adopted the policy in 2008. Before it came the Lesotho Telecommunications Policy 1999 and the ICT Policy for Lesotho 2005. The Lesotho ICT Policy 2021 was in draft in March 2022.

Text. The Ministry of Communications, Science and Technology published the full text, which the government's website hosts.

Period. The policy states no end year or review date.

Delivery plan. The policy states no budget line for its own implementation and provides for a Universal Service Fund drawing up to two percent of operators' net operating income.

Reporting. The National Digital Policy of December 2024 says the monitoring system planned under the ICT Policy for Lesotho 2005 was never established.

Last twelve months. The ministry sought consultants in mid-2025 to review the 2008 policy and draft a Lesotho Communications Policy (2025), with bids closing on 21 July 2025.

Not held. No delivery plan and no report against the 2008 policy is held, and its finance is known only from the 2008 text. The ICT Policy 2021 is held only as a draft and the 2025 review only as a tender, and nothing is dated in the last twelve months.

MAR.short: A telecommunications sector policy note adopted in 2019 ran to 2023; whether a successor is being prepared is not known, so no stage is set.
MAR.summary: Not held. The Note d'orientations générales du secteur des télécommunications à horizon 2023, adopted on 26 December 2019, ran to 2023, and no successor note is held as adopted or in preparation. No report against its targets, no finance for it and no event in the twelve months to 30 September 2026 is held.

MDG.short: A national ICT for development policy dates from 2004, with targets assessed in 2022; whether its text is public or still open is not known.
MDG.summary:
Governance and finance. The MPTDN formulated the Politique nationale des TIC pour le développement in 2004 with support from UNDP.

Standing. A JICA study of March 2022 describes the 2004 policy as the Malagasy government's main ICT policy.

Text. The JICA study reports the policy as setting seven strategic objectives.

Period. The policy's targets run to 2015 for the digital network and to ten years from 2004 for users and engineers.

Delivery plan. The targets include a digital network covering every fivondronana by 2015, 10 million ICT users and 30,000 ICT engineers. The policy states no cost.

Reporting. In March 2022 JICA assessed progress against the policy's objectives: legal and regulatory reform was relatively advanced, while network extension and the training of ICT engineers were behind for lack of funds.

Last twelve months. The latest account of the policy is JICA's of March 2022.

Not held. The policy's text, an act adopting it and a stated period are not held, so whether the 2004 policy is still open is not known. No mandated body or finance since September 2023 is held, and no event in the twelve months to 30 September 2026.

MLI.short: A national ICT policy was adopted in 2005; whether its text is public and what period it covers are not known.
MLI.summary:
Governance and finance. The Politique nationale des TIC 2005 names financing as one of its six priorities, alongside the legal framework, infrastructure, content and applications, media, and cooperation.

Standing. The Government adopted the national information and communication technology policy in 2005. It followed the Déclaration de politique sectorielle des télécommunications, which the Government adopted in 2000.

Text. The national digital economy strategy of November 2014, Mali Numérique 2020, sets out the 2005 policy's six priorities.

Period. The policy dates from 2005.

Delivery plan. The 2000 telecommunications declaration set the country's telecommunications objectives and an action programme. The 2005 policy is built on six priorities.

Reporting. Mali Numérique 2020 states in 2014 that the Government adopted the policy.

Last twelve months. The policy was adopted in 2005, and the telecommunications declaration before it in 2000.

Not held. No text of the 2005 policy is held, and no source says it is unpublished. No period, delivery plan, results report, mandated body or budget line is held for it, and nothing is dated within the last twelve months; its adoption is known only from a 2014 document.

MOZ.short: Mozambique's Information Society Policy was adopted in 2018 with no end date; whether results against its targets are reported is not known.
MOZ.summary:
Governance and finance. Resolution 19/2018 gives the National Institute of Electronic Government (INAGE) the task of mobilising the money, materials and staff for the policy. The policy says its implementation depends on internal and external finance and private investment, and names no budget line. In 2022 INTIC said its work aimed to implement the policy.

Standing. The Council of Ministers approved the Política para a Sociedade da Informação on 20 March 2018 by Resolution 17/2018, in force from 21 June 2018. It revokes the Política de Informática of 2000.

Text. The full text is printed in the Boletim da República, I Série, no. 122, of 21 June 2018.

Period. The policy states no end date and no review year.

Delivery plan. The policy says an Operational Plan sets the actions, those responsible and the calendar for each five years of the Strategic Plan, and states no cost. Resolution 52/2019 approved the 2019-2028 Strategic Plan to put the policy into operation.

Reporting. INTIC's activity report for 2022 says its efforts that year aimed to implement the policy and its Strategic Plan.

Last twelve months. INTIC's 2022 activity report names the policy as approved by Resolution 17/2018.

Not held. No report against the policy's own targets is held, and the Operational Plan that carries its actions is not held. Nothing dated in the past three years says which body is responsible for the policy or how it is financed.

MRT.short: A sector policy declaration was adopted in January 2013; whether its text is public and whether it is still in force are not known.
MRT.summary:
Governance and finance. The ministry's presentation, published in April 2019, names better regulation of the sector as one of the declaration's four pillars.

Standing. The Déclaration de politique sectorielle is adopted: the ministry's presentation states that a new sector policy declaration was adopted in January 2013.

Text. The ministry's presentation gives the declaration's four pillars as competition and investment, consumer protection, the sector's spillovers for the economy, and better regulation.

Period. The presentation dates the declaration's adoption to January 2013.

Delivery plan. The presentation sets the declaration out as four pillars, the first of them competition and investment.

Reporting. The ministry's presentation, published in April 2019, describes the declaration as new and as adopted in January 2013.

Last twelve months. The ministry's account of the declaration dates from April 2019.

Not held. The text of the declaration is not held. Nothing gives its period, a delivery plan, a report against it, a mandated body or a budget line, and nothing on it is dated after April 2019.

MUS.short: A national ICT policy issued in 2007 ran to 2011; whether a successor is being prepared is not known, so no stage is set.
MUS.summary: Not held. The National ICT Policy 2007-11, issued in September 2007, ended in 2011, and no successor sector policy is held as adopted or in preparation. The National ICT Strategic Plan it relies on, any report against it and any event in the twelve months to 30 September 2026 are not held.

MWI.short: Malawi has a National ICT Policy dated 2013 with its text public; whether the 2022 draft policy was adopted is not known.
MWI.summary:
Governance and finance. The Digital Government Strategy of September 2019 says it will assist the Ministry of Information in implementing the targets in the National ICT Policy.

Standing. The National ICT Policy 2013 is listed in the policy framework of a 2025 management plan for the government data centre. A UNCDF scan of May 2023 calls it outdated and in need of updating, and the Presidential Delivery Unit produced a draft National ICT and Digitalization Policy in 2022.

Text. An essay of March 2026 links a copy of the 2013 policy's text in the ITU national strategies repository.

Period. The 2022 draft is titled 2022-2026.

Delivery plan. The Digital Government Strategy of 2019 lists an action to update the National ICT Policy, owned by the Ministry of Information and the Department of E-Government.

Reporting. The same strategy says the government carried out an ICT sector review during 2013-2017.

Last twelve months. A GSMA report of August 2026 lists the National ICT Policy 2013 among the prior policies on which current digital strategies build.

Not held. The act and date that adopted the National ICT Policy 2013 are not known, and no period is given for it. No delivery plan of the policy and no report against it is held, nothing on its governance is dated within three years, and whether the 2022 draft was validated or adopted is not known.

NAM.short: Namibia launched a national ICT policy in January 2026; its text, end year, delivery plan and budget are not known.
NAM.summary:
Governance and finance. The National ICT Policy 2026 sets out clear roles for the institutions responsible for implementing and monitoring ICT development, The Namibian reported in January 2026.

Standing. The Ministry of ICT launched the policy at Opuwo in January 2026. It follows the Overarching ICT Policy 2009, which the National Broadband Policy gazetted on 14 August 2020 says it is built on, and the National ICT Policy / Broadband Policy, which the ITU's repository lists among Namibia's strategies.

Text. The Namibian reported the policy's launch on 29 January 2026.

Period. The minister said at the launch that the policy would guide the ICT sector over the next five years. The ITU's repository gives the earlier National ICT Policy / Broadband Policy a time frame of 2018 to 2022.

Delivery plan. The 2026 policy gives institutions their roles in implementing ICT development.

Reporting. For the earlier National ICT Policy / Broadband Policy, the ITU's repository records training programmes as evidence of implementation.

Last twelve months. The ICT minister launched the policy in January 2026.

Not held. The text of the National ICT Policy 2026 is not held, and nothing held links to it or quotes it from an official site. Its period has no end year, and no delivery plan, report against it or budget line is on record.

NER.short: A telecommunications and ICT sector policy was adopted in 2013 and ended in 2020; no successor sector policy is known, so no stage is set.
NER.summary: Not held. The Document de politique sectorielle des télécommunications et des TIC 2013-2020 ended in 2020, and no successor sector policy is held as adopted or in preparation; an update was instructed in July 2017 and no updated policy is held. Nothing is held on the policy's text, on a mandated body or its finance, or on any event in the twelve months to 30 September 2026.

NGA.short: Nigeria's telecommunications policy of 2000 is still in force and is being rewritten in 2026; its finance and reporting against its targets are not known.
NGA.summary:
Governance and finance. The National Telecommunications Policy 2000 assigns policy formulation to the Ministry of Communications and regulation to the Nigerian Communications Commission, and sets up a National Frequency Management Council in the Ministry.

Standing. The Minister of Communications' preface of May 2000 presents the policy as approved by the President, and the Commission's consultation paper of 9 February 2026 calls it the subsisting sector policy, in force for twenty-five years.

Text. The Ministry of Communications published the full text, in seventeen chapters, in May 2000.

Period. The consultation paper states no end date for the policy, whose Chapter 16 provides for review from time to time.

Delivery plan. The consultation paper proposes to add an implementation matrix with milestones, dependencies and responsible parties, which the 2000 text does not have.

Reporting. Chapter 16 of the policy names annual reports among its three implementation instruments, beside implementation machinery and a national forum.

Last twelve months. In February 2026 the Commission published fifteen proposals for rewriting the policy and invited comments by 20 March 2026, and in May 2026 it held a review workshop with regulators, operators and investors.

Not held. No report against the policy's own targets is held, and no source of finance is stated. The committees set up to review the policy belong to the rewrite, which is still being drafted and has not replaced the 2000 text.

RWA.short: Rwanda has an ICT sector plan for 2024-2029, published in 2025; whether results against it have been reported is not known.
RWA.summary:
Governance and finance. The ICT Sector Strategic Plan 2024-2029 commits the Ministry of ICT and Innovation and its affiliated agencies to deliver its programmes. The ministry convened the sector working group's review of the plan under the finance ministry's guidance on 22 November 2024.

Standing. The ministry published the plan, dated 1 January 2025 on its cover, as one it is committed to implement. A sector review of 22 November 2024 was convened to validate it.

Text. The plan is a PDF on the ministry's own site.

Period. The plan covers the financial years 2024/25 to 2028/29. The plan before it covered 2018-2024.

Delivery plan. The plan's contents list an implementation plan and a section on cost and financing, with budget allocated across priority areas. The November 2024 review sets out its targets, among them 1.5 million citizens trained in coding and ICT skills and 50,000 digital jobs.

Reporting. The sector review for 2023/24 reports against the 2018-2024 plan, and put digitised public services at 91% against a target of 100% by 2024.

Last twelve months. After a cabinet briefing on 24 July 2026 the ministry set 30 June 2027 as the date 3G is switched off nationwide, as part of the plan.

Not held. No report, review or evaluation of results against the 2024-2029 plan's own targets is held. No source ties a domestic budget line to the plan, and its costing is known from the contents list only, with no figures.

SDN.short: The National ICT Strategy 2021-2025 ended in 2025; whether a successor is being prepared is not known, so no stage is set.
SDN.summary: Not held. The National ICT Strategy 2021-2025 ran to 2025, and nothing held records a successor sector policy announced, in drafting or validated. No text, delivery plan or date of adoption is held, and nothing is dated in the last twelve months.

SEN.short: Senegal validated a sector policy letter for 2025-2029 in February 2025; whether it has been adopted is not known.
SEN.summary:
Governance and finance. The secretary general of the ministry chaired the final validation workshop for the Lettre de politique sectorielle 2025-2029 in February 2025.

Standing. The Lettre de politique sectorielle 2025-2029 is validated: the final validation workshop with the sector's actors was reported on 10 February 2025, and terms of reference dated July 2026 say the Ministry of Telecommunications and Digital has validated it.

Text. The terms of reference of July 2026 refer to the letter as the ministry's validated sector policy.

Period. The letter covers 2025 to 2029.

Delivery plan. The letter is tied to the National Development Strategy 2025-2029, as the terms of reference of July 2026 state.

Reporting. The terms of reference of July 2026 record the letter as validated by the ministry.

Last twelve months. Terms of reference of July 2026 state that the letter has been validated; the validation workshop was reported in February 2025.

Not held. No adoption of the letter is on record. Its text, a delivery plan, a report against it, a mandated body, a budget line and any dated event in the twelve months to 30 September 2026 are not held.

SLE.short: The 2009 ICT policy, reviewed in 2017, was replaced in 2021 by a national digital policy; no successor is known, so no stage is set.
SLE.summary: Not held. No sector policy is in force: the National ICT Policy approved on 28 October 2009 and reviewed in 2017 was replaced in 2021 by the National Digital Development Policy, and no sector successor is held as adopted or in preparation. No report against the 2009 policy and no budget line for it are held, and nothing is dated inside the last twelve months.

SOM.short: A National ICT Policy and Strategy for 2025-2029 was reported approved in 2025; whether its text is published is not known.
SOM.summary:
Governance and finance. The Ministry of Communications and Technology published a notice on 11 November 2025 for a consultant firm to prepare the National ICT Policy and Strategy 2025-2029. The consultancy is paid from an IDA grant under the Regional Digital Integration Project.

Standing. The minister told the WSIS+20 forum on 9 July 2025 that the Council of Ministers approved the National ICT Policy earlier in 2025. The notice of 11 November 2025 seeks a firm to renew the 2019-2024 policy as a 2025-2029 one, over about four months.

Text. The ministry published the full text of the National ICT Policy and Strategy 2019-2024 on its own site.

Period. The notice gives the new policy's period as 2025 to 2029, after one the Cabinet adopted on 28 November 2019 for 2019 to 2024.

Delivery plan. The 2019-2024 policy set a table of actions and targets, each with a year of delivery, and left the cost of each line to be determined.

Reporting. In August 2025 the minister said the Starlink launch supports the goals of the 2019-2024 policy.

Last twelve months. Expressions of interest for the consultancy were due on 29 November 2025.

Not held. The text of the 2025-2029 policy, a delivery plan for it and any report against its targets. The minister's statement of July 2025 and the notice of November 2025 differ on whether the policy is approved or still to be written. No domestic budget line is stated.
