SSD.short: A national ICT policy published in 2012 is public and was said in 2025 to be in implementation; its period, plan and results are unknown.
SSD.summary:
Governance and finance. The minister of ICT and postal services spoke for the policy at the 30th EACO Assemblies in Juba, reported in June 2025.

Standing. The Government of South Sudan published its National ICT Policy in 2012 as a government policy statement. In June 2025 the minister said the government is implementing the revised ICT Policy of 2012.

Text. The policy text is public on the ICT Policy Africa document page as a government publication.

Period. The policy is dated 2012.

Delivery plan. The text sets sector policy for posts, telecommunications and information technology.

Reporting. The minister's June 2025 statement that the policy is being implemented gave no figure or measure against the policy's targets.

Last twelve months. The latest statement on the policy is the minister's, published on 12 June 2025.

Not held. The policy's period, a delivery plan, a mandated body, a budget line and any report against its own targets are not held, and nor is an adopting act: the 2012 date is the publisher's. Nothing is dated in the twelve months to 30 September 2026.

STP.short: An ICT sector strategy was prepared in 2012 and was still awaiting adoption in June 2015; whether it was ever adopted is not known.
STP.summary:
Governance and finance. The ICT Sector Strategy was prepared in 2012 under the Central African Backbone project, which the World Bank financed; the programme as a whole carried an IDA grant of SDR 9.8 million.

Standing. The strategy was prepared in 2012 after wide consultation with stakeholders. In June 2015 its adoption by the Council of Ministers was still pending.

Text. The World Bank's completion report on the project, prepared in June 2015, names the strategy as prepared and not yet adopted.

Period. The strategy dates from 2012, the year it was prepared.

Delivery plan. The strategy was itself a product of the Central African Backbone project, prepared under it in 2012.

Reporting. The World Bank's completion report of June 2015 records the strategy as awaiting adoption by the Council of Ministers.

Last twelve months. In June 2015 the strategy was still waiting for the Council of Ministers to adopt it, three years after it was prepared.

Not held. Whether the strategy was adopted, dropped or replaced after June 2015. No text, period, delivery plan or report on it is held, and nothing is dated within the last twelve months.

SWZ.short: Eswatini has an ICT infrastructure policy adopted in 2006 with no end year; its delivery plan and reporting are not known.
SWZ.summary:
Governance and finance. Cabinet adopted the National Information and Communication Infrastructure (NICI) Policy in August 2006.

Standing. The policy is adopted. A stakeholder validation workshop endorsed the draft ICT policy in January 2006, and Cabinet adopted it that August as what the document calls the Swaziland National Information and Communication Infrastructure (NICI) Policy.

Text. The government site gov.sz hosts the policy as a PDF, in one file with its Implementation Plan 2012-2016. The document's published date is 1 August 2006.

Period. The policy is published with an Implementation Plan covering 2012 to 2016.

Delivery plan. The Implementation Plan 2012-2016 sits in the same document as the policy on the government site.

Reporting. The policy document records its own adoption in 2006 and its launch in 2007.

Last twelve months. The Prime Minister launched the policy on 3 August 2007.

Not held. No period of the policy's own is held: the only one on record, to 2016, is the Implementation Plan's. No adopted delivery plan, no report against the policy, no body or budget in the last three years and nothing dated in the last twelve months is held.

SYC.short: Seychelles has a National ICT Policy from 2007 with its text public; whether it has a delivery plan or reports results is not known.
SYC.summary:
Governance and finance. The National ICT Policy 2007 carries a foreword by the Minister for National Development and sets five focus areas: infrastructure, the legal and regulatory framework, human resources, industry and government.

Standing. The policy is published as the National ICT Policy for Seychelles, and a World Bank report of September 2026 treats it as in force.

Text. The full text is on the SCRA website as a PDF.

Period. The policy states no end year or period; it sets a vision and policy statements.

Delivery plan. The policy says it lays the foundation for a later National ICT Strategic Plan.

Reporting. The World Bank's Seychelles Country Growth and Jobs Report says digital skills are a core pillar of the policy.

Last twelve months. In September 2026 the World Bank named the policy beside the National Development Strategy (2024-2028) as carrying digital skills.

Not held. No delivery plan and no report against the policy is held, and nothing on a mandated body or a budget line in the last three years. The policy document is undated: 2007 is the date it is recorded as published, and the World Bank report gives no adoption date or scope.

TCD.short: A sector ICT plan adopted in 2017 ended in 2021; whether a successor is being prepared is not known, so no stage is set.
TCD.summary: Not held. No sector policy is on record as following the Plan Tchad Numérique 2017-2021, adopted or in preparation. No text, delivery plan, report, mandated body, finance or event in the last twelve months is held for that plan, the NICI plan 2007-2027 or the 1997 sector policy declaration.

TGO.short: A digital economy sector policy declaration of 2017 ran to 2022; whether a successor is being prepared is not known, so no stage is set.
TGO.summary: Not held. The Déclaration de politique du secteur de l'économie numérique 2018-2022, adopted in October 2017, reached the end of its period in 2022, and no successor sector policy is held as adopted or in preparation. Its text, delivery plan and finance are not held, nor is any report against it; the one fact on its steering bodies dates from 2017, and no event in the twelve months to 30 September 2026 is held.

TUN.short: Tunisia has a national digital strategy but no ICT or telecommunications sector policy is held, so no stage is set.
TUN.summary: Not held. No ICT or telecommunications sector policy is held as adopted or in preparation. The instruments held are national digital strategies, a ministry's annual performance plan and a programme, none of which is a sector policy.

TZA.short: Tanzania adopted its National ICT Policy in 2016 and a costed strategy ran to 2020/21; whether the 2023 review was adopted is not known.
TZA.summary:
Governance and finance. The ICT Commission, under the Ministry of ICT, has the role of ensuring the National ICT Policy is implemented, a November 2024 case study states. The policy's December 2016 implementation strategy names the Government budget, development partners and the private sector as its financing sources.

Standing. The National ICT Policy 2016 was signed by the Minister for Works, Transport and Communication in May 2016 as the Government's revision of the 2003 policy. A June 2025 report cites it as the country's ICT policy. The ministry issued a successor text dated June 2023, which states no adoption date.

Text. The full policy is published as a PDF on the ministry's website.

Period. The policy's implementation strategy covers 2016/17 to 2020/21.

Delivery plan. The strategy estimates that Tsh. 248.2 billion is required over its five years, with a logframe of 22 objectives giving targets, indicators, time frames and responsible institutions.

Reporting. The June 2023 successor text says the ministry will design a monitoring and evaluation system and evaluate after five years.

Last twelve months. In August 2026 The Citizen reported the ICT Commission's director general describing the 2016 policy as the one that followed the 2003 policy.

Not held. The 2016 policy's own period, any report of results against its targets, and a budget line tied to it in the past three years. Whether the 2023 successor text has been adopted is not known.

UGA.short: Uganda has a National ICT Policy of 2014, with a replacement drafted in 2022; whether the 2014 text is public is not known.
UGA.summary:
Governance and finance. The Ministry of ICT and National Guidance's report for the fourth quarter of 2021/22 shows its E-Services department running the drafting and Cabinet submission of a replacement National ICT Policy, on an output that also covers the National Cyber Security Strategy.

Standing. The Vision for a Digital Uganda 2040, of September 2022, lists the National ICT Policy 2014 among Uganda's key policies, as being reviewed. The final draft of its replacement, dated May 2022, names it among the key policies of the sector's current policy environment.

Text. The final draft of the replacement is online on the website of the consultant who prepared it.

Period. A case study of August 2024 describes Uganda's policy environment as starting with the National ICT Policy of 2003.

Delivery plan. The 2022 draft carries no implementation plan and says the ministry will develop a road map to inform an implementation matrix.

Reporting. The ministry's report of June 2022 says drafting of the replacement was complete and awaiting Cabinet approval. The Ministry of Finance's monitoring report for 2022/23 says stakeholder engagement was finalised, pending submission to the Cabinet Secretariat.

Last twelve months. Terms of reference issued by NITA-U in August 2026 cite a "Draft National ICT Policy, 2022" for the ICT sector's share of GDP.

Not held. No text of the National ICT Policy 2014 is held, and nothing gives its period, a delivery plan or a report against it. No adoption of the 2022 draft is on record, and nothing dated since 2023 says where it stands.

ZAF.short: South Africa adopted an ICT policy white paper in 2016, and whether it has a delivery plan or reports against its targets is not known.
ZAF.summary:
Governance and finance. In 2019/20 the Department of Telecommunications and Postal Services developed ICT policy and legislation for the sector through its Programme 3, ICT Policy Research and Capacity Development.

Standing. The Department issued the National Integrated ICT Policy White Paper in Government Gazette 40325 of 3 October 2016.

Text. The White Paper is published as a gazette file on gov.za and on the department's website, dcdt.gov.za.

Period. The White Paper's stated main purpose is to unlock ICTs to eliminate poverty and reduce inequality by 2030.

Delivery plan. In 2019/20 the Department pursued its legislative programme in line with the White Paper.

Reporting. The Department's 2019/20 annual report records, against the indicator "ICT legislation and policies in line with the White Paper", that the Digital Development Fund Bill, the Data and Cloud Policy and a framing document for the White Paper's review were developed.

Last twelve months. A World Bank report of June 2026 lists the White Paper among the key anchors of South Africa's policy framework, and a discussion document on universal access of October 2026 lists it as a policy instrument.

Not held. No delivery plan for the White Paper is held, and no report against its own targets. How the policy is financed and what came of the review framed in 2019/20 are not known.

ZMB.short: Zambia has a National ICT Policy published in 2023 with no end year; whether results against it have been reported is not known.
ZMB.summary:
Governance and finance. The National ICT Policy 2023 makes the ministry responsible for ICTs answerable for coordinating, implementing, monitoring and evaluating it, with ZICTA regulating the sector. It lists the national budget among seven possible sources of finance and states no budget line or amount.

Standing. The Ministry of Technology and Science published the policy on 11 October 2023 as the government's revision of the National ICT Policy 2006. In December 2025 the policy working group of an ITU event in Lusaka recognised it as the overarching framework governing ICTs in Zambia.

Text. The full text is on the ministry's website as a PDF.

Period. The policy states no end year. It is anchored on Vision 2030 and sets no term of its own.

Delivery plan. A ZDA sector profile of September 2024 says the 2022 to 2026 ICT Policy Implementation Plan lists seventeen investment actions, among them district fibre, a national internet exchange point, regional data centres and rural Wi-Fi, with no costs given.

Reporting. The policy gives monitoring and evaluation of its implementation to the ministry and the Cabinet Office.

Last twelve months. On 12 November 2025 the Ministry of Community Development and Social Services launched guidelines it said were aligned with the policy, TechAfrica News reports.

Not held. No report, review or evaluation against the policy's targets, and no adoption date beyond the text's publication. The implementation plan carries no costs and no budget line is tied to the policy.

ZWE.short: Zimbabwe has a public National ICT Policy for 2022 to 2027 with an uncosted action plan; results against its targets are not known.
ZWE.summary:
Governance and finance. The 2022 text of the National ICT Policy 2022-2027 names the Ministry of ICT, Postal and Courier Services as coordinator, with a National ICT Policy Advisory Council led by the Minister and a Policy Implementation Secretariat, and ties no budget line or amount to the policy.

Standing. The policy carries a presidential foreword and replaces the policy of 2016-2020, and Cabinet's briefing of 14 July 2026 names it among the frameworks of the national digital agenda.

Text. The full text of the policy, published in 2022, is public.

Period. The policy titles itself for 2022 to 2027, and an article of November 2025 gives it the same period.

Delivery plan. The policy's implementation plan sets out actions by priority area, with responsible bodies and periods from 2023 to 2027, and states no costs.

Reporting. The 2022 text gives the Policy Implementation Secretariat the task of tracking implementation.

Last twelve months. Cabinet named the policy on 14 July 2026, and on 20 July 2026 the head of the statistics agency referred to an ICT Policy for 2026 to 2030.

Not held. No report, review or evaluation against the policy's targets is held, and no adoption date is stated. The policy's bodies and finance are known only from the 2022 text, and nothing held gives the standing or text of the ICT Policy 2026-2030.

AGO.short: Angola's quality institute was a correspondent member of ISO in 2026; no international standard on information technology or data adopted nationally is known.
AGO.summary:
Membership and adoption. Angola's standards body is the Instituto Nacional da Qualidade e Infra-estruturas, known as INIQ. ISO's member register lists it as a correspondent member, on a page read in August 2026. In March 2026 the institute published its catalogue of standards for the year, adding 140 Angolan standards after committee work and public consultation. The account of the catalogue names none on information technology or data, and none taken from an international standard.

Requirement and standard-setting. The register shows the institute as an observing member on the technical committees it follows, and does not name them. It also shows the institute observing on ISO's policy development committees. The central bank's move of its real-time payments system to an international message format, completed in July 2026, is listed below.

Not held. No source held names an international standard on information technology or data adopted as a national standard.

The standard sets out how software compares and sorts strings of text. The national digital services centre opened in July 2026 is listed below.

MDG.summary:
Membership and adoption. Madagascar's standards body is the Bureau des Normes de Madagascar. A United Nations Development Programme assessment of the country's digital readiness, published in December 2025, says the bureau is a correspondent member of ISO and that public information shows no programme of standards on artificial intelligence or data governance. The assessment names no international standard on information technology or data adopted as a Malagasy one.

Requirement and standard-setting. The same assessment says most data centres meet local rules or their own standards and hold no international information security certificate. In March 2026 the government called for an audit of the national identity management system against international standards on information security and privacy. The audit is listed below.

Not held. No source held names an international standard on information technology or data adopted as a national standard.

MLI.summary:

ISO's member register lists it as a member body, the full class of membership, on a page read in September 2026. The register adds that the agency belongs to the West African programme for harmonising standards. It names no international standard on information technology or data that Mali has adopted as a national one.

Requirement and standard-setting. The register shows the agency with participating and observing seats on technical committees and does not name them. Mali's biometric passport, whose production restarted in October 2025, is listed below. The security ministry's announcement says the passport is produced to international civil aviation standards.

Its register of the national information security certification scheme, as at 31 December 2025, lists certificates against MS ISO/IEC 27001:2022, the Mauritian Standard form of the international standard on information security management. The bureau's annual report for 2021/2022 says it runs that scheme under regulations of 2008. The register shows ten certificates, all issued by the bureau. Neither states the bureau's class of membership of ISO.

Requirement and standard-setting. In July 2026 a minister spoke of adopting the same standard in the national cybersecurity framework, in an account of the postal sector's defences against attack. A workshop in March 2026 took the bureau's information security scheme to the public service. An industry certification framework is listed below.

Its online catalogue of Sudanese Standards gives each standard's ISO equivalent where there is one. The catalogue carries no date and was read in August 2026. It lists Sudanese Standard 4469:2018, an information technology standard on the yield of printer toner cartridges, as equivalent to ISO 19752:2017, and Sudanese Standard 1633-1:2015, on metadata for records, as equivalent to ISO 23081-1:2006. The catalogue does not state the organisation's class of membership of ISO.

Requirement and standard-setting. In January 2026 the central bank issued a cybersecurity framework for banks and financial institutions. It applies to that sector and is listed below, with the passport signing certificate Sudan lodged in the international civil aviation directory.

It names no international standard on information technology or data adopted as a Senegalese one.
