UGA.short: Uganda's 2026 information security policy requires public bodies to comply with the international information security standard; its part in writing such standards is not known.
UGA.summary:
Membership and adoption. The Uganda National Bureau of Standards notified its work programme for January to June 2026 to the ISO/IEC Information Centre, under the World Trade Organization's code of good practice for standards bodies. The programme lists the Ugandan standards the bureau planned to develop in that half-year.

Requirement and standard-setting. The National Information Technology Authority's National Information Security Policy 2026, launched on 15 July 2026, describes itself as setting mandatory requirements for ministries, departments, agencies and local governments. It says cloud services, programming interfaces, artificial intelligence and industrial control systems must be deployed and managed in compliance with ISO/IEC 27001:2022, the international standard on information security management, and that organisations must apply the ISA/IEC 62443 standards to industrial control systems. The minister launched the policy with its framework.

Not held. No source from the last three years naming the standards body or a public body as a participating member, chair or secretariat of an ISO or IEC committee on information technology or data is held. No source held states the standards bureau's membership of ISO, or names an international standard adopted as a Ugandan one.

ZAF.short: Nothing held names the standards body as a member of ISO or IEC, or says it belongs to neither, so no stage is set.
ZAF.summary: Not held. Nothing held names the country's standards body as a member of ISO or IEC, or says it belongs to neither.

ZMB.short: Nothing held names the standards body as a member of ISO or IEC, or says it belongs to neither, so no stage is set.
ZMB.summary: Not held. Nothing held names the country's standards body as a member of ISO or IEC, or says it belongs to neither.

ZWE.short: Zimbabwe listed the international information security standard as a national one in 2026; no rule requiring public bodies to meet it is known.
ZWE.summary:
Membership and adoption. Zimbabwe's standards body is the Standards Association of Zimbabwe. Its accreditations page, updated to February 2026, lists ZWS ISO/IEC 27001:2022, on information security management systems, as a Zimbabwe Standard, the national form of the international standard. The association's catalogue to March 2025 carries a section of standards adopted from the African standards organisation. Neither states the association's class of membership of ISO.

Requirement and standard-setting. The accreditations page says the association's scheme for certifying organisations against the standard was accredited in February 2026 by the Southern African regional accreditation service. The page names no organisation, public or private, certified under the scheme. A banking group's certificate against the same standard, announced in June 2026, is listed below.

Not held. No source held names a law, decree, regulation, directive or circular requiring public bodies to meet a named international standard on information technology or data.

AGO.short: Angola has an interoperability framework written and none adopted; whether public bodies will be required to follow it is not known.
AGO.summary:
Framework adopted. Angola has a framework written and not adopted. The Instituto de Modernização Administrativa's terms of reference of February 2026 say a seven-month study with 25 public institutions produced a Framework and Roadmap of Interoperability, with organisational, semantic, technical and infrastructure guidelines and a phased roadmap. A regional progress report says the institute completed the framework study and its platform roadmap in the first half of 2026, as the basis for buying the interoperability platform. Neither names an instrument adopting it.

Required and followed. The same study found that 27% of systems across the 25 institutions were interconnected, mostly point to point, with fragmented governance and no common standards. The document names no decree making the framework compulsory. It gives no date by which the framework is to be adopted.

Not held. No source held says a government interoperability framework is adopted and published.

BDI.short: A May 2024 notice sought a consultant to develop Burundi's government interoperability framework, with no drafting begun; nothing dated since is known.
BDI.summary:
Framework adopted. A World Bank-financed PAFEN notice of 3 May 2024 seeks a consultancy to develop a Government Interoperability Framework (Cadre d'Interopérabilité du Gouvernement) and an interoperability strategy setting standards and protocols. The work is in phase 2, to follow once the deliverables of phase 1 are validated, and the notice states that no drafting had begun.

Required and followed. The nearest fact held is the same notice of 3 May 2024 for the e-government technical assistance. It describes the Government Interoperability Framework and the interoperability strategy that would set its standards and protocols as still to be developed, in phase 2, which follows once the deliverables of phase 1 are validated. The notice states that no drafting had begun on that date, 3 May 2024.

Not held. Nothing held shows a government interoperability framework adopted and published, or a text requiring public bodies to follow one.

BEN.short: Benin instituted its interoperability framework by decree in 2020; no source held names the body that enforces it.
BEN.summary:
Framework adopted. Benin has a framework in force. The Cadre d'interopérabilité, published by the state digital agency, is instituted by decree 2020-209 of 18 March 2020 and sets four levels, juridical, organisational, semantic and technical, and five common infrastructure components. A new architecture policy for state information systems, setting principles, technical rules and standards to make public systems interoperable, went to sectoral consultation in Cotonou on 30 June 2026.

Required and followed. The agency's legal note of July 2026 treats the framework as in place: it sets the registration, technical and contractual conditions for connecting to the national exchange platform, with a national interoperability committee supervising. No source names a body that enforces the framework itself or counts the bodies connected under it.

Not held. No source held says public bodies are required to follow the framework: a decree, law, regulation or circular that makes it compulsory and names the body that enforces it.

BFA.short: Burkina Faso adopted a general interoperability framework by prime ministerial order in 2018; whether public bodies must follow it is not known.
BFA.summary:
Framework adopted. Burkina Faso has a framework in force. The Référentiel général d'interopérabilité, a normative document fixing the rules for compatibility between public administrations' information systems, was adopted by order of the Prime Minister on 23 May 2018.

Required and followed. The account of the adoption is a news report of 15 October 2019, more than a year after the order, and is the only source held on the framework. It names no body charged with enforcing the rules and reports no ministry or agency whose systems have been checked against them. Nothing held is dated after 2019, so the framework stands on that report: no source says it has been revised, replaced or withdrawn, and none counts the administrations that follow it.

Not held. No source held says public bodies are required to follow the framework: a decree, law, regulation or circular that makes it compulsory and names the body that enforces it.

BWA.short: Botswana's 2025 Digital Services Act requires an information exchange framework, and one is being aligned with donor support; none is issued.
BWA.summary:
Framework adopted. Botswana has a framework in preparation. Section 12 of the Digital Services Act, assented to in October 2025, requires the Digital Services Authority to establish a standardised Framework for Secure Exchange of Information, covering secure communication, identity verification, data integrity and interoperability. The Act comes into force by ministerial order. A European Union-funded project running from August 2024 to August 2027 is working with the government to improve and align the National Interoperability Framework, its standards, guidelines and tools.

Required and followed. The project lists a harmonised and operational national interoperability framework for e-government services as an expected result, to be reached by 2027. The Act does not say the exchange framework has been issued. No public body is reported as bound by either text yet.

Not held. No source held says a government interoperability framework is adopted and published.

CAF.short: Nothing held says Central African Republic has a government interoperability framework, or says it has none, so no stage is set.
CAF.summary: Not held. Nothing held names a government interoperability framework, or says there is none.

CIV.short: Cote d'Ivoire adopted a general interoperability framework by decree in 2021 and binds public bodies to it; the enforcing body is not named.
CIV.summary:
Framework adopted. Cote d'Ivoire has a framework in force. Decree 2021-913 of 22 December 2021 adopts the Référentiel Général d'Interopérabilité des Systèmes d'Information, annexed to it, as the general framework of technical rules for the interoperability of information systems. The annex lists the standards that are recommended, those under observation and those at the end of their life.

Required and followed. The decree was made on the joint report of the ministers for the digital economy and for the public service, who are charged with carrying it out. Its third article binds public bodies to comply with the framework. It names no separate body that enforces compliance. The government exchange platform is noted below: no source ties it to the framework, and none counts the public bodies that comply with it.

Not held. No source held says public bodies are required to follow the framework: a decree, law, regulation or circular that makes it compulsory and names the body that enforces it.

CMR.short: Cameroon's draft e-government law, validated by officials in November 2025, would set interoperability rules for public bodies; it is not adopted.
CMR.summary:
Framework adopted. Cameroon's rule is in a draft law. A workshop at Ebolowa from 3 to 14 November 2025 gave technical validation to the draft e-government bill on access to public information and the digital transformation of the administration, after which the text was ready for ministers to finalise. The experts' recommendations covered interoperability.

Required and followed. The project that supports the reform says the bill provides that administrations must make their information systems compatible, with GovTech Cameroun setting the security and interoperability norms. That is what the law would require once passed. The bill has not been adopted, and no body is yet bound by it. The same account, published on 20 November 2025, gives no date for its passage through parliament.

Not held. No source held says a government interoperability framework is adopted and published.

COD.short: DR Congo's government adopted draft public-sector digital norms, including an interoperability standard, in April 2022; whether any order makes them compulsory is not known.
COD.summary:
Framework adopted. The Ministry of Digital held a workshop on 2-3 February 2022 that analysed and validated five books of public-sector digital standards, Book 5 being the Référentiel Général d'Interopérabilité. The government adopted the draft digital norms and standards for the public sector on 15 April 2022, in the same five books, including that referential.

Required and followed. On the adoption of 15 April 2022, the minister said the norms would be given legal force by ministerial order (arrêté), and the article does not report one as issued. The February 2022 workshop provided for a restricted commission to finalise the texts of the five books before promulgation. The government therefore adopted the draft norms, the Référentiel Général d'Interopérabilité among them, while the legal fixing was still to follow.

Not held. Nothing held shows a decree, law, regulation or order making the framework compulsory and naming the body that enforces it.

COG.short: Congo said in September 2026 it is developing a national digital architecture as the reference for connecting public systems; none is adopted.
COG.summary:
Framework adopted. Congo has a framework in development. The digital economy ministry's news page of 2 September 2026 says the country is committing to develop a National Digital Architecture built on the principles of digital public infrastructure, described as the reference framework for interconnecting public and private information systems. The page cites no instrument adopting it.

Required and followed. The architecture is still in development, so nothing yet binds public bodies to it. The page is the only held account of the framework, and it gives no timetable for its completion, names no body that will hold it, and reports no ministry or agency connecting systems under it. Systems named in the same reporting are noted below. No public body is reported as bound by it yet.

Not held. No source held says a government interoperability framework is adopted and published.

COM.short: Nothing held says Comoros has a government interoperability framework, or says it has none, so no stage is set.
COM.summary: Not held. Nothing held names a government interoperability framework, or says there is none.

CPV.short: Cape Verde's minister said in 2023 that interoperability rules were planned for 2024; nothing says drafting has begun, so no stage is set.
CPV.summary: Not held. Nothing held names a government interoperability framework, or says there is none.

DJI.short: Djibouti's state information systems agency issued a national interoperability framework in 2022; whether public bodies must follow it is not known.
DJI.summary:
Framework adopted. Djibouti has a framework issued. The Agence Nationale des Systèmes d'Information de l'État issued the Cadre d'Interopérabilité de Djibouti as the national interoperability framework, setting principles, four layers of interoperability, legal, organisational, semantic and technical, and a conceptual model for integrated public services. The document is dated 2022.

Required and followed. The framework came out of a government-funded project: a consultancy says it drafted the national interoperability framework for the agency in a project that ran from May 2022 to April 2023 and is marked finished. Neither source names a decree or circular that makes the framework compulsory for ministries, and neither counts the public bodies that exchange data under it. No source says the framework has been revised, replaced or withdrawn since it was issued.

Not held. No source held says public bodies are required to follow the framework: a decree, law, regulation or circular that makes it compulsory and names the body that enforces it.

DZA.short: Algeria's decree of December 2025 makes a national interoperability system the only route for data exchange between public bodies; use is not yet reported.
DZA.summary:
Framework adopted. Algeria has a rule in force. Presidential decree 25-320, published in the Journal officiel of 30 December 2025, sets up a national data governance scheme made of a data classification reference, a data-source cataloguing reference and the national interoperability system for secure exchange between public bodies. On 20 September 2026 the Council of Ministers ordered a further presidential decree on the secure digital interoperability plan between state bodies.

Required and followed. The decree makes the national interoperability system the exclusive framework for data exchange between public institutions and administrations, requires each body to classify and catalogue its data to gain access, and puts the system under the High Commission for Digitalisation. No source names the bodies exchanging data under it.

Not held. No source from the last three years naming or counting public bodies that exchange data under the framework, or are certified as meeting it, is held.

EGY.short: Nothing held says Egypt has a government interoperability framework, or says it has none, so no stage is set.
EGY.summary: Not held. Nothing held names a government interoperability framework, or says there is none.

ERI.short: A 2022 index recorded no government interoperability framework in Eritrea; nothing dated since says whether one exists, so no stage is set.
ERI.summary: Not held. No framework or draft is on record, and no source dated in the last three years says the government has neither.

ETH.short: Ethiopia approved a government interoperability framework by 2019; a 2023 assessment found the main services portal did not follow it.
ETH.summary:
Framework adopted. Ethiopia has a framework approved. The Ministry of Innovation and Technology's library of guidelines and standards lists the Ethiopian Government Interoperability Framework of 2019 with the status Approved, and the ministry's e-government assessment of February 2023 refers to the approved framework. In July 2024 the ministry was leading an interoperable digital government initiative, with a governance and compliance document for the framework attached.

Required and followed. The 2023 assessment found that the E-Services Portal offers no data interoperability features, a departure from the approved framework, and that an enterprise architecture stands alone, out of line with the national one. No source names an instrument that makes the framework compulsory. None names a body that enforces it, or counts the public bodies whose systems comply with it.

Not held. No source held says public bodies are required to follow the framework: a decree, law, regulation or circular that makes it compulsory and names the body that enforces it.

GAB.short: Gabon's digital agency was drawing up a national interoperability framework in December 2025; whether it is adopted or required is not known.
GAB.summary:
Framework adopted. The ANINF is drawing up a national interoperability framework (cadre national d'interopérabilité) under the Gabon Digital programme, as reported on 22 December 2025, and lists interoperability of public systems among the remaining challenges. A World Bank appraisal document of 15 June 2021 recorded the baseline for a common interoperability framework governing secure data exchange within government as No. The project was to define and adopt the Common Interoperability Framework and a National Strategy of Interoperability.

Required and followed. The appraisal document of 15 June 2021 set the baseline for government entities actively and securely exchanging data on the government interoperability platform at 0, with a target of 5. The legal text making the Common Interoperability Framework applicable was still to be drafted under the project.

Not held. Nothing held shows a framework adopted and published, or a text requiring public bodies to follow one.

GHA.short: Ghana adopted an e-government interoperability framework in 2008; a 2022 draft update calls its implementation ineffectual.
GHA.summary:
Framework adopted. Ghana has a framework adopted in 2008. The National Information Technology Agency's draft update says the first Government of Ghana e-government interoperability framework, with the Government of Ghana Enterprise Architecture, was adopted in 2008. Version 2.0 of the framework is labelled a draft for stakeholder review; the draft is dated 2022.

Required and followed. The draft says implementation of the 2008 framework was ineffectual and that the framework is out of date. It gives no count of the public bodies that follow it. No source names an instrument that makes either version compulsory for ministries and agencies, or says that version 2.0 has been approved since the review. No source says the 2008 framework has been withdrawn, so it stands with its year.

Not held. No source held says public bodies are required to follow the framework: a decree, law, regulation or circular that makes it compulsory and names the body that enforces it.

GIN.short: Guinea's digital agency lists interoperability rules at version 0.2.2, with no date and no adopting act, so no stage is set.
GIN.summary: Not held. No framework or draft is on record, and no source dated in the last three years says the government has neither.

GMB.short: The Gambia said in April 2026 that a national enterprise architecture framework governs interoperability; it was still being validated a month later.
GMB.summary:
Framework adopted. The Gambia has a framework in preparation. The Ministry of Communications and Digital Economy told a United Nations commission in April 2026 that a national enterprise architecture framework, led by the government ICT agency, is ensuring interoperability across government systems through open standards, shared services and national governance. The statement gives no date of adoption.

Required and followed. The ministry's statement names the Gambia ICT Agency as leading the framework. It cites no decree, regulation or circular that makes the framework compulsory for ministries, and names no ministry or agency that exchanges data under it. Nothing held says the architecture has been adopted or published since the statement, or gives a date by which it will be. No public body is reported as bound by it.

Not held. No source held says a government interoperability framework is adopted and published.

GNB.short: Guinea-Bissau approved a national interoperability regulation by decree in October 2025; who enforces it is not known.
GNB.summary:
Framework adopted. Guinea-Bissau has a regulation in force. The Council of Ministers approved the draft decree on the Regulation on Interoperability of Systems and Digital Platforms of Public and Private Services in July 2025. The government then approved the regulation through Decree 27/2025, published in the Boletim Oficial of 31 October 2025, setting common technical standards so that systems can exchange data.

Required and followed. The regulation followed a feasibility study for an interoperability framework, platform and enterprise architecture, commissioned under a World Bank-backed programme, which in August 2026 reported the national interoperability regulation as approved. No source names the body that enforces it or counts the bodies following it. The decree's own text is not held, so what it requires of each public body is not stated.

Not held. No source held says public bodies are required to follow the framework: a decree, law, regulation or circular that makes it compulsory and names the body that enforces it.

GNQ.short: A 2024 World Bank diagnostic says Equatorial Guinea has no national interoperability framework; none is reported as being written.
GNQ.summary:
Framework adopted. Equatorial Guinea has no framework. A World Bank diagnostic of 2024 states that the government has no national interoperability framework and no government enterprise architecture framework. A report of July 2024 says the diagnostic recommends a national interoperability framework, describing it as currently absent.

Required and followed. The diagnostic says public sector systems do not communicate with each other, and that interoperability, where it is achieved, is arranged ministry by ministry without central coordination. No source dated since 2024 reports a framework being drafted, and none names an instrument on data exchange between public bodies. No source names a body charged with writing one, or a date by which one is due. A statement that there is no framework counts here for three years from its date.

Not held. No source held says a framework is being written.

KEN.short: Kenya's ICT Authority has published a government interoperability framework whose approval is blank, and said in 2025 it was still to be finalised.
KEN.summary:
Framework adopted. Kenya has a framework published and not approved. The ICT Authority's second edition of the Government Enterprise Architecture and Government Interoperability Framework sets out an interoperability charter and data, technical and metadata standards, but leaves its approval date and document history blank. After a workshop with ministries and agencies on 6 and 7 November 2025, the Authority said it would develop and finalise the national standards and interoperability framework. A supplier that ran a pilot for the ministry to June 2025 wrote a further framework document based on the European model.

Required and followed. The second edition says it is to be adopted by the whole government, ministries, counties and agencies. In September 2026 the Cabinet Secretary cited the framework as the basis for a cross-border service pilot.

Not held. No source held says a government interoperability framework is adopted and published.

LBR.short: An April 2026 executive order requires Liberia's new technology office to produce an interoperability framework; nothing says drafting has begun, so no stage is set.
LBR.summary: Not held. Nothing held names a government interoperability framework, or says there is none.

LBY.short: A regional commission proposed an interoperability framework for Libya in December 2025; nothing says drafting has begun, so no stage is set.
LBY.summary: Not held. No framework or draft is on record, and no source dated in the last three years says the government has neither.

LSO.short: Lesotho's finance minister said in February 2025 that a government interoperability framework is being developed; whether it is adopted or compulsory is not known.
LSO.summary:
Framework adopted. On 19 February 2025 the Minister of Finance and Development Planning told Parliament that the Government of Lesotho Enterprise Architecture and Interoperability Framework is being developed, to improve efficiency and avoid fragmented ICT deployment across government. The government had issued terms of reference for the Government of Lesotho Enterprise Architecture and a standalone e-Government Interoperability Framework on a page dated 22 July 2024.

Required and followed. The 2024 national digital transformation strategy cites the absence of an overarching digital government architecture and gaps in interoperability. The strategy says a digital government interoperability framework should be defined and implemented. It lists defining and implementing a government interoperability framework as a very high priority action, led by the Ministry of Information, Communications, Science, Technology and Innovation.

Not held. No source held says a government interoperability framework is adopted and published.

MAR.short: Nothing held says Morocco has a government interoperability framework, or says it has none, so no stage is set.
MAR.summary: Not held. Nothing held names a government interoperability framework, or says there is none.

MDG.short: Madagascar published its interoperability framework in 2022 and made a decree on interoperability's institutions in 2025; whether it is compulsory is not known.
MDG.summary:
Framework adopted. Madagascar has a framework published. The digital governance unit published version 1.0.2 of the Cadre d'interopérabilité, described as the first official interoperability framework in Madagascar, validated on 10 November 2022 after drafts from December 2021. The page is addressed for action to all public services.

Required and followed. A decree followed: decree 2025-1959 on the institutional framework of interoperability in Madagascar is listed on a legal portal, by title only. A later article says an exchange system is implemented within a legal framework reinforced by that decree. The decree's text is not held, so what it requires of public bodies, and which body it charges with enforcement, are not stated. No source counts the public services that exchange data under the framework.

Not held. No source held says public bodies are required to follow the framework: a decree, law, regulation or circular that makes it compulsory and names the body that enforces it.

MLI.short: Nothing held says Mali has a government interoperability framework, or says it has none, so no stage is set.
MLI.summary: Not held. Nothing held names a government interoperability framework, or says there is none.

MOZ.short: Mozambique's 2017 decree binds all public bodies to its interoperability framework, with the ICT regulator enforcing; which bodies comply is not known.
MOZ.summary:
Framework adopted. Mozambique has a regulation in force. Decree 67/2017, approved by the Council of Ministers on 17 October 2017 and published on 1 December 2017, approves the Regulation of the e-Government Interoperability Framework. The regulation is being revised: a national workshop that opened on 11 June 2026 was the last consultation on the revised text before its final approval.

Required and followed. The decree applies to all public administration bodies, central and local, obliges them to use a single interoperability platform and integrate their systems, and charges the national ICT institute with inspecting compliance and sanctioning breaches. No source from the last three years names or counts the bodies that comply. The 2017 regulation stays in force until the revised text is approved.

Not held. No source from the last three years naming or counting public bodies that exchange data under the framework, or are certified as meeting it, is held.

MRT.short: Mauritania's digital ministry was drafting a framework of public digital service standards in March 2026; it is not adopted.
MRT.summary:
Framework adopted. Mauritania has a framework being written. A report of 27 March 2026 says the digital transformation ministry held a three-day workshop to develop a unified framework of standards for public digital services, to ensure greater interoperability.

Required and followed. At the workshop the ministry presented a technical study and an implementation mechanism for stakeholders' comments before full adoption. The framework is therefore not yet in force, and the report names no decree, order or circular that would make it compulsory for public bodies, nor a body that would enforce it. No ministry or agency is reported as building or connecting its systems to the standards. The report gives no date for the workshop itself and no timetable for adoption.

Not held. No source held says a government interoperability framework is adopted and published.

MUS.short: Mauritius issued an e-government interoperability framework in 2002; whether public bodies must follow it is not known.
MUS.summary:
Framework adopted. Mauritius has a framework issued. The government issued version 1.0 of the Mauritius e-Government Interoperability Framework in November 2002, setting technical standards and specifications for interoperability across government information systems.

Required and followed. The framework covers data exchange between public agencies. One source is held on it, and it reports version 1.0 of 2002 as the framework: no later version is named. No source says the framework has been replaced or withdrawn, so it stands with its year. None names a decree, regulation or circular that makes it compulsory for ministries and agencies, a body that enforces it, or the public bodies that exchange data under it. Nothing held on the framework is dated after the paper that reports it.

Not held. No source held says public bodies are required to follow the framework: a decree, law, regulation or circular that makes it compulsory and names the body that enforces it.

MWI.short: Malawi's ICT ministry proposed a binding government data sharing regulation in June 2026; it is not adopted.
MWI.summary:
Framework adopted. Malawi has a rule proposed and not adopted. A report of 11 June 2026 says the Ministry of ICT has proposed a Government Data Sharing Regulation, a binding rule with a common digital standard so that government systems can communicate.

Required and followed. The proposed regulation would route all government data exchange through the National Data Centre, and would be compulsory once made. It has not been made: the report describes a proposal, gives no date for its adoption and names no body that would enforce it. No ministry or agency is reported as exchanging data under it. Systems named in the same reporting are noted below, since no source ties them to a framework. The report gives no timetable for the regulation.

Not held. No source held says a government interoperability framework is adopted and published.

NAM.short: Namibia drafted an interoperability framework in 2016 and updated the document in 2021-2022; nothing says the government adopted it.
NAM.summary:
Framework adopted. Namibia has a framework drafted and not adopted. The Office of the Prime Minister drafted an Interoperability Framework for Namibia, modelled on Estonia's X-Road, and consulted stakeholders on it in 2016. The supplier of the exchange platform says that in 2014 it introduced an interoperability platform and a corresponding framework in Namibia.

Required and followed. The same supplier says that, in a 2021-2022 capacity-building project for the Office of the Prime Minister, it helped Namibia update its interoperability framework document. None of the three accounts says the government adopted or published the framework, names an instrument making it compulsory, or counts the public bodies that follow it. The exchange platform itself is noted below. No source held is dated after 2024.

Not held. No source held says a government interoperability framework is adopted and published.

NER.short: Nothing held says Niger has a government interoperability framework, or says it has none, so no stage is set.
NER.summary: Not held. Nothing held names a government interoperability framework, or says there is none.

NGA.short: Nigeria's IT agency took over a government enterprise architecture framework in March 2026; whether agencies must follow it is not known.
NGA.summary:
Framework adopted. Nigeria has a framework handed over and in use. A report of 27 March 2026 says the National Information Technology Development Agency took over the Nigeria Government Enterprise Architecture framework from the Korean cooperation agency, after two and a half years of work on it and its reference models.

Required and followed. The report describes the framework as now operational and enabling data exchange across government agencies. It does not name the agencies or count them. It cites no regulation, circular or other instrument that makes the framework compulsory for ministries, departments and agencies, and no source held says the agency enforces it. Nothing held says whether the framework has been published for agencies to follow, or names the body that would check their systems against it.

Not held. No source held says public bodies are required to follow the framework: a decree, law, regulation or circular that makes it compulsory and names the body that enforces it.

RWA.short: Rwanda approved a national data sharing policy for public institutions in May 2025; whether they must follow it is not known.
RWA.summary:
Framework adopted. Rwanda has a policy approved. A news report says Rwanda approved its National Data Sharing Policy in May 2025, to provide a framework for data exchange between public institutions, with safeguards on privacy and on access to restricted data.

Required and followed. Before the policy, a 2019 survey of eight public agencies found no common standards, guidelines, interoperability framework or enterprise architecture, and recommended publishing one, and found no law obliging agencies to interoperate, with integration left to each agency's own initiative. No source dated since the policy's approval names an instrument that makes it compulsory, a body that enforces it, or the institutions exchanging data under it. The policy's text is not held, so what it requires of each institution is not stated.

Not held. No source held says public bodies are required to follow the framework: a decree, law, regulation or circular that makes it compulsory and names the body that enforces it.

SDN.short: Nothing held says Sudan has a government interoperability framework, or says it has none, so no stage is set.
SDN.summary: Not held. Nothing held names a government interoperability framework, or says there is none.

SEN.short: Senegal presented a national interoperability framework and a draft decree in 2026; neither is adopted.
SEN.summary:
Framework adopted. Senegal has a framework and a decree in draft. The digital ministry says the first phase of its interoperability project, whose deliverables a steering committee validated on 26 March 2026, produced a national interoperability framework and a draft decree. It announced that on 5 May 2026 it would present the draft decree governing the interoperability platform and introduce the framework, exchange architectures, technical standards and security requirements.

Required and followed. A separate project is writing a Government Enterprise Architecture, a common reference for policies, processes, data, applications and digital infrastructure; a workshop on 29 July 2026 reviewed its diagnostic phase and proposed the target architecture. In August the ministry said the inventory of state systems was still to be drawn up.

Not held. No source held says a government interoperability framework is adopted and published.

SLE.short: Sierra Leone's ICT ministry said in October 2025 it had developed a government enterprise architecture framework; it is not issued.
SLE.summary:
Framework adopted. Sierra Leone has a framework developed and not issued. The Ministry of Communication, Technology and Innovation said in October 2025 that a Government Enterprise Architecture Framework it developed will serve as a national guide for digital integration.

Required and followed. The ministry says it trained over 100 ICT officers from ministries, departments and agencies in enterprise architecture. Its statement does not say the framework has been adopted or published, cites no instrument that would make it compulsory for those ministries and agencies, and names no body that would enforce it. No ministry or agency is reported as exchanging data under it. Systems named in the same reporting are noted below, since no source ties them to the framework.

Not held. No source held says a government interoperability framework is adopted and published.

SOM.short: Somalia's e-government strategy of August 2025 says the federal government has no interoperability framework; none is reported as being written.
SOM.summary:
Framework adopted. Somalia has no framework. The Ministry of Communications and Technology's e-Government Strategy 2025-2029 states that the Federal Government of Somalia still has no enterprise architecture or interoperability framework, leaving digital government initiatives fragmented in silos. The strategy is dated August 2025.

Required and followed. The strategy is the only source held that speaks to the question. What it plans is noted below; it does not report that drafting of a framework has begun. No source dated since August 2025 reports a framework in preparation, and none names a decree, regulation or circular on how federal ministries and agencies exchange data, or a body that would be charged with enforcing one. A statement that there is no framework counts here for three years from its date.

Not held. No source held says a framework is being written.

SSD.short: Nothing held says South Sudan has a government interoperability framework, or says it has none, so no stage is set.
SSD.summary: Not held. Nothing held names a government interoperability framework, or says there is none.

STP.short: Sao Tome and Principe published a first draft interoperability framework in 2021; an interoperability law was still a bill in 2023.
STP.summary:
Framework adopted. Sao Tome and Principe has a framework in draft. The national cybersecurity strategy, whose final version is dated 15 December 2023, lists among the country's milestones that the Quadro Nacional de Interoperabilidade was published in November 2021. The published text is version 0.1.

Required and followed. The strategy says a Lei de Interoperabilidade was at the time a draft bill. No law or decree therefore makes the framework compulsory for public bodies. The strategy also records that an interoperability platform was first conceived in 2020, alongside the framework. It names no body that enforces the framework and counts no ministry or agency that exchanges data under it. Nothing held is dated after December 2023. No approved version 1.0 of the framework is reported.

Not held. No source held says a government interoperability framework is adopted and published.

SWZ.short: An October 2022 assessment found a government interoperability framework proposal submitted but not yet adopted; whether it has since been adopted is not known.
SWZ.summary:
Framework adopted. The International Organization for Migration's assessment of Eswatini, from a mission in October 2022, says the country has processes in place for a government interoperability framework and a submitted proposal for it. The assessment names the framework as the Government Interoperability Framework (GIF), with the Ministry of ICT as its owner. It treats the GIF as a submitted proposal, not yet adopted, and the mission that produced it took place in October 2022.

Required and followed. The same assessment recommends concrete steps on the submitted proposal and its timely approval by the cabinet. The assessment also describes a data-sharing platform hosted by RSTP, which it names alongside the framework proposal. The platform and the framework proposal are both listed in the assessment's findings for Eswatini.

Not held. No source held says a government interoperability framework is adopted and published.

SYC.short: Nothing held says Seychelles has a government interoperability framework, or says it has none, so no stage is set.
SYC.summary: Not held. Nothing held names a government interoperability framework, or says there is none.

TCD.short: A 2019 thesis quoting the 2017-2021 digital plan said no normative framework existed; nothing recent is known, so no stage is set.
TCD.summary: Not held. No framework or draft is on record, and no source from the last three years says the government has neither.

TGO.short: Togo's digital agency holds its common interoperability framework as a draft guide, version 1.0, as at September 2026.
TGO.summary:
Framework adopted. Togo has a framework in draft. The Agence Togo Digital sets out the government's Cadre Commun d'Interopérabilité in its Guide de l'Architecture d'Entreprise, and the guide's version-control page shows version 1.0 with the status Brouillon, a blank version date and an empty revision history.

Required and followed. The page was captured on 6 September 2026 and carries no date of its own. It names no decree, order or circular adopting the guide or making it compulsory for ministries and agencies, and no body that would enforce it. No ministry or agency is reported as exchanging data under it. Rules for single systems named in the same reporting are not assessed here. The guide's text beyond its version page was not read for this study.

Not held. No source held says a government interoperability framework is adopted and published.

TUN.short: Tunisia set rules for electronic data exchange between public bodies by decree-law and decree in 2020; whether they are enforced is not known.
TUN.summary:
Framework adopted. Tunisia has rules in force. Decree-law 2020-31 of the Head of Government, published in the Official Journal of 10 June 2020, concerns electronic data exchange between public bodies and their users and between the bodies themselves. Government decree 2020-777 of 5 October 2020 sets the conditions and procedures for that exchange, implementing the decree-law.

Required and followed. The decree defines a national interoperability operator and an interoperability system. The passages held show the titles and definitions and not the provisions that follow, so no source held states that public bodies are obliged to use the system or that the operator enforces the rules. No source counts the bodies exchanging data under them. No source says the decree-law or the decree has been amended or repealed.

Not held. No source held says public bodies are required to follow the framework: a decree, law, regulation or circular that makes it compulsory and names the body that enforces it.

TZA.short: Tanzania's e-government agency approved an interoperability framework in 2016; whether public institutions must follow it is not known.
TZA.summary:
Framework adopted. Tanzania has a framework approved. The e-Government Agency issued the e-Government Interoperability Framework, version 1.0, approved by its chief executive in February 2016.

Required and followed. The framework sets common standards and technical guidelines for public institutions to exchange data. It is the agency's own document, and it is the only source held that states the rule: the news read for this study reports new government systems and names no change to the framework. No source held names a law, regulation or circular that makes the framework compulsory for public institutions, says the agency enforces it, or counts the institutions that comply. No source says the 2016 framework has been replaced or withdrawn, so it stands with its year.

Not held. No source held says public bodies are required to follow the framework: a decree, law, regulation or circular that makes it compulsory and names the body that enforces it.

UGA.short: Uganda issued an e-government interoperability framework in 2021 and renewed it in 2026; whether public bodies must follow it is not known.
UGA.summary:
Framework adopted. Uganda has a framework issued and renewed. The published Uganda e-Government Interoperability Framework, issued by the ICT ministry and the national IT authority and dated 6 May 2021, sets twelve principles and six interoperability layers for e-government systems. The renewal was launched with a multi-agency workshop in Kampala in February 2026, and by May 2026 the government had renewed the Government Enterprise Architecture and the framework, with World Bank support.

Required and followed. The Ministry of Health's guidelines of January 2023 say the government has spelled out how sectors exchange information in the framework. No source names an instrument that makes the framework compulsory or counts the bodies following it. No source names the body that enforces the renewed framework.

Not held. No source held says public bodies are required to follow the framework: a decree, law, regulation or circular that makes it compulsory and names the body that enforces it.

ZAF.short: South Africa was updating its minimum interoperability standards and government-wide architecture in 2026; no source held says the current ones are in force.
ZAF.summary:
Framework adopted. South Africa has its standards under revision. The Operation Vulindlela report for the first quarter of 2026/27, from the National Treasury and the Presidency, says work progressed during the quarter on updating the Minimum Interoperability Standards and the Government-Wide Enterprise Architecture.

Required and followed. The report says the updated standards are to be progressed and tested in priority digital services by September 2026. It does not say what force the existing standards have, cites no instrument that makes them compulsory for departments and names no body that enforces them. No department is reported as certified against them. Exchange systems named in the same reporting are noted below, since no source ties them to the standards. The report names no date for their approval.

Not held. No source held says a government interoperability framework is adopted and published.

ZMB.short: Zambia issued a public service interoperability standard in 2019; no decree or law making it compulsory is held.
ZMB.summary:
Framework adopted. Zambia has a standard issued. The government, through the electronic government division in the Office of the President, issued the Public Service ICT Electronic Government Interoperability Standard, first edition, in a final version dated February 2019. The text describes itself as the electronic government interoperability framework for all ministries, provinces and spending agencies.

Required and followed. The standard is a government-issued document and cites no decree or law behind it. It says of itself that the division enforces it and that systems must comply to join the government's ICT infrastructure. No source dated since 2019 names a law, regulation or circular that makes it compulsory, or counts the ministries and agencies whose systems have been checked against it.

Not held. No source held says public bodies are required to follow the framework: a decree, law, regulation or circular that makes it compulsory and names the body that enforces it.

ZWE.short: Zimbabwe handed an enterprise architecture blueprint to government ICT directors in May 2026; nothing says it is published or binding.
ZWE.summary:
Framework adopted. Zimbabwe has an architecture written and not published. A supplier says it completed an enterprise architecture framework, roadmap and change plan for the government in a project running from September 2023 to September 2024, with staff from over 40 ministries, departments and agencies in its workshops. In May 2026 the Enterprise Architecture Model blueprint was officially handed over, and is expected to guide the integration of government digital systems and public services.

Required and followed. The ICT minister said the blueprint was handed to the nation's ICT directors at an e-Government Unit conference on 7 May 2026, with a government service bus planned so that ministries share data once. No source names an instrument making the blueprint compulsory.

Not held. No source held says a government interoperability framework is adopted and published.

AGO.short: A 2018 presidential decree makes a national interoperability plan binding on public services; whether it requires them to share data is not known.
AGO.summary:
Law or decree in force. Angola's Presidential Decree 46/18 of 14 February 2018 approves the national plan for a global interoperability architecture across the central and local administration of the state. It took effect on publication and is a binding act of the President. The plan it approves says that the measures it needs at the level of law are still to be legislated.

Sharing required and the law applied. The 2018 decree states that adherence to the plan is mandatory for the services of the public administration. What is made mandatory is the plan and its architecture; the decree is not recorded as obliging a public body to hand data to another, to connect to an exchange platform, or to stop asking people for what the state already holds. No regulation or order made under it since 2023 is recorded.

Not held. No source held says the law in force requires public bodies to share data, to connect to the government's exchange platform, or not to ask a person for what another public body already holds.

BDI.short: Nothing held names a law or decree on public bodies sharing data for Burundi, or a draft, so no stage is set.
BDI.summary: Not held. Nothing held names a law, decree or regulation on public bodies sharing data, or a draft of one, or says there is none.

BEN.short: A 2020 decree sets up the national data exchange platform; whether public bodies are required to use it is not known.
BEN.summary:
Law or decree in force. Benin's Decree 2020-209 of 18 March 2020, issued by the Presidency, sets up XRoad BJ, the national interoperability platform through which public bodies exchange data. The decree is the founding instrument of the platform, and no later text is recorded as amending or replacing it.

Sharing required and the law applied. The 2020 decree is recorded as setting up the platform, with nothing on an obligation for ministries and agencies to connect to it or to exchange their data through it. No regulation or order made under the decree since 2023 is recorded, and no public body is named as exchanging data because the decree requires it. The platform is run for the Presidency by the agency for information systems and digital technology.

Not held. No source held says the law in force requires public bodies to share data, to connect to the government's exchange platform, or not to ask a person for what another public body already holds.

BFA.short: A 2018 order of the Prime Minister sets interoperability rules for public administrations; whether it requires them to share data is not known.
BFA.summary:
Law or decree in force. Burkina Faso adopted its general interoperability reference, the Référentiel général d'interopérabilité, by an order of the Prime Minister dated 23 May 2018. The order fixes the rules that make the information systems of the different public administrations compatible with each other. It is a regulation of the head of government and not an act of parliament or a decree.

Sharing required and the law applied. The reference was the subject of a training seminar for the IT directorates of ministries from 15 to 17 October 2019, a year after the order was signed. Nothing recorded says the order obliges administrations to exchange data or to connect to a common platform, and no regulation or order made under it since 2023 is recorded. No administration is named as exchanging data because the order requires it.

Not held. No source held says the law in force requires public bodies to share data, to connect to the government's exchange platform, or not to ask a person for what another public body already holds.

BWA.short: A 2025 act tells public bodies not to collect what another body already holds; no rules made under it are recorded.
BWA.summary:
Law or decree in force. Botswana's Digital Services Act, 2025 (Act No. 22 of 2025) was passed by the National Assembly on 14 August 2025 and assented to on 17 October 2025. It provides for public bodies exchanging data through an information gateway and under a framework for the secure exchange of information, and for one body to retrieve data from another. The Act starts on a date the minister sets by order in the Gazette.

Sharing required and the law applied. The Act says a public or private body shall avoid collecting information that another body already holds, and that citizens and businesses are to give the same information only once, to be shared and reused as needed. A body that does not comply with the directions of the authority the Act sets up can be fined up to P500,000. No regulation or order made under the Act is recorded.

Not held. No regulation, decree or order made under it, and no public body named as exchanging data because it requires them to, dated in the last three years, is held.

CAF.short: Nothing held names a law or decree on public bodies sharing data for Central African Republic, or a draft, so no stage is set.
CAF.summary: Not held. Nothing held names a law, decree or regulation on public bodies sharing data, or a draft of one, or says there is none.

CIV.short: A 2017 ordinance binds every administrative authority to connect to the state's exchange platform; whether it has been applied since 2023 is not known.
CIV.summary:
Law or decree in force. Cote d'Ivoire's Ordinance 2017-500 of 2 August 2017, made by the President in the Council of Ministers, governs electronic exchanges between users and administrative authorities and between the administrative authorities themselves. It has a chapter on the interoperability of electronic services, and no repeal is recorded.

Sharing required and the law applied. Chapter V of the ordinance says the state sets up an interoperability platform for electronic services to which every administrative authority is bound to connect, and that the authorities must follow the general interoperability framework. The ordinance also bars an authority from asking a user again for information the administration already holds. No decree or order applying the ordinance since 2023 is recorded, and no authority is named as connected to the platform because the ordinance requires it.

Not held. No regulation, decree or order made under it, and no public body named as exchanging data because it requires them to, dated in the last three years, is held.

CMR.short: A draft e-government law described in 2025 would have administrations share data; it has not been passed.
CMR.summary:
Law or decree in force. Cameroon has a bill and no law in force. The government's digital transformation project described in November 2025 a draft e-government law on access to public information and the digital transformation of the administration, one of the texts examined at a workshop in Ebolowa. No promulgation is recorded, and no decree or regulation on public bodies sharing data is recorded as in force.

Sharing required and the law applied. The draft, as the project describes it, provides that administrations must make their information systems compatible so that they can share data securely, and gives a body named GovTech Cameroun the task of steering interoperability. These are terms of a bill that has not been passed. With no law in force, nothing has been made under one and no administration is named as exchanging data because a law requires it.

Not held. No source held says a law, decree or regulation on public bodies sharing data is in force.

COD.short: Nothing held names a law or decree on public bodies sharing data for DR Congo, or a draft, so no stage is set.
COD.summary: Not held. Nothing held names a law, decree or regulation on public bodies sharing data, or a draft of one, or says there is none.

COG.short: Nothing held names a law or decree on public bodies sharing data for Congo, or a draft, so no stage is set.
COG.summary: Not held. Nothing held names a law, decree or regulation on public bodies sharing data, or a draft of one, or says there is none.

COM.short: Nothing held names a law or decree on public bodies sharing data for Comoros, or a draft, so no stage is set.
COM.summary: Not held. Nothing held names a law, decree or regulation on public bodies sharing data, or a draft of one, or says there is none.

CPV.short: A 2020 government resolution requires state bodies to share data; whether any regulation or application has followed is not known.
CPV.summary:
Law or decree in force. Council of Ministers Resolution 54/2020, approved on 19 March 2020 and published in Boletim Oficial no. 37 of 27 March 2020, took effect the day after publication and applies to all direct and indirect State administration services. It is a government resolution, not a law. Its measure e orders a legal diploma on interoperability of public administration information systems to be drafted and approved, and its measure f orders an interoperability framework.

Sharing required and the law applied. Measure g of the resolution establishes that public administration services and bodies must share among themselves the public data and documents needed for a given process or service, subject to personal data protection rules. Measure r orders steps to operationalise the once-only principle, with the citizen's consent. The resolution was published on 27 March 2020.

Not held. No regulation, decree or order made under the resolution, and no public body named as exchanging data because it requires them to, dated in the last three years, is held.

DJI.short: Nothing held names a law or decree on public bodies sharing data for Djibouti, or a draft, so no stage is set.
DJI.summary: Not held. Nothing held names a law, decree or regulation on public bodies sharing data, or a draft of one, or says there is none.

DZA.short: A December 2025 presidential decree makes a national system the only channel for data exchange between public bodies; its application is not yet recorded.
DZA.summary:
Law or decree in force. Algeria's Presidential Decree 25-320 of 30 December 2025, published in Official Journal no. 87, sets up a national data governance system. Within it, a national interoperability system secures the exchange of data between public institutions and administrations. In September 2026 a further presidential decree on a secure digital interoperability plan was reported as being drawn up on the President's instruction.

Sharing required and the law applied. The 2025 decree makes the national interoperability system the exclusive framework for exchanging digital data between public institutions and administrations, over a secure national interconnection network set aside for the purpose. Each body must classify and catalogue its data to gain access. No order made under the decree is recorded, and no institution is named as exchanging data through the system because the decree requires it.

Not held. No regulation, decree or order made under it, and no public body named as exchanging data because it requires them to, dated in the last three years, is held.

EGY.short: Nothing held names a law or decree on public bodies sharing data for Egypt, or a draft, so no stage is set.
EGY.summary: Not held. Nothing held names a law, decree or regulation on public bodies sharing data, or a draft of one, or says there is none.

ERI.short: Nothing held names a law or decree on public bodies sharing data for Eritrea, or a draft, so no stage is set.
ERI.summary: Not held. Nothing held names a law, decree or regulation on public bodies sharing data, or a draft of one, or says there is none.

ETH.short: The Council of Ministers sent a draft data governance proclamation to parliament in September 2026; nothing is in force.
ETH.summary:
Law or decree in force. Ethiopia has a bill and no law in force. On 28 September 2026 the Council of Ministers referred a draft National Data Governance Proclamation to the House of Peoples' Representatives, a text designed to make government services work through interoperable systems. The same meeting is reported as approving a draft National Data Management Proclamation meant to ease data sharing, interoperability and reuse.

Sharing required and the law applied. The draft is described as designed to facilitate data sharing, interoperability and the reuse of data across government. Whether it would oblige public bodies to share is not stated in either report, and the House had not passed it by the end of September 2026. With no proclamation in force, nothing has been made under one and no public body is named as exchanging data because a law requires it.

Not held. No source held says a law, decree or regulation on public bodies sharing data is in force.

GAB.short: A 2025 ordinance makes it compulsory for administrations to interconnect and exchange information; whether it has been applied is not known.
GAB.summary:
Law or decree in force. Gabon's Ordinance 0006/PR/2025 regulating digitalisation was signed by the President on 12 August 2025 and published in the Official Journal on 30 August 2025. It applies to all services of the state and to public and private bodies, and sets a legal framework for e-government for the first time.

Sharing required and the law applied. The ordinance makes it compulsory for administrations to interconnect, so that they exchange information and procedures are simpler, and puts the interoperability of information systems at its centre. It also requires public administrations to digitise their services. No decree or order applying the ordinance is recorded, and no administration is named as exchanging data because the ordinance requires it. The ordinance was published in the Official Journal within three weeks of its signature.

Not held. No regulation, decree or order made under it, and no public body named as exchanging data because it requires them to, dated in the last three years, is held.

GHA.short: A data harmonisation bill went to public consultation in November 2025 and a data exchange act is proposed; nothing is in force.
GHA.summary:
Law or decree in force. Ghana has a bill and no law in force. The National Information Technology Agency's draft Data Harmonisation Bill 2025 would give a legal basis for data sharing, common standards and the integration of systems across public and private institutions. Public consultation was set for 19 to 27 November 2025, with Cabinet and Parliament to follow. In July 2026 a representative of the communications minister said a Data Exchange Act was also proposed.

Sharing required and the law applied. The proposed Data Exchange Act is described as a law to improve interoperability and allow secure data sharing among government agencies. Neither text had been passed by the end of September 2026. With no law in force, nothing has been made under one and no public body is named as exchanging data because a law requires it.

Not held. No source held says a law, decree or regulation on public bodies sharing data is in force.

GIN.short: A 2019 arrêté between the health and territorial administration ministries covers vaccination and birth certificates; whether any wider law requires sharing is not known.
GIN.summary:
Law or decree in force. UNICEF Guinea lists a government interoperability arrêté between the Ministry of Health and the Ministry of Territorial Administration and Decentralisation (MATD), published in May 2019, for promoting vaccination and obtaining birth certificates. Its scope is health and civil registration only. The arrêté is authored by the government, and UNICEF Guinea gives only the month of publication, May 2019, for a text covering the Ministry of Health and MATD.

Sharing required and the law applied. The nearest held fact is the same May 2019 arrêté, which UNICEF Guinea describes as running between the Ministry of Health and the Ministry of Territorial Administration and Decentralisation. It is listed for two purposes, promoting vaccination and obtaining birth certificates, and UNICEF Guinea dates it to May 2019.

Not held. No source held says a law requires public bodies to share data, to connect to the government's exchange platform, or not to ask a person for what another public body already holds.

GMB.short: Nothing held names a law or decree on public bodies sharing data for Gambia, or a draft, so no stage is set.
GMB.summary: Not held. Nothing held names a law, decree or regulation on public bodies sharing data, or a draft of one, or says there is none.

GNB.short: A decree of October 2025 approved a national interoperability regulation; whether it requires public bodies to share data is not known.
GNB.summary:
Law or decree in force. Guinea-Bissau's national regulation on the interoperability of the digital systems and platforms of public and private services was approved by Decree 27/2025 and published in the Official Bulletin of 31 October 2025. The Council of Ministers had approved it in draft on 10 July 2025. The regional digital project again announced the regulation's approval in August 2026.

Sharing required and the law applied. The regulation is described as one that lets public bodies share information securely. The reports do not say that it obliges public bodies to share data, to connect to an exchange platform, or to stop asking people for what another body already holds. No order made under the regulation is recorded, and no public body is named as exchanging data because the regulation requires it.

Not held. No source held says the law in force requires public bodies to share data, to connect to the government's exchange platform, or not to ask a person for what another public body already holds.

GNQ.short: Nothing held names a law or decree on public bodies sharing data for Equatorial Guinea, or a draft, so no stage is set.
GNQ.summary: Not held. Nothing held names a law, decree or regulation on public bodies sharing data, or a draft of one, or says there is none.

KEN.short: Nothing held names a law or decree on public bodies sharing data for Kenya, or a draft, so no stage is set.
KEN.summary: Not held. Nothing held names a law, decree or regulation on public bodies sharing data, or a draft of one, or says there is none.

LBR.short: An executive order of April 2026 mandates interoperable government systems, with legislation due within a year; no law is in force.
LBR.summary:
Law or decree in force. Liberia has an executive order and no law. Executive Order No. 163, signed by President Boakai on 22 April 2026, creates a national digitalisation and modernisation initiative and an office of technology, digitalisation and innovation. Draft legislation to make the arrangement permanent is due within twelve months of the order.

Sharing required and the law applied. The order mandates interoperable digital systems across ministries, agencies and commissions and introduces a government interoperability framework. It provides that data sharing between them be governed by formal agreements on access, use and accountability. These are the terms of an order that legislation is meant to replace. With no law in force, nothing has been made under one and no ministry is named as exchanging data because a law requires it.

Not held. No source held says a law, decree or regulation on public bodies sharing data is in force.

LBY.short: Nothing held names a law or decree on public bodies sharing data for Libya, or a draft, so no stage is set.
LBY.summary: Not held. Nothing held names a law, decree or regulation on public bodies sharing data, or a draft of one, or says there is none.

LSO.short: Nothing held names a law or decree on public bodies sharing data for Lesotho, or a draft, so no stage is set.
LSO.summary: Not held. Nothing held names a law, decree or regulation on public bodies sharing data, or a draft of one, or says there is none.

MAR.short: A framework bill covering interoperability between government institutions was under government review in November 2025; nothing is in force.
MAR.summary:
Law or decree in force. Morocco has a bill and no law in force. A framework bill known as Digital X.0, covering artificial intelligence, data governance, digital identity and interoperability, was under review by the General Secretariat of the Government in November 2025. It was still being worked on before going to parliament, and the minister delegate for digital transition said it clarifies how data moves between government institutions.

Sharing required and the law applied. The bill is described as setting a model in which any exchange of information between public agencies is authorised by the user, through consent that can be traced. That is a condition on sharing and not a duty to share. The bill had not been passed by the end of September 2026. With no law in force, nothing has been made under one and no agency is named as exchanging data because a law requires it.

Not held. No source held says a law, decree or regulation on public bodies sharing data is in force.

MDG.short: A draft decree on electronic signature and interoperability was validated at a workshop in September 2025; nothing is in force.
MDG.summary:
Law or decree in force. Madagascar has a draft decree and no law in force. In September 2025 the ministry of digital development held a workshop to validate a draft decree on electronic signature and interoperability. The text would set up a regulatory framework for interoperability of its own, with a digital governance unit and a national interoperability committee. No adoption by the government is recorded.

Sharing required and the law applied. The draft is described by what it would set up: a framework, a unit and a committee. The report does not say the decree would oblige public bodies to exchange data or to connect to a common platform. The decree had not been adopted by the end of September 2026. With nothing in force, no rule has been made under it and no public body is named as exchanging data because a decree requires it.

Not held. No source held says a law, decree or regulation on public bodies sharing data is in force.

MLI.short: Nothing held names a law or decree on public bodies sharing data for Mali, or a draft, so no stage is set.
MLI.summary: Not held. Nothing held names a law, decree or regulation on public bodies sharing data, or a draft of one, or says there is none.

MOZ.short: A 2017 decree obliges public bodies to share data and use one exchange platform; a revised regulation was still in consultation in June 2026.
MOZ.summary:
Law or decree in force. Mozambique's Decree 67/2017 of 1 December 2017, made by the Council of Ministers under the Electronic Transactions Law, approves the regulation of the e-government interoperability framework. It applies to every institution of the public administration and took effect 180 days after publication. A revised regulation went to its final consultation at a national workshop on 11 June 2026, and the regulator described the review in December 2025.

Sharing required and the law applied. The decree obliges public administration bodies to share the data they hold and to reuse data held by other state bodies. They must reuse data a citizen has already supplied through the interoperability platform, and must use the single platform. The revised regulation had not been approved by the end of September 2026, so no rule made under the decree since 2023 is recorded, and no body is named as exchanging data because it requires them to.

Not held. No regulation, decree or order made under it, and no public body named as exchanging data because it requires them to, dated in the last three years, is held.

MRT.short: A 2022 decree governs electronic exchanges between administrative authorities; whether it requires them to share data is not known.
MRT.summary:
Law or decree in force. Mauritania's Decree 2022-009, made by the Prime Minister and published in Official Journal no. 1505, governs electronic exchanges between users and administrative authorities and between the administrative authorities themselves. The Council of Ministers heard it on 3 November 2021. It applies to any information exchanged electronically between administrative authorities.

Sharing required and the law applied. The decree sets a general security reference that the authorities' information systems must meet when they exchange information electronically. It governs how exchanges are made; it is not recorded as obliging an authority to share its data, to connect to an exchange platform, or to stop asking users for what another authority already holds. No order made under it since 2023 is recorded, and no authority is named as exchanging data because the decree requires it.

Not held. No source held says the law in force requires public bodies to share data, to connect to the government's exchange platform, or not to ask a person for what another public body already holds.

MUS.short: A 2022 Civil Status Act amendment lets the Bank of Mauritius share population data for Central KYC; any wider sharing law is not known.
MUS.summary:
Law or decree in force. On 15 April 2022 the Bank of Mauritius Governor said, in opening remarks at the signing of memoranda of understanding, that legislative amendments to the Civil Status Act enable the Bank to share information retrieved from the Central Population Database with Central KYC participants. The amendment is limited to the Central KYC purpose, and the Governor named the Central Population Database as the source of the information shared.

Sharing required and the law applied. The nearest held fact is the same speech of 15 April 2022, in which the Governor of the Bank of Mauritius says the amendment to the Civil Status Act enables sharing between the Bank and Central KYC participants. The Governor describes the amendment as enabling sharing from the Central Population Database for Central KYC.

Not held. No source held says the law in force requires public bodies to share data, to connect to the government's exchange platform, or not to ask a person for what another public body already holds.

MWI.short: A government data sharing regulation was proposed in June 2026; nothing in force requires public bodies to exchange data.
MWI.summary:
Law or decree in force. Malawi has a draft regulation and no law in force. In June 2026 the Ministry of Information and Communications Technology proposed a Government Data Sharing Regulation to govern the national data exchange platform, Boma Lathu. The regulation had not been made by the end of September 2026.

Sharing required and the law applied. The minister said in June 2026 that government institutions still share citizens' data by email, on USB drives and on paper, and that a binding regulation on exchange through the platform is the missing piece. No instrument in force requires public bodies to exchange data. With no regulation in force, nothing has been made under one and no institution is named as exchanging data because a rule requires it.

Not held. No source held says a law, decree or regulation on public bodies sharing data is in force.

NER.short: A 2019 electronic transactions law lets administrations exchange data and sets a framework they must use; later use under it is not known.
NER.summary:
Law or decree in force. Niger's Loi 2019-03 of 30 April 2019 on electronic transactions was promulgated and published in the Journal Officiel. Its Title VII on electronic administration lets administrations exchange information, documents and acts electronically (Art. 29). Art. 35 institutes a General Interoperability Framework for administrative information systems, to be set by decree.

Sharing required and the law applied. The same law exempts an applicant from supplying a supporting document when the administration can obtain it directly from the administration or services concerned (Art. 33), replacing it with a sworn declaration. The framework's data directories, norms and standards are those the administration must use (Art. 35). No regulation or order made under it is recorded, and no public body is named as exchanging data because it requires them to.

Not held. No regulation, decree or order made under the law, and no public body named as exchanging data because it requires them to, dated in the last three years, is held.

With nothing in force, no rule has been made under it and no public body is named as exchanging data because a decree requires it.
