Local governments recording. Four Puntland local governments, Galkacyo north, Garowe, Qardho and Bosaso, used the system to collect taxes in October 2022. In Galmudug and Benadir no local government or district had a financial management system; Benadir's districts collect no taxes, and the regional administration's agents collect property taxes, permits and licences, in November 2022.

Not held. No total of local governments is given, so the four counted are a floor and not a share. Nothing is dated inside the last twelve months, and whether district records reach the state system since 2021 is not established.

SSD.short: A digital revenue system was launched for Juba City Council in September 2026; the council is still leaving manual collection. No other council is named.
SSD.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. Stateman Software & Telecom Ltd is named as the developer, implementer and managing company of what Juba City Council calls its Digital Revenue Collection & Management System, working in partnership with the council, in October 2022. In September 2026 the Central Equatoria State Government launched a digital revenue collection system and e-services for the council; no vendor or funder is named.

What is recorded. A council notice of 21 October 2022 invites all businesses within the council and its blocks to register their data on the new system. Registration and access to services had started, and manual payments for council services are to end.

Where the record is held. Businesses register their data at the council's block headquarters offices, by the notice of October 2022.

Last twelve months. The state government launched the council's digital revenue system in September 2026, and the council's first executive meeting under its caretaker mayor, reported on 8 October 2026, put the move from manual to digital collection at the centre of its priorities.

Local governments recording. The roll-out covers Juba City Council and its blocks, and was announced as just started in October 2022. In October 2026 the council was still described as moving from manual collection to a digital system.

Not held. Where the record is held is not stated, and no local government other than Juba City Council is named. Whether the system of October 2022 stayed in use is not established, and no figure for collection on the system launched in September 2026 is held.

STP.short: Nothing is held on local governments' revenue records, digital or paper, and no system is named, so no stage is set.
STP.summary: Not held. No source on local government revenue records is held, and no system of any class is named. Nothing is shown either way, including absence.

SWZ.short: One council, Manzini, billed ratepayers by account and took payment by phone in 2024; other local governments' records are not known.
SWZ.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The rates are billed and collected by the Municipal Council of Manzini, on its notice of April 2024.

What is recorded. For 2024/2025 the council issued rates bills to individual ratepayers by post, email and bulk SMS, and keeps their contact and ownership details; payments carry the plot or account number. In December 2020 it said rates had been billed in April 2020 and some property owners had not paid since.

Where the record is held. Ratepayers check their rates balance and pay on the USSD code *440#, as of April 2024.

Last twelve months. The latest dated event is of April 2024, when the council introduced the USSD code for checking balances and paying, alongside bulk SMS of bill amounts, for the 2024/2025 billing year.

Local governments recording. One council, the Municipal Council of Manzini, billed its ratepayers for 2024/2025, as it did in April 2020.

Not held. Where the record is held, who finances the billing, and whether any local government other than Manzini keeps such a record are not established; no total of local governments is given. Nothing is dated inside the last twelve months.

SYC.short: Nothing is held on local governments' revenue records, digital or paper, and no system is named, so no stage is set.
SYC.summary: Not held. No source on local government revenue records is held, and no system of any class is named. Nothing is shown either way, including absence.

TCD.short: One commune, Mongo, began a taxpayer census for a digital tax system in April 2025; whether any commune records payments digitally is not known.
TCD.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The taxpayer census is run by the commune of Mongo in partnership with the firm IT Solution Center, each enumerator accompanied by a collector and a municipal police officer, in April 2025.

What is recorded. The census covers shops, bakeries and restaurants, and is described as the start of a digital tax system in which payments are to be recorded directly, as of April 2025.

Where the record is held. Payments are to be recorded in the commune's management system, which it calls the système de gestion communal, by the account of April 2025.

Last twelve months. The latest dated event is of 2 April 2025, when Mongo launched the ten-day taxpayer census, to move local tax collection to a digital system.

Local governments recording. One commune, Mongo, began the census in April 2025 as the start of its digital tax system.

Not held. Whether any commune records its payers or their payments in a system, and where such a record is held, is not established. No commune other than Mongo is named, and nothing is dated inside the last twelve months.

TGO.short: One commune, Lacs 1, started a project to digitalise municipal tax registration in 2021; whether it went into use is not known.
TGO.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The municipal tax project in Lacs 1 is worked on with UNDP, which says it equipped about sixty communes with office furniture and IT equipment from 2020, as of May 2021.

What is recorded. After a visit on 27 May 2021, UNDP and the commune of Lacs 1, at Aného, were said to have initiated a project to digitalise the registration of municipal taxes, alongside one for civil-status acts.

Where the record is held. The project to digitalise the registration of municipal taxes belongs to the commune of Lacs 1 and UNDP, on UNDP's account of May 2021.

Last twelve months. The latest dated event is the visit of 27 May 2021, after which the tax project was initiated.

Local governments recording. One commune, Lacs 1, had the tax digitalisation project in May 2021, among the about sixty that UNDP says it equipped from 2020.

Not held. What is recorded and where it is held are not established, and no start of use is stated for the Lacs 1 project. Nothing is dated after May 2021.

TUN.short: Communes entered their business-tax rolls in a system shared with the Ministry of Finance in 2022; how many communes do so is not known.
TUN.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The municipal revenue system GRB 2.0 was developed by the GIZ-run REMO project in partnership with the Ministry of the Interior, which ran from 1 May 2022 to 30 April 2026 as a German-Tunisian cooperation programme.

What is recorded. For the business tax, the commune president lists the taxable persons and the amounts due and enters the list in the commune's GRB system, a GIZ study said in March 2022. Ceremony fees were then receipted from a stub book at the commune's cash office.

Where the record is held. The commune's entry is visible on the GRB network to the regional treasurer and the municipal receiver of the Ministry of Finance, who follow collection (March 2022).

Last twelve months. The REMO project, which produced GRB 2.0, ended on 30 April 2026.

Local governments recording. In 2024 a cooperation project in Bizerte was developing GRB 2.0 and electronic payment of municipal fees for that commune. The 2022 study calls GRB the communes' system.

Not held. No count or share of communes entering their rolls in GRB is given, and what is known of its use dates from March 2022. No plan naming the system is held.

TZA.short: By February 2023, 169 of 184 councils had started using a centrally hosted billing system; the share recording today is not known.
TZA.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The local government ministry, PMO-RALG, manages TAUSI, the revenue system the councils use, the Controller and Auditor General recorded for 2024/25, and the 2026/27 budget speech assigns its development to that ministry. In his report on 2023/24 the auditor recommended that the ministry secure funding for TAUSI's full rollout in all 184 local government authorities.

What is recorded. The auditor reviewed the bills issued through TAUSI to 30 June 2025 and found TZS 1.22 billion issued by seven authorities unpaid; the revenue manual he cites requires a bill to update the taxpayer's record on payment. A ministry official said on 10 September 2025 that some councils issue receipts that do not come from the system.

Where the record is held. TAUSI is a centrally hosted application (audit of 2024/25). Some councils and village governments still keep forest-product revenue in books and hard-copy documents, the forestry division said in August 2026.

Last twelve months. The budget speech of 11 June 2026 commits the ministry and the revenue authority to finish linking TAUSI to the national tax system, and to add modules for buildings and for registering traders.

Local governments recording. By February 2023 169 councils had started to use TAUSI, the minister told the National Assembly; the auditor counts 184 local government authorities. In 2023/24 16 of them collected through the older LGRCIS instead, and by December 2024 the property tax module was in 47 of the 184.

Not held. No share of local government authorities recording in TAUSI has been published since February 2023; the newer figures concern one module or the authorities still on the older system. No domestic budget line for the system is stated.

UGA.short: A revenue system was in use in nine cities in late 2024; the share of local governments recording in it is not known.
UGA.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The Ministry of Local Government runs E-LogRev (March 2024), under a contract with Tucksee Pty Limited that does not clearly require the source code to pass to government, the Auditor General reported in December 2024. The system is funded by both the finance ministry and URA TREP, and the local government ministry has no IT strategic plan.

What is recorded. In IRAS, the mayor of Nansana said in March 2024, the system fixes the assessment and records payments against a catalogue of fees.

Where the record is held. The Auditor General found no formal access policy for the E-LogRev database (December 2024).

Last twelve months. At the half-year of 2024/25 local governments' own revenue reached 37 per cent of the annual budget, against 24.35 per cent at the same point of 2019/20, which the finance ministry attributes to the IRAS rollout.

Local governments recording. The finance ministry's monitoring covered IRAS in nine cities in the first half of 2024/25, with the tenth, Jinja, still on E-LogRev. In March 2024 IRAS was reported rolled out in 98 districts, 21 municipalities and nine cities and E-LogRev operational in 48 local governments. The Auditor General's report on 2022/23 counted 124 activated local governments, 39 of them without the equipment to run the system.

Not held. Where the record is held is not stated, and no total of local governments is given against which the counts can be set. Nothing is dated inside the last twelve months.

ZAF.short: Municipalities bill property rates per property and owner from their own billing systems, as described in 2023; how many do so is not known.
ZAF.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. National Treasury's budget circular of 7 December 2023 has each municipality reconcile its valuation roll to its billing system and send the reconciliation to the Treasury every quarter, within 10 working days of the quarter's end.

What is recorded. The circular says every municipality's property-rates billing report holds, for each property, the market value, the category, the amount billed, the owner and any rebate, exemption or reduction, with a unique identifier that ties the property to the valuation roll (December 2023).

Where the record is held. The billing record stays in the municipality's own billing system; what goes to National Treasury, through its GoMuni upload portal, is the reconciliation (December 2023).

Last twelve months. National Treasury set the quarterly reconciliation in its circular of 7 December 2023.

Local governments recording. The circular describes the billing report of every municipality, on the ground that all municipal financial systems take the valuation roll as their basis (December 2023).

Not held. No count or share of municipalities billing from a system is given. Nothing is held on who owns, plans or pays for the billing systems, and nothing is dated inside the last twelve months.

ZMB.short: A council revenue system was at proof of concept in eight councils in March 2026; whether it is live anywhere is not known.
ZMB.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. Smart Zambia, the state digital agency, announced the e-Council system in March 2026 as part of the national e-government plan.

What is recorded. The e-Council system is planned to let councils identify their revenue streams and track collections in real time (March 2026). A policy brief of May 2024 found councils' property tax administration weakened by outdated cadastres and poor record keeping, with many tax maps covering a fraction of rateable properties.

Where the record is held. The same brief says most local councils still run on manual systems, and the few partly digitalised work in silos at department or section level (May 2024).

Last twelve months. In March 2026 the government's chief technical officer said all 116 local authorities were connected to the government network and had solar power, ahead of an e-Council rollout planned for 2026.

Local governments recording. The first phase is a proof of concept in eight councils, among them Ndola, Kitwe, Solwezi, Chingola, Kalulushi, Kalumbila and Chilanga, with a demonstration of the system expected by 19 June 2026 before it is extended to the rest (March 2026).

Not held. Nothing shows the e-Council system live in any council, or that the June 2026 demonstration took place. No plan period and no finance are stated, and the statement that most councils work manually dates from May 2024.

ZWE.short: In 2024 about 83 of 92 local authorities used a shared digital system; whether most record revenue payers in it is not known.
ZWE.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. In May 2023 the Deputy Minister of Local Government and Public Works said LADS would become a business unit of her ministry, with the Harare Institute of Technology as consultant, and that its further development would be paid for from a government devolution grant.

What is recorded. Kwekwe City Council bills on the Promun package, with sections for utility billing, accounts receivable, cashiering and credit control (August 2026). Mutare's finance department runs the LADS debt management module (October 2021). At Gwanda, the Auditor-General reported for 2024, 27 stands sold in 2019 were still not billed.

Where the record is held. The Harare Institute of Technology says LADS links local authorities' financials and billing to the national public financial management system (November 2024). The Auditor-General's report on 2024 says most local authorities had no ERP system for revenue collection and ran processes that were manual or partly automated.

Last twelve months. In June 2025 the institute said its InstaPark parking system was in use in 15 municipalities.

Local governments recording. Around 83 of Zimbabwe's 92 local authorities use at least one LADS module, the institute told the Harare Commission of Inquiry in November 2024.

Not held. Which LADS modules the 83 local authorities use, and whether any of them records revenue, is not stated. No fact on governance is dated inside the last three years, and no event inside the last twelve months.

AGO.short: Private money reached Anda and Africell in 2026, but whether earlier years saw any is not known.
AGO.summary:
Private money put into a digital business, with its year. In March 2026 BFA Asset Management put $1.2 million from its Kimbo Fund into Anda, an Angolan motorcycle-taxi mobility start-up. Breega, Speedinvest and 4DX Ventures had put $3.4 million into Anda in total, with no round dates given. In 2026 EXIM Bank of the United States committed $100 million to Africell for technology investment in Angola.

Money raised inside the country. The $1.2 million for Anda came from BFA Asset Management of Luanda, a firm spun off from Banco de Fomento Angola, announced in March 2026.

Private money the government brought into a public digital project. The state is selling a 15% stake in the mobile operator Unitel in 2026.

Not held. Every amount held from 2024 on was signed or started in the same year, and nothing earlier is held.

BDI.short: Lumitel put about USD 5.6 million into a rural 4G contract in 2026; whether private money came in other years is not known.
BDI.summary:
Private money put into a digital business, with its year. In 2026 Lumitel Burundi, a subsidiary of Vietnam's Viettel group, signed a USD 10 million contract with the PAFEN project to extend rural 4G, and financed 56 per cent of it itself, about USD 5.6 million. That is the only amount held from 2024 onward, and it is dated to the publication on 3 March 2026, as the page itself carries no date.

Money raised inside the country. The money came from a foreign group's subsidiary, Lumitel, which pays 56 per cent of the rural 4G contract from its own funds, and no local raise is stated in that source.

Private money the government brought into a public digital project. The government of Burundi, through the PAFEN project, co-finances the remaining 44 per cent of the USD 10 million rural 4G contract, and so brought Lumitel's private 56 per cent, about USD 5.6 million, into a public connectivity project in 2026, with the state and the company sharing the cost of the same contract.

Not held. Only one amount is held from 2024 on, so whether private money came in more than one year is not known.

BEN.short: MTN Group committed over USD 215 million in 2025, but no money raised inside Benin or brought in by the government is known.
BEN.summary:
Private money put into a digital business, with its year. In 2025 MTN Group committed over USD 215 million of its own money in Benin through 2026, spent on a 5G rollout, fibre expansion and a new MTN Benin headquarters. The commitment was announced at the Benin Investment Forum in May 2025 and is the only private amount held for the country from 2024 on.

Money raised inside the country. No money raised inside Benin is held; MTN, a South African group, put in the USD 215 million itself, dated 2025.

Private money the government brought into a public digital project. No private money brought in by the government is held; The MTN commitment was self-funded and approved by MTN.

Not held. The amount held was signed or started in the same year, 2025, so no earlier or later private money is shown. Nothing shows money raised inside Benin, or private money the government brought into a public project.

BFA.short: No private money put into a digital business in Burkina Faso is held, and none is reported absent, so no stage is set.
BFA.summary: Not held. Nothing held names private money put into a digital business in the country, or says there is none.

BWA.short: Private money of GBP 10 million was committed to a Botswana tech fund in April 2026; whether more came in other years is not known.
BWA.summary:
Private money put into a digital business, with its year. In April 2026 Pula Investments, the family office of UK financier Stephen Lansdown, anchored Botswana Tech Fund, which TechCabal reports has GBP 10 million (USD 13.5 million) in committed capital, with a first close of GBP 5 million (USD 6.7 million). The fund is run from Botswana with Launch Africa.

Money raised inside the country. Nothing from 2024 on is held; In May 2021 members of Angel Network Botswana, a Botswana investor network, put P250,000 (USD 22,000) into the online marketplace Ponatshego, per the World Bank.

Private money the government brought into a public digital project. There is a government-backed startup programme launched in March 2026 with Scalar International, which states no private amount.

Not held. Only one amount is held from 2024 on, so whether private money came in more than one year is not known.

CAF.short: No private money put into a digital business in the country is known for 2024 or later, so no stage is set.
CAF.summary: Not held. No private money put into a digital business in the country is known, and none is known to be absent.

CIV.short: Development finance institutions put money into two Ivorian firms in 2024; whether Ivorian investors or public projects drew private money is not known.
CIV.summary:
Private money put into a digital business, with its year. The Dutch development bank FMO approved an equity investment of EUR 2.40 million in Hub2 (Connekt 4 SAS), effective August 2024. Hub2 is a fintech providing mobile wallet and payment services in Francophone Africa, and the investment sits under FMO's Ventures Program 2. Invest International approved a concessional loan of USD 0.325 million to PAIX Indigo B.V., part of the Paix Group, in 2024. The loan paid for a feasibility study for a data centre in Côte d'Ivoire.

Money raised inside the country. The equity in Hub2 came from outside the country: FMO is a Dutch development bank, and the investment was made under its own Ventures Program 2.

Private money the government brought into a public digital project. The 2024 money went to a payments fintech and a data centre developer, both private companies, and not to a government project.

Not held. Any investment in an Ivorian digital business since 2024 beyond the two above, any money from investors of the country itself, and any private money in a public digital project.

CMR.short: Private companies committed $75 million in September 2026 and $225 million over three years from 2025; money raised inside Cameroon is not known.
CMR.summary:
Private money put into a digital business, with its year. In September 2026 the US company Cybastion committed $75 million to digital infrastructure in Cameroon, including an AI-ready data center in Douala with a dedicated power plant, as Biometric Update reports. In 2025 MTN Cameroon said it is investing US$225 million over three years in its own operations, chiefly its fintech division and national network coverage.

Money raised inside the country. No amount raised on a Cameroonian market or put in by a Cameroonian bank, fund or investor is held for 2024 or later. The MTN Cameroon pledge is financed by the company itself, in its own network and fintech operations, with no separate recipient named.

Private money the government brought into a public digital project. No public digital project with a stated private amount is held for 2024 or later, and no government co-investment is recorded. There is the private data center commitment in Douala, a US company's investment in which no public project is named and no government money is stated.

Not held. No source from 2024 on names an amount put in by a bank, pension fund, insurer, investor or company of Cameroon itself, or raised on the country's own market.

COD.short: A fund lent USD 32.8 million and Helios Towers committed over USD 100 million to towers in 2026; where it was raised is not known.
COD.summary:
Private money put into a digital business, with its year. In 2026, EAAIF, a PIDG fund managed by Ninety One in London, signed a USD 32.8 million senior secured loan to Eastcastle Infrastructure DRC, within an upsized USD 179 million facility, to build 728 towers. On 31 March 2026, Helios Towers DRC signed an investment agreement for more than USD 100 million in shared telecom towers, which the company says it is investing itself.

Money raised inside the country. No fact held says where any of this money was raised. Vodacom Congo says it spends on average USD 140 million a year on its network in the DRC and plans a USD 670 million long-term programme, stated on 8 October 2026.

Private money the government brought into a public digital project. No amount is held. The national investment promotion agency ANAPI was the counterparty to the Helios tower agreement in March 2026.

Not held. Where the money was raised, and any private money in a public digital project, is not established.

COG.short: A USD 3 million seed round for a Brazzaville delivery platform came in 2024, but whether more private money followed is not known.
COG.summary:
Private money put into a digital business, with its year. In June 2024 Uma Ventures, a Hong Kong-based venture capital firm, led a USD 3 million seed round for Noki Noki, a delivery platform based in Brazzaville. The money went into a privately owned company that operates in the Congolese capital, and the investor who led the round is based abroad. Trendtype reported the round on 24 June 2024.

Money raised inside the country. The one 2024 round, Noki Noki's USD 3 million seed round, was led by Uma Ventures of Hong Kong, so that money came from outside Congo and was not raised on the Congolese market.

Private money the government brought into a public digital project. The one 2024 round, Noki Noki's USD 3 million seed round led by Uma Ventures, went to a private Brazzaville delivery platform, not to a project of the Congolese state.

Not held. Whether private money came into Congolese digital businesses in any year other than 2024 is not known. Money raised inside Congo and private money brought into a public digital project are not known either.

COM.short: The IFC lent EUR 25 million to a telecom firm in 2025; money raised at home and in public projects is not known.
COM.summary:
Private money put into a digital business, with its year. The International Finance Corporation, the World Bank Group's private-sector lender, agreed in June 2025 to lend EUR 25 million to Yas Comoros, an AXIAN Telecom subsidiary, to pay for 5G, fibre-to-the-home, fibre-to-the-office and inter-island connectivity. There is an IFC commitment of USD 27 million to Yas Comoros, a commercial loan approved and starting in 2025, the same year as the June agreement.

Money raised inside the country. The 2025 lender, the IFC, is not a Comorian body, so the money in this loan came from outside the country.

Private money the government brought into a public digital project. The 2025 loan went to Yas Comoros, an AXIAN Telecom subsidiary, for network connectivity, and it is a private firm's loan rather than a government project.

Not held. Money raised inside Comoros, and private money brought into a public digital project, are not known. Every amount held from 2024 on was signed or started in the same year.

CPV.short: Nothing held names private money put into a digital business in Cabo Verde, or says there is none, so no stage is set.
CPV.summary: Not held. Nothing held names private money put into a digital business in the country, or says there is none.

DJI.short: No private money put into a digital business in Djibouti is held, and none is reported absent, so no stage is set.
DJI.summary: Not held. Nothing held names private money put into a digital business in the country, or says there is none.

DZA.short: Private investors put about USD 5 million into one Algerian start-up in December 2025; private money in government digital projects is not known.
DZA.summary:
Private money put into a digital business, with its year. In December 2025 a group of private investors led by Tell Group, a financial services company, with the Algerian conglomerate Groupe Industriel Babahoum Algerie (GIBA) taking part, put 600 million dinars (about USD 5 million) into the Algerian travel-tech start-up VOLZ, per TechCabal.

Money raised inside the country. The VOLZ round was raised in dinars from Algerian investors, and TechCabal calls it the largest Algerian start-up round in dinars. Tell Group's USD 5 million is recorded as approved equity, starting in 2025.

Private money the government brought into a public digital project. None is held; Algeria's government committed USD 1 billion in October 2025 to a financing fund for African start-ups.

Not held. Every amount held from 2024 on was signed or started in the same year.

EGY.short: Private money came into Egyptian digital firms in 2024 to 2026, led by 2026 rounds; no government-led public project with private money is known.
EGY.summary:
Private money put into a digital business, with its year. In 2026 Mubadala and the EBRD co-led a USD 35 million pre-Series C round for Paymob, Partech led a USD 13 million Series A for Synapse Analytics, Algebra Ventures led a USD 12.5 million Series A for Blnk and Launch Africa and Antler MENAP co-led a USD 2.8 million seed round for Fincart. In 2025 Konecta put USD 50 million into a Cairo hub; in 2024 Africa50 put USD 15 million into Raya Data Center and Huawei USD 300 million into its Cairo cloud region.

Money raised inside the country. In 2026 Blnk raised USD 24.6 million in local-currency debt from Egyptian banks. In May 2025 Fawry raised EGP 497.5 million by securitising microloans through Capital for Securitisation Company, and Hassan Allam committed USD 400 million to Egyptian data centres in 2026.

Private money the government brought into a public digital project. Hassan Allam committed USD 400 million in 2026 to a data-centre licence, a private project.

Not held. No source from 2024 on has a signed public-private partnership, concession or joint venture in which a private partner puts a named amount into a public digital project, or a state fund that private investors have paid into.

ERI.short: No private money put into a digital business in Eritrea is held, and none is reported absent, so no stage is set.
ERI.summary: Not held. Nothing held names private money put into a digital business in the country, or says there is none.

ETH.short: Foreign investors put money into Ethiopian digital firms in 2024 to 2026, mainly Safaricom Ethiopia; no domestic or government-brought private money is known.
ETH.summary:
Private money put into a digital business, with its year. Safaricom PLC of Kenya injected KES 21.3 billion into Safaricom Ethiopia in the year to March 2026, lifting its stake from 51.3% to 54.1%, and added Sh1.4 billion in the quarter to June 2026. The International Finance Corporation committed a USD 200 million commercial loan to Safaricom Ethiopia in 2024. Dodai, an Addis Ababa e-mobility company, closed a USD 13 million Series A in April 2026, USD 8 million equity and USD 5 million debt, with British International Investment among the investors. FMO committed USD 15.7 million in a commercial loan to Cooperative Bank of Oromia in 2024.

Money raised inside the country. Safaricom PLC of Kenya holds 54.1% of Safaricom Ethiopia.

Private money the government brought into a public digital project. Ethio telecom, which is state-owned, extended the deadline of its public share offering in January 2025.

Not held. No source from 2024 on names an amount put in by a bank, pension fund, insurer, investor or company of Ethiopia itself, or raised on its own market.

GAB.short: Private money reached Gabon's mobile money business in 2022, but no deal from 2024 is known, so no stage is set.
GAB.summary: Not held. No source dated from 2024 names an amount of private money put into a digital business in the country.

GHA.short: Private money reached Ghanaian digital businesses from 2024 to 2026, mainly telecom and fintech; money raised inside Ghana is not known.
GHA.summary:
Private money put into a digital business, with its year. Africa50, Oikocredit and three other funds put USD 14 million of equity into Zeepay Ghana, closing in April 2024. Google committed USD 37 million to an AI research centre in Accra from 2025. In 2026, IFC put a US$2.4 million convertible loan into Complete Farmer, and Village Capital's facility put USD 500,000 into three startups. MTN committed US$1.1 billion over three years and Telecel US$200 million to their networks.

Money raised inside the country. Nothing held names it. Scancom PLC (MTN Ghana) invested GHS 1.9 billion in its network and digital platforms in the first half of 2026.

Private money the government brought into a public digital project. Nothing held names it. Parliament approved a 20-year electronic road toll concession in July 2026.

Not held. No source from 2024 on names an amount put in by a bank, pension fund, insurer, investor or company of Ghana itself, or raised on its own market.

GIN.short: MIGA committed USD 373 million and USD 27 million to two Orange companies in Guinea in 2024; money raised inside Guinea is not known.
GIN.summary:
Private money put into a digital business, with its year. In 2024 MIGA committed USD 373 million in an active guarantee to Orange Guinee SA, a telecoms operator, under a project listed as Sonatel equity. In the same year MIGA committed USD 27 million in a second active guarantee, to Orange Finances Mobiles Guinee SA for mobile money, also listed as Sonatel equity.

Money raised inside the country. MIGA's two 2024 guarantees, of USD 373 million and USD 27 million, name Orange Guinee SA and Orange Finances Mobiles Guinee SA as the companies they were committed to.

Private money the government brought into a public digital project. MIGA's 2024 guarantee of USD 373 million was committed to Orange Guinee SA, a telecoms operator, and the record names no public project.

Not held. Every amount held from 2024 on was signed or started in the same year, so nothing shows money raised inside Guinea or private money brought into a state project.

GMB.short: Private money came in as US$50 million in December 2025 and GMD 6.1 billion in July 2026; domestic investors are not known.
GMB.summary:
Private money put into a digital business, with its year. In December 2025 the state telecoms operator GAMTEL signed a US$50 million public-private partnership with SYSROAD SA HOLDING to raise its national backbone from 40Gbps to 800Gbps. In July 2026 the financier YCELL Co. Ltd. committed GMD 6.1 billion to modernise the network of GAMCEL, the state mobile operator, under a Share Investment and Network Modernization Agreement that also gives it an 80% equity stake, about US$83.6 million in all.

Money raised inside the country. The GAMTEL backbone partner, SYSROAD SA HOLDING, is a Senegal-based systems integrator.

Private money the government brought into a public digital project. GAMTEL is the public partner in the national broadband partnership, and the private partner finances the upgrade of the national broadband network. The US$50 million agreement was signed in December 2025.

Not held. No bank, pension fund, insurer, investor or company of the country itself is named as putting in money since 2024, and nothing was raised on the Gambian market.

Private money the government brought into a public digital project. The 2025 guarantee went to Orange Bissau S.A., a telecoms operator, which is a company and not a state project; MIGA's cover for it is active and started in 2025.

GNQ.short: No private money put into a digital business is known, and none is known to be absent, so no stage is set.

KEN.short: Private money has come in since 2024, from IFC, DFC and Airtel Africa among others, but money raised inside Kenya is not known.
KEN.summary:
Private money put into a digital business, with its year. IFC committed USD 11 million in equity to IHS Kenya in 2024, the US DFC USD 25.5 million in a commercial loan to M-KOPA Kenya in 2024 and Airtel Africa USD 147 million for a Nxtra data centre at Tatu City in 2025. Private money the government brought into a public digital project. There is a 2026 public notice by the National Transport and Safety Authority on a partnership for smart driving licences, with no amount given.

LBR.summary:
Private money put into a digital business, with its year. In 2026 the Austrian company OeSD International is to finance about US$54.7 million of nationwide ID enrolment and infrastructure under a Build, Operate and Transfer concession, which the National Identification Registry says is signed and awaits legislative ratification. In 2024 MIGA committed USD 81 million as a guarantee to Orange Liberia Inc. for its telecom expansion.

Money raised inside the country. MIGA's USD 81 million guarantee in 2024 went to Orange Liberia Inc., and the source names no local lender or investor.

Private money the government brought into a public digital project. The government of Liberia brought OeSD International into the national ID and civil registration upgrade through a signed public-private partnership described as about US$54 million, reported in September 2026 and still needing parliamentary approval.

LBY.summary: Not held. Nothing held names private money put into a digital business in the country, or says there is none.

LSO.summary:
Private money put into a digital business, with its year. Convalt Energy, a US company, signed a binding agreement with Lesotho's Ministry of Energy on 4 June 2026 for Project Kobong, a hydropower and AI data centre valued at about US$6.2 billion (Lesotho Tribune). The Tribune calls it the largest foreign investment commitment in Lesotho's history, with construction targeted for 2029 subject to feasibility. Its chief executive says the project was launched on 31 July 2026 (TechAfrica News).

Money raised inside the country. None held; Project Kobong's investor is Convalt Energy, a US company (TechAfrica News).

Private money the government brought into a public digital project. None held; The Kobong agreement was signed with the Ministry of Energy (Lesotho Tribune).

Not held. Whether any of the Kobong money has been paid in is not known, and no amount raised inside Lesotho is held.

MAR.short: Morocco's startups drew over USD 25 million in the first half of 2026; who put it in is not known.
MAR.summary:
Private money put into a digital business, with its year. TechCabal reports that Morocco's startups attracted more than USD 25 million in total funding in the first half of 2026. That is the sum across all startup deals in those six months, not one investment, and no investor or company is named for any part of it.

Money raised inside the country. The USD 25 million-plus that Morocco's startups drew in the first half of 2026 is reported as a country total, with no split between Moroccan and foreign investors.

Private money the government brought into a public digital project. No private deal in a government digital project is reported for 2024 or later. The only private money reported is the first-half 2026 startup total of more than USD 25 million, which is not tied to any public project.

Not held. Only one amount is held from 2024 on, so whether private money came in more than one year is not known.

MDG.short: Two development-bank loans to AXIAN Telecom in 2025 brought private money in; whether any was raised locally or by the state is not known.
MDG.summary:
Private money put into a digital business, with its year. The African Development Bank approved a $160 million senior loan to AXIAN Telecom in January 2025, with over $10 million for 22,000 women entrepreneurs in Madagascar through the MVola platform. The European Investment Bank announced $100 million to AXIAN Telecom on 10 April 2025 for 4G and 5G, $40 million of it for Madagascar and $60 million for Tanzania. Both lenders are development finance institutions, and both loans went to the same private telecoms group.

Money raised inside the country. Nothing held shows money raised inside Madagascar. The African Development Bank's January 2025 loan went to a Mauritius-headquartered company working across nine countries, so the money came from outside the country.

Private money the government brought into a public digital project. Nothing held shows the government bringing private money into a public digital project. The Economic Development Board of Madagascar, the state investment agency, has had a regional antenna at Manakara since July 2025, and no amount is stated.

Not held. Nothing held shows what happened to either 2025 commitment after the year it was made, or how much reached Madagascar beyond the stated shares. No money raised at home or brought by the government is held.

MLI.short: No private money put into a digital business is known, and nothing says there is none, so no stage is set.

MRT.short: No private money put into a digital business in Mauritania is known, nor whether there is none, so no stage is set.

MUS.short: No source from 2024 names an amount of private money put into a digital business in Mauritius, so no stage is set.

MWI.short: A mobile operator put in MK30.87 billion in 2025 and US$31 million reported in 2026; who else invests is not known.
MWI.summary:
Private money put into a digital business, with its year. In 2025 TNM plc, a Malawian mobile operator, invested MK30.87 billion of its own money in network infrastructure, mainly modernisation, 4G site expansion and 5G rollout. In August 2026 TNM said it had invested US$31 million of its own money in network capacity and coverage across Malawi, with no date given for the spending. In both cases the company is its own financier, and neither report says where its money comes from.

Money raised inside the country. TNM, a Malawian operator, paid for its 2025 network spending itself, covering modernisation, 4G site expansion and the 5G rollout, with no bank, fund or share issue named behind it.

Private money the government brought into a public digital project. Both network investments were TNM's own money, with no state partner named and no public digital project attached to either amount.

Not held. No amount from 2024 on is held from a Malawian bank, pension fund, insurer or investor, or raised on Malawi's own market. No private partner is held putting a named amount into a public digital project.

NAM.short: Paratus put N$600 million into a mobile network in 2025, a Namibian bank lent N$405 million in 2026; private money in public projects unknown.
NAM.summary:
Private money put into a digital business, with its year. In the year to September 2025 Paratus Group invested a further N$600 million (US$33.7 million) in its new private mobile network in Namibia, one-third of it for a digital technology stack. That follows N$1.42 billion (US$79.8 million) put into network infrastructure since 2018.

Money raised inside the country. On 25 March 2026 RMB Namibia, a Namibian bank, announced a seven-year N$405 million social loan to Telecom Namibia, the state-owned operator, for network modernisation and broadband expansion.

Private money the government brought into a public digital project. The nearest case is the 2026 loan to the state-owned Telecom Namibia, which is a bank loan to an operator and not a partnership with a stated private contribution.

Not held. No public-private partnership, concession or joint venture since 2024 is known in which a private partner puts a named amount into a public digital project, and no state fund that private investors paid into.

NER.short: Telecom operators put US$7.5 million into rural connectivity by mid-2024; whether more came in other years is not known.
NER.summary:
Private money put into a digital business, with its year. Telecom operators awarded rural connectivity contracts under the World Bank-backed Smart Villages project had put in US$7,522,666 of private sector investment by 30 June 2024, against a closing target of US$25 million for December 2025. It is the only private amount for Niger from 2024 on.

Money raised inside the country. The Smart Villages money came from telecom operators awarded rural connectivity contracts under the project, and no other private digital investment in Niger since 2024 is recorded.

Private money the government brought into a public digital project. The government's public project, Smart Villages for rural growth and digital inclusion (P167543), counts the operators' investment as private money raised through the project, measured at mid-2024 against its US$25 million target.

Not held. Whether private money came in more than one year from 2024 is not known, and neither is where the operators' money was raised.

NGA.short: Private investors put money into Nigerian digital firms in 2024 to 2026, some raised at home; private money in public projects is not known.
NGA.summary:
Private money put into a digital business, with its year. Terra Industries closed its seed round at USD 52 million in 2026, with Norleo Space Investments among the new investors. Moove raised USD 250 million in a Series C in August 2026. Standard Bank Group agreed in October 2026 to buy shares in OPay for up to USD 200 million, subject to OPay's US listing. In 2024 Development Partners International led a USD 110 million Series C in Moniepoint, and in 2025 Visa put USD 10 million into Moniepoint.

Money raised inside the country. ThriveAgric raised N5.3 billion in August 2026 from institutional investors in the first series of a commercial paper programme approved by Nigeria's SEC. Dimension Data Limited raised N4.05 billion in July 2026 in a naira bond from high-net-worth investors to expand its fibre network.

Private money the government brought into a public digital project. In 2026 JICA committed USD 10.6 million as a grant to the Nigeria Sovereign Investment Authority for a project supporting startups that address social challenges.

Not held. No public-private partnership, concession or joint venture signed since 2024 has a private partner putting a named amount into a public digital project, and no state fund has taken in private investors' money.

RWA.short: Private investors put in USD 44 million and USD 11.2 million in 2025; where the startup money came from is not known.
RWA.summary:
Private money put into a digital business, with its year. In 2025 British International Investment committed USD 44 million in equity to Paradigm Tower Ventures, a shared telecom infrastructure company, an investment British International Investment lists as active and starting in 2025. In the same year, Disrupt Africa's tally counts USD 11.2 million raised by two Rwandan tech startups, naming neither the financiers nor the startups, and giving no split between the two.

Money raised inside the country. No amount raised inside Rwanda is held for 2024 or later. There is the 2025 tally of USD 11.2 million for two startups, which does not say whether the financiers are Rwandan or foreign.

Private money the government brought into a public digital project. No private amount tied to a government digital project is held for 2024 or later. There is a venture debt fund backed by the state-owned development bank, which is public money rather than private investment, reported in August 2026, and it is the only item of its kind held. Its owner is the Development Bank of Rwanda, a state body. Its owner is the Development Bank of Rwanda, a state body.

Not held. Every amount held from 2024 on was signed or started in the same year. Who financed the two startups, and where they are from, is not held.

SDN.short: No private money put into a digital business in Sudan is named, and it is not known whether any exists, so no stage is set.
SDN.summary: Not held. Nothing names private money put into a digital business in the country, or says there is none.

Private money put into a digital business, with its year. US company Cybastion announced a $300 million investment in September 2026, and Helios Towers a $150 million plan of its own money in July 2026. British International Investment committed $32 million to Wave in 2025, and in 2024 $27 million to Sonatel, where the IFC committed $40 million. The US DFC committed $5 million to QuantumID in 2024. Tanel raised a $2.1 million seed round in 2024 from Alan and Ventures Platform.

Money raised inside the country. Nothing held names an amount from a Senegalese bank, fund or company. Sonatel, an Orange Group subsidiary, took its 2024 loans from outside lenders.

Private money the government brought into a public digital project. Nothing held shows this. The Cybastion announcement names no instrument, projects or timetable.

Not held. No source from 2024 on names an amount put in by a bank, pension fund, insurer, investor or company of Senegal itself, or raised on the country's own market.

SLE.summary:
Private money put into a digital business, with its year. Orange Sierra Leone committed USD 50 million in 2025, self-funded and put into its own business, for a network modernisation toward 4G and 5G readiness. The commitment is described as active. It is the only private amount held dated 2024 or later, so the page names one deal and one year.

Money raised inside the country. Nothing held shows money raised inside Sierra Leone. There is the same Orange Sierra Leone commitment of USD 50 million in 2025, which the company funded itself and which is stated as a commitment, not as a raise.

Private money the government brought into a public digital project. Nothing held shows an amount the government brought in from private sources. There is the November 2025 opening of the Orange Sierra Leone data centre in Bo, where the President reaffirmed the government's commitment to enabling private investment.

Not held. Whether private money came in more than one year is not known, because only one amount dated 2024 or later is held. No money raised inside the country and no private money brought in by the government is held.

SOM.short: Nothing is known of private money put into a digital business in Somalia, or of there being none, so no stage is set.
SOM.summary: Not held. Nothing held names private money put into a digital business in Somalia, or says there is none.

SSD.short: Finnfund put USD 10 million into a telecom energy company across 2024 and 2025; money raised inside the country is not known.
SSD.summary:
Private money put into a digital business, with its year. Finnfund, Finland's development finance institution, put USD 5 million in 2024 into Communication and Renewable Energy Infrastructure (CREI), which supplies solar-hybrid power to MTN South Sudan's telecom sites. A follow-on of USD 5 million started in 2025 and was reported in February 2026, bringing Finnfund's total in the company to USD 10 million, 40% of the USD 25 million project financing.

Money raised inside the country. CREI, the company Finnfund financed, is registered in Mauritius, and its investor is Finnish.

Private money the government brought into a public digital project. NCT South Sudan and Bayobab are rolling out a national backbone fibre network, announced in March 2026, with no private amount given.

Not held. No amount from a bank, pension fund, insurer, investor or company of South Sudan itself since 2024 is known, nor any raised on its own market. No private amount in the government's fibre project is known.

STP.summary: Not held. No source dated 2024 or later names an amount of private money put into a digital business in the country.

SYC.summary:
Private money put into a digital business, with its year. Fusepay, a Seychelles-founded fintech, closed a $350,000 pre-seed round in August 2025, backed by Hustle Fund, Everywhere Ventures, First Check Ventures, Startup Istanbul and an angel investor. That makes five named backers in one round, and the amount is the only one held for 2024 or later.

Money raised inside the country. Fusepay is Seychelles-founded; the round's named backers and the angel investor are given without a stated home base, so how much of the round came from Seychelles is not given.

Private money the government brought into a public digital project. There is the Fusepay pre-seed round, a private raise by a payments business, with no government role or public project named, and no private money alongside a state-led digital project is held.

Not held. Only one amount is held from 2024 on, so whether private money came in more than one year is not known.

TGO.summary:
Private money put into a digital business, with its year. In 2024 the International Finance Corporation committed USD 54 million to Togocom, an Axian Group subsidiary for a telecom expansion loan, the earliest of the four deals. In February 2025 Gozem, a Lomé-based super app, closed a USD 30 million Series B round with MSC Group and Al Mada Ventures. In 2026 the IFC committed a further USD 10 million to Gozem, and BGK committed USD 28 million to Cyber Defense Africa.

Money raised inside the country. The Togo-based companies that took this money include Gozem, based in Lomé, and Togocom, a subsidiary of Axian Group.

Private money the government brought into a public digital project. The lenders and investors above dealt directly with companies, not with a government body: Togocom, Gozem and Cyber Defense Africa.

Not held. No amount from 2024 on is named from a bank, pension fund, insurer, investor or company of Togo itself, or raised on Togo's own market. No private money the government brought into a public digital project is shown.

TUN.short: Nothing held names private money put into a digital business in the country, or says there is none, so no stage is set.
TUN.summary: Not held. Nothing held names private money put into a digital business in the country, or says there is none.

TZA.short: Foreign and corporate money reached Tanzanian digital firms every year from 2024 to 2026, but none from Tanzanian investors is known.
TZA.summary:
Private money put into a digital business, with its year. In 2024 Norrsken22 put $8 million into NALA's Series A, British International Investment lent $20 million to Helios Towers' Tanzanian arm and bought $20 million of a Helios Towers bond, and InfraCo Africa put $2 million into Mawingu. In 2025 MIGA guaranteed $40 million for Airtel Money Tanzania, Wingu Africa put $50 million into a data centre and Axian Telecom paid $5 million for GOfiber. In 2026 Liquidity extended NALA a $25 million credit facility and Vodacom Group put $28 million into the M-Pesa platform.

Money raised inside the country. Vodacom Tanzania raised its capital spending 85.1% to TZS 323.9 billion in the year to March 2026.

Private money the government brought into a public digital project. The regulator disclosed KCB's 22.23% stake in Pesapal in September 2026.

Not held. No amount from 2024 on is held from a bank, pension fund, insurer, investor or company of Tanzania, or raised on its own market.

UGA.short: Four private deals of USD 15 million, 12 million, 1.6 million and 420,000 came in during 2024, but money raised inside Uganda is not known.
UGA.summary:
Private money put into a digital business, with its year. In January 2024 Gateway Partners lent USD 15 million to Watu Credit Uganda, a two- and three-wheeler asset-finance company, through Alpen Capital's Africa Credit Opportunities Fund. In 2024 the Belgian Investment Company for Developing Countries committed USD 12 million to TowerCo Of Africa Uganda for rural telecom towers, and ElectriFI put USD 1.6 million into the e-bike start-up Gogo Electric. In September 2024 Rexial, a direct-debit payments start-up, raised a USD 420,000 seed round.

Money raised inside the country. No money raised inside Uganda is held; Rexial, a Ugandan start-up, raised a USD 420,000 seed round in September 2024, from investors the source does not name.

Private money the government brought into a public digital project. No private money brought in by the government is held; The Belgian Investment Company for Developing Countries loan of USD 12 million went to a private tower company, starting 2024.

Not held. Every amount held from 2024 on was signed or started in the same year, so no later private money is shown. Nothing shows money raised inside Uganda, or private money the government brought into a public project.

ZAF.short: Private investors put money into South African digital firms from 2024 to 2026; no private deal in a public project is known.
ZAF.summary:
Private money put into a digital business, with its year. An Actis-led consortium completed the purchase of the Swiftnet tower platform from Telkom in 2025 for about US$370 million. Microsoft committed US$329 million to Azure South Africa and Equinix US$438 million to data centres, both in 2026. Teraco secured an R8 billion syndicated loan in 2024. Proparco is investing US$20 million in Frogfoot, Vox and Hypa, and Quona Capital led an US$8.4 million Series A in Jem, both in 2026.

Money raised inside the country. South African investors, led by the Public Investment Corporation, put together the R300 million first close of Mamor Capital Ventures' fund in 2026. The DNI Consortium holds 34.8% of Frogfoot and Vox after a 2026 capital raise valuing them at R14.4 billion.

Private money the government brought into a public digital project. The Technology Innovation Agency and the Small Enterprise Development and Finance Agency joined the same Mamor first close, a private fund, in 2026.

Not held. No source from 2024 on has a signed public-private partnership, concession or joint venture in which a private partner puts a named amount into a public digital project. Nor is there a state fund that private investors have paid into.

ZMB.short: Acumen put US$5M into Sun King Zambia and Lupiya pledged K500 million, both in 2026; private money in other years is not known.
ZMB.summary:
Private money put into a digital business, with its year. In 2026, Acumen's Hardest-to-Reach Catalyze initiative closed a US$5 million equity investment in Sun King's Zambian subsidiary, a pay-as-you-go solar company whose customers repay by mobile money, a business built on digital payments.

Money raised inside the country. In July 2026, Lupiya, a Zambian digital lender, said it will put a further K500 million into loans to Zambian small businesses, farmers, traders and women entrepreneurs over the next decade, from its own money.

Private money the government brought into a public digital project. The nearest private money to a state-linked sector is IFC's US$75 million senior loan to the tower operator IHS Zambia in 2021, lent to a private company and not to a public project, and made before the period counted.

Not held. Every amount held from 2024 on was signed or started in the same year, 2026. Whether private money came in across other years is not known.

BEN.short: Benin had a draft open data decree under discussion in December 2022 and no portal data published; no adopted policy is known.
BEN.summary:
Policy adopted. In December 2022 a World Bank open data readiness assessment, written for the Government of Benin, said the draft access to information bill and its Open Data decree were under discussion within the government, with no clear date for sending them to parliament and little progress in over 12 months. It named adoption of the bill and decree as the first priority. From January 2022 to September 2024, Expertise France ran a technical assistance project supporting the national agency ASSI in setting up Benin's open data initiative, with a first axis of putting in place an open data regulation.

Portal run and data published. The same assessment said the national open data portal, built on CKAN and developed by the digital agency ASIN in 2021, was being finalised and was due to be officially launched in 2023. It reported no data published on it, and said no open data licence or law yet existed.

Not held. No source held says an open data policy is adopted and still running.

Terms of reference issued in March 2026 for a programme of open data hackathons funded by the European Union refer to the policy's expected adoption by Parliament. No source held says the policy has been approved or launched, gives the date it was written or names the ministry that wrote it.

Portal run and data published. No source held names a government open data portal in Botswana, or a ministry that has released data under the policy. The hackathon programme was planned around the policy's adoption, which had not taken place by March 2026. No source held says which ministry would run a portal, or whether public bodies already release data in open formats ahead of the policy.

Not held. No source held says an open data policy is adopted and still running.

No source held says the policy or the law has been adopted. No source held gives a date for either.

The open data portal promised in the previous action plan was never made public and was under development at the Ministry of State Modernisation and Public Administration, with completion set for January 2025. The minister told a parliamentary committee in November 2023 that the portal was a 2024 project financed by the World Bank. No source held says it has opened.

In December 2025 the minister listed its launch among the policies Egypt has adopted for digital transformation.

The brief calls for a standardised framework and a unified portal to close that gap, since the vision rests on those other instruments alone.

The OGP Malawi Secretariat announced on 3 September 2025 that Malawi had officially launched its new Open Data Portal as part of the Third OGP National Action Plan, giving citizens access to government budget, development project and public service delivery data through dashboards and downloadable datasets. In November 2025 the CSEA brief states that most government datasets stay in PDF reports.

It was handed to the Ministry of Finance for submission to Cabinet in December 2016 and presented to the Permanent Secretary of Finance in February 2017. Portal run and data published. The same report says the national open data portal opendata.go.tz, launched in September 2015 and managed by the eGovernment Agency, held 163 datasets (755 resources) from 11 institutions in 4 sectors by June 2017, double the year before. The portal ran under the Chief Secretary's January 2015 circular as the interim directive.

AGO.short: In 2026 journalists, the opposition and the bar association criticised Angola's new false-information law; whether anyone has been punished under it is not known.
AGO.summary:
Public criticism of government policy. Leaders of the Sindicato dos Jornalistas Angolanos, the Comissao de Carteira e Etica and the Forum das Mulheres Jornalistas called the penalties of the new Law Against False Information on the Internet excessive and inhibiting, reported on 22 August 2026. UNITA, the largest opposition party, voted against the bill in the National Assembly on 21 May 2026, and the bar association had told the Assembly president on 27 January 2026 that the bill threatens free expression and needs reformulation. A jurist of the civic movement Mudei said the law's definition is unclear and several NGOs plan a court challenge with the bar association.

Cuts and blocks, and a bar on them. No cut or block is held for Angola. On 23 January 2026 UNITA abstained when the National Assembly approved the cybersecurity bill in general, saying it feared internet cuts on election and protest days.

Punishment for speech, and its removal. No arrest or charge for speech is held. The Law Against False Information on the Internet, Lei n.o 6/26, was published in the Diario da Republica on 4 August 2026 with prison of up to 10 years, and the bar association cited sanctions of 2 to 10 years for executives.

Not held. Nothing held says whether anyone in Angola was punished for what they said or published in the last twelve months, or that no one was.

Access Now's #KeepItOn report counts 4 internet shutdowns in Cameroon in 2025, one a cross-border cut that reached the Central African Republic through the WACS cable.

Punishment for speech, and its removal. No arrest or charge for speech is held. The nearest held fact is the 2010 cybercrime law, law n°2010/012 of 21 December 2010, whose provisions workshop participants said limit free expression.

Not held. Nothing held says who ordered the 2025 shutdowns or when they ended, and no source says whether a bar on such cuts exists.

GAB.summary:
Public criticism of government policy. Nine civil-society organisations, including ROLBG, SOS Prisonniers, Tournons la Page Gabon and the Ligue nationale des droits humains, met in Libreville on 11 July 2026 and called the suspension unconstitutional and disproportionate, demanding its repeal. On 25 July 2026 the group APSAD presented a report finding self-censorship among public-debate actors and urged an end to blanket suspensions.

Cuts and blocks, and a bar on them. The communications regulator, the HAC, suspended social media in Gabon by decision no. 0002/HAC/2026, until further notice. The Presidency's spokesman defended the suspension as temporary and conservatory on 17 July 2026, with no lifting date given. Gabon Mail Infos reported on 6 October 2026 that it was still in force. Maroc Telecom lists temporary restrictions on certain internet uses in Gabon for February 2026. No bar on such cuts is held.

Punishment for speech, and its removal. Nothing is held on a person arrested or an outlet closed for what was said, nor on a law repealed. The nearest held fact is the APSAD finding of self-censorship among public-debate actors and rules short of international standards.

Not held. Nothing held says anyone in Gabon was arrested or charged for speech, or that any law was repealed. No source gives the date the suspension began, or says a court or other body has barred it.

GHA.summary:
Public criticism of government policy. On 19 September 2026 Democracy Hub, a civil-society group, through its adviser Oliver Barker-Vormawor, criticised on JoyNews the police detention, the denial of bail and the evidence-gathering in the Salomey Awiti Bafoh prosecution. The same day the MP John Ntim Fordjour said that Section 208 is applied selectively against government critics.

Cuts and blocks, and a bar on them. Nothing is held on a cut to internet access or a block on a platform in Ghana, or on any bar against one. The nearest held fact is the Presidency's letter on a national stakeholder engagement on hate speech and abusive online content.

Punishment for speech, and its removal. Senior nursing officer Salomey Awiti Bafoh was arrested on 13 September 2026 and charged at the Adentan Circuit Court with abetment of publishing false news under sections 20(1) and 208 of the Criminal Offences Act, for allegedly helping redistribute videos from a UK-based TikTok account. She pleaded not guilty and was denied bail and remanded. The National Commission for Civic Education chairperson said, as reported on 1 September 2026, that the repeal of criminal libel and seditious laws in 2001 strengthened democratic development.

Not held. Nothing held says an outlet was suspended or closed for what it published in the last twelve months, or that any access to a platform was cut.

GIN.short: In September 2026 the regulator barred France 24, and social media have been restricted since 28 July; who ordered the restrictions is not known.
GIN.summary:

The Union pour la defense des consommateurs, through its president Bany Sidibe, denounced the social media restrictions on 4 August 2026 as a state decision harming the right to information. It and the Association des blogueurs de Guinee demanded the return of access to all social networks.

Cuts and blocks, and a bar on them. Facebook, YouTube and TikTok were blocked from 28 July 2026, according to the bloggers association ABLOGUI, and Jeune Afrique reported WhatsApp difficulties too. On 17 September 2026 the HAC ordered the telecoms regulator ARPT to block all France 24 digital access points and Canal+ Guinée to cut its signal. The ECOWAS Court found that restrictions on internet access from October to December 2020 violated rights to information and expression.

Punishment for speech, and its removal. On 17 September 2026 the HAC revoked the national broadcasting authorisation of France 24 and withdrew its correspondents accreditations. The Media Foundation for West Africa report, as reported on 14 August 2026, cites the suspension of critical media outlets in Guinea. No repeal is held.

Not held. No source says who ordered the social media restrictions of July 2026, or when they ended. Nothing held says a person was arrested for speech in the last twelve months.

GNB.summary:
Public criticism of government policy. No source held reports public criticism of government policy in the window. The nearest held fact is that on 26 November 2025, the day the military seized power, citizens reported restrictions on social platforms.

Cuts and blocks, and a bar on them. On 26 November 2025, citizens reported widespread restrictions on Facebook, YouTube, TikTok and Instagram, which the Media Foundation for West Africa says the military imposed. The source gives no end date, and no held source names a bar on such cuts.

Punishment for speech, and its removal. No source held reports a person punished for speech, or a punishing law removed. The nearest held fact is the same report, which says the military imposed restrictions on social platforms on the day it took power.

Not held. No source held says when the social media restrictions ended, or that anyone criticised policy in public or was punished for speech.

GNQ.short: Equatorial Guinea arrested the author of a viral video about the vice-president in 2026; policy criticism is not known, so no stage is set.
GNQ.summary: Not held. No source dated in the last three years says a newspaper, broadcaster, party or group inside the country criticised a government policy in public, and none says the internet was cut in the last twelve months.

KEN.short: The Court of Appeal struck down Kenya's false-publication offences in 2026 and the National Assembly has appealed; who ordered the 2025 Telegram block is unknown.
KEN.summary:
Public criticism of government policy. The Bloggers Association of Kenya returned to court in 2025 to challenge the amendment to the Computer Misuse and Cybercrimes Act. On 4 September 2026 the Consumer Federation of Kenya won a High Court order quashing the Attorney-General's opinion clearing the Digital Superhighway tenders, and on 24 August 2026 an opposition leader said the electoral commission's contract specifications were tailor-made for one company.

Cuts and blocks, and a bar on them. Access Now counts three internet shutdowns in Kenya in 2025, including an exam-time block of Telegram, the third year running, now being litigated. KICTANet's network ran its first rapid-response protocol during a 2024 Telegram shutdown. No held source gives a law or court ruling that bars cuts.

Punishment for speech, and its removal. Kenya's Court of Appeal struck down the sections of the Computer Misuse and Cybercrimes Act on false publication; the sections carried fines up to KSh 5 million and up to ten years in prison, and the National Assembly has appealed to the Supreme Court. Neither article gives the ruling's date.

Not held. No law, ruling of the country's own court or undertaking given in court in the last three years bars the government from cutting the internet.

LBR.short: In September 2026 police arrested a man under the Cybercrime Act over posts about the Vice President; the court outcome is not known.
LBR.summary:
Public criticism of government policy. On 24 September 2026 the Press Union of Liberia, the Center for Media Studies and several civil society groups called the Cybercrime Act's provisions on false information and offensive communication vague and a weapon to silence critics. On 31 August 2026 the Center for Transparency and Accountability in Liberia and other groups pressed the Liberia Telecommunications Authority chairman to disclose revenue from the gateway monitoring system, which he has refused to do.

Cuts and blocks, and a bar on them. No held source reports a cut or block of internet access, or a law or ruling that bars one. The nearest held fact is the Liberia Telecommunications Authority's temporary management of the International Gateway Monitoring System.

Punishment for speech, and its removal. In September 2026 police arrested Jerry Nyanti Wratto in Monrovia, charged him and sent him to court under the Cybercrime Act over Facebook and TikTok posts about the Vice President. The Vice President asked for his release, and no court outcome is given. A 2019 law, the KAK Act, decriminalised sedition and criminal libel against the President.

Not held. No source held gives the outcome of the Wratto case, a cut or block of internet access, or a bar on one.

LBY.short: Nothing held shows public criticism of policy, an internet cut or a punishment for speech, so no stage is set.
LBY.summary: Not held. Nothing held says government policy is criticised in public inside the country, that the internet was cut, or that anyone was punished for what they said.

LSO.short: Nothing held shows public criticism of policy, an internet cut or a punishment for speech, so no stage is set.
LSO.summary: Not held. Nothing held says government policy is criticised in public inside the country, that the internet was cut, or that anyone was punished for what they said.

MAR.short: Nothing held shows public criticism of policy, an internet cut or a punishment for speech, so no stage is set.
MAR.summary: Not held. Nothing held says government policy is criticised in public inside the country, that the internet was cut, or that anyone was punished for what they said.

MDG.short: In September 2026 a news site questioned the cybercrime bill's digital police powers; it is not known whether anyone was punished for speech.
MDG.summary:
Public criticism of government policy. On 3 September 2026 Madagascar-Tribune questioned the government's cybercrime bill n°042/2026, saying the permanent access powers of its new digital police raise issues of public freedoms and of balance with freedom of expression, and contrasting it with the stalled access-to-information bill.

Cuts and blocks, and a bar on them. No held source reports a cut of internet access or a bar on one. The nearest held fact is the Council of Ministers decision of 8 July 2026 to block pornographic websites, which is a block of named sites and not of access.

Punishment for speech, and its removal. No held source reports a person punished for speech, or a punishing law removed. The nearest held fact is the same bill n°042/2026, whose digital police unit would hold permanent access powers.

Not held. No source says the country went the last twelve months with no one punished for what they said or published.

MLI.short: Mali sentenced two journalists in 2026 over public remarks and tried a third; policy criticism is not known, so no stage is set.
MLI.summary: Not held. No source dated in the last three years says a newspaper, broadcaster, party or group inside the country criticised a government policy in public, and none says the internet was cut in the last twelve months.

MOZ.short: In March 2026 civil society and opposition criticised telecommunications regulations as allowing internet shutdowns; whether anyone was punished for speech is not known.
MOZ.summary:
Public criticism of government policy. Civil society bodies and opposition parties strongly criticised the government's new telecommunications regulations in March 2026 as allowing internet shutdowns on national security grounds, and journalist and press freedom activist Tomas Vieira Mario condemned the minister's defence on Facebook and called for the regulations to be overhauled.

Cuts and blocks, and a bar on them. No cut or block is held. The nearest held fact, from a Club of Mozambique report, is that the March 2026 criticism concerned regulations said to allow shutdowns, and that the minister denied any attempt to restrict use of the internet.

Punishment for speech, and its removal. No arrest, charge or sentence for speech is held. The nearest held fact is that a named journalist publicly condemned the minister's defence of the regulations in March 2026, the day after the minister spoke.

Not held. No source says the country went the last twelve months with no one punished for what they said or published.

MRT.short: Nothing held shows public criticism of policy, an internet cut or a punishment for speech, so no stage is set.
MRT.summary: Not held. Nothing held says government policy is criticised in public inside the country, that the internet was cut, or that anyone was punished for what they said.

MUS.short: Nothing held shows public criticism of policy, an internet cut or a punishment for speech, so no stage is set.
MUS.summary: Not held. Nothing held says government policy is criticised in public inside the country, that the internet was cut, or that anyone was punished for what they said.

MWI.short: Civil society criticised budget and surveillance plans in 2026; whether anyone was punished for speech in the last twelve months is not known.
MWI.summary:
Public criticism of government policy. Civil society groups told parliamentary committees on 9 March 2026 that the proposed 2026/27 education budget falls short of the 20 percent UNESCO benchmark. A group calling itself the Concerned Citizens of Malawi People Power Movement publicly criticised the communications regulator MACRA by January 2026 for not briefing the public on its social media monitoring system procurement.

Cuts and blocks, and a bar on them. No cut or block is held. The nearest held fact is that civil society groups challenged the legality of MACRA's $1.5 million social media monitoring contract and called for its suspension.

Punishment for speech, and its removal. No arrest or charge in the last twelve months is held. The nearest held fact is that journalist Joshua Chisa Mbele was arrested in January 2022 after sharing on Facebook a document alleging corruption involving government officials.

Not held. No source says the country went the last twelve months with no one punished for what they said or published.

NAM.short: A think tank criticised a draft data bill in 2022; nothing held shows internet cuts or punishment for speech, so no stage is set.
NAM.summary: Not held. No source dated in the last three years says a newspaper, broadcaster, party or group inside the country criticised a government policy in public, and none says the internet was cut in the last twelve months.

NER.short: Niger punished journalists from 2023 to 2026; nothing held shows public criticism of policy or a recent internet cut, so no stage is set.
NER.summary: Not held. No source dated in the last three years says a newspaper, broadcaster, party or group inside the country criticised a government policy in public, and none says the internet was cut in the last twelve months.

NGA.short: In 2026 the State Services department prosecuted Omoyele Sowore for criticising the president, then paused the case until after the 2027 election.
NGA.summary:
Public criticism of government policy. The Socio-Economic Rights and Accountability Project and the Nigerian Guild of Editors called in August 2026 for enforcement of Section 24 of the Cybercrimes Act to be suspended. On 18 July 2026 the Rule of Law and Accountability Advocacy Centre urged the National Assembly to withdraw or revise parts of the Data Protection (Amendment) Bill that could let regulators shut digital platforms.
