Cuts and blocks, and a bar on them. No cut in the last twelve months is counted. The nearest held fact is that the federal government announced an indefinite suspension of Twitter on 5 June 2021 and telecom providers were directed to block it.

Punishment for speech, and its removal. The Department of State Services is prosecuting Omoyele Sowore under the Cybercrimes Act for describing President Tinubu as a criminal; its Director-General announced on 30 August 2026 that the prosecution would be suspended until after the 2027 election. On 31 August 2026 SERAP and Sowore's lawyer demanded that the DSS withdraw the charges.

Not held. Nothing held says a person was arrested, charged or jailed, or an outlet suspended or closed, for what was said or published, other than the Sowore prosecution.

RWA.short: Nothing held says whether policy is criticised in public, the internet was cut, or anyone was punished for speech, so no stage is set.
RWA.summary: Not held. Nothing held says government policy is criticised in public inside the country, that the internet was cut, or that anyone was punished for what they said.

SDN.short: In August 2026 a court in El Obeid jailed a pharmacist for six years over a private call opposing the war; no repeal is known.
SDN.summary:
Public criticism of government policy. The Sudanese Journalists Syndicate condemned the detention of journalist Gurashi Awad on 14 August 2026 and called for the immediate repeal of the 2007 Cybercrime Act, which it described as restrictive of fundamental liberties.

Cuts and blocks, and a bar on them. MTN Sudan suspended internet service in the afternoons on 13 to 15 April 2026, the days of the Sudanese Certificate Examinations, in accordance with government directives, and the source calls it the sixth consecutive year of exam-period shutdowns.

Punishment for speech, and its removal. A criminal court in El Obeid sentenced pharmacist Ahmed Suleiman Ahmed al-Waqi to six years in prison in August 2026 over a private phone conversation opposing the war, under the Criminal Act and the Cybercrime Law.

Not held. Nothing held says a cut was barred or a penalty for speech repealed.

SEN.short: In 2026 23 MPs challenged the media regulator law in court; whether anyone was punished for speech last year is not known.
SEN.summary:
Public criticism of government policy. The Association of Online Press Publishers and Professionals (APPEL), a Senegalese professional body, with Paradigm Initiative, backed a constitutional challenge lodged by 23 MPs on 10 March 2026 against the media regulator law over risks of administrative censorship, in Paradigm Initiative's account. The Conseil constitutionnel gave its Decision n° 2/C/2026 on that law on 7 April 2026.

Cuts and blocks, and a bar on them. RSF says that in early 2024 restrictions such as internet shutdowns undermined the right to inform in Senegal, without saying who ordered them or for how long. CIPESA says shutdowns were imposed during the 2023 unrest and that a court found they violated freedom of expression and access to information.

Punishment for speech, and its removal. Nothing held names a person punished for speech or publication. The nearest held fact is the law itself: the deputies adopted the bill creating the Conseil national de régulation des médias on 3 March 2026, and it carries the number Loi n° 2026-09.

Not held. No source says the country went the last twelve months with no one punished for what they said or published.

SLE.short: Parliament repealed the criminal libel provisions in 2020, but nothing recent is known on public criticism or internet cuts, so no stage is set.
SLE.summary: Not held. No source dated in the last three years says a newspaper, broadcaster, party or group inside the country criticised a government policy in public, and none says the internet was cut in the last twelve months.

SOM.short: In March 2025 police shut Risaala Media and arrested five journalists; whether anyone was punished for speech in the past year is not known.
SOM.summary:
Public criticism of government policy. Defenders Coalition Somalia, a Somali civil-society group, with DefendDefenders, criticised the Official Information Bill approved by the Council of Ministers in March 2024 in a joint UN review submission dated 28 October 2025. They objected to its broad confidentiality and national-security exemptions, its lack of independent oversight and the secrecy in which it was drafted.

Cuts and blocks, and a bar on them. No cut of a connection is held. The nearest held fact is that the government closed 82,000 social media pages it called extremist-linked in 2026, as Hiiraan reported on 4 September 2026.

Punishment for speech, and its removal. On 18 March 2025 armed police stormed the Risaala Media station in Mogadishu, took it off air and arrested five named journalists without a court warrant, after it was first to report the bombing of the president's convoy. The submission gives no law for the arrests.

Not held. No source says the country went the last twelve months with no one punished for what they said or published.

SSD.short: The regulator ordered social media blocked in January 2025; nothing held says when it ended or whether policy is criticised, so no stage is set.
SSD.summary: Not held. No source dated in the last three years says a newspaper, broadcaster, party or group inside the country criticised a government policy in public, and none says the internet was cut in the last twelve months.

STP.short: Nothing held says whether policy is criticised in public, the internet was cut, or anyone was punished for speech, so no stage is set.
STP.summary: Not held. Nothing held says government policy is criticised in public inside the country, that the internet was cut, or that anyone was punished for what they said.

SWZ.short: In April 2026 an outlet published an investigation holding the ICT ministry to account; whether anyone was punished for speech is not known.
SWZ.summary:
Public criticism of government policy. An opinion piece in Independent News Eswatini says that the Swazi Bridge outlet published an investigation on 12 April 2026 holding the ICT ministry to account for how its memorandum of understanding with Google Cloud EMEA was communicated, which the piece calls a failure of communication.

Cuts and blocks, and a bar on them. No cut or block of a connection or a site is held. The nearest held fact is that MISA, the media body, engaged the Eswatini government on expression and media freedom, in a blog dated 27 February 2026.

Punishment for speech, and its removal. No arrest, charge or sanction for speech is held. The nearest held fact is a promised access to information law, which MISA's account of its talks with the government names, with no date given for it.

Not held. No source says the country went the last twelve months with no one punished for what they said or published.

SYC.short: Nothing held says whether policy is criticised in public, the internet was cut, or anyone was punished for speech, so no stage is set.
SYC.summary: Not held. Nothing held says government policy is criticised in public inside the country, that the internet was cut, or that anyone was punished for what they said.

TCD.short: Internet access in Lac province has been cut since October 2024 and was still limited in September 2026; who ordered it is not known.
TCD.summary:
Public criticism of government policy. Internet Society Chad, a civil-society chapter, called on the authorities in a communique of 11 February 2025 to restore access in Lac province and said alternatives to a total cut exist. The Association des Médias en Ligne du Tchad (AMET) said on 5 August 2026 that the regulator HAMA's suspension of applications to create new media must respect press freedom and citizens' right to pluralistic information, while backing action against fake pages.

Cuts and blocks, and a bar on them. Internet access in Lac province has been cut since 28 October 2024 and was still off on 11 February 2025, with security reasons mentioned as possible. A citizen's open letter to the president, reported on 10 September 2026, says connectivity in Lac has been heavily limited for nearly two years and was still limited. Neither source names who ordered it or gives an end date.

Punishment for speech, and its removal. No arrest, charge or sanction for speech is held. The nearest held fact is that HAMA suspended the examination of applications to create online newspapers, reported on 4 August 2026.

Not held. Who ordered the cut of internet access in Lac province, and when it ends, are not held.

TGO.short: Access Now reports 2025 protest throttling in Togo, but not where, who ordered it or when it ended, so no stage is set.
TGO.summary: Not held. No source dated in the last three years says a newspaper, broadcaster, party or group inside the country criticised a government policy in public, and none says the internet was cut in the last twelve months.

TUN.short: Journalists were sentenced to prison in 2026 over what they wrote and said; whether any twelve months pass without such a case is not known.
TUN.summary:
Public criticism of government policy. The National Union of Tunisian Journalists, with Human Rights Watch, Amnesty International and RSF, denounced Decree-Law 2022-54 as a tool of repression in a report dated 16 July 2026, and the union called for the annulment of the El Mekki judgment.

Cuts and blocks, and a bar on them. Nothing is held on cuts or blocks. The nearest held fact is the RSF 2026 index, which ranks Tunisia 137th of 180.

Punishment for speech, and its removal. On 15 July 2026 the Sfax Court of Appeal sentenced journalist Haythem El Mekki to one year in prison under Article 86 of the Telecommunications Code over a social-media post about a Sfax hospital, after a first-instance court had dismissed the case. Journalists Borhen Bsaies and Mourad Zeghidi were sentenced to one year, reduced to eight months, under Decree-Law 54; RSF also reports the El Mekki sentence.

Not held. Nothing held shows a twelve-month stretch in which no one was arrested, charged or jailed, and no outlet suspended or closed, for what was said or published.

TZA.short: The internet was cut nationwide around the 29 October 2025 election; who ordered it and whether another cut has followed is not known.
TZA.summary:
Public criticism of government policy. Nothing is held on public criticism of policy. The nearest held fact is that the Legal & Human Rights Centre filed a case at the East African Court of Justice on 8 December 2025 alleging a nationwide internet shutdown by the government.

Cuts and blocks, and a bar on them. Access Now reports a five-day nationwide internet blackout during the 29 October 2025 election, and counts 8 internet shutdowns in Tanzania in 2025. The Legal & Human Rights Centre alleges a total shutdown from 29 October to 4 November 2025. The Internet Governance Project puts the cost at an estimated US$250 million in losses during the 2025 election period.

Punishment for speech, and its removal. The Tanzania Communications Regulatory Authority suspended the online content licence of JamiiForums for 90 days from 6 September 2025 over content it called misleading and insulting to the Government and the President, and blocked access to the platform. A complaint filed in August 2026 alleges the leader of the opposition was jailed on capital charges in 2025 for calling for electoral reforms.

Not held. Nothing held shows a twelve-month stretch with no cut or block of the internet or a service, or who ordered the October 2025 blackout.

UGA.short: The government cut the internet for four days around the January 2026 election and kept social media blocked; when those blocks ended is not known.
UGA.summary:
Public criticism of government policy. The Uganda Law Society condemned the shutdown, its vice president saying no state of emergency had been declared so the order was illegal and unconstitutional. At a Kampala briefing on 27 February 2026, UGANET and other civil society organisations criticised blanket internet shutdowns and urged legal safeguards against them.

Cuts and blocks, and a bar on them. The Uganda Communications Commission directed all mobile operators and internet providers to suspend public internet access from 18:00 on 13 January 2026, two days before the presidential election. Access Now describes it as a cut of internet and social media; the blackout lasted four days. On 18 January the Commission's executive director said social media and messaging applications stayed restricted after general access returned, and they were still blocked more than a week later.

Punishment for speech, and its removal. Nothing is held on anyone punished for speech. The nearest held fact is that a CIPESA submission to Uganda's fourth-cycle Universal Periodic Review names sections 24 and 25 of the Computer Misuse Act.

Not held. Nothing held shows a twelve-month stretch with no cut or block of the internet or a service.

ZAF.short: Nothing held says whether policy is criticised in public, the internet was cut, or anyone was punished for speech, so no stage is set.
ZAF.summary: Not held. Nothing held says government policy is criticised in public inside the country, that the internet was cut, or that anyone was punished for what they said.

ZMB.short: A vlogger got nine months in September 2026 over a post about a presidential aide; whether any year passes without such cases is unknown.
ZMB.summary:
Public criticism of government policy. The Net Rights Coalition said on 8 August 2026 that arrests, detention and summoning of journalists under the Cyber Crimes Act No. 4 of 2025 signal a chilling environment and called for amendments to the cyber laws. The Christian Churches Monitoring Group said the electoral system change and delimitation were done with insufficient consultation.

Cuts and blocks, and a bar on them. Nothing is held on a cut or block in the last twelve months. The nearest held fact is that Access Now says authorities reportedly blocked WhatsApp, Facebook, Twitter and Instagram during the 12 August 2021 elections, lifted after civil society challenged the order in court.

Punishment for speech, and its removal. On 15 September 2026 the Lusaka Magistrates Court sentenced vlogger Joseph Chishimba to nine months under section 54 of the Cyber Security and Cyber Crimes Act No. 2 of 2021 over a WhatsApp screenshot about a presidential aide. Police in Mansa arrested Kennedy Mwansa for allegedly insulting the president in a TikTok video, charging him under the Cyber Crimes Act. The EU observation mission said the August 2026 elections took place amid arrests for online speech offences, mostly over criticism of the president.

Not held. Nothing held shows a twelve-month stretch in which no one was arrested, charged or jailed for what was said or published.

ZWE.short: In June 2026 a Zimbabwean media-freedom body criticised the national AI strategy; whether anyone was punished for speech in the last year is not known.
ZWE.summary:
Public criticism of government policy. On 23 June 2026 MISA Zimbabwe, a media-freedom body inside the country, published an analysis criticising the Zimbabwe National AI Strategy 2026-2030, including its proposed National Reality Check Platform for truth-verification, as lacking legal safeguards for freedom of expression.

Cuts and blocks, and a bar on them. CIPESA says the state security minister ordered an internet shutdown in January 2019 amid nationwide fuel-price protests, through an intercept directive to mobile network operators, and that the High Court ruled that month that the minister had no authority under the Interception of Communications Act to order it.

Punishment for speech, and its removal. No arrest, charge or sentence for speech is held in the evidence for this country. CIPESA's note on the fourth-cycle review lists offences of false information, cyberbullying, incitement, insulting the President, sovereignty and national interest.

Not held. No source says the country went the last twelve months with no one punished for what they said or published.

AGO.short: Angola's 2020 payment system law is in force and since 2022 lets non-bank companies be authorised; no rule to connect providers is known.
AGO.summary:
Law or rules in force. Angola's payments law is Lei n.º 40/20 of 16 December 2020, the Lei do Sistema de Pagamentos de Angola, and the Banco Nacional de Angola makes binding notices under its article 6. Aviso n.º 2/22 of February 2022 sets the rules for access to payment service activity, Aviso n.º 4/25 of August 2025 those for opening and running e-money accounts, and Aviso n.º 1/26 of January 2026 those for acquirers that are not banks.

Non-banks licensed and providers required to connect. Aviso n.º 2/22 lets non-bank financial institutions based in Angola provide payment services, e-money issuance among them, as payment service companies authorised by the central bank. Since January 2026 only such authorised companies may act as non-bank acquirers of payment terminals and cash machines.

Not held. No rule held requires mobile money providers and banks to connect to each other or to a national or regional switch.

BDI.short: Burundi's 2018 payment system law is in force, and a 2024 regulation licenses non-bank payment institutions; no rule to connect providers is known.
BDI.summary:
Law or rules in force. Burundi's Loi n°1/07 of 11 May 2018 on the national payment system is in force, and the central bank's oversight framework, published in November 2025, cites it as the current law, whose article 9 lets the bank issue regulations. Under it the bank made Règlement n°002/2024, revising a 2017 regulation on payment services and payment institutions: no one may provide payment services without the central bank's licence.

Non-banks licensed and providers required to connect. The central bank licenses payment institutions under the 2024 regulation, and its framework lists them apart from commercial banks and microfinance institutions as operators of e-money platforms. Every licensed payment service provider is to be inspected on site at least every two years. The regulation's date within 2024 is not given, and no rule is named that requires providers to connect to each other.

Not held. No rule held requires mobile money providers and banks to connect to each other or to a national or regional switch.

BEN.short: Benin is under the regional central bank's 2024 payment rules, which license non-banks; in 2026 it ordered all providers to connect.
BEN.summary:
Law or rules in force. Benin is bound by the rules of the BCEAO, the central bank of the eight-state West African Economic and Monetary Union. Instruction n°001-01-2024 on payment services, applied since January 2024, obliges every company offering payment services in the union to hold a licence or stop, and distinguishes payment institutions from banks, microfinance institutions and e-money institutions.

Non-banks licensed and providers required to connect. Four companies held payment institution licences in Benin at 31 August 2026: Julaya Bénin, Open SI, FedaPay Bénin and QOS Integrated Center Bénin. The union's banking commission counted three licensed e-money issuers there at the end of 2025. In April 2026 the BCEAO told every bank, e-money institution and payment institution to connect to its instant payment platform, PI-SPI, by 30 June, and on 25 June moved the deadline to 30 September 2026, with microfinance institutions given until 30 June 2027.

Not held. Nothing on the four questions.

BFA.short: Burkina Faso is under the regional central bank's 2024 payment rules, which license non-banks; in 2026 it ordered all providers to connect.
BFA.summary:
Law or rules in force. Burkina Faso is bound by the rules of the BCEAO, the central bank of the eight-state West African Economic and Monetary Union. Payment institutions are licensed under its instruction of 23 January 2024 on payment services, which sets them apart from banks, microfinance institutions and e-money institutions; the BCEAO counted 34 licensed across the union at 31 August 2026.

Non-banks licensed and providers required to connect. Two payment institutions are licensed in Burkina Faso: INTOUCH Burkina, since 9 May 2025, and KERRY Payments Burkina, since 2 September 2025. The union's banking commission counted one licensed e-money issuer there at the end of 2025. In April 2026 the BCEAO told every bank, e-money issuer and payment institution to connect to its instant payment platform, PI-SPI, by 30 June, and on 25 June moved the deadline to 30 September 2026.

Not held. Nothing on the four questions.

BWA.short: Botswana's electronic payment regulations, amended in April 2026, license payment companies that are not banks; no rule requiring providers to connect is known.
BWA.summary:
Law or rules in force. The Bank of Botswana regulates payments under the Electronic Payment Services Regulations. Amendments made by the Minister of Finance as Statutory Instrument No. 46 of 2026, under the Bank of Botswana Act, took effect on 2 April 2026, and providers had to comply at once. Operating a service without the Bank's licence is an offence.

Non-banks licensed and providers required to connect. The amended regulations require anyone operating an electronic payment service, e-money issuance and money transfer included, to hold a Bank of Botswana licence and to be a company incorporated in Botswana. They do not apply to banks licensed under the Banking Act, so the licence is one for companies that are not banks. The Bank told the public to use licensed providers.

Not held. No rule held requires mobile money providers and banks to connect to each other or to a national or regional switch.

CAF.short: The Central African Republic is under the 2018 regional payment services regulation, which licenses non-banks; none was licensed there by 2023.
CAF.summary:
Law or rules in force. The Central African Republic is bound by CEMAC regulation n°04/18 of 21 December 2018 on payment services, which the regional central bank's financial inclusion strategy, published in February 2025, describes as governing payment establishments and mobile money across the six member states of the Central African Economic and Monetary Community.

Non-banks licensed and providers required to connect. The 2018 regulation created payment establishments, licensed to provide payment services without being tied to a bank; subsidiaries of mobile operators and fintech companies can be licensed where they meet its requirements. The strategy lists six licensed across the region by July 2023: two in Cameroon, one in Chad, two in Congo and one in Gabon. None of the six was in the Central African Republic.

Not held. No rule held requires mobile money providers and banks to connect to each other or to a national or regional switch.

CIV.short: Côte d'Ivoire is under the regional central bank's 2024 payment rules, with ten non-bank payment institutions licensed; in 2026 all providers were ordered to connect.
CIV.summary:
Law or rules in force. Côte d'Ivoire is bound by the rules of the BCEAO, the central bank of the eight-state West African Economic and Monetary Union. Instruction n°001-01-2024 on payment services, applied since January 2024, obliges every company offering payment services in the union to hold a licence or stop; payment institutions are licensed under it.

Non-banks licensed and providers required to connect. Ten payment institutions were licensed in Côte d'Ivoire at 31 August 2026, the newest on 27 April 2026, and in 2025 Djogana Pay became the country's fourth e-money institution after Orange Money, MTN Mobile Money and Moov Money. In April 2026 the BCEAO told every bank, e-money institution and payment institution to connect to its instant payment platform, PI-SPI, by 30 June, and on 25 June moved the deadline to 30 September 2026.

Not held. Nothing on the four questions.

CMR.short: Cameroon licenses payment institutions that are not banks under regional rules, the newest in July 2026; no rule requiring providers to connect is known.
CMR.summary:
Law or rules in force. Cameroon's regulatory framework lets payment institutions, and also banks and microfinance institutions, offer payment services under the conditions the regulation sets. A licence is granted by order of the finance minister on a decision of COBAC, the banking commission of the six-state Central African Economic and Monetary Community.

Non-banks licensed and providers required to connect. Konoom Cameroun was licensed as a payment institution by arrêté n°681/MINFI of 21 July 2026, following COBAC decision n°D-2026/092; Orange Money Cameroun and Mobile Money Corporation, the MTN subsidiary, were already licensed. COBAC's 2025 annual report counts seven licensed payment institutions in the region, those two among them. No rule is named that requires mobile money providers and banks to connect to each other or to a national or regional switch, so Cameroon answers the first three questions and not the fourth.

Not held. No rule held requires mobile money providers and banks to connect to each other or to a national or regional switch.

COD.short: The Democratic Republic of the Congo's 2018 payment systems law is in force; whether it licenses non-banks is not known.
COD.summary:
Law or rules in force. Loi n° 18-019 of 9 July 2018 on payment systems and securities settlement systems is the Democratic Republic of the Congo's payments law. It was published in the Journal Officiel on 23 July 2018. No regulation made under it by the central bank is named, and no amendment to it is reported.

Non-banks licensed and providers required to connect. The 2018 law defines electronic money and payment orders. It is not said whether companies that are not banks can be licensed under it, and no rule is named that requires mobile money providers and banks to connect to each other or to a national switch. The Democratic Republic of the Congo therefore answers the first two questions only: a law in force, with its reach to non-banks and to connection between providers not stated.

Not held. No source held says the law or rules in force license payment providers or e-money issuers that are not banks, or names one licensed under them.

COG.short: Congo has two licensed payment institutions that are not banks, reported for 2025; the rules they are licensed under are not named.
COG.summary:
Law or rules in force. Congo's payment institutions are licensed by COBAC, the banking commission of the six-state Central African Economic and Monetary Community, whose 2025 annual report covers the payment institutions licensed in the region. The commission reports each year on the institutions it supervises in the six member states.

Non-banks licensed and providers required to connect. Mobile Money Congo SA and Mobile Commerce Congo SA are the payment institutions operating in Congo, neither of them a bank, and their revenues rose 28.1% to FCFA 20.6 billion in 2025. No law or regulation is named as the one they are licensed under, and no rule is named that requires mobile money providers and banks to connect to each other or to a national or regional switch. Congo therefore reaches the third question on the licences alone.

Not held. No rule held requires mobile money providers and banks to connect to each other or to a national or regional switch.

COM.short: The Comoros has had central bank e-money rules since 2017, under a 2015 payments decree; whether they license non-banks is not known.
COM.summary:
Law or rules in force. The Central Bank of the Comoros issued Regulation n°01/2017/BCC/DSBR in 2017, setting the conditions for carrying on e-money activity. It rests on decree n°15-026/PR of 3 March 2015 on payment systems, means of payment and payment incidents. The regulation gives only the year it was made, and no later amendment is reported.

Non-banks licensed and providers required to connect. The 2017 regulation sets conditions for e-money activity. It is not said whether companies that are not banks can be licensed under it, and no rule is named that requires mobile money providers and banks to connect to each other or to a national switch. The Comoros therefore answers the first two questions only: rules in force, with their reach to non-banks and to connection between providers not stated.

Not held. No source held says the law or rules in force license payment providers or e-money issuers that are not banks, or names one licensed under them.

CPV.short: Cabo Verde's 2018 decree-laws on payments are in force and let the central bank authorise non-bank institutions; no rule to connect providers is known.
CPV.summary:
Law or rules in force. Cabo Verde legislated on payments in three decree-laws published on 28 November 2018. Decreto-legislativo n.º 7/2018 sets the regime for regulating and operating the payment system, and Decreto-legislativo n.º 8/2018 regulates payment services and the issue, distribution and redemption of electronic money. All three appeared in the same issue of the Boletim Oficial, n.º 78, and the Banco de Cabo Verde is the regulator under each.

Non-banks licensed and providers required to connect. Payment institutions and e-money institutions, financial institutions distinct from banks, are authorised by the Banco de Cabo Verde under the third, Decreto-legislativo n.º 9/2018, which governs access to their activity. The postal service, Correios de Cabo Verde, may also issue e-money. No licensed institution is named, and no rule is named that requires providers to connect to each other or to a national switch.

Not held. No rule held requires mobile money providers and banks to connect to each other or to a national or regional switch.

DJI.short: Djibouti's 2016 national payment system law is in force; whether it licenses non-banks is not known.
DJI.summary:
Law or rules in force. Loi n° 118/AN/15/7ème L, the law creating the National Payment System, was adopted by the National Assembly and promulgated in 2016. It applies across Djibouti to every payment service and system. It is known as the Loi sur le Système de Paiement National. No regulation made under it by the central bank is named, and no amendment to it is reported.

Non-banks licensed and providers required to connect. The 2016 law covers payment services and systems. It is not said whether companies that are not banks can be licensed under it, and no rule is named that requires mobile money providers and banks to connect to each other or to a national switch. Djibouti therefore answers the first two questions only: a law in force, with its reach to non-banks and to connection between providers not stated.

Not held. No source held says the law or rules in force license payment providers or e-money issuers that are not banks, or names one licensed under them.

DZA.short: Algeria's 2023 banking law and 2025 regulation license payment providers that are not banks; the first mobile operator subsidiary was authorised in September 2026.
DZA.summary:
Law or rules in force. Algeria's Loi n° 23-09 of 21 June 2023 on money and banking provides for payment service providers and counts electronic money among payment instruments. Under it the Bank of Algeria made Regulation no. 25-02 of 14 April 2025 on their authorisation, licensing and operation, and instruction no. 06-2025 of 17 August 2025 on how they are organised.

Non-banks licensed and providers required to connect. The 2023 law lists payment service providers apart from banks, and the 2025 regulation lets a company be licensed as one by the Governor of the Bank of Algeria once the Monetary and Banking Council has authorised it. On 23 September 2026 the Council authorised Djezzy Payment Services, a subsidiary of a mobile operator, to set itself up as a provider; it has twelve months to apply for the licence.

Not held. No rule held requires mobile money providers and banks to connect to each other or to a national or regional switch.

EGY.short: Egypt's central bank issued licensing rules for payment providers in 2025; whether companies that are not banks can be licensed is not known.
EGY.summary:
Law or rules in force. The Central Bank of Egypt issued Rules for Licensing and Registration of Payment System Operators and Payment Service Providers in June 2025, with transitional provisions for existing payment institutions. In September 2025 it issued regulations on governance, internal control and fit and proper criteria, with which operators and providers must comply within a year.

Non-banks licensed and providers required to connect. The 2025 licensing rules apply to payment system operators and payment service providers. It is not said whether a company that is not a bank can be licensed under them, and no rule is named that requires mobile money providers and banks to connect to each other or to a national switch. Egypt therefore answers the first two questions only.

Not held. No source held says the law or rules in force license payment providers or e-money issuers that are not banks, or names one licensed under them.

ERI.short: Nothing held names a payments law or e-money rules for Eritrea, or says there are none, so no stage is set.
ERI.summary: Not held. Nothing held names a payments law, e-money rules or a draft of either, or says there is none.

ETH.short: Ethiopia's 2020 central bank directives license payment operators and wallet issuers that are not banks; no rule requiring providers to connect is known.
ETH.summary:
Law or rules in force. The National Bank of Ethiopia introduced two sets of rules in 2020: the Payment Instrument Issuers directives and the Payment Systems Operators directive. Firms are licensed and operating under both. The Reporter gave this account of the two frameworks in July 2026. No act of parliament on payments is named.

Non-banks licensed and providers required to connect. The operators directive created four licence categories, for switch, point-of-sale, cash machine and payment gateway operators, under which companies that are not banks, Chapa, Arifpay, Santimpay and Kacha among them, were licensed. The issuers directives let telecom operators launch mobile wallets. No rule is named that requires mobile money providers and banks to connect to each other or to a national switch, so Ethiopia answers the first three questions and not the fourth.

Not held. No rule held requires mobile money providers and banks to connect to each other or to a national or regional switch.

GAB.short: Gabon is under the 2018 regional payment regulation, with non-bank payment institutions operating; a national digital payments ordinance was before parliament in 2026.
GAB.summary:
Law or rules in force. Gabon is bound by CEMAC regulation n°04/18 of 21 December 2018 on payment services, which a BEAC instruction of 5 May 2026 supplements. A national text is in preparation: the Council of Ministers adopted a draft ordinance on digital payments on 29 January 2026, and on 22 May the digital economy minister defended the bill ratifying it before the National Assembly's finance committee.

Non-banks licensed and providers required to connect. The regional regulation governs payment institutions distinct from credit institutions, which must report monthly to the central bank. COBAC's 2025 report names Airtel Money Gabon and Clikpay Gabon in Gabon's payment institution sector, which earned FCFA 24.7 billion in 2025. No rule is named that requires providers to connect to each other.

Not held. No rule held requires mobile money providers and banks to connect to each other or to a national or regional switch.

GHA.short: Ghana's 2019 payments act licenses e-money issuers that are not banks, and mobile money interoperability was mandated in 2018.
GHA.summary:
Law or rules in force. Ghana's Payment Systems and Services Act, 2019 (Act 987) has applied since February 2020. The Bank of Ghana acts under it: on 14 July 2026 it revoked a licence under section 13. The Act sets licensing requirements for payment service providers and electronic money issuers.

Non-banks licensed and providers required to connect. The Act requires payment service providers and electronic money issuers to hold a Bank of Ghana licence. Zeepay Ghana, a fintech company, held a dedicated electronic money issuer licence until the Bank revoked it in July 2026 over inadequate cash backing of its e-money. Ghana mandated mobile money interoperability in 2018; the rule that did so is not named. The Bank of Ghana assesses licence applicants on financial stability, technology, compliance with anti-money-laundering rules and consumer protection.

Not held. Nothing on the four questions.

GIN.short: Central bank decisions from 2015 license non-bank e-money companies; as of 2026 no rule is known requiring providers to connect to a switch.
GIN.summary:
Law or rules in force. The BCRG's Comite des agrements issued Decision D/2015/003/CAM of 31 March 2015 on e-money issuance and e-money establishments. It binds from its date of signature and was published in the Journal Officiel, as reproduced in the BCRG's December 2017 compendium of banking texts.

Non-banks licensed and providers required to connect. The decision places e-money establishments among financial establishments, not banks, and constitutes them as Guinean limited companies. It requires them to obtain a BCRG licence, with a decision due within 90 days of a complete file. Decision D/2015/008/CAM of 3 June 2015 sets their minimum share capital at GNF 2 billion, to be held in Guinean francs and employed in Guinea. Article 5 of banking law L/2013/060/CNT, promulgated by decree on 28 November 2013, allows service providers other than credit institutions to be authorised, in a limited way, to provide and manage means of payment under rules set by a Comite des agrements decision. At the 22 July 2026 NimbaPay launch the BCRG Vice-Governor called NimbaPay a strategic opportunity, not a regulatory constraint.

Not held. No rule is held that requires mobile money providers and banks to connect to each other or to a national or regional switch.

GMB.short: The Gambia's 2011 mobile money regulation authorises providers that are not banks, beside a 2013 payments act; no rule to connect providers is known.
GMB.summary:
Law or rules in force. The Gambia has two texts. The central bank's Mobile Money Regulation, 2011, made under the Central Bank of The Gambia Act 2005, took effect on 15 October 2011. The Electronic Payments System Act 2013 defines the establishment and operation of the electronic payments system.

Non-banks licensed and providers required to connect. The 2011 regulation provides for retail transfers by persons not licensed as banks or financial institutions, and has the central bank authorise such payment service providers: limited liability companies registered in The Gambia, with core capital of GMD 10 million and a security deposit of GMD 5 million. No rule is named that requires mobile money providers and banks to connect to each other or to a national switch.

Not held. No rule held requires mobile money providers and banks to connect to each other or to a national or regional switch.

GNB.short: Guinea-Bissau is under the regional central bank's 2024 payment rules, with two non-banks licensed; in 2026 all providers were ordered to connect.
GNB.summary:
Law or rules in force. Guinea-Bissau is bound by the rules of the BCEAO, the central bank of the eight-state West African Economic and Monetary Union. Payment institutions are licensed under its Instruction n°001-01-2024 on payment services, and 34 were approved across the union at 31 August 2026.

Non-banks licensed and providers required to connect. The banking commission's register lists one payment institution and one e-money institution in Guinea-Bissau, INTOUCH Guinée-Bissau and Finances Mobiles Bissau, neither a bank; the first was approved on 25 June 2025. The BCEAO required every bank, e-money issuer and payment institution to connect to its instant payment platform, PI-SPI, by 30 June 2026, and on 25 June moved the deadline to 30 September; five institutions in Guinea-Bissau were authorised on the platform at 31 July 2026.

Not held. Nothing on the four questions.

GNQ.short: Equatorial Guinea is under the 2018 regional payment services regulation, which licenses non-banks; none was licensed there by 2023.
GNQ.summary:
Law or rules in force. Equatorial Guinea is bound by CEMAC regulation n°04/18 of 21 December 2018 on payment services, which the regional central bank's financial inclusion strategy, published in February 2025, describes as governing payment establishments and mobile money across the six member states of the Central African Economic and Monetary Community.

Non-banks licensed and providers required to connect. The 2018 regulation created payment establishments, licensed to provide payment services without being tied to a bank; subsidiaries of mobile operators and fintech companies can be licensed where they meet its requirements. The strategy lists six licensed across the region by July 2023: two in Cameroon, one in Chad, two in Congo and one in Gabon. None of the six was in Equatorial Guinea.

Not held. No rule held requires mobile money providers and banks to connect to each other or to a national or regional switch.

KEN.short: Kenya's 2011 payment system act and 2014 regulations authorise mobile money operators; a replacement bill was published for comment in September 2026.
KEN.summary:
Law or rules in force. Kenya's National Payment System Act 2011 is the legal framework for payment systems and providers, and the National Payment System Regulations 2014 put it into operation. It is the current Act. In September 2026 the National Treasury and the Central Bank of Kenya published a draft National Payment System Bill, 2026 to repeal and replace it, with comments due by 9 October.

Non-banks licensed and providers required to connect. Mobile phone money transfer operators are authorised as payment service providers under the 2011 Act and the 2014 regulations, in categories that include e-money issuer and small money issuer. No rule is named that requires mobile money providers and banks to connect to each other or to a national switch.

Not held. No rule held requires mobile money providers and banks to connect to each other or to a national or regional switch.

LBR.short: Liberia's central bank mobile money regulations were in force in 2024; whether they license companies that are not banks is not known.
LBR.summary:
Law or rules in force. The Central Bank of Liberia's Mobile Money Regulations are the framework governing electronic money and mobile money operators in Liberia, where more than 11 million mobile wallets operate. The Central Bank of Liberia is the regulator.

Non-banks licensed and providers required to connect. The regulations govern mobile money operators. It is not said that those operators are companies other than banks, or that they are licensed under the regulations, and no rule is named that requires mobile money providers and banks to connect to each other or to a national switch. Liberia therefore answers the first two questions only: rules in force, with their reach to non-banks and to connection between providers not stated. The year the regulations were made is not given. Nor is any payments act of parliament named.

Not held. No source held says the law or rules in force license payment providers or e-money issuers that are not banks, or names one licensed under them.

LBY.short: Libya's 2022 electronic transactions law covers e-money, and the central bank licenses electronic payment companies; no rule to connect providers is known.
LBY.summary:
Law or rules in force. Libya's Law No. 6 of 2022 on Electronic Transactions defines electronic money and, in article 70, provides that it is issued by commercial banks and other financial institutions under controls set by the Central Bank of Libya.

Non-banks licensed and providers required to connect. The Central Bank's circular 18 of 2025 is addressed to electronic payment companies it has licensed, and binds them. It defines an electronic payment service provider as an entity licensed by the Central Bank to provide electronic payment services and e-wallets. The licence is therefore one a company that is not a bank can hold. No rule is named that requires those companies and banks to connect to each other or to a national switch.

Not held. No rule held requires mobile money providers and banks to connect to each other or to a national or regional switch.

LSO.short: Lesotho's 2014 payment systems act is in force; a bill to replace it and license all payment providers reached second reading in May 2026.
LSO.summary:
Law or rules in force. Lesotho's Payment Systems Act, 2014 was published in the Government Gazette on 12 September 2014 and came into operation that day. On 5 May 2026 the Minister of Finance moved the Payment System Bill, 2025 for second reading in the National Assembly, to repeal and replace it.

Non-banks licensed and providers required to connect. The bill would license all payment service providers, fintech companies included. The 2014 Act frames interbank payment systems and the issue and use of payment instruments. It is not said that companies other than banks can be licensed under the Act in force, and no rule is named that requires mobile money providers and banks to connect to each other or to a national switch.

Not held. No source held says the law or rules in force license payment providers or e-money issuers that are not banks, or names one licensed under them.

MAR.short: Morocco's 2014 banking law licenses payment institutions that are not banks, and they were active in 2026; no rule requiring providers to connect is known.
MAR.summary:
Law or rules in force. Morocco's Law 103-12 on credit institutions, enacted on 24 December 2014, defines means of payment, electronic money among them, and payment services, and regulates payment institutions. Bank Al-Maghrib supervises them; in July 2026 it cut the cap on domestic card interchange fees from 0.65% to 0.50%, effective 1 October 2026.

Non-banks licensed and providers required to connect. The law defines payment institutions as entities offering payment services, separate from credit institutions, and requires them to obtain Bank Al-Maghrib's approval before operating. Bank Al-Maghrib and the Competition Council said in July 2026 that newly licensed payment institutions and older ones were taking up card acquiring. No rule is named that requires providers to connect to each other. Payment institutions also open accounts remotely alongside banks, under a 2020 ruling of the data protection commission.

Not held. No rule held requires mobile money providers and banks to connect to each other or to a national or regional switch.

MDG.short: Madagascar's 2017 e-money law licenses e-money institutions that are not banks; no rule requiring providers to connect is known.
MDG.summary:
Law or rules in force. Madagascar's Loi n°2016-056 on electronic money and electronic money institutions was adopted by both chambers in December 2016, cleared by the High Constitutional Court on 27 January 2017 and promulgated on 2 February 2017. The banking supervision commission, the CSBF, applies it: it issues instructions and audits the institutions.

Non-banks licensed and providers required to connect. The law requires any legal entity running e-money operations to be approved by the CSBF as an e-money institution, a limited company separate from credit institutions and microfinance institutions. The CSBF grants and withdraws those licences, and in June 2026 the central bank governor announced audits of the institutions. No rule is named that requires them and banks to connect to each other.

Not held. No rule held requires mobile money providers and banks to connect to each other or to a national or regional switch.

MLI.short: Mali is under the regional central bank's 2024 payment rules, which license non-banks; in 2026 it ordered all providers to connect.
MLI.summary:
Law or rules in force. Mali is bound by the rules of the BCEAO, the central bank of the eight-state West African Economic and Monetary Union. Payment institutions are licensed under its Instruction n°001-01-2024 on payment services, which sets them apart from banks, microfinance institutions and e-money institutions.

Non-banks licensed and providers required to connect. Two payment institutions are licensed in Mali: INTOUCH Mali, since 9 May 2025, and CAURIDOR, since 3 September 2025. The union's banking commission counted two licensed e-money issuers there at the end of 2025. In April 2026 the BCEAO told every bank, e-money issuer and payment institution to connect to its instant payment platform, PI-SPI, by 30 June, and on 25 June set 30 September 2026 as the new deadline.

Not held. Nothing on the four questions.

MOZ.short: Mozambique passed a new payment system law in July 2026, licenses mobile operators' e-money institutions and requires them to join the instant payment system.
MOZ.summary:
Law or rules in force. Mozambique replaced its payments law in 2026. Lei n.º 15/2026 of 2 July approves the National Payments System Law and revokes Lei n.º 2/2008; parliament approved it in April and the president promulgated it in June. The central bank had made Aviso n.º 1/GBM/2026 under the 2008 law in February.

Non-banks licensed and providers required to connect. Three electronic money institutions authorised by the central bank, M-Pesa, e-Mola and M-Kesh, belong to the three mobile operators. Article 8 of the regulation annexed to the Aviso makes participation in the instant payment system compulsory for electronic money institutions and for credit institutions above a set size. A report of July 2026 likewise says participation by digital wallet operators in the instant payment system, which joins banks, microbanks and e-money institutions, is mandatory.

Not held. Nothing on the four questions.

MRT.short: Mauritania's 2021 electronic payments law and 2022 instruction license payment institutions that are not banks; no rule requiring providers to connect is known.
MRT.summary:
Law or rules in force. Mauritania's Loi n°2021-014 of 5 July 2021 on electronic payment services and means regulates payment service providers and e-money issuers, and repealed a 2006 ordinance. Under it the central bank issued Instruction no. 03/GR/2022 of 31 March 2022 regulating payment institutions. The law has 113 articles and was published in Journal Officiel n°1490 of 30 July 2021.

Non-banks licensed and providers required to connect. The law bars anyone except banks from carrying on the business of a payment institution, or issuing and distributing e-money, without the central bank's prior licence. The instruction defines payment institutions as legal entities licensed by the central bank other than credit institutions, with minimum capital and a guarantee deposit of 20 million ouguiya each. No rule is named that requires providers to connect to each other.

Not held. No rule held requires mobile money providers and banks to connect to each other or to a national or regional switch.

MUS.short: Mauritius's 2018 payment systems act licenses non-bank payment providers, with new rules for aggregators in 2026; no rule to connect providers is known.
MUS.summary:
Law or rules in force. The National Payment Systems Act 2018 was assented to on 29 November 2018 and makes the Bank of Mauritius the regulator of payment systems and payment service providers. It was last amended in April 2026, and the Bank's Guideline for Payment Aggregators, issued under section 17, took effect on 31 August 2026.

Non-banks licensed and providers required to connect. Section 9(1) of the Act provides that no one other than the central bank or a bank may act as a payment service provider without the Bank's licence. The 2026 guideline requires non-bank companies that want to act as payment aggregators to obtain that licence, and gave existing ones until 31 August 2026 to apply. No rule is named that requires providers to connect to each other.

Not held. No rule held requires mobile money providers and banks to connect to each other or to a national or regional switch.

MWI.short: Malawi's Payment Systems Act is in force and was amended in August 2026; whether it licenses non-banks is not known.
MWI.summary:
Law or rules in force. Malawi has a Payment Systems Act in force. On 6 August 2026 Parliament passed an amendment to it removing its provisions on cheques, and the Finance Minister said detailed regulations would follow. Because Parliament amended it, the Act was already law before August 2026. The report does not name the regulations to come.

Non-banks licensed and providers required to connect. The amendment deals with cheques. It is not said whether companies that are not banks can be licensed under the Act, and no rule is named that requires mobile money providers and banks to connect to each other or to a national switch. Malawi therefore answers the first two questions only: a law in force, with its reach to non-banks and to connection between providers not stated. The year the Act was first passed is not given.

Not held. No source held says the law or rules in force license payment providers or e-money issuers that are not banks, or names one licensed under them.

NAM.short: Namibia's 2023 payment system act is in force, and 2026 rules license non-bank payment providers; no rule requiring providers to connect is known.
NAM.summary:
Law or rules in force. Namibia's Payment System Management Act 14 of 2023 was promulgated on 28 July 2023 and commenced on 8 August 2023. The Bank of Namibia makes determinations under its section 45: PSD-10 on fees and charges took effect on 24 December 2025, PSD-1 on licensing on 6 January 2026 and PSD-12 on operational and cybersecurity standards on 3 July 2026.

Non-banks licensed and providers required to connect. PSD-1 sets a licensing process for payment services by non-bank financial institutions and defines an electronic money issuer as a licensed payment service provider. PSD-10 applies to all payment service providers, defined as banking institutions and non-bank financial institutions, and binds e-money issuers and providers of e-money wallets and instant payments. No rule is named that requires providers to connect to each other.

Not held. No rule held requires mobile money providers and banks to connect to each other or to a national or regional switch.

NER.short: Niger is under the regional central bank's rules, with one non-bank e-money issuer licensed in 2025; in 2026 all providers were ordered to connect.
NER.summary:
Law or rules in force. Niger is bound by the rules of the BCEAO, the central bank of the eight-state West African Economic and Monetary Union, which licenses e-money issuers and supervises them with the union's banking commission. The commission's 2025 report counts one licensed e-money issuer in Niger at 31 December 2025, among 18 across the union.

Non-banks licensed and providers required to connect. That issuer is not a bank. In April 2026 the BCEAO told every bank, e-money issuer and payment institution in the eight states, Niger included, to be connected to its instant payment platform, PI-SPI, by 30 June 2026. By a communiqué of 25 June it set 30 September 2026 as the new deadline for them, and 30 June 2027 for microfinance institutions.

Not held. Nothing on the four questions.

NGA.short: Nigeria's central bank licenses mobile money operators and payment providers, reported in 2026; the rules it does so under are not named.
NGA.summary:
Law or rules in force. The Central Bank of Nigeria already licenses mobile money operators, payment service providers and digital banks, operators told a public hearing on 2 March 2026. The hearing was on the Nigerian Fintech Regulatory Commission Bill 2025, which would create a single regulator to license and supervise all fintech services and passed second reading in the House of Representatives on 28 October 2025.

Non-banks licensed and providers required to connect. The central bank's licences go to mobile money operators and payment service providers, OPay among the operators that said so at the hearing. The law or rules under which it grants them are not named, and no rule is named that requires mobile money providers and banks to connect to each other or to a national switch. Nigeria therefore reaches the third question on the licences alone.

Not held. No rule held requires mobile money providers and banks to connect to each other or to a national or regional switch.

RWA.short: Rwanda's central bank directive of January 2026 requires banks and e-money issuers to route all transfers through one national platform from July 2026.
RWA.summary:
Law or rules in force. The National Bank of Rwanda issued Directive No. 45/2026 on 9 January 2026. It required domestic retail payments between banks and electronic money issuers to move to the eKash platform, the national instant payment rail. RSwitch gave the account of the directive that ITWeb Africa reported.

Non-banks licensed and providers required to connect. From 14 July 2026 every transfer between bank accounts and electronic money issuers, account to wallet, wallet to account, account to account and wallet to wallet, is routed through eKash. The Rwanda Bankers' Association states that the directive took effect on that date, so that banks and e-money issuers all run on the single rail. The directive binds the e-money issuers with the banks; the law under which those issuers are licensed is not named.

Not held. Nothing on the four questions.

SDN.short: Sudan's 2020 central bank regulation licenses non-bank mobile payment companies; a 2026 circular asks them to connect to a switch not yet available.
SDN.summary:
Law or rules in force. Sudan's central bank regulates payments under its Regulation on Licensing and Organising Mobile Payment Financial Institutions 2020, approved on 28 December 2020 under the Banking Business Organisation Act, and a Payment Systems Regulation of 2013. Circular 7/2026 of 31 March 2026 cites both as its basis and sets binding minimum rules for financial services over USSD.

Non-banks licensed and providers required to connect. The 2020 regulation has the central bank license companies, not banks, to run mobile payment and open e-money wallet accounts; their names may not include the word bank. The 2026 circular lets those institutions and licensed electronic payment providers offer USSD financial services alongside banks. It asks providers to connect to a national switch once one is available, and sets no date.

Not held. No rule held requires mobile money providers and banks to connect to each other or to a national or regional switch.

SEN.short: Senegal is under the regional central bank's 2024 payment rules, with eleven non-bank payment institutions licensed; in 2026 all providers were ordered to connect.
SEN.summary:
Law or rules in force. Senegal is bound by the rules of the BCEAO, the central bank of the eight-state West African Economic and Monetary Union. Its instruction of 23 January 2024 on payment services is the rule under which payment institutions are licensed, and obliges every fintech offering payment services in the union to obtain a licence or stop.

Non-banks licensed and providers required to connect. Eleven payment institutions were licensed in Senegal at 31 August 2026, Flutterwave Sénégal and Julaya Sénégal among them, and the banking commission counted five licensed e-money issuers at the end of 2025; Wave has held an e-money licence since April 2022. By a communiqué of 25 June 2026 the BCEAO set 30 September 2026 as the deadline for banks, e-money institutions and payment institutions to connect to its instant payment platform, PI-SPI.

Not held. Nothing on the four questions.

SLE.short: Sierra Leone's 2022 payment systems act is in force and licenses payment providers that are not banks; no rule requiring providers to connect is known.
SLE.summary:
Law or rules in force. Sierra Leone's National Payment Systems Act, 2022 was assented to on 2 June 2022, commenced on 23 June 2022 and repealed the Payment Systems Act 2009. The Bank of Sierra Leone's Guidelines for E-money have been completed and gazetted, with guidelines on remittance business and directives for the national switch.

Non-banks licensed and providers required to connect. Section 6 of the Act bars anyone from providing payment services or operating a system without a Bank of Sierra Leone licence, and sets conditions for e-money issuers; section 8 exempts only banks and financial institutions from needing a new licence. The licence is therefore one for companies that are not banks, and the Act gives mobile money operators a seat on its payments council. No rule is named that requires providers to connect to each other.

Not held. No rule held requires mobile money providers and banks to connect to each other or to a national or regional switch.

SOM.short: Somalia's 2020 mobile money regulations are in force, and both houses had passed a payment system bill by January 2026; its signing is not known.
SOM.summary:
Law or rules in force. The Central Bank of Somalia made the Mobile Money Regulations, Amended 2020 under the Central Bank of Somalia Act 2012, setting out the licensing, conduct and supervision of mobile money service providers. A National Payment System Bill is before parliament: the House of the People passed it on 8 November 2025 and the Upper House passed its third reading on 11 January 2026.

Non-banks licensed and providers required to connect. The 2020 regulations license mobile money service providers. It is not said that those providers are companies other than banks, and no rule is named that requires mobile money providers and banks to connect to each other or to a national switch. Whether the bill has been signed into law is not reported.

Not held. No source held says the law or rules in force license payment providers or e-money issuers that are not banks, or names one licensed under them.

SSD.short: South Sudan's central bank was validating a draft National Payment System Bill in August 2026; no payments law or e-money rules are in force.
SSD.summary:
Law or rules in force. South Sudan has a bill and no law. The Bank of South Sudan opened a five-day workshop on 10 August 2026 to validate the National Payment System Bill, 2025, which covers mobile money, e-money, payment switches and settlement, before its next stage of consideration. At its close on 14 August the governor called for faster progress; the bill had not been passed.

Non-banks licensed and providers required to connect. The bill would set licensing frameworks as the regulatory foundation for mobile money and electronic banking, the governor said in urging its swift passage. With no law or rules in force, no company that is not a bank is licensed under one and no rule requires providers to connect. South Sudan therefore answers the first question only.

Not held. No source held says a payments law or e-money rules are in force.

STP.short: São Tomé and Príncipe's 2018 payment system law lets the central bank license non-bank providers; no rule requiring providers to connect is known.
STP.summary:
Law or rules in force. São Tomé and Príncipe's Lei n.º 17/2018, published on 7 September 2018, sets the legal regime for regulating, overseeing and managing the National Payment System, and covers payment services, the issue of electronic money among them. The central bank's organic law, Lei n.º 03/2025, makes it responsible for regulating payment systems and lets its board adopt binding regulations.

Non-banks licensed and providers required to connect. The 2018 law lets the central bank authorise and license payment service providers, defined as any entity providing payment services, e-money issuance included. Banks are treated apart: they need no new authorisation to provide payment services. The licence is therefore open to companies that are not banks. No licensed provider is named, and no rule is named that requires providers to connect to each other.

Not held. No rule held requires mobile money providers and banks to connect to each other or to a national or regional switch.

SWZ.short: Eswatini's 2023 payment system act licenses mobile money providers, and since December 2024 all providers must join the national payment switch.
SWZ.summary:
Law or rules in force. Eswatini's National Payments System Act, 2023 regulates payment systems and payment service providers and repealed a 2011 clearing and settlement act. The central bank said in November 2025 that licensing runs under it now and that it was finalising regulations on timelines and requirements.

Non-banks licensed and providers required to connect. A new mobile money provider must go through the central bank's licensing process; three mobile money operators, MTN MoMo and Instacash among them, are in the interoperable system. At the launch of fast payments on the Eswatini Payment Switch on 11 December 2024 the Governor said participation is mandated for all payment service providers offering local payments, with the remaining participants expected to be live by the end of January 2025.

Not held. Nothing on the four questions.

SYC.short: Seychelles' 2014 payment system act and 2022 e-money regulations license issuers that are not banks; no rule requiring providers to connect is known.
SYC.summary:
Law or rules in force. Seychelles' National Payment System Act, 2014 commenced on 18 August 2014. Under it the Central Bank made the Electronic Money Regulations, 2022, which commenced on 12 December 2022, and on 15 December 2025 amended its licensing and authorisation regulations.

Non-banks licensed and providers required to connect. The 2022 regulations set capital and liquidity rules for electronic money issuers other than banks, with initial capital of SCR 1,000,000, and treat issuers that are banks or credit unions as separate cases. The 2025 amendment sets the conditions on which the Central Bank may license any company incorporated under the Companies Act as a payment service provider. No rule is named that requires providers to connect to each other. The amended regulations exempt banks and credit unions from annual fees only.

Not held. No rule held requires mobile money providers and banks to connect to each other or to a national or regional switch.

TCD.short: Chad is under the 2018 regional payment services regulation, with three non-banks licensed by 2026; no rule requiring providers to connect is known.
TCD.summary:
Law or rules in force. Chad is bound by the CEMAC regulation of 21 December 2018 on payment services, which replaced 2011 rules covering e-money issuance only and is the framework under which Chad's payment establishments are licensed. The regional central bank's register lists it as a text for all six member states.

Non-banks licensed and providers required to connect. Moov Money Tchad, a telecom subsidiary, holds a payment establishment licence from the regional banking commission, COBAC, confirmed in July 2026; it is the third company that is not a bank so licensed in Chad, after Airtel Money in 2023 and the fintech Konoom in 2025. In February 2026 the finance ministry signed conventions with four such operators on mobile money for state payments. No rule is named that requires providers to connect to each other.

Not held. No rule held requires mobile money providers and banks to connect to each other or to a national or regional switch.

TGO.short: Togo is under the regional central bank's rules, with a new e-money institution licensed in 2025; in 2026 all providers were ordered to connect.
TGO.summary:
Law or rules in force. Togo is bound by the rules of the BCEAO, the central bank of the eight-state West African Economic and Monetary Union, which licenses e-money institutions across the union. The banking commission's 2025 report says the number of licensed e-money issuers rose from 14 to 18 in 2025, Togo's Tmoney among the new approvals.

Non-banks licensed and providers required to connect. Tmoney was licensed as an e-money institution in September 2025. In April 2026 the BCEAO told every bank, e-money issuer and payment institution in the eight states to be connected to its instant payment platform, PI-SPI, by 30 June 2026, and on 25 June moved the deadline to 30 September, with microfinance institutions given until 30 June 2027. Nine institutions in Togo were authorised on the platform at 31 July 2026.

Not held. Nothing on the four questions.

TUN.short: Tunisia's 2016 banking law licenses non-bank payment establishments, with new central bank rules in September 2026; no rule to connect providers is known.
TUN.summary:
Law or rules in force. Tunisia's Law n° 2016-48 of 11 July 2016 on banks and financial institutions sets the framework for payment services and payment establishments in its articles 20 and 21. The central bank issued Circular n° 2026-10 on payment establishments on 25 September 2026, replacing a 2018 circular; it takes effect three months after publication.

Non-banks licensed and providers required to connect. Article 20 of the law has payment services run by a specialised payment establishment, which is not a bank, with minimum capital of 5 million dinars. In March 2026 OFT Tunisie, a subsidiary of Ooredoo, received definitive authorisation as one. The 2026 circular lets payment establishments open client payment accounts, transfer funds and issue electronic payment instruments. No rule is named that requires providers to connect to each other.

Not held. No rule held requires mobile money providers and banks to connect to each other or to a national or regional switch.

TZA.short: Tanzania's 2015 National Payment Systems Act is in force and covers electronic money; whether non-banks are licensed under it is not known.
TZA.summary:
Law or rules in force. Tanzania's National Payment Systems Act, 2015 was assented to on 25 April 2015 and gazetted on 22 May 2015. It regulates payment systems, payment instruments and electronic money under Bank of Tanzania licensing. The Bank of Tanzania is the licensing authority. No regulation made under the Act is named, and no amendment to it is reported.

Non-banks licensed and providers required to connect. The 2015 Act puts electronic money under Bank of Tanzania licensing. It is not said that companies other than banks are licensed under it, and no rule is named that requires mobile money providers and banks to connect to each other or to a national switch. Tanzania therefore answers the first two questions only: a law in force, with its reach to non-banks and to connection between providers not stated.

Not held. No source held says the law or rules in force license payment providers or e-money issuers that are not banks, or names one licensed under them.

UGA.short: Uganda's 2020 National Payment Systems Act is in force, and the central bank licenses two mobile money operators; no rule to connect providers is known.
UGA.summary:
Law or rules in force. Uganda's law is the National Payment Systems Act, 2020. Bank of Uganda officials told a parliamentary committee on 14 September 2026 that the bank's oversight of wallet providers, payment firms and deposit-taking institutions rests on it.

Non-banks licensed and providers required to connect. The bank's payment systems director said at the same hearing that the wallet providers it licenses and supervises are MTN and Airtel, mobile money operators that are not banks, under the 2020 Act. No rule is named that requires mobile money providers and banks to connect to each other or to a national switch, so Uganda answers the first three questions and not the fourth. The hearing was part of a committee inquiry into the central bank.

Not held. No rule held requires mobile money providers and banks to connect to each other or to a national or regional switch.

ZAF.short: South Africa's 1998 payment system act is in force and has no licence for non-banks; a bill to change that was promised in September 2026.
ZAF.summary:
Law or rules in force. South Africa's National Payment System Act of 1998 regulates the payment system and gives the Reserve Bank responsibility for clearing and settlement; it is twenty-eight years old and still the law. The Reserve Bank governor said on 1 September 2026 that a National Payment System Bill, moving regulation from the kind of entity to the kind of activity, would soon go out for public comment.

Non-banks licensed and providers required to connect. South Africa has no dedicated mobile money licence for companies that are not banks, an MTN executive said in September 2026, so fintech companies must work through a licensed bank to move money. The Reserve Bank is preparing an equivalent through an authorisation framework and the bill.

Not held. No source held says the law or rules in force license payment providers or e-money issuers that are not banks, or names one licensed under them.

ZMB.short: Zambia's 2007 National Payment Systems Act is in force; whether it licenses companies that are not banks is not known.
ZMB.summary:
Law or rules in force. Zambia's National Payment Systems Act was enacted by parliament on 12 April 2007, to give legal backing to the operation of payment mechanisms in Zambia and to empower the Bank of Zambia to regulate them. No regulation made under it is named, and no amendment to it is reported.

Non-banks licensed and providers required to connect. The 2007 Act empowers the Bank of Zambia to regulate payment mechanisms. It is not said whether companies that are not banks can be licensed under it, and no rule is named that requires mobile money providers and banks to connect to each other or to a national switch. Zambia therefore answers the first two questions only: a law in force, with its reach to non-banks and to connection between providers not stated.

Not held. No source held says the law or rules in force license payment providers or e-money issuers that are not banks, or names one licensed under them.

ZWE.short: Zimbabwe's 2001 National Payment Systems Act is in force; whether it licenses companies that are not banks is not known.
ZWE.summary:
Law or rules in force. Zimbabwe's National Payment Systems Act (Chapter 24:23), Act 21 of 2001, commenced on 16 November 2001. It provides for the recognition, operation, regulation and supervision of payment and clearing systems. The text held is consolidated to 31 December 2016. No regulation made under it is named, and no later amendment is reported.

Non-banks licensed and providers required to connect. The 2001 Act covers payment and clearing systems. It is not said whether companies that are not banks can be licensed under it, and no rule is named that requires mobile money providers and banks to connect to each other or to a national switch. Zimbabwe therefore answers the first two questions only: a law in force, with its reach to non-banks and to connection between providers not stated.

Not held. No source held says the law or rules in force license payment providers or e-money issuers that are not banks, or names one licensed under them.

AGO.short: Only surveillance, identification and personnel systems are held, to 2026; whether stations record on paper or digitally is not known, so no stage is set.
AGO.summary: Not held. No source held states whether stations record reports or cases on paper or digitally, in what system, or in how many stations.

BDI.short: Only traffic, statistics and staff systems are held, the latest from 2026; how stations record reports is not known, so no stage is set.
BDI.summary: Not held. Nothing held states whether stations record reports or cases on paper or digitally, in what system, or in how many stations.

BEN.short: Only fingerprint, criminal-file and public online services are held, to 2026; how stations record reports is not known, so no stage is set.
BEN.summary: Not held. Nothing held states whether stations record reports or cases on paper or digitally, in what system, or in how many stations.

BFA.short: A computerised occurrence book for police and gendarmerie stations was over 80% built in December 2023; whether any station uses it is not known.
BFA.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The computerised main courante platform, as the security ministry names its occurrence-book system, belongs to the Ministère de l'Administration Territoriale, de la Décentralisation et de la Sécurité, whose director of information systems reported on it to a delegation of the digital transition ministry in late December 2023.

Records made digitally. In late December 2023 the platform was not yet operational: the digital transition ministry put it at more than 80 per cent built.

How the record is made. The platform is to replace the physical registers in which main courantes are kept at police commissariats and gendarmerie brigades, and in late December 2023 those registers were still the record.

Last twelve months. The ministry's director of information systems said in late December 2023 that the platform would be operational by mid-January 2024, once amendments were taken in.

Stations doing the digital entry. In late December 2023 no commissariat or gendarmerie brigade was using the computerised main courante.

Not held. Nothing dated on or before 30 September 2026 says the platform went live in any commissariat or brigade. No plan, source of finance, count of stations or event in the last twelve months is held.

BWA.short: Only cameras, traffic enforcement and tablets for statistics are held, to 2026; how stations record reports is not known, so no stage is set.
BWA.summary: Not held. Nothing held states whether stations record reports or cases on paper or digitally, in what system, or in how many stations.

CAF.short: Only one specialised unit's case system (2026) and donated equipment are held; how stations record reports is not known, so no stage is set.
CAF.summary: Not held. Nothing held states whether police stations or gendarmerie brigades record reports or cases on paper or digitally, in what system, or in how many stations.

CIV.short: Only cameras, fingerprint files and online court documents are held, to 2026; how stations record reports is not known, so no stage is set.
CIV.summary: Not held. Nothing held states whether police stations or gendarmerie brigades record reports or cases on paper or digitally, in what system, or in how many stations.

CMR.short: A digital system for investigation and case information existed in 2020 and was barely used; which stations use it, if any, is not known.
CMR.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. GIZ's factsheet on its support to the Cameroonian police, status June 2020, presents the digitised investigations and proceedings system as the Délégation générale à la sûreté nationale's own, and says the DGSN must also overcome unreliable internet connection, electricity and computer equipment.

Records made digitally. In June 2020 the police had a digitised system for processing and transmitting information on investigations, criminal proceedings, arrest warrants, fines and current sanctions.

How the record is made. The system processes and transmits information on investigations and criminal proceedings, on the June 2020 factsheet's account.

Last twelve months. At June 2020, the date of GIZ's factsheet on its programme with the Cameroonian police, the digitised system for investigations and criminal proceedings was barely used.
