Stations doing the digital entry. GIZ put the system's slight use down to weak institutional and management capacity at the Délégation générale à la sûreté nationale in its factsheet of June 2020.

Not held. Which units use the system, whether any is outside the capital, where and how entries are made and how many stations enter are not held. Nothing is held since June 2020.

COD.short: Police documents were typed or handwritten on paper in 2023; whether any station has had a digital system since is not known.
COD.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. A police statement must by law be written out and signed by the officer who drafts it, on pain of nullity, the programme officer of the Ligue des droits de la personne dans la région des Grands Lacs told Canada's Immigration and Refugee Board on 15 March 2023.

Records made digitally. A case is referred to the Congolese National Police by a written and signed complaint, the Executive Secretary of Héritiers de la justice told the board on 9 March 2023.

How the record is made. Police documents in criminal proceedings are typed, and the record of the parties' hearings is handwritten in most cases, he said in March 2023 after consulting lawyers at the South Kivu Court of Appeal.

Last twelve months. The samples supplied to the board in March 2023 were blank paper forms of findings, arrest and witness testimony reports.

Stations doing the digital entry. The typed and handwritten police documents were described in March 2023 for the country as a whole.

Not held. Nothing dated after March 2023 is held on how stations record, and neither account of that month says in terms that no digital system exists. Nothing is held on a system for stations, its owner, plan or finance, or on the last twelve months.

COG.short: A 2014 survey of two towns found police stations working by hand; the rest of the country is not known, so no stage is set.
COG.summary: Not held. The one statement that stations work by hand is a survey of commissariats in Pointe-Noire and Nkayi from January 2014; nothing is held on Brazzaville, the rest of the country or the gendarmerie beyond one brigade, and nothing dated since. Who would own a station system, and anything from the last twelve months, is not held.

COM.short: Only a criminal-record directorate (2026) and a driving-licence programme are held; how stations record reports is not known, so no stage is set.
COM.summary: Not held. Nothing held states whether stations record reports or cases on paper or digitally, in what system, or in how many stations.

CPV.short: Complaints ran digitally from national police stations to the courts by March 2026; how many stations use the system is not known.
CPV.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The criminal-process subsystem of what the Ministry of Justice calls the Sistema de Informação da Justiça was developed by the state's NOSi with the justice institute IMIJ and handed to the ministry on 16 March 2026. The order bringing it into phased operation was issued jointly by the Ministry of Justice and the Ministry of Internal Administration on 27 December 2024.

Records made digitally. The Ministry of Justice says the subsystem takes in the Polícia Nacional's stations and the Polícia Judiciária's delegations, so that the handling of complaints is essentially digital from the police to the courts. By 16 March 2026 it had processed about 25,000 police reports and more than 18,000 cases from end to end.

How the record is made. The ministry says the system integrates the stations and the delegations with the courts, complaints being handled digitally in the one system.

Last twelve months. On 16 March 2026 NOSi formally handed the subsystem over. The stated target is all courts fully digital within three years.

Stations doing the digital entry. The joint order of 27 December 2024 makes use of the electronic criminal process obligatory in the Polícia Nacional.

Not held. No count or share of Polícia Nacional stations using the system, and no account of how a station enters the complaint. No plan or finance for it, and nothing on rural stations.

DJI.short: Only body cameras (2026), a gendarmerie intranet and a fingerprint file are held; how stations record reports is not known, so no stage is set.
DJI.summary: Not held. Nothing held states whether police stations or gendarmerie brigades record reports or cases on paper or digitally, in what system, or in how many stations.

DZA.short: Only public online services, traffic-fine payment and criminal registers are held, to 2026; how stations record reports is not known, so no stage is set.
DZA.summary: Not held. Nothing held states whether police stations or gendarmerie brigades record reports or cases on paper or digitally, in what system, or in how many stations.

EGY.short: A rights group said in 2021 that stations often lack the means to type reports; digital recording is not known, so no stage is set.
EGY.summary: Not held. The one statement on stations, from January 2021, says they often lack the technology to write reports on a computer; it names no system, no place and no count of stations, and does not say that stations record on paper only. Who would own a station system, and anything from the last twelve months, is not held.

ERI.short: A 2017 state report names a police computerized data system; how stations record reports is not known, so no stage is set.
ERI.summary: Not held. No source held states whether stations record reports or cases on paper or digitally, in what system, or in how many stations.

ETH.short: A criminal records system covering crime report to sentence was still being built in January 2026; no station is known to use it.
ETH.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The Ministry of Justice says CRIMS, as it names its Criminal Records Information Management System, is being developed by the Ethiopian Artificial Intelligence Institute for the ministry, the Federal Police Commission and the Addis Ababa Police Commission to work in jointly, steered by a coordinating committee, in an item published on 20 January 2026.

Records made digitally. The system is under development and not yet in use, and is to record digitally everything from the crime report through investigation, charge, trial and sentence, the ministry said in January 2026.

How the record is made. Its modules cover report intake, investigation, juvenile offenders, offence type, biometric data, and prosecutors' and courts' decisions, on the ministry's account of January 2026.

Last twelve months. In January 2026 the ministry reported a coordinating-committee forum, with the minister and senior leaders of the three bodies, at which the system was said to be in development.

Stations doing the digital entry. In August 2023 the ministry was training federal investigating police and prosecutors, about 100 in all, in order to launch the system widely.

Not held. No station, place or way of making the record is given for the system, and no launch is recorded since the 2023 training. No plan or source of finance is stated.

GAB.short: A vendor presented a case-file system design in January 2026; whether any force uses it is not known, so no stage is set.
GAB.summary: Not held. The only records system held is a vendor's design presented at a Libreville seminar on 10 January 2026, with no adoption by the police, the gendarmerie or a ministry stated and no station using it. No dated statement says how stations record today, and no plan, finance or count of stations is held.

GHA.short: Case dockets were held digitally in 55 police stations across seven regions in 2022; the total of stations, and anything since, is not known.
GHA.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The Government of Ghana launched what it calls the Case Tracking System in 2018, with the support of USAID, as a common platform for the Police Service, the Attorney General's office, the Prisons Service, the Legal Aid Commission, the Economic and Organised Crime Office and the Judicial Service.

Records made digitally. The Asokwa Municipal Police Commander said in May 2022 that the system had eliminated the use of paper as case dockets in the prosecution of criminal cases. The Legal Resources Centre reported in 2022 that 2,475 cases had been registered on it from December 2021.

How the record is made. The commander said he could monitor cases in all stations within his jurisdiction from his office through the system, with unstable internet and electricity hindering it. In the Volta Region, 104 laptops, 95 tablets and 93 connectivity units were given out to run it, by the centre's 2022 report.

Last twelve months. On 23 May 2022 the project was being supported by USAID, whose Justice Sector Support Activity also paid for an awareness campaign.

Stations doing the digital entry. The Legal Resources Centre reported in 2022 that 55 police stations and 3 prisons services were using the system, in seven regions and over 40 districts: Greater Accra, Ashanti, Northern, Volta, Bono, Western and Eastern. In July 2019 the West African Police Information System had more than 35 units in the capital, shared among police, immigration and prisons, and none in the regions.

Not held. No total of stations to set beside the 55, and nothing on the system since 2022. Whether the first report of an occurrence is recorded digitally, and whether rural stations use the system.

GIN.short: Ten police and gendarmerie units in Greater Conakry were equipped in 2021; whether any enters records is not known, so no stage is set.
GIN.summary: Not held. The facts held on a station system are a decree of 13 May 2019 creating the police data centre and its information system, which names no station, and an account dated 31 March 2021: ten police and gendarmerie units of Greater Conakry equipped, with no total of units, no statement that any was entering records, and the digitising of procès-verbaux stated as an intention. Nothing newer shows preparation, a pilot or a system running, and no dated statement says how stations record today.

GMB.short: The police chief said in March 2026 that documentation is on paper; what became of a 2021 pilot is not known.
GMB.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. UNDP's terms of reference of 22 April 2021 state that the crime-reporting app will be owned by the Gambia Police Force, and UNDP reports that in 2020 it supported the work technically and financially with UN Peacebuilding Fund money.

Records made digitally. The Inspector General of Police, at a media briefing reported on 24 March 2026, described the force's documentation as paper-based. UNDP reports that in 2020 it supported a Mobile Data Collection App within the police's digitalised case management system and trained 24 officers to use it.

How the record is made. The Inspector General said the force needs to move from paper-based documentation to a digitalised mode, as reported on 24 March 2026.

Last twelve months. At the briefing reported on 24 March 2026 the Inspector General put digitalisation of police workflow and records management as work still to come.

Stations doing the digital entry. UNDP's terms of reference of 22 April 2021 describe a mobile app for crime reporting by police officers as in its pilot phase, to be extended to other police stations in phases.

Not held. What became of the case management system and the crime-reporting app after April 2021, and how many stations took part in the pilot. Who owns, plans or pays for digital station records has not been stated in the last three years.

GNB.short: A 2024 student project states that police stations have no system for recording occurrences; how stations record is not known.
GNB.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. A steering committee of several entities oversees the centre for collecting and processing criminal information that Guinea-Bissau calls SIPAO, and INTERPOL accompanies it and the European Union finances it, the Minister of Justice and Human Rights said on 17 April 2023.

Records made digitally. Guinea-Bissau does not have a system for recording criminal occurrences in police stations, the author of an undergraduate final project at IFBA in Brazil stated in August 2024.

How the record is made. The author gave that absence as the first reason for building a prototype, a web application tested in 2024 by ten users of Guinean nationality.

Last twelve months. INTERPOL described the West African Police Information System on 12 September 2025 as strengthening information exchange and coordination among the region's law enforcement agencies.

Stations doing the digital entry. A new SIPAO service beside the Guarda Nacional command in Bissau was described in August 2024 as a centre where all police forces work and share information. The centre's director named extension to all law-enforcement institutions as the main challenge still ahead in 2024.

Not held. How stations record is not held, and the statement that no station system exists is one author's, with no source cited. No station is named as entering its cases at the criminal-information centre in Bissau, and nothing is held on a plan, on the last twelve months or on stations.

GNQ.short: A project to interconnect police stations is in the 2026 budget law; how stations record reports is not known, so no stage is set.
GNQ.summary: Not held. No source held states whether stations record reports or cases on paper or digitally, in what system, or in how many stations.

KEN.short: Seventy-six stations around Nairobi had a digital occurrence book in 2023; in 2026 one was still being procured, and its use now is not known.
KEN.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The National Police Service presented the programme that carries digital Occurrence Books to Parliament on 13 May 2026 as its own investment, and the Interior Cabinet Secretary said on 1 April 2026 that the government was itself procuring the digital occurrence book. On 26 March 2025 the service asked development partners for Sh20 billion for digitisation, the digital Occurrence Book included.

Records made digitally. The occurrence book. The service's annual report for 2022 says its Digital Occurrence Book was launched at Kasarani Sub-County, Nairobi, on 21 November 2019, and on 30 June 2023 the Interior Cabinet Secretary said complaints, statements and details of criminal activity made at stations are recorded in it.

How the record is made. On 30 June 2023 the Deputy Inspector General of Administration Police said reports entered at the station were open to monitoring by ward, county and regional commanders and the Inspector General.

Last twelve months. On 13 May 2026 the Inspector General told a parliamentary committee that digital Occurrence Books would come within three to four months. On 28 August 2026 the Interior Cabinet Secretary said they would accompany police communication centres set up first in Nairobi, Mombasa, Nyeri, Nakuru, Eldoret and Kisumu.

Stations doing the digital entry. The Star reports that 76 police stations in and around Nairobi had their Occurrence Books digitised by 30 June 2023. On 13 May 2026 the Inspector General told MPs the service did not yet have digital Occurrence Books.

Not held. What became of the Nairobi system after June 2023, and whether any station outside the capital area records digitally. No domestic budget line and no dated plan naming the system.

LBR.short: Six officers in the capital's county began entering crime reports on tablets in a 2021 pilot; whether any station outside it does is not known.
LBR.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The Liberia National Police was the first to roll out the case management system under the Ministry of Justice, in 2021. The UN Joint Rule of Law Programme supported its design, development and roll-out, and the crime statistics system was developed with UNDP support.

Records made digitally. UNDP reported in March 2023 an officer entering crime reports into a tablet as they come in, with suspects' biodata, photos and GPS locations. The case management system records the parties, the offences, the proceedings and the outcome of a case, and was up and running at the police in June 2022.

How the record is made. The Crime Statistics Information System, as UNDP names it, is online and in two parts: a smartphone or tablet on which the officer enters the report, and a portal that aggregates the reports for police decision-makers. Case data is captured on a web and mobile application that works online and offline, by UNDP's account of April 2022.

Last twelve months. FrontPageAfrica reported in 2026 that Nyehn Town Police Station, the only police facility serving Todee District, has no computers.

Stations doing the digital entry. The crime statistics system went live at police headquarters on 25 January 2021, with training for 15 personnel. Six officers were chosen to pioneer it in Montserrado County, the seat of the capital, that month.

Not held. No fact shows either system in use at a station outside Montserrado County, and no count or share of stations entering records is held; the newest facts on use are of 2021 to 2023. Nothing is held on who owns, plans or pays for the systems since 2022, or on any change in the last twelve months.

LBY.short: Tripoli's police stations got a digital system for investigation reports in December 2025; use outside the capital is not known.
LBY.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The Tripoli Security Directorate launched its digital transformation system itself at its headquarters on 31 December 2025, with the Attorney General, the security director and a representative of the acting Minister of Interior present, the Libyan News Agency reports.

Records made digitally. Among the components inaugurated that day is a system for the evidence-gathering reports of police stations and traffic sections. On 3 May 2025 Tripoli's security director told the heads of investigation of the police stations and traffic departments, whose officers receive reports and complaints and open the case minutes, to attend to the running of "the digital system".

How the record is made. The instruction of May 2025 names the digital system as a primary source for the database and for documenting legal rights.

Last twelve months. The directorate inaugurated its digital transformation system, including the police-station investigation-reports system, on 31 December 2025.

Stations doing the digital entry. The agency's report of the launch names the system as one for police stations and traffic sections of the Tripoli Security Directorate.

Not held. No station outside the Tripoli Security Directorate is shown using a records system, and no count of stations, plan or source of finance is given. How the record is made is not stated.

LSO.short: An inspection begun in 2023 found posts without stationery keeping registers by hand; what other stations do is not known, so no stage is set.
LSO.summary: Not held. The one fact on station records, from the Ombudsman's inspection begun in July 2023, shows named posts without stationery keeping registers and forms by hand; it does not say that stations record on paper only, nor what the other inspected stations do. No records system for stations is named, and nothing is held on its owner, the records made, the stations or the last twelve months.

MAR.short: Police stations record complaints and cases in connected national systems, cases in 16 of 22 commands in 2025; the share of stations is not known.
MAR.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The Direction Générale de la Sûreté Nationale (DGSN), the national police, built GESTARR with its own technical staff and holds its data on a central DGSN server. Its own teams built the case-management system added to GESTARR in 2024.

Records made digitally. Complaints lodged at a police arrondissement are managed in GESTARR (October 2019). In 2024 the DGSN added a system for crime and misdemeanour cases at the arrondissements, each case followed through investigation to submission to the judicial authorities. Its 2025 review says the system it calls Qadaya handles crime and misdemeanour cases in real time.

How the record is made. In October 2019 the arrondissements' information was stored on a central DGSN server and shared between arrondissements across the Kingdom, on a platform that links the arrondissements to each other and to the Sûreté nationale's central services.

Last twelve months. The DGSN's review of 2025 says Qadaya's rollout continued during the year and reached 16 of the 22 police commands, with national coverage in view.

Stations doing the digital entry. GESTARR was in almost all the Kingdom's arrondissements in October 2019, and its generalisation was completed in 2023, when the DGSN counted 454 police arrondissements and had the case system on trial in 350 police posts. The case system was in use in 12 commands in 2024, among them the regional sûretés of Ouarzazate, Errachidia, Taza and Al Hoceima, and Qadaya covered 16 of the 22 commands in 2025.

Not held. The share of police arrondissements entering their records: the DGSN counts commands, not stations. No plan or finance for the systems is stated, and nothing dated places the Royal Gendarmerie's brigades in or out of a record system.

MDG.short: The police opened an online platform for reporting violence and disappearances in 2026; how stations record reports is not known, so no stage is set.
MDG.summary: Not held. No source held states whether stations record reports or cases on paper or digitally, in what system, or in how many stations.

MLI.short: An online criminal-record service opened in 2026; how stations record reports is not known, so no stage is set.
MLI.summary: Not held. No source held states whether stations record reports or cases on paper or digitally, in what system, or in how many stations.

MOZ.short: Police kept almost no digital records in 2007 and stations used no computers; whether any station records digitally now is not known.
MOZ.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. An information technology plan for the Polícia da República de Moçambique had not been achieved at all by October 2007, its needs assessment waiting on a bilateral funding agreement with Spain, UNDP's evaluators stated.

Records made digitally. The evaluation mission, visiting stations and commands in September 2007, verified the almost complete absence of digital records of autos, case files or any other procedure across the force.

How the record is made. In 2007 piles of paper served as case file archives, and stations lacked paper and typewriter ribbons, the mission found.

Last twelve months. Club of Mozambique reported on 23 August 2024 a public security management information system for the Ministry of the Interior, described as nationwide in scope.

Stations doing the digital entry. In September 2007 the use of information technology was non-existent at district and police station level, and most stations the mission visited had a computer that did not work or outdated typewriters.

Not held. Nothing dated after 2007 is held on how stations record, so the owner, plan and finance of a station records system and the last twelve months are not held. No fact says that stations enter reports or cases in the gender-based violence register or in the public security information system.

MRT.short: A police information system launched in June 2025 runs in Nouakchott's commissariats, 34 centres linked; use by stations outside the capital is not known.
MRT.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The central office for collecting police information, in the judicial police directorate of the General Directorate of National Security, supervises the police information system, which the directorate calls WAPIS and which its Director General launched on 19 June 2025.

Records made digitally. The system is meant to digitise the work of police commissariats and to document the reports and complaints made at commissariats and their offices, a report of the launch states.

How the record is made. Central commissioners and heads of judicial police sections in the commissariats register in a database held by the central office, to which police centres are being linked, by the same report of 19 June 2025.

Last twelve months. On 19 June 2025 the Director General put the system to work for central directors, the regional directors of the Nouakchott wilayas, central commissioners and heads of judicial police sections in the commissariats.

Stations doing the digital entry. At the launch the director of the central office gave the centres linked as 27 of the National Police and 7 of the National Gendarmerie, and the report puts the rollout across Nouakchott's commissariats at 90 per cent complete.

Not held. No source shows the system in use at a station outside Nouakchott, and the 34 centres linked are given with no place and no total of stations. No plan or source of finance is stated.

MUS.short: All police stations had computers linked to the headquarters complaint and case system in 2025; how many stations enter records in it is not known.
MUS.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The Crime Occurrence Tracking System is the police's own, answered for by the Commissioner of Police through the Prime Minister as Minister of Home Affairs, with the government's Central Informatics Bureau working with the police on its replacement, as the National Assembly heard on 17 June 2025.

Records made digitally. The Prime Minister told the Assembly on 17 June 2025 that the system manages and tracks complaints and declarations from initial reporting to final case disposal, and has been operational since 2011. Défi Media reported in March 2023 that statements made at police stations, once handwritten in Occurrence Books, have been entered in it since 2015.

How the record is made. The system is a digital platform connecting all police stations to the main server at Police Headquarters, used on personal computers in the stations (June 2025). The entries are made directly on computers linked to a server (March 2023).

Last twelve months. On 17 June 2025 the Prime Minister said the system had been enhanced but never upgraded since 2011, and that the police had begun to replace it with a new case management system, with a special consultant to be retained.

Stations doing the digital entry. The Prime Minister said on 17 June 2025 that all police stations are equipped with personal computers for the system, which Défi Media's account of his reply also carries.

Not held. The number of police stations and the share of them entering records in the system: the one figure is of stations equipped. No plan or finance for the system is stated, and nothing is dated in the twelve months to 30 September 2026.

MWI.short: Officers were trained in July 2026 for a crime management system's introduction, after a 2022 pilot in six districts; stations using it are not known.
MWI.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The Crime Management System is the Malawi Police Service's own platform, launched in partnership with UNDP, which said so in July 2026. The earlier case management system for sexual and gender-based violence was rolled out with support from the Spotlight Initiative, funded by the European Union from 2019 to 2023.

Records made digitally. The system covers a case from the moment it is reported until its final disposal, by UNDP's account of July 2026. In 2022 officers entered cases into a crime record system combined with the gender-based violence one.

How the record is made. At a conference in September 2024 the police said it was working towards digitising its processes, a crime management system among them, and UNDP's assessment found most justice-sector processes still on paper.

Last twelve months. On 29 July 2026 the police and UNDP opened a three-day training on the system in Lilongwe, for officers from across the country ahead of its introduction in stations.

Stations doing the digital entry. In 2022 the combined system was piloted in six districts: Mzimba, Nkhata Bay, Ntchisi, Dowa, Nsanje and Machinga. In July 2026 the Crime Management System was being introduced across stations and formations, with the trained officers as its early adopters.

Not held. No source names or counts a station using the Crime Management System, and whether the system piloted in six districts in 2022 stayed in use is not stated. How a record is entered in the new system, a current plan naming it and who pays for it are not held, and nothing held describes rural stations.

NAM.short: The police have had a digital case system since 2010; in 2022 not all units had it, and which stations enter reports is not known.
NAM.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The Ministry of Safety and Security launched the E-Policing eco-system, as it names the force's system, in 2010 at a cost of N$22 million, the minister said on 8 July 2016.

Records made digitally. In July 2016 the eco-system comprised 16 databases, case docket management among them. A paper of May 2022 says e-policing in Namibia records, stores and shares police information electronically.

How the record is made. A 2022 University of Namibia study of police stations in the Omusati region found that officers there record by hand, first in the station crime register and then in paper files kept in cabinets or boxes, and that no digital record system was in place in those stations.

Last twelve months. In May 2022 officers at Okahandja police station saw storing the occurrence book electronically as duplication of data.

Stations doing the digital entry. In May 2022 implementation was immature, because not all units of the Namibian Police had been introduced to the system.

Not held. No source says which stations enter reports or cases in the e-policing system, how many do, or whether it is past a pilot; the one study of stations, in the Omusati region in 2022, found none doing so there. No plan, source of finance or event of the last twelve months is held, and nothing is dated after 2022.

NER.short: In 2019 a team of eight in Niamey entered cases into the police database; whether any station outside the capital records digitally is not known.
NER.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The national police's Direction de la Police Technique et Scientifique in Niamey works the database, and its director is responsible for recording criminal acts in Niger, EUCAP Sahel Niger reported on 23 May 2019. The system, launched in Niger in 2012, is financed by the European Union under the Emergency Trust Fund for Africa and implemented by INTERPOL with EUCAP Sahel Niger.

Records made digitally. The database, which Niger calls the Système d'Information Policière en Afrique de l'Ouest (SIPAO), holds offences, criminals' identities and criminal proceedings, and the team recording criminal acts had entered more than 8,000 cases by May 2019.

How the record is made. Cases are entered by a team of 8 under the director in Niamey, while operators are being trained to record data directly from their own service, by the same report of May 2019.

Last twelve months. EUCAP Sahel Niger reported on 23 May 2019 that 700 new cases were recorded in the month.

Stations doing the digital entry. In May 2019 the entry was made in Niamey, by the team of 8.

Not held. Nothing since May 2019 says the system reached stations outside Niamey or still runs. No count of stations is held, and what the Niamey team enters from is not stated.

NGA.short: Stations made statements, reports and the crime diary by hand in 2021 and 2022; whether that still holds is not known.
NGA.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The Ministry of Police Affairs' press unit said in June 2021 that divisional police stations lack basic ICT infrastructure.

Records made digitally. The ministry's press unit stated in June 2021 that statements and reports in police stations are made manually, and that most criminal records of offenders and property across the country are not made electronically. A paper by Jimoh, Wajiga and Garba, published in June 2022, found criminal records kept by hand in a crime diary or ledger at the stations its authors observed.

How the record is made. Sources writing to Canada's Immigration and Refugee Board in October 2020 described statements and police reports written on a standard paper form at the division, with some records kept electronically at state commands or police headquarters. In June 2021 the ministry said writing a statement, generating a report for citizens and entering biodata were done manually.

Last twelve months. The 2022 paper described crime reporting and detailing in stations as a manual method.

Stations doing the digital entry. A law-firm partner told the Board in October 2020 that use of computer networks and electronic databases was still very low among police formations.

Not held. Whether stations still record by hand after 2022 is not known. What the Smart Police Station launched in Gombe State in June 2026 records, who owns and funds any station record system, and how many stations enter records digitally are not held.

RWA.short: The investigation bureau processes criminal case files in the justice ministry's electronic system, by its 2024 history; whether stations enter them is not known.
RWA.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The Ministry of Justice manages the Integrated Electronic Case Management System, the Rwanda Investigation Bureau's history of its first years, published in October 2024, states.

Records made digitally. The bureau has incorporated the system to process criminal investigation files, by the same history, which the bureau wrote of its own work and which covers the years 2017 to 2023.

How the record is made. The handling of cases is digitalised from investigation to final judgment through the system, the bureau's history states.

Last twelve months. The bureau's history, published in October 2024, covers 2017 to 2023 and gives the system as the place its investigation files are processed.

Stations doing the digital entry. The history gives the entry of criminal investigation files as the bureau's own, in the system the justice ministry manages.

Not held. Whether the bureau's stations and posts enter the case file themselves, where and how the entry is made, and how many stations do it are not established. Nothing is dated inside the last twelve months.

SDN.short: Police stations took reports on paper in 2022, before the war; how they record now is not known.
SDN.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The police plan for 2024 to 2030, as reported in June 2026, lists digital systems development among its 39 projects in 21 programmes.

Records made digitally. A thesis abstract from Sudan University of Science and Technology, of 2022, proposes converting the reports taken in Sudanese police stations to an electronic system.

How the record is made. The same abstract describes the system for reports in police stations as the old paper one. Its subject is the report that opens the legal procedure for medical treatment after an incident, known as Form 8.

Last twelve months. Police databases were reported in June 2026 as restored after the war, and as having helped settle administrative and financial matters and the payment of entitlements.

Stations doing the digital entry. The 2022 thesis reports no electronic report system in use in police stations.

Not held. How stations have recorded reports since 2022, and since the war began, is not known. Which records any station system would cover, who owns and funds it, and how many stations use one are not held.

SEN.short: The gendarmerie showed a report-drafting tool still in design in October 2025; how stations record today is not known, so no stage is set.
SEN.summary: Not held. No dated statement says how stations or gendarmerie brigades record today. The one records tool held was shown at a design workshop on 2 October 2025, its technical form not stated and its use in the units still under discussion; no training, delivery, plan or finance is held for it.

SLE.short: Police records were paper-based in 2024 and statements still taken on stationery in July 2026; whether the planned case system has begun is not known.
SLE.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The Sierra Leone Police's Strategic Development Plan 2025-2029 names what it calls an e-Case Management System, for case tracking and processing, as key intervention 4.3, with Crime Services the responsible directorate. The plan says government allocation, limited and late, remains the force's main funding.

Records made digitally. The plan sets the system against a 2024 baseline: a survey on the status of case management in 2025, implementation of its recommendations from 2026 to 2028 and an effective system as the 2029 target.

How the record is made. The plan lists a transition from a paper-based to a digital records management system among its priorities, on a 2024 baseline. A report of 27 July 2026 says stationery would be kept mainly for operational work such as statement-taking and physical record-keeping.

Last twelve months. The force handed 39 laptops to Local Unit Commanders for electronic correspondence, as reported on 27 July 2026.

Stations doing the digital entry. The 2025-2029 plan describes internet connectivity as poor in most police facilities, and schedules it for the six regional headquarters in 2025 and provincial divisional headquarters in 2027 and 2028.

Not held. Whether the 2025 survey of case management was done, or any other step taken to prepare the planned system. No count of stations, and no budget for the system.

SOM.short: Police used paper-based systems in April 2024, when a donor-funded case system was tendered for Mogadishu only; whether police now use one is not known.
SOM.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The International Development Law Organization (IDLO) procures the planned case management system with the Office of the Attorney General, which is to receive the source code on completion, and the vendor reports to IDLO (April 2024). The money is from the United States Department of State, under its two-year Somalia Justice Support Programme.

Records made digitally. IDLO stated on 19 April 2024 that the police use paper-based systems, and that the planned system would be the first electronic case management system for Somalia's federal justice institutions.

How the record is made. On the same date IDLO said the police and the Custodial Corps had never made a serious attempt to develop an electronic case management system.

Last twelve months. IDLO invited bids on 19 April 2024, due 3 June 2024, for a system to be developed over 15 months.

Stations doing the digital entry. The tender's criminal investigation module would let investigators create a complaint when it is received at a police station or call centre; its first phase covers only the Criminal Investigation Department in Mogadishu, and nothing was built in April 2024. In Puntland, a member state with its own police, computer stations for nine regional investigation offices, linked to a server in Garowe, were still to be installed in 2021, on equipment given by the European Union's mission.

Not held. Whether the police enter reports or cases in any system built since the 2024 tender is not known, and no station is named as doing so. A plan naming a station record system and anything dated in the last twelve months are not held.

SSD.short: A case system shared by courts, justice ministry and police ran in Juba only in 2021; how many stations use it is not known.
SSD.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. UNDP supported the setup in Juba of a unified case management system for the courts, the justice ministry and the South Sudan National Police Service, its rule of law report on 2021 states.

Records made digitally. UNDP reports that 10,836 cases, 2,508 of them brought by female claimants, were recorded in 2021 through the system, which it names the Case Monitoring Information Management System, set up for the judiciary, the Ministry of Justice and Constitutional Affairs and the police service.

How the record is made. The police service uses a paper-based system for handling crime reporting, with crime files misplaced or lost from police shelves, the abstract of a thesis listed on 7 June 2026 states.

Last twelve months. The thesis listed on 7 June 2026 describes a web application for crime reports that its researcher built and tested for Jubek State; the application is the researcher's own.

Stations doing the digital entry. UNDP's report on 2021 places the case management system in Juba only.

Not held. No count of police stations using the Juba system is held, nor how many of its cases the police entered or whether the file passes digitally to the court. Nothing on the system is dated after 2021, and the thesis gives no year of its own.

STP.short: A police crime-statistics system was being put in place in 2024; how stations record reports is not known, so no stage is set.
STP.summary: Not held. No source held states whether stations record reports or cases on paper or digitally, in what system, or in how many stations.

SWZ.short: Police trainers were trained in 2025 to enter cases in a justice ministry system; whether any station enters cases is not known.
SWZ.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The Integrated Electronic Case Management System, which Eswatini calls IECMS, is the Ministry of Justice's programme, with a Technical Working Group supporting its training sessions and Synergy International Systems supporting implementation, Independent News reported in August 2025.

Records made digitally. Royal Eswatini Police Service officers were trained on entering new cases into the system and were walked through all the components of a docket at the ministry's training of trainers in August 2025.

How the record is made. At the Mbabane and Manzini One Stop Centres the police record by hand in occurrence books, and police, prosecution and social welfare keep separate paper registers, UNICEF's evaluators stated in 2025.

Last twelve months. The training of police trainers on the system was reported on 20 August 2025.

Stations doing the digital entry. At the Manzini One Stop Centre the police complete paper forms that go to headquarters every 2 to 3 months and are not kept on site, UNICEF's evaluators stated in 2025.

Not held. No station, region or start date is held for police entry of cases in the IECMS, and the paper recording is described at two One Stop Centres only, not at stations nationally. A plan, the finance and whether the police case file passes digitally to the court are not held.

SYC.short: Police stations are all connected to a national case system, by a 2025 vendor account; how many enter their own records is not known.
SYC.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The vendor Winsoft, in an account published on 6 January 2025, says the Seychelles Police Department wanted the case app and brought in Transmedia, a British Claris partner, to build it, and that the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime funded and supported the project.

Records made digitally. The app manages cases from start to finish and is the repository of every case recorded, by Winsoft's account of January 2025. Development began with the intake form for incident reports, the record of a single crime; digitising the Occurrence Book itself, the daily record of incidents, was listed as an enhancement to come.

How the record is made. The app runs on desktop computers or iPads as a central resource holding every case, and officers search crimes from other districts (January 2025).

Last twelve months. Winsoft's account of 6 January 2025 says the department has continued to evolve its use of the app since deployment.

Stations doing the digital entry. The detective commander of Mont Fleuri station is quoted by Winsoft, in January 2025, saying all police stations are connected. The same account says the database is bedding in at headquarters in Victoria.

Not held. The number of police stations and the share of them entering their own records: the one figure is a station commander's statement that all are connected, with no year. No plan is stated, and nothing is dated in the twelve months to 30 September 2026.

TCD.short: A police data centre was inaugurated in 2025; how stations record reports is not known, so no stage is set.
TCD.summary: Not held. No source held states whether stations record reports or cases on paper or digitally, in what system, or in how many stations.

TGO.short: Police said in April 2026 all police and gendarmerie stations have the regional police information tool; whether any enters reports in it is not known.
TGO.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. SIPAO, the West African police information system, is an ECOWAS programme implemented by INTERPOL with European Union funding, and was handed to ECOWAS and the national authorities on 8 April 2025, after that funding ended.

Records made digitally. A police divisional commissioner said on 14 April 2026 that the country's commissariats and gendarmerie brigades have SIPAO as a tool.

How the record is made. The tool in the stations is that of the regional programme, SIPAO, on the commissioner's account of 14 April 2026.

Last twelve months. The police stated on 14 April 2026 that every station has the tool, a year after the programme's handover of 8 April 2025.

Stations doing the digital entry. All commissariats and gendarmerie brigades in Togo have the SIPAO tool, the police said on 14 April 2026.

Not held. No source held states whether any station enters reports or cases in the tool, which records, or how, and the police give no count of stations. No plan or source of finance is held.

TUN.short: Twenty-one model National Guard and National Security centres were under construction in 2025; how stations record reports is not known, so no stage is set.
TUN.summary: Not held. No source held states whether stations record reports or cases on paper or digitally, in what system, or in how many stations.

TZA.short: A digital case file system was installed and central stations in 23 regions connected by April 2024; whether stations enter cases is not known.
TZA.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The Minister for Home Affairs told Parliament in May 2024 that the ministry had installed the digital case file management information system itself, in carrying out the Criminal Justice Commission's recommendations. The ministry's 2024/25 budget carried TZS 40.5 billion for strengthening the ICT system, installing the biometric system and buying police radios.

Records made digitally. The case file. The minister said in May 2024 that the ministry has installed a digital case file management information system, to be connected with the criminal justice institutions.

How the record is made. By April 2024 the regional Central Police Stations were connected over the national broadband backbone and linked to the Office of the Director of Public Prosecutions.

Last twelve months. In May 2024 the minister said police stations in other regions were still being connected to the system.

Stations doing the digital entry. The minister said that by April 2024 the Central Police Stations in 23 regions had been connected.

Not held. Whether a station enters the case file when the case is opened, how many stations there are in all, and whether the link to the prosecutor carries the case file. No plan or funding source for the system, and nothing dated after May 2024.

UGA.short: Digital case files were piloted in ten Kampala divisions in 2017, with upcountry stations outside in 2021; use since is not known.
UGA.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The Uganda Police Force's ICT Directorate developed the Crime Records Management System itself, and the force resolved in October 2022 to embark on the Electronic Policing Information System, ePIS. A UNODC consultancy notice of 2023 gives the ePIS programme four interventions: business process reform, automation of case management, enabling infrastructure and digital skilling.

Records made digitally. The case file. The force said in December 2017 that its crime records system processes and tracks the progress of case files. A journal article of June 2024 says ePIS is to manage all cases registered and investigated by the police from inception to conclusion.

How the record is made. The UNODC notice of 2023 calls the force's collection, processing and sharing of data largely manual. The Independent reported in 2021 that stations had one records officer for case files and detectives kept the files of their own cases.

Last twelve months. In June 2024 ePIS was in its design phase.

Stations doing the digital entry. In December 2017 the crime records system was being piloted in ten divisions of Kampala Metropolitan. The Independent reported in 2021 that it had been upgraded and tested in Kampala, with tests in upcountry stations to follow. The justice sector's bulletin of May 2024 lists lack of internet connectivity at upcountry police stations among the obstacles.

Not held. Whether any station outside Kampala Metropolitan enters cases digitally, how many stations the Kampala pilot covered and whether it still runs. No costing, period or funding source for ePIS, and nothing dated in the twelve months to 30 September 2026.

ZAF.short: Case dockets were captured digitally at 998 of 1,157 police stations in May 2021, 86.3% of all police stations; the rural share is not known.
ZAF.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The South African Police Service runs the case docket system as its own. Its Strategic Plan 2025 to 2030, tabled on 4 April 2025, lists the enhancement of case docket management, with full functionality in 2027/28. The 2025/26 plan funds its information systems from Programme 1 of Vote 28.

Records made digitally. When a complaint is taken at a station and the elements of a crime exist, a case docket is opened and captured on what the police call the Crime Administration System and the Investigate Case Docket Management System, by the Acting Minister's reply to a question of 31 December 2025.

How the record is made. The docket is captured at the station's Community Service Centre, signed off on the system by the Shift Commander and verified on it at station, provincial and national level, with a physical docket kept beside it. In May 2021 the docket system depended on the station's network link.

Last twelve months. On 11 April 2025 the Police Minister announced a partnership with the private sector to digitise case dockets and upgrade five police stations.

Stations doing the digital entry. The police told Parliament's police committee on 4 May 2021 that the docket system was in 998 police stations with 159 still to be covered, 86.3% of all police stations. The 159 registered cases on the old system, which fed the same database. In 2023/24, 789 of 1,160 stations sent complainants text messages about a docket through the system.

Not held. No count of stations registering dockets on the system later than May 2021, and no rural share. Whether the first report of an occurrence is recorded digitally, and whether the docket passes digitally to the prosecutor or the court.

ZMB.short: Stations recorded on paper in 2024; network equipment for 40 arrived by February 2026, and whether any yet records digitally is not known.
ZMB.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The Zambia Police Strategic Plan 2023-2026 gives guidelines for an e-record management system for the service's electronic records, by a University of Zambia study. The service's Technical Services Directorate, the Ministry of Home Affairs and Internal Security and the SMART Zambia Institute build and run the police's electronic systems.

Records made digitally. In 2024 the occurrence books, crime register books and docket movement books were kept on paper at headquarters and across the service. Headquarters had a Police Information Management System, a database of police records including crime reports and case files, officials told the study between November 2024 and January 2025. UNDP said in November 2021 that an Electronic Occurrence Book had been rolled out to the Victim Support Unit.

How the record is made. Statements are recorded and dockets opened by hand, so complainants and witnesses attend a station in person, informants told the study between November 2024 and January 2025.

Last twelve months. The SMART Zambia Institute received routers, switches, access points and firewalls for 40 police stations, to connect them to a centralised digital system, as reported on 3 February 2026.

Stations doing the digital entry. In 2024 the occurrence book, crime register and docket were digitised nowhere in the service, and rollout from headquarters to divisions and stations was planned.

Not held. No fact shows a station entering a report or a case digitally, and who enters the records held in the headquarters database is not stated. The centralised system the 40 stations are to join is not yet in place, with no pilot, station count or source of finance given for it.

ZWE.short: An electronic docket system was announced in December 2025 as coming soon; whether any station yet records digitally is not known.
ZWE.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The Home Affairs minister said on 17 January 2024 that computerising police operations, under what he called the ZRP Integrated Information System, is part of the ministry's ICT strategy approved by Cabinet in 2022, and that the police had finished a needs assessment and were looking for a partner. In December 2021 the Information minister said government would bear all costs of digitising rural stations.

Records made digitally. The officer commanding Harare Province said, in remarks reported on 9 December 2025, that the police would soon move to an electronic system for processing all dockets.

How the record is made. The force's Horizon 2025 strategic plan, as reported on 16 December 2021, decries the manual management of information, which it says makes information hard to retrieve and leads to its loss and destruction.

Last twelve months. In December 2025 the Zimbabwe Republic Police presented the planned electronic docket system as a measure against bribery in the handling of case files.

Stations doing the digital entry. The Information minister said after Cabinet on 14 December 2021 that a pilot study for digitising rural police stations had been completed, with gadgets and connectivity still to be provided.

Not held. Which stations, if any, entered reports or dockets in a system by 30 September 2026, and which record the planned system will hold. How the system is to be paid for has not been stated since 2021.

AGO.short: The telecommunications ministry put its draft artificial intelligence law out for public comment in 2025; what the 41 contributions said is not known.
AGO.summary:
Consultation and what was published of it. The Ministry of Telecommunications, Information Technologies and Social Communication put its draft Law on Artificial Intelligence, of 86 articles, on its public consultation portal in September 2025. The report attached to the draft says the consultation was open to all public and private bodies and to interested individuals. The ministry published the draft itself on the portal. On 27 August 2026 the portal showed 18 contributions from companies, 18 from specialists and 5 from the general public.

Required consultation and standing body. The report attached to the draft law says the consultation was held before the draft goes to the Council of Ministers. A coordination committee for the national financial inclusion strategy was set up by Despacho Presidencial 201/23.

Not held. No published report of a consultation on a digital law or policy, no comments received and no written answer to them is held from the last three years.

BDI.short: Government met companies and civil society in 2025 on its national data governance strategy; what they said is not known.
BDI.summary:
Consultation and what was published of it. A nationwide workshop on 18 April 2025 brought together public bodies, companies and civil society to set Burundi's priorities for its National Data Governance Strategy, by the account of the United Nations Economic Commission for Africa. The strategy was validated on 7 November 2025 at a workshop presided over by the Vice-Minister of Finance, Budget and Digital Economy. The commission says companies, academics and civil society took part in the process. Its page is the published account of both workshops.

Required consultation and standing body. The Ministry of Finance, Budget and Digital Economy hosted the Central Africa Internet Governance Forum in Bujumbura from 16 to 21 February 2026, a regional forum with no named national law or policy before it.

Not held. No published report of a consultation on a digital law or policy, no comments received and no written answer to them is held from the last three years.

The ministry had drafted it with the private sector, universities, research centres, civil society and the diaspora. On 27 August 2025 it opened a workshop on the national artificial intelligence action plan with the same groups, whose conclusions feed the draft plan. On 11 June 2024 a committee of the transitional legislative assembly heard FED-numérique, Internet Society Burkina Faso and two independent specialists on the information systems security bill, and some of them handed in written observations.

Required consultation and standing body. The committee's report of July 2024 says the government's draft of that bill had earlier gone to a national validation workshop with other ministries, civil society and the private sector.

On 30 and 31 July 2025 it held a workshop at Yamoussoukro to validate the draft national strategy and action plan for moving to IPv6, with about twenty public and private bodies, among them Orange CI, MTN CI, Moov Africa, Huawei and CODINORM.

COD.summary:
Consultation and what was published of it. ARPTC, the post and telecommunications regulator of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, opened a public consultation on bringing 5G to the country, announced in a communiqué dated 18 March 2025. On 6 August 2026 the digital economy minister held a working session with people from the digital sector on interministerial order no. 015 of 20 July 2026, which sets the duties, taxes and fees of the digital sector. The session followed a public outcry over the order and was reported by the state news agency the next day.

Required consultation and standing body. The Réseau des acteurs du numérique, an industry body, was among those the minister met on 6 August 2026 about the order.

COG.summary:

It followed a mission of 2 to 6 June that consulted 21 institutions from government, regulators, universities, the private sector, civil society and development partners. The commission had announced consultations in Brazzaville and Pointe-Noire with telecom operators, financial institutions, universities and digital businesses, and a workshop that would include civil society and the private sector.

CPV.summary:

The Conselho Consultivo da Economia Digital, a consultative council on the digital economy, held its third ordinary meeting on 25 November 2025, chaired by the minister. The ministry also ran a national diagnostic phase, and the contributions of business, civil society, young innovators and national experts are to feed the final text.

GHA.short: The information technology agency put a draft data harmonisation bill out for public comment in November 2025; whether the comments were published is not known.
GHA.summary:
Consultation and what was published of it. The National Information Technology Agency put out its draft Data Harmonisation Bill 2025 for public consultation, announced on 23 October 2025 and set to run from 19 to 27 November 2025. It invited citizens, universities, the private sector and the general public to make submissions through the consultation document on its website. In 2023 Ghana's Open Government Partnership secretariat and Multi-Stakeholder Forum wrote the fifth national action plan with civil society organisations and government agencies, in consultative meetings and a workshop in October 2023. The plan carries commitments on misinformation on digital platforms, on amending the Electronic Communications Act 2008, and on data sharing and open data.

Required consultation and standing body. The Open Government Partnership Multi-Stakeholder Forum is a steering body whose members include civil society and parliament.

Not held. No report of a consultation on a digital law or policy, no comments received and no written answer to them is held from the last three years. Nothing held states a rule that required a consultation, or a view given by a standing body on a named digital law or policy.

GIN.short: A government agency put a draft state information security policy to digital-sector people in April 2025; whether a report was published is not known.
GIN.summary:
Consultation and what was published of it. ANSSI, an agency under Guinea's Ministry of Posts, Telecommunications and the Digital Economy, held a workshop to validate the draft State Information Systems Security Policy, which it calls the PSSIE, in April 2025. Representatives of public institutions, cybersecurity experts and people working in the digital sector attended. They analysed the draft's parts, added to them and validated them.

Required consultation and standing body. Guinea has a multi-stakeholder group for transparency in the extractive industries, covered in a validation report of 2026. Its steering committee has an open data policy of its own, which covers data on extractive revenue. The digital ministry and UNDP held a validation workshop on a report assessing readiness for artificial intelligence, reported in December 2025.

Not held. No report of a consultation on a digital law or policy, no comments received and no written answer to them is held from the last three years. Nothing held states a rule that required a consultation, or a standing body that gave a view on a digital law or policy.

The Public Utilities Regulatory Authority published the draft Broadcasting and Online Content Regulations, 2026 on 2 April 2026, one of seven draft instruments released together. It invited licensees, sector ministries, industry, consumer groups, civil society organisations and the general public to comment between 1 and 10 April 2026. On 2 and 3 July 2025 people from government, the private sector, civil society and universities gave inputs on the draft National Data Policy at a national validation workshop. Government and private institutions reviewed the draft E-Commerce Policy and Strategy in groups at a workshop on 24 September 2025. In November 2025 telecom executives, consultants and development partners reviewed the regulator's proposed tools for regulating telecom prices.

Required consultation and standing body. The government's National Policy Development Handbook 2025 is a guide to the policy cycle, and it says it requires inclusive and participatory processes.

Not held. No report of a consultation on a digital law or policy, no comments received and no written answer to them is held from the last three years. Nothing held shows a consultation held because a rule required it, or a standing body that gave a view.

GNB.short: The regulator opened a public consultation on a draft electronic transactions law in May 2026; who replied and what was published is not known.
GNB.summary:
Consultation and what was published of it. The Board of Guinea-Bissau's national regulator, ARN-TIC, opened a public consultation on the draft Electronic Transactions Law with a notice, Aviso n.º 01/CA/ARN/2026, published on 8 May 2026. The notice was addressed to "interested parties" and asked for their responses in writing, by email, by 28 May 2026. The regulator's own name for the draft is Projeto de Lei das Transações Eletrónicas.

Required consultation and standing body. The consultation on the draft law rests on the notice of the regulator's Board, which set its own terms for who could respond, how and by when. After the military takeover of 26 November 2025, citizens reported restrictions across the country on Facebook, YouTube, TikTok and Instagram.

Not held. No report of a consultation on a digital law or policy, no comments received and no written answer to them is held from the last three years. Nothing held says who responded to the notice, states a rule that required a consultation, or names a standing body that gave a view.

KEN.short: In 2026 the ministry and regulator asked the public about communications regulations and an AI policy and published replies; no standing body's view is known.
KEN.summary:
Consultation and what was published of it. The Ministry of Information, Communications and the Digital Economy, with the Communications Authority, asked the public on 26 August 2025 for views on the draft Kenya Information and Communications Regulations, then published a matrix of comments beside the revised drafts and called a public validation forum for 15 to 17 September 2026. The State Department for ICT and the Digital Economy opened the draft Artificial Intelligence and Other Emerging Technologies Policy for written comment from 21 July to 4 August 2026. The Communications Authority said on 22 September 2026 that it had published the submissions on its draft internet telephony guidelines with its own position on them, and it answered in writing the public comments on its line deactivation and number recycling rules, reported on 12 October 2026. The Ministry held a validation workshop on the draft National Data Governance Policy on 5 February 2026 with the private sector, academia and civil society in the room.

Required consultation and standing body. The Ministry said on 26 August 2026 that the public participation on the regulations was in line with Article 10 of the Constitution and sections 5 and 8 of the Statutory Instruments Act. Its notice of 21 July 2026 on the artificial intelligence policy said the process followed the Constitution, which it said requires public participation in developing policies.

Not held. No source from the last three years says a standing body with members from outside government gave its view on a named digital law or policy.

LBR.short: In 2026 the telecoms regulator consulted on satellite guidelines under its 2009 procedure and published its responses; no standing body's view is known.
LBR.summary:
Consultation and what was published of it. The Liberia Telecommunications Authority put its draft Satellite Communications Guidelines out for written comment from 23 February to 9 March 2026, asking licensed service providers, satellite operators and others for their views, and held public forums on 5 March and 29 May 2026 with mobile operators, internet service providers and satellite companies. It published a Consultation Report on 3 April 2026 giving its responses to the written submissions. The Authority also held a public consultation on its Draft Infrastructure Regulations in Paynesville, reported on 12 October 2026, with internet service providers, mobile network operators and licensees. The Ministry of Posts and Telecommunications, with the African Union Commission, held a two-day consultation in Monrovia on 13 and 14 November 2025 to prepare the National Data Policy, with civil society, academia, the private sector and the media.

Required consultation and standing body. The Authority says the satellite consultation was conducted under Part III, Section 11(4) of the Telecommunications Act of 2007, and its consultation document states that it ran in accordance with the Authority's published Guidelines for Consultation Process of 2009.

Not held. No source from the last three years says a standing body with members from outside government gave its view on a named digital law or policy.

LSO.summary:

The Ministry of Information, Communications, Science, Technology and Innovation circulated the draft Cybersecurity Bill 2026 for stakeholder review in August 2026. On 23 September 2026 it opened a second consultation workshop on the bill in Maseru, lasting two days, with the Lesotho Communications Authority and UNDP, as the Department of Information reports.

Required consultation and standing body. The ministry launched a National Cybersecurity Forum in July 2026 that brings together public bodies, companies, academics, civil society and the technical community. With the Lesotho Communications Authority it first held the forum in Maseru on 29 July 2026. The Computer Crime and Cyber Security Bill 2024 would set up a National Cybersecurity Advisory Council to advise the government on cybersecurity policy.

Not held. No published report of a consultation on a digital law or policy is held from the last three years, nor the comments received, nor a written answer to them.

They met in three workshops, on digital training for young people, digital skills for women and access to digital public services for people with disabilities. Their proposals are to feed the update of the third national Open Government action plan, for 2024 to 2028, as LeNew reported on 8 September 2026.

Required consultation and standing body. The Ministry of Digital Transition and Administrative Reform holds the action plan, which carries commitments on digital inclusion. A preliminary draft law, number 62.25 on climate change and the carbon market, went to public consultation, reported in September 2026; it is not a digital law.

It also held consultation sessions in the provinces with people from the public sector, companies, civil society and academia. Earlier, INTIC put its draft Regulation on Cloud Computing Service Providers to public consultation until 30 March 2025, with a companion draft regulation on data centres.

Required consultation and standing body. A National Commission for Artificial Intelligence, established by decree, is to assess the final strategy before it goes to the government. The minister also convened a working group across sectors to review the strategy.

The ministry's Secretary General described the workshop as a consultation with those concerned, among them representatives of companies, civil society and academia.

Required consultation and standing body. The WARDIP-Mauritanie project, under the Ministry of Digital Transformation, published a provisional award notice on 7 May 2026 for technical assistance to build a national platform for citizen participation, which it calls the Plateforme de participation citoyenne. The notice is a procurement, and names no digital law or policy put to the public.

Not held. No published report of a consultation on a digital law or policy is held from the last three years, nor the comments received, nor a written answer to them.

MACRA, acting as the Data Protection Authority, held a consultation meeting in Lilongwe on 15 July 2026 on draft data protection regulations and proposed registration fees of K50,000 to K7 million by turnover, attended by companies such as United General Insurance. In February 2026 the Department of E-Government opened a two-day national validation workshop in Lilongwe on the draft National Digital Transformation Strategy and the draft National AI Strategy, with government institutions, regulators, companies, civil society and academia. A GSMA report says the ministry, supported by UNDP, published the draft digital transformation strategy and a five-year roadmap for consultation that month.

NAM.summary:

Namibia's Ministry of Information and Communication Technology put its draft Data Protection Bill out for public comment in October 2022, asking for written submissions by 30 November 2022, with the draft available from its website and from regional council offices. The ACTION Namibia Coalition, a civil society group, filed a 19-page submission with the ministry on that date, and IPPR says a version of its own paper on the bill went in as the coalition's input. The Communications Regulatory Authority of Namibia later invited written submissions by 29 August 2025 on the minister's proposed policy directive to raise the minimum broadband speed, after consultations held by the ministry on 21 May 2025 and by the regulator on 11 July 2025.

Required consultation and standing body. The regulator and the chamber of commerce have a three-year memorandum of understanding, reported in July 2026, with a joint steering committee that oversees the memorandum itself.

The Nigerian Communications Commission issued a consultation paper on 19 June 2026 on zero-rated access to educational platforms, asking for written comments by 9 July, and held a public forum on it in Abuja with the telecom operators' association ALTON and uLesson Group among those present. The Nigeria Data Protection Commission held a workshop in Lagos with private companies on its Data Privacy Framework for e-Commerce, reported in September 2026. The technology agency NITDA took a draft National Innovation Hubs Standard Framework to more than 60 hub operators, startup founders and investors in Lagos, reported on 7 September 2026. The National Assembly held a public hearing on 10 November 2025 on the National Digital Economy and E-Governance Bill, where the telecom operators' association presented a position paper.

The Open Government Partnership's reviewers say the 2023-2025 action plan, which includes an open contracting portal, was written through a steering committee of government and civil society.

It asked for contributions from operators, alternative infrastructure operators, public developers, equipment makers, integrators, consultancies and individuals. On 10 August 2026 it published a synthesis of the twenty-one contributions it received, setting out where they agreed and the differing positions expressed.

Required consultation and standing body. The Conseil national du Numérique is a consultative body of 20 public, private and civil-society members under the Prime Minister's office. Cabinet then approved the National Data Protection Policy and a new Data Protection and Right to Access Information Act, reported on 22 April 2026; that report says the reform builds on years of consultations with civil society groups, the media, security institutions and development partners.

Required consultation and standing body. MoCTI held the inaugural meeting of its Technology, Innovation and Entrepreneurship Advisory Council, reported on 5 February 2026; the council has members from the private sector and academia.
