SOM.short: The regulator consulted companies, civil society and consumer representatives on two draft rules in 2026; whether what they said was published is not known.
SOM.summary:
Consultation and what was published of it. The National Communications Authority of Somalia held a one-day consultation on 16 February 2026 on its draft Telecom Consumer Protection Regulation, at which telecommunications operators, internet service providers, submarine cable operators and consumer representatives gave their views. It then convened a national consultation meeting, reported on 25 April 2026, on its draft Cybersecurity Risk Management and Compliance Framework, with government institutions, private companies, the education sector, civil society and technical experts taking part, to gather input before the framework is finished.

Required consultation and standing body. The Ministry of Communications and Technology's Digital Inclusion Policy for Advancing Access to ICT Services for Marginalised Groups, dated August 2025, says it was validated by a workshop of interested parties.

Not held. No published report of a consultation on a digital law or policy, the comments received or a written answer to them from the last three years is held.

SSD.short: A workshop on the data protection bill was held with civil society, reported in 2026; whether what was said was published is not known.
SSD.summary:
Consultation and what was published of it. South Sudan's regulator, the National Communication Authority, and Digital Rights Frontlines, a civil society organisation, convened a two-day consultative workshop on the Data Protection Bill 2025 (Version 1.0), reported on 5 May 2026. More than 30 people took part, among them members of parliament, civil society organisations, the UNMISS legal unit and the regulator itself.

Required consultation and standing body. The South Sudan Internet Governance Forum is a national forum of government and people outside it, with a Multistakeholder Advisory Group, and is known as SS-IGF; its 2026 meeting was held in Juba, reported on 4 July 2026. The National Constitutional Review Commission is consulting the public on the permanent constitution, reported in August 2026.

Not held. No published report of a consultation on a digital law or policy, the comments received or a written answer to them from the last three years is held.

STP.short: The national cybersecurity strategy was put out for public comment in 2025; whether anything said in reply was published is not known.
STP.summary:
Consultation and what was published of it. In September 2025 AGER, under the STP Digital project, put the National Cybersecurity Strategy of São Tomé and Príncipe 2024-2028 out for public consultation, together with the action plan annexed to it. It invited contributions by telephone and by email within 30 days of publication. The notice of the consultation is on AGER's website.

Required consultation and standing body. AGER convened the first Fórum de Governança da Internet de São Tomé e Príncipe on 28 to 30 July 2026, the country's internet governance forum, known as FGI STP. Government, the private sector, academia, civil society and the technical community took part in it. The forum was not a consultation on a named law or policy.

Not held. No published report of a consultation on a digital law or policy, the comments received or a written answer to them from the last three years is held.

SWZ.short: In 2026 the Ministry of ICT held validation meetings on draft data governance and science policies; whether it published what it heard is not known.
SWZ.summary:
Consultation and what was published of it. The Ministry of ICT's Department of Research, Science, Technology and Innovation held a two-day validation session in February 2026 on the draft review of the National STI Policy and the combined 4IR and 5IR Strategy, which covers artificial intelligence, automation and data governance. The department's director said the draft was brought back to those consulted to refine, and ESEPARC, an economic policy research centre, presented. The Ministry also held a validation workshop at Ezulwini, reported on 22 July 2026, on the draft National Data Governance Policy (2027-2031). It brought together government ministries, regulators, the private sector, civil society, academia and development partners.

Required consultation and standing body. The long title of the Computer Crime and Cybercrime Act 2022 names a National Cybersecurity Advisory Council.

Not held. No report of a consultation on a digital law or policy, no comments received and no written answer to them from the last three years is held.

SYC.short: In 2023 and 2024 the financial regulator consulted on a virtual asset law and published a response; no rule requiring it is known.
SYC.summary:
Consultation and what was published of it. On 20 December 2023 the Financial Services Authority, for the Ministry of Finance, launched a public consultation on the proposed Virtual Asset Service Providers framework. It invited written responses and held a live session on 9 January 2024, in person and online, attended by about 50 to 60 people, with further sessions for Securities Act licensees, corporate service providers and virtual asset providers already operating. The Ministry and the Authority published a consultation response dated 7 March 2024 summarising the consultation, which drew about 15 detailed written responses.

Required consultation and standing body. The National AML/CFT Committee approved and launched that consultation. The Cabinet approved the holding of a Digital Economic Transformation Forum with members from several sectors, on record in September 2026.

Not held. No source from the last three years says a consultation on a digital law or policy was held because a law, decree or published procedure required it.

TCD.short: In 2026 the telecommunications ministry consulted business, academia and civil society on a draft data governance strategy; whether it published the results is not known.
TCD.summary:
Consultation and what was published of it. The Ministry of Telecommunications, Digital Economy and Digitalisation of Administration, with ECA and GIZ, held consultations in N'Djamena on 13 to 15 May 2026 for the National Data Governance Strategy, with a workshop on 21 May to validate the findings. The private sector, academia, civil society organisations, telecom operators and fintech companies were listed among the participants. A three-day workshop opened on 18 May 2026 included technology incubators and information-security specialists, and its working groups were to produce contributions for the drafting. On 7 October 2026 the Minister opened a national validation workshop on the draft and asked the academic and civil society representatives present to read it and say frankly what they think.

Required consultation and standing body. IGF Tchad, a national internet governance forum, was created in 2014.

Not held. No report of a consultation on a digital law or policy, no comments received and no written answer to them from the last three years is held.

TGO.short: Nothing held shows people outside government were asked about a digital law or policy, so no stage is set.
TGO.summary: Not held. Nothing held says people outside government were asked for their views on a digital law or policy, or that they were not.

TUN.short: In 2025 and 2026 the telecommunications regulator put fibre-sharing rules out for public comment; whether it published what it was told is not known.
TUN.summary:
Consultation and what was published of it. The Instance Nationale des Télécommunications, the telecommunications regulator, ran a first public consultation from 26 September to 26 November 2025 on the conditions for sharing fibre-optic access infrastructure. It opened a second from 6 March to 2 April 2026 on the rules for that sharing, which any contributor could answer by email or post. The E-Government Unit of the Presidency of the Government drew up the 2023-2025 open government action plan, whose commitments cover open data and the digitalisation of administrative services, through three regional workshops in Gafsa, Kairouan and Kef. Over 320 proposals were collected through a digital participation portal, workshops, email and public structures, and the Tunisian Civil Forum for OGP took part, as a results report published on 4 August 2026 states.

Required consultation and standing body. Government decree 2018-328 of 29 March 2018 requires public consultation on public policies and draft texts, with a published consultation report.

Not held. No report of a consultation on a digital law or policy, no comments received and no written answer to them from the last three years is held.

TZA.short: In 2026 regulators and academic institutions gave views on a draft data governance strategy at a workshop; whether they were published is not known.
TZA.summary:
Consultation and what was published of it. On 12 March 2026 the United Nations Economic Commission for Africa, working with the Government of Tanzania, convened a national validation workshop in Dodoma on the draft Tanzania Electronic Data Governance Strategy, known as TZeDGS. Regulatory authorities, academic institutions and sectoral agencies took part in the workshop and gave their views on the draft, and what they said informed refinements to the strategy. The Ministry of Communication and Information Technology closed the workshop.

Required consultation and standing body. The Africa Internet Governance Forum 2025 was held in Dar es Salaam, with the Government of Tanzania as host. National consultations on the East African Community's Regional AI Strategy were held in Tanzania on 12 February 2026.

Not held. No report of a consultation on a digital law or policy, no comments received and no written answer to them from the last three years is held.

ZAF.short: Parliament, the communications regulator and the Treasury put digital bills and draft rules out for public comment in 2026; what they heard is not known.
ZAF.summary:
Consultation and what was published of it. Parliament's communications committee took written submissions on the Electronic Communications Amendment Bill from the public, industry bodies and civil society until 21 September 2026. The communications regulator, ICASA, published draft amendments to its radio spectrum regulations on 15 May 2026 and held public hearings on 19 and 20 August for those who had sent written comments. The Department of Communications and Digital Technologies put its draft national artificial intelligence policy out for public comment on 10 April 2026 and later withdrew it. The National Treasury and the Reserve Bank asked for written comments by 30 September 2026 on a draft crypto asset manual, and said comments on the draft capital flow regulations published on 17 April were being considered. The universal service agency opened a public consultation on the 2010 determination on universal access, reported on 10 October 2026.

Required consultation and standing body. ICASA gave notice on 4 September 2026 of an inquiry under section 4B of the ICASA Act into the affordability of telecommunications services, inviting written answers to a questionnaire and public comment on a discussion document. A gazette of 30 September 2026 withdrew that notice and carried a new draft notice inviting comment on a questionnaire and a discussion document.

Not held. No published report of a consultation on a digital law or policy, no comments received and no written answer to them is held from the last three years.

ZWE.short: In 2025 the ICT ministry consulted academia, business and civil society on its draft artificial intelligence strategy; whether a report was published is not known.
ZWE.summary:
Consultation and what was published of it. The Ministry of ICT, Postal and Courier Services held a National Multi-Stakeholder Consultation in Harare on 28 August 2025, followed by sessions in Bulawayo on 9 September and Masvingo on 11 September 2025. The sessions were held to interrogate and validate the Kadoma Draft of the National Artificial Intelligence Strategy 2026-2030. In the strategy the Ministry credits contributions from academia, the private sector, civil society and diaspora representatives, alongside government and development partners.

Required consultation and standing body. The National Artificial Intelligence Strategy 2026-2030 says a National AI Council is to be established. It names AI & Ethics Dare, a public consultation forum, as a way citizens shape policy on artificial intelligence, and its appendix proposes a National Digital Regulatory Committee with members from several sectors.

Not held. No report of a consultation on a digital law or policy, no comments received and no written answer to them from the last three years is held.

AGO.short: Angola's standards institute, formed in 2021, added 140 national standards in 2026; whether any covers information technology or data is not known.
AGO.summary:
Standards body and its standards. Angola's standards body is the National Institute of Quality Infrastructure, formed by Presidential Decree 95/21 of 20 April 2021, which merged the standardisation institute and the accreditation institute. The decree gives it the coordination of national standardisation and the job of developing, publishing and approving Angolan standards. The institute made its 2026 catalogue available on 9 March 2026, with 140 new national standards in the annual update, approved after technical committee work and public consultation. The announcement names no standard on information technology or data.

Certification. The international standards organisation's member register records the institute as a public body, under a statute approved in April 2021, that draws up and sells technical standards and holds correspondent membership. It records no certification against a standard on information technology or data.

Not held. No source held names a national standard on information technology or data.

BDI.short: Burundi's standards bureau signed a cooperation memorandum with its Congolese counterpart in 2025; no national standard on information technology or data is known.
BDI.summary:
Standards body and its standards. Burundi's standards body is the Bureau burundais de normalisation et de contrôle de la qualité. On 29 August 2025 it signed a memorandum in Bujumbura with the Office congolais de contrôle, its counterpart in the Democratic Republic of Congo, on cooperation in standardisation, quality control and certification. The report of the signing, which presents the memorandum as a step to reduce non-tariff barriers to trade between the two countries, names no standard on information technology or data that the bureau has issued.

Certification. The memorandum of August 2025 covers certification as one of three fields of cooperation between the two bodies, with standardisation and quality control. The report says nothing of certification against a standard on information technology or data, and names no organisation that the bureau has certified.

Not held. No source held names a national standard on information technology or data.

BEN.short: Benin's standards agency was set up by order in 2017; no national standard on information technology or data is known.
BEN.summary:
Standards body and its standards. Benin's standards body is the Agence nationale de Normalisation, de Métrologie et du Contrôle Qualité. The international standards organisation's member record states that it was established by Order 2017-031 of 23 January 2017 as a public institution under the Ministry of Industry, with the mandate to manage the national standardisation system. The record names no national standard on information technology or data.

Certification. The same record gives the agency the mandate to implement the national certification system as well as the standardisation system. It names no scheme for certifying an organisation against a standard on information technology or data, and no organisation certified by the agency. The agency's national conformity mark, reported for electrical equipment, is listed below.

Not held. No source held names a national standard on information technology or data.

BFA.short: Burkina Faso's standards agency has had its statutes since 2016; no national standard on information technology or data is known.
BFA.summary:
Standards body and its standards. Burkina Faso's standards body is the Agence Burkinabè de Normalisation, de la Métrologie et de la Qualité. Decree 2016-357 of 13 May 2016 approves its statutes as a public administrative establishment, created by a 2012 decree under the 2007 law on standardisation, certification, accreditation and quality, and charges it with drawing up and issuing national standards. On 4 February 2026 the agency signed a framework convention with the telecoms regulator on managing object identifiers, which names the regulator's executive secretary as the national registration authority. Neither text names a national standard on information technology or data.

Certification. The 2016 statutes rest on a law that covers certification and accreditation as well as standardisation. They name no scheme for certifying an organisation against a standard on information technology or data.

Not held. No source held names a national standard on information technology or data.

BWA.short: Botswana's standards bureau, established by a 1995 Act, publishes a yearly programme of standards work; none on information technology or data is known.
BWA.summary:
Standards body and its standards. The Botswana Bureau of Standards was established by the Standards Act of 1995, which commenced on 1 August 1996, as a body corporate with a Standards Council, charged with preparing and publishing Botswana Standards. It publishes an annual work programme of standards projects; issue 341, updated on 16 April 2026, covers April 2026 to March 2027. In November 2025 the trade minister told Parliament that the bureau had developed voluntary national standards on school uniforms. None of the three sources names a standard on information technology or data.

Certification. The Standards Act is the nearest text held, and it names no certification against a standard on information technology or data. Neither does the work programme of April 2026.

Not held. No source held names a national standard on information technology or data.

CPV.short: Cabo Verde's standards institute listed 25 national standards in 2024, none on information technology or data.
CPV.summary:
Standards body and its standards. Cabo Verde's standards body is the Instituto de Gestão da Qualidade e da Propriedade Intelectual, which publishes the list of Cabo Verdean standards, updated in March 2024. The list runs from NCV 001:2015 to NCV 025:2023. Of its 25 national standards, 21 are on agricultural, fisheries and food products and four on tourism; it holds none on information technology, information security, software or data. The list does not state the law that set the institute up.

Certification. The catalogue of March 2024 is the nearest text held. It lists standards and no certification scheme. Certificates held by a port company, a data centre and the state's digital agency against international standards are listed below, and none names the institute or a certifier accredited in the country.

Not held. No source held names a national standard on information technology or data.

DJI.short: Djibouti's standards agency, created by law in 2021, set up its first two technical committees in 2025; neither covers information technology or data.
DJI.summary:
Standards body and its standards. Djibouti's standards body is the Agence Djiboutienne des Normes et de la Qualité, created by a law of 7 January 2021 as a public industrial and commercial body attached to the commerce ministry and named the national reference body for drawing up standards. A decree of 4 May 2022 organises it. The Council of Ministers of 13 January 2026 examined its 2026 budget of 134.9 million Djibouti francs, up from 112.1 million in 2025, and recorded that in 2025 it made two technical committees operational, for agri-food products and for electrical and household appliances. No standard on information technology or data is named.

Certification. The 2022 decree charges the agency with certifying conformity to standards and accrediting the bodies that assess it. It names no scheme for information technology or data.

Not held. No source held names a national standard on information technology or data.

DZA.short: Algeria's standards institute holds a national standard on ordering text in information technology, due for revision in 2026; certification against such standards is not known.
DZA.summary:
Standards body and its standards. Algeria's standards body is the Algerian Institute of Standardisation, created by executive decree 98-69 of 21 February 1998 as a public industrial and commercial establishment under the industry ministry, charged with drawing up, publishing and disseminating Algerian standards. Its draft national standardisation programme for 2026, published in February 2026, lists the revision of an existing national standard, NA 13037, against the 2025 edition of the international standard on comparing and ordering character strings in information technology.

Certification. The 1998 decree also charges the institute with adopting conformity marks and authorising their use. Nothing in it, or in the draft programme for 2026, names certification against a standard on information technology or data, or an organisation certified against one.

Not held. No source held says the standards body or a certifier accredited in the country offers certification against a national standard on information technology or data.

EGY.short: Egypt's standards organisation issued a national standard on exchanging electricity metering data in 2025; certification against such standards is not known.
EGY.summary:
Standards body and its standards. The Egyptian Organization for Standardization and Quality states that it is the sole official body for preparing and issuing Egyptian standards, set up by Presidential Decree 2 of 1957 and given its present name by Presidential Decree 83 of 2005. Its register lists Egyptian Standard 7982-1/2025, endorsed on 1 October 2025, which adopts the international standard on the exchange of electricity metering data and is classed under information technology. The standard is not obligatory. A ministerial decision of 2022 lets an international or foreign standard stand where no Egyptian one exists.

Certification. The register entry for the 2025 standard is the nearest text held, and it names no certifier and no organisation certified against the standard.

Not held. No source held says the standards body or a certifier accredited in the country offers certification against a national standard on information technology or data.

ERI.short: Eritrea's standards institution was established by proclamation in 1995; no national standard on information technology or data is known.
ERI.summary:
Standards body and its standards. Eritrea's standards body is the Eritrean Standards Institution, established by Proclamation No. 75 of 1995 as an autonomous body with legal personality. The proclamation makes it the sole national organ for standardisation, quality assurance and metrology, and gives it the power to prepare compulsory Eritrean Standards. The record of the proclamation, dated 20 September 1995, is an abstract and the only source held on the institution, and it names no standard on information technology or data.

Certification. The 1995 proclamation covers quality assurance as well as standardisation and measurement. The record held names no scheme for certifying an organisation against a standard on information technology or data, and no organisation the institution has certified against any standard.

GHA.summary:
Standards body and its standards. Ghana's standards body is the Ghana Standards Authority. The Ghana Standards Authority Act, 2022, Act 1078, was assented to and published in the Gazette on 30 June 2022, and was amended by the Ghana Accreditation Service Act, 2023. An industry brief of 2024 names the authority as the national standards body. On 19 March 2026 it hosted a steering committee meeting on the second phase of a metrology institute project with Germany's metrology institute, and on 4 September 2026 the communications minister said it works with two regulators to see that cell sites meet approved radiation and safety levels. None of these names a standard on information technology or data.

Certification. The 2022 Act is the nearest text held; only its citation and history are held, and they name no certification scheme.

Not held. No source held names a national standard on information technology or data.

GIN.short: Guinea's standards institute was organised by decree in 2023; no national standard on information technology or data is known.
GIN.summary:
Standards body and its standards. Guinea's standards body is the Institut Guinéen de Normalisation et de Métrologie. A presidential decree read on national television on 7 January 2023 fixes its attributions, organisation and operation as a public administrative body under the industry and finance ministries. The decree charges it with drafting national standards, or adopting foreign or international ones, and with publishing them. The report of the decree names no standard on information technology or data that the institute has issued.

Certification. The decree of January 2023 is the only text held on the institute. The national conformity mark it provides for is listed below. The report names no scheme for certifying an organisation against a standard on information technology or data, and no organisation the institute has certified.

GMB.short: The Gambia's standards bureau listed an information security standard as a national standard in 2022; certification against it is not known.
GMB.summary:
Standards body and its standards. The Gambia Standards Bureau was established by an Act of Parliament in 2010 to develop and publish national standards in all sectors and to provide conformity assessment and metrology services. Its director general said in 2026 that it has more than 70 staff, having absorbed the former weights and measures department. The bureau's 2022 catalogue lists GAMS ISO/IEC 27001:2005, on information security management systems, as a Gambian Standard adopted from the international one. The international standards organisation lists the bureau as a correspondent member.

Certification. The 2022 catalogue says the bureau provides conformity assessment services. It names no certification scheme for the information security standard, which adopts the 2005 edition of the international one, and no organisation certified against it.

Not held. No source held says the standards body or a certifier accredited in the country offers certification against a national standard on information technology or data.

KEN.short: Kenya's standards bureau has existed since 1974; a national standard on information technology or data issued by it is not known.
KEN.summary:
Standards body and its standards. Kenya's standards body is the Kenya Bureau of Standards, which a 2026 release says has existed since 1974 and provides standards development, metrology, conformity assessment, training and certification. In August 2026 it was led by a director general and overseen by a National Standards Council. The ICT Authority's Government Data Centre Standard, approved in January 2020, names the bureau as the source of information on valid national and international standards and says it took part in developing the authority's standards under a memorandum of understanding. None of the three names a national standard on information technology or data that the bureau has issued.

Certification. The 2026 release lists certification among the bureau's services, and names no scheme for information technology or data.

Not held. No source held names a national standard on information technology or data.

LBR.short: Liberia established its standards authority by an Act published in 2022; no national standard on information technology or data is known.
LBR.summary:
Standards body and its standards. Liberia's standards body is the Liberia Standards Authority. An Act to amend the Executive Law and establish the authority was published by the commerce ministry on 5 August 2022. Its preamble cites the quality infrastructure of the Economic Community of West African States and the country's obligations under the World Trade Organization's agreement on technical barriers to trade. Only the preamble of the Act is held, and it names no national standard on information technology or data.

Certification. The Act's preamble is the only text held on the authority. It names no scheme for certifying an organisation against a standard on information technology or data, and no organisation the authority has certified. The country's national quality policy is listed below.

LBY.short: Libya's standards centre, created by a 1990 law, adopted new standards in 2026; none is known to cover information technology or data.
LBY.summary:
Standards body and its standards. Libya's standards body is the National Centre for Standardization and Metrology, created by Law 5 of 1990, issued on 15 May 1990. The law charges the centre with quality control and with preparing, adopting and supervising standards, and makes the standards it adopts binding nationwide. On 3 February 2026 the centre's supreme committee, meeting at the planning ministry, adopted its plan for 2026 and a number of Libyan standards. The report of the meeting names none of them as a standard on information technology or data.

Certification. The 1990 law gives the centre quality control as well as standard-setting. Neither it nor the report of the 2026 meeting names certification against a standard on information technology or data.

LSO.summary:
Standards body and its standards. Lesotho's standards body is the Lesotho Standards Institution. The trade and industry minister said on 16 September 2020 that the institution, created by an Act published in 2014, was now operational as the country's national standards body, with a mandate to develop and publish national standards. The minister's address is the only source held on the institution, and it names no national standard on information technology or data.

Certification. The minister's address of 2020 sets out the institution's mandate to develop and publish standards. It names no scheme for certifying an organisation against a standard on information technology or data, and no organisation the institution has certified. The communications regulator's quality-of-service rules of 2023 are listed below.

MDG.summary:
Standards body and its standards. Madagascar's standards body is the Bureau des Normes de Madagascar, which was created by decree 98-944 of 4 November 1998 and is now governed by decree 2014-1570 of 30 September 2014. A United Nations Development Programme assessment published in December 2025 describes it as the national standards body and a correspondent member of the international standards organisation, and says public information shows no specific programme on standards for artificial intelligence or data governance. Neither source names a national standard on information technology or data.

Certification. The bureau's own description of its activities is the nearest text held. It names no scheme for certifying an organisation against a standard on information technology or data, and no organisation the bureau has certified.

MLI.short: Mali's standards agency, created in 2012, had its budget cut for 2026; no national standard on information technology or data is known.
MLI.summary:
Standards body and its standards. Mali's standards body is the Agence Malienne de Normalisation et de Promotion de la Qualité, created by an ordinance of 19 March 2012 as a public administrative body with legal personality and financial autonomy, charged with implementing national policy on standardisation and quality promotion. The international standards organisation records it as Mali's national standards body and a full member. Its board, meeting on 29 January 2026, adopted a 2026 budget of 243.3 million CFA francs, against 318.4 million in 2025. None of the three names a national standard on information technology or data.

Certification. The 2012 ordinance charges the agency with creating and managing the national conformity mark. It names no certification against a standard on information technology or data.

MOZ.short: Mozambique's standards institute certifies quality management under a 2022 decree; no national standard on information technology or data is known.
MOZ.summary:
Standards body and its standards. Mozambique's standards body is the Instituto Nacional de Normalização e Qualidade. Decree 8/2022 of 14 March 2022 approves the regulation on standardisation and conformity assessment and gives the institute the job of coordinating standardisation and implementing Mozambican technical standards. On 7 May 2026 the economy ministry and the institute announced that a certificate of conformity becomes mandatory from 1 June 2026 for listed imports, among them rice, fortified foods, used vehicles, tyres and construction steel. Neither names a standard on information technology or data.

Certification. The 2022 decree also charges the institute with certifying management systems, products, services and people. Six are held by public bodies: the Passport and Immigration Office, the national computer emergency response team, the Mauritius Revenue Authority, the central information systems division of the technology ministry, the police information technology unit and the National Sanctions Secretariat.

SWZ.summary:

Togo's standards body is the Agence togolaise de normalisation, which the agriculture ministry describes as a technical structure of the Haute Autorité de la Qualité et de l'Environnement. The ministry says the agency drew up 46 national standards, all on agri-food value chains such as rice, soya, poultry and meat, which were presented in Lomé on 17 and 18 August 2026. A notice approved on 16 December 2025 proposes 15 standards for compulsory declaration, on cosmetics, paints, toys, chemicals, paper, appliances and cables. Its own site, in August 2026, says it develops, publishes, maintains and withdraws Zambian National Standards, that it has developed standards in sectors that include information and communication technology, and that there are more than 6,500 Zambian National Standards and more than 50 international standards adopted as national ones. ZWE.summary:

The National Quality Policy 2021–2025 says it develops national standards but rests on no enabling legislation, and that the government will legislate for it and rename it. AGO.summary:

Angola and Mozambique signed a memorandum in June 2026 under which Mozambique's state telecommunications operator and state broadcaster would carry their signals over Angola's ANGOSAT-2 satellite, with a commercial agreement still to be made final. Angola's space programme office signed a commercial pilot agreement with Telecom Namibia, reported in August 2026, to test the satellite as backhaul for the Namibian network. On land, a company secured a US$31 million loan in November 2023 to pay for a data centre in Luanda and three fibre routes, one of them from Luanda through Lusaka to Dar es Salaam.

In service and carrying another country's traffic. The pilot with Telecom Namibia is a test of the satellite on a working network, and the memorandum with Mozambique awaits its commercial agreement.

BFA.summary:
Shared link or facility agreed and under construction. A telecommunications company based in Morocco began investing about US$100 million in 2020 in a terrestrial fibre cable linking Morocco, Mauritania, Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger. The cable is the company's own, built to join its subsidiaries in the four countries to its home network, and the investment ran from 2020 to 2022.

In service and carrying another country's traffic. The 5,700 km cable is recorded as completed in 2022. It runs from Morocco to Niger through Mauritania, Mali and Burkina Faso, and lets the company's subsidiary in landlocked Burkina Faso reach international bandwidth over the parent's network. Burkina Faso has no coast, and the cable gives that subsidiary a route over land to the capacity its parent holds.

It provides for cooperation on cross-border fibre interconnection, internet transit and wholesale capacity, and for the development of the corridor between Buitepos, on the Namibian border, and Ngoma. The memorandum is between the two companies, and names the corridor as work to be developed.

In service and carrying another country's traffic. A fibre route into Zimbabwe from the Botswana border was live and carrying traffic on 3 July 2026. The two companies behind it describe the section from Plumtree to Bulawayo as the first active route of its network into Zimbabwe and as linking Zimbabwe to Botswana.

Not held. No source held reports the link or facility carrying another country's traffic in the last three years: capacity sold or traffic carried across the border, or a user from the other country named.

CAF.short: Fibre links to Cameroon and Congo have been in service since February 2023; how much traffic they carry is not known.
CAF.summary:
Shared link or facility agreed and under construction. The six central African states are developing the Central African Backbone to join their national fibre networks, with about $273 million from member states and partners, as reported in August 2026. The government received grants from the African Development Bank and the European Union for its part of the project. A regional prospectus lists the country among eleven in a USD 9 million project for six new data centres, one of them here, which is still being defined.

In service and carrying another country's traffic. The national fibre backbone was inaugurated on 6 February 2023: 935 km of fibre on land and under rivers, joined to Cameroon at Gamboula and to Congo at Bomassa. The project closed in September 2023 with both cross-border links installed. The authorities judged in May 2026 that reaching the sea cables through the networks of coastal neighbours had markedly improved speeds.

Not held. No source held reports the link or facility carrying another country's traffic in the last three years: capacity sold or traffic carried across the border, or a user from the other country named.

In service and carrying another country's traffic. RASCOM's director general said on 31 July 2026 that the organisation's services are already in use in Côte d'Ivoire. His example was the national broadcaster, RTI, which used RASCOM satellite capacity during the Africa Cup of Nations in 2023. The user he names is Ivorian. He names no other country's operator using the same capacity, and gives no figure for what is carried.

Not held. No source held reports the link or facility carrying another country's traffic in the last three years: capacity sold or traffic carried across the border, or a user from the other country named.

In service and carrying another country's traffic. The Central African Republic's fibre backbone was inaugurated on 6 February 2023 with 935 km of fibre installed and working. It joins the Central African Republic to Cameroon at Gamboula, and to Congo, as one part of the Central African Backbone project that the African Development Bank and the European Union paid for.

In service and carrying another country's traffic. A company activated a 2,000 km fibre route from Mombasa to Goma in February 2026, through Nairobi, Kampala and Kigali, giving the east of the country a direct path to the sea cables on the Kenyan coast. The company said on 9 February 2026 that the route was already carrying traffic for its first wholesale customers, with partner companies in Uganda and Kenya. It said again on 9 September 2026 that the route was live and carrying traffic.

The three operators presented the project to prospective carriers in Addis Ababa on 7 September 2026, ahead of deployment and commercial launch.

The African Union's register of its Convention on Cyber Security and Personal Data Protection, known as the Malabo Convention, dated 2 February 2026 records Rwanda as having signed it on 16 April 2019, ratified it on 14 November 2019 and deposited the instrument on 21 November 2019. The register counts 21 signatures and 20 instruments deposited among the Union's 55 member states, and the convention has been in force since 8 June 2023. The National Bank of Rwanda and the Bank of Ghana signed a memorandum on 25 February 2025 to let fintech firms licensed by one operate under the other.

Taken into national law and applied across a border. No national law, decree or regulation passed to give effect to a shared African legal text is recorded for Rwanda, and nor is a licence or signature recognised, a request between authorities answered or a ruling under one. The African Union's register lists the dates each state signed, ratified and deposited, and says nothing of national law.

Not held. No source held says a national law or rule was passed to give effect to a shared text.

BDI.short: Burundi joined East Africa's shared roaming area in 2024, and regional figures for 2025 show its cross-border calls more than doubling.

It took part in the Community's Digital for Development Forum in Arusha in June 2026 and in its technical committee on telecommunications in May 2026.

What was agreed put into effect and in use. Burundi entered the East African Community One Network Area on 1 August 2024, with regulations from its regulator cutting regional roaming tariffs. The regional regulators' organisation reports that inbound cross-border voice traffic rose 126 per cent in 2025, from 89.6 million to 202.9 million minutes, and attributes the rise to that accession.

The Algerian-Tunisian joint technical commission on communications and ICT cooperation held its fourth session in Tunisia in June 2026, a standing body of the two governments, and agreed joint projects. None of the projects is reported as started. Published figures of its use, a decision of a joint body or a review of what was delivered in the last three years are not recorded.

Not held. No source held gives figures of use, a decision of a joint body, or a review of what an agreement has delivered, in the last three years.

TZA.short: Tanzania is in East Africa's shared roaming area, and regional figures for 2025 show its outbound cross-border calls up by more than half.
TZA.summary:
Part taken in regional digital policy. Tanzania is one of the seven member states of the East African Communications Organisation, with its regulator submitting data for 2024 and 2025. It took part in the third steering committee of the Eastern Africa regional digital integration project in Nairobi on 5 and 6 May 2026. The steering committee was reported by the East African Community's secretariat, which runs the project with the Intergovernmental Authority on Development.

What was agreed put into effect and in use. The regional regulators' organisation reports Tanzania's One Network Area cross-border voice traffic for 2025 as 148 million inbound minutes, up 36.4 per cent, and 577.7 million outbound minutes, up 59 per cent from 363.3 million. The One Network Area is the East African Community's shared roaming arrangement, under which roaming tariffs between member states were cut.

Not held. Nothing on the four questions.

UGA.short: Uganda is in East Africa's shared roaming area, with 2025 call figures published, and won a seat on the African telecommunications union's council in 2026.
UGA.summary:
Part taken in regional digital policy. Uganda was elected to a four-year seat on the administrative council of the African Telecommunications Union in Abuja on 24 July 2026. It chairs and hosted in Kampala the Northern Corridor Integration Projects cluster meeting with Kenya, Rwanda and South Sudan in August 2026, and is a member state of the East African Communications Organisation.

What was agreed put into effect and in use. The regional regulators' organisation reports that Uganda's inbound One Network Area cross-border voice traffic fell 28 per cent in 2025, from 1,103.2 million to 794.4 million minutes, which it attributes to internet calling services replacing voice. The same report covers the One Network Area, the East African Community's shared roaming arrangement, under which roaming tariffs between member states were cut.

Not held. Nothing on the four questions.

ZAF.short: South Africa pays dues to the African telecommunications union, budgeted for 2026; no digital agreement signed or seat won is known.
ZAF.summary:
Part taken in regional digital policy. South Africa's budget provides a membership transfer of 2.073 million rand to the African Telecommunications Union for 2026/27. Its delegates took part in the Southern African Development Community's regional workshop on data governance in Harare in August 2026. It hosted and chaired the Community's summit in August 2026, with digitised borders a chairship priority, and was a launching partner of the African Union development agency's semiconductor advisory group. An agreement signed, a meeting hosted or chaired, or a seat won in the last three years is not recorded.

What was agreed put into effect and in use. The nearest held fact is the digitised borders priority of its regional chairship, set in August 2026; no border system is reported as started under it. A roaming cut, a joint body set up, a regional guideline adopted as a national rule or a shared service opened is not recorded, and neither are figures of use or a decision of a joint body.

Not held. No source held dates an agreement signed, a meeting hosted or chaired, or a seat won, in the last three years.

ZMB.short: A Zambian was elected secretary general of the African telecommunications union in July 2026; nothing agreed is known to be in effect.
ZMB.summary:
Part taken in regional digital policy. The conference of plenipotentiaries of the African Telecommunications Union elected Kezias Kazuba Mwale of Zambia as secretary general in Abuja on 24 July 2026, with 21 of 34 votes. Zambia's minister of technology and science spoke at the close of the conference, in which Zambia's delegation took part.

What was agreed put into effect and in use. The nearest held fact is the election of the secretary general, an office won; no rule or service adopted in Zambia under a regional agreement is reported. A roaming cut, a joint body set up, a regional guideline adopted as a national rule or a shared service opened is not recorded, and neither are figures of use or a decision of a joint body.

Not held. No source held says a thing the country agreed has been put into effect.

ZWE.short: Zimbabwe's minister chairs Smart Africa's council of ICT ministers, as of 2026; nothing agreed is known to be in effect.
ZWE.summary:
Part taken in regional digital policy. Zimbabwe's ICT minister chairs Smart Africa's council of ICT ministers, reported in August 2026. Zimbabwe's ministry hosted in Harare the Southern African Development Community's regional workshop on data governance in August 2026, a three-day meeting on harmonising data policy. Its data protection authority holds the second vice presidency of the Network of African Data Protection Authorities, and Zimbabwe was the 26th state to join Smart Africa.

What was agreed put into effect and in use. The nearest held fact is the Harare workshop on harmonising data policy; no harmonised rule adopted in Zimbabwe is reported. A roaming cut, a joint body set up, a regional guideline adopted as a national rule or a shared service opened is not recorded, and neither are figures of use or a decision of a joint body.

Not held. No source held says a thing the country agreed has been put into effect.

AGO.short: Since 2023 births are entered digitally at offices in Luanda and three other cities; most offices use paper, and the digital count is not known.
AGO.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The Ministry of Justice and Human Rights runs civil registration through its directorate DNIRN and introduced RCI, as it names its civil registration system, in 2023. Presidential Decree 267/24 of 28 November 2024 approved a plan to December 2026 for a single database fed daily by civil registration. Nascer com Registo, the government's maternity registration programme, is financed by the European Union, ANGOP reported on 4 March 2026.

Events registered digitally. Births have been registered in RCI since 2023 at civil registration posts. Angola told the registrars general on 18 July 2026 that biographic and biometric data are collected when the birth entry is issued.

How the record is made. In RCI the birth is entered at the post, in a system with a centralised database. The older SIRC has no central database and the majority of civil registration units still rely on paper records, as of 2024.

Last twelve months. Novo Jornal reported on 5 May 2026 that identification and civil registration posts in almost the whole country had been without their system for four months. A civil registration post opened on 3 March 2026 in the provincial hospital's maternity at Mbanza Kongo.

Local offices doing the digital entry. RCI is in Luanda's registries and in one post each in Huambo, Benguela and Lubango, as of 2024. The World Bank's diagnostic counts 39 civil registration units in Luanda province and at least 255 in the country in 2023.

Not held. No source counts the offices registering in the central system, and deaths in a digital system are not described. No source says the outage reported on 5 May 2026 has ended.

BDI.short: Digital civil registration runs in about twelve pilot communes in 2026, most acts still on paper; how the pilot record is made is not known.
BDI.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The interior ministry presents the civil registration reform and its pilot digitalisation as the government's, with the World Bank, UNICEF, UNECA and UNDP as supporting partners, in its presentation of 18 July 2026. Its director general for territorial administration put the platform's cost at about BIF 15 billion on 6 May 2026.

Events registered digitally. The project launched at Rumonge on 19 July 2024 is for the digital registration of births and deaths at the commune's civil status service, at its seat and in its zones.

How the record is made. The ministry's director general told the African registrars general on 18 July 2026 that the majority of civil-status acts are still recorded in physical registers and that Burundi has no single national database of them. The ministry's director general said on 6 May 2026 that the legal framework still rests on manual registration procedures.

Last twelve months. On 6 May 2026 the ministry presented a digital platform for civil registration and biometric identity card production, its infrastructure nearly complete and awaiting a decree. On 11 August 2026 it stated that the government continues to scale up the platform.

Local offices doing the digital entry. The ministry's presentation of 18 July 2026 records a pilot digitalisation project in 12 communes. On 10 August 2026 thirteen communes had a biometric registration system, with civil registration digitalised in pilot communes.

Not held. No source says the system is past its pilot, how the digital record is made in the pilot communes or where it is held. No plan with a current period and no domestic budget line for the platform is on record.

BEN.short: Births are registered digitally at maternity desks in ten pilot health facilities since August 2025; how other local offices make the record is not known.
BEN.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. ANIP, the national identification agency, runs the one-stop birth registration desk with its own teams and the Ministry of Health's health workers. Benin's playbook of May 2026 states that ANIP is attached to the Presidency and is in charge of the population register and the national civil-status file. ANIP began the reform with the support of the WURI project and UNICEF.

Events registered digitally. From 20 August 2025 the declaration and registration of a birth are done on site in about ten public health facilities. In six months 17,071 children were declared there and 13,069 registered, ANIP reported on 24 February 2026.

How the record is made. Desk agents at Natitingou and Djougou register the child in the system at the maternity, working on tablets and centralised databases, La Nation reported on 16 July 2026. Paper declaration forms remained in use during the pilot.

Last twelve months. The pilot ended in February 2026 and a consolidation phase is running in the same ten facilities, with generalisation three to four months behind the initial calendar, ANIP's director general said on 16 July 2026.

Local offices doing the digital entry. The desk's pilot was launched on 20 August 2025 at CHU-MEL Cotonou and runs in ten public health facilities. On 24 February 2026 the desk was running in 10 health facilities, with gradual national scale-up among the prospects.

Not held. How ANIP's communal units and the civil-status centres make the record is not described, so deaths and offices beyond the ten pilot facilities are not established. No plan with a period is on record.

BFA.short: Birth-entry software was deployed in 170 civil registration centres in 2025; the total number of centres, and how many register in it, is not known.
BFA.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The Direction générale de la modernisation de l'état civil trains commune agents on the platform it calls VENEEM. The Stratégie nationale de l'état civil 2023-2027 was adopted by joint order on 25 January 2024. In 2024, 2.52% of its financing came from the state budget, 33.46% from local authorities and 64.01% from partners.

Events registered digitally. The country's delegate told an Abidjan symposium in December 2024 that births are declared directly from health centres through a national application. Agents of the commune of Pouni were trained from 31 August to 2 September 2026 to enter births, marriages and deaths.

How the record is made. The Pouni training covered entering events in real time by smartphone, at central offices and secondary centres alike. A November 2024 account says the platform captures events where they occur, on computers and smartphones. The Code des personnes et de la famille, in its 2025 text, institutes a national digital civil-status register.

Last twelve months. Agents of the commune of Koloko were trained on the software and given equipment, as reported on 22 June 2026. On 25 June 2026 the director general for the modernisation of civil status said deployment in communes was continuing.

Local offices doing the digital entry. The ministry reported the software deployed in 30 main and 140 secondary centres in 2025, and in 20 main and 96 secondary centres in 2024.

Not held. The total number of centres, how many of the 170 register in the software and whether the 2025 count includes 2024's. Where the record is held, and whether deaths are entered beyond one commune's training.

BWA.short: A national system registered births and deaths in 2024; how many of the 35 district offices enter records in it is not known.
BWA.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The Department of Civil and National Registration of the Ministry of Labour and Home Affairs operates the registration offices and holds the records of the Births and Deaths Registration System. Its recurrent provision of P108,505,050 for 2026/27 covers the system's maintenance among others. A 2019 health ministry roadmap scheduled a registration strategic plan for 2021-2026.

Events registered digitally. The system registers births, stillbirths and deaths, and was the source for the 49,180 births and 14,070 deaths registered in 2024.

How the record is made. Statistics Botswana in August 2026 calls the system "partially automated and decentralized", designed to give real-time statistics and integrated with the National Identification System, which has assigned a birth registration number at birth since 2003. A September 2015 report says births and deaths records pass online from local and regional offices to a central repository.

Last twelve months. The minister told Parliament on 6 March 2026 that of about 15 hospital kiosks set up to register births on site, 9 were operating and 6 had closed, chiefly for lack of staff. On 24 February 2026 he said online registration of births and deaths was built and would go live with the 1-Gov platform.

Local offices doing the digital entry. The department operates 35 district registration offices and 17 on-site registration points at hospitals and clinics, as Statistics Botswana reported in August 2026. Electronic on-site registration had opened in 13 hospitals by September 2015.

Not held. How many of the 35 district offices and 17 on-site points enter records in the system, and whether the entry is made at the office. No plan in force is held, and the kiosk closures are undated.

CAF.short: A civil registration application was still being developed in July 2026 and offices register on paper; the number of pilot offices is not known.
CAF.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The territorial administration ministry, through its Direction Générale de la Décentralisation et de l'État Civil, is preparing the deployment of a civil registration application with CIVIPOL as technical operator. The Politique Nationale de l'État Civil was adopted by the Head of State on 4 April 2025. The supporting MODERO project is financed by the European Union.

Events registered digitally. The software under development is to cover births, marriages and deaths, the director general said on 18 July 2026. UNICEF's profile of 2017 gives births and deaths as processed by hand on paper.

How the record is made. The director general described an all-paper system on 18 July 2026, with 70% of civil registration centres without electricity. Civil registration registers were distributed to communes of the Ouham, and registers for declaring births to the maternity of Bossangoa university hospital, UNDP reported in April 2026.

Last twelve months. In July 2026 the ministry was preparing to deploy the application, which was not yet deployed. An operational map of 45 centres had been validated by 18 July 2026.

Local offices doing the digital entry. The country's delegate told an Abidjan symposium in December 2024 that the digitalisation of civil status was at the pilot phase and should extend to 40 localities in 2025.

Not held. No office is shown entering a birth or a death digitally. How many offices were in the pilot, what it piloted and the period the national policy covers are not held.

CIV.short: In March 2026 the registrar said 98 per cent of civil status centres were computerised and connected; whether any registers births digitally is not known.
CIV.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. ONECI, the national civil status and identification office, is the executing arm of the national civil status policy, the Minister of the Interior and Security said on 16 June 2025. A convention of 2 March 2026 implements the Stratégie nationale de l'état civil et de l'identification. The 2026 finance law appropriates FCFA 500 million from domestic revenue for modernising civil status.

Events registered digitally. The software ONECI supplied to the centres, which AIP names Citiweb, is intended for the digital registration of births, marriages, deaths and other civil status acts.

How the record is made. The World Bank said on 18 September 2025 that the registry is still on paper. The decree of 2 October 2019 keeps the paper register as the legal record and permits acts to be established by computer beside it.

Last twelve months. At the end of 2025 ONECI supplied all town hall and sub-prefecture centres with computers carrying the software, and began training agents. From 27 to 29 July 2026 it trained 44 agents of the Gôh region.

Local offices doing the digital entry. ONECI's director general said on 2 March 2026 that 98 per cent of civil status centres were computerised and connected to the software, and on 11 August 2026 that its Système national de gestion de l'état civil was deployed in 699 centres.

Not held. The evidence does not say that any centre registers a birth in the software: every figure is of centres equipped, computerised or with the system deployed, and neither the 98 per cent nor the 699 comes with a total of centres. How the record is made at an equipped centre is not established.

CMR.short: In September 2026, 60 of 432 principal civil status centres were digitised, 13.9 per cent; the share of all local offices is not known.
CMR.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. BUNEC, the national civil status office, works under the supervision of the decentralisation ministry. Its National Strategic Plan for the Modernisation of the Civil Status System 2025-2029 was launched on 11 September 2025. The equipment in the communes comes through UNDP projects, Legal Identity II in the East Region and a Denmark-funded one in ten municipalities.

Events registered digitally. UNDP reported in September 2025 that Maroua 3 council issues birth, marriage and death certificates, producing birth certificates on the system while the parent waits. In the East Region birth acts were being produced in the system UNDP names SIGEC by August 2026.

How the record is made. Each East Region commune receives its own server, workstations and network with the software installed, UNDP reported in August 2026. In an interview published on 8 October 2026 BUNEC's Director General describes paper as the dominant process, with digital registration in selected councils only.

Last twelve months. On 7 January 2026 Limbe I Council issued the first birth certificate from a digitalised system in the North-West and South-West regions. By August 2026 two East Region centres, Bertoua 1er and the Bertoua City Council, were in production.

Local offices doing the digital entry. On the figures BUNEC's Director General gave on 14 September 2026, 60 of the country's 432 principal civil status centres were digitised, 13.9 per cent, against 42 in April 2022. The country also has 2,439 secondary centres.

Not held. The share of all local offices is not published: the 60 are counted against principal centres only, and the secondary centres are outside the figure. The evidence does not establish that a record made in a commune is held in the national register, and it states no national budget line.

COD.short: In August 2025 one commune of the capital was piloting digital civil registration; whether any birth or death has been registered digitally is not known.
COD.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The Ministry of Interior and Security is responsible for civil registration through its Civil Registration Division, as of March 2019. The one pilot is executed by four United Nations entities and financed by the UN's Joint SDG Fund, UNFPA reported on 18 August 2025. A national civil-registration strategy and a master plan for digitising the centres were still to be written on 1 October 2026.

Events registered digitally. UNFPA stated on 18 August 2025 that the Masina pilot aims to automate the collection and management of data on births, marriages and deaths.

How the record is made. Government terms of reference posted on 3 April 2026 state that the civil registers are mostly manual and are not integrated into any central file. In March 2019 the Civil Registration Division reported that each act is written on paper with four carbon copies.

Last twelve months. A UNDP tender closing on 25 April 2026 sought a consultant to assess the digitalisation of civil registration and support the design of digital registration tools. On 23 July 2026 a sector office in Walikale, North Kivu, had been out of birth registers for several months.

Local offices doing the digital entry. One commune, Masina in Kinshasa, has a pilot at its municipal civil-status office, UNFPA reported on 18 August 2025. In March 2019 the Civil Registration Division counted 979 local offices, 102 urban and 877 rural, none using a computer or mobile device.

Not held. No fact says an event has been registered digitally: the Masina pilot's births and deaths are stated as its aim, and its own dates and results are not given. No count of offices is held newer than the 979 of March 2019.

COG.short: A civil registration system was built and validated by September 2026 but no office uses it; whether older urban systems still run is not known.
COG.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The state agency ACSI designed and built the civil registration system Congo calls SIFEC for the Interior ministry's territorial administration directorate. On 20 February 2026 the validation workshop's main recommendation was that the human, material and financial means to deploy it be provided. The World Bank's Congo Digital Acceleration Project counts an operational civil registration database among its results. The agency placed the computerisation of civil-status events in its programme under the national policy for the reform and modernisation of civil status 2022-2026.

Events registered digitally. None. SIFEC's Births, Marriages and Deaths modules were under validation in February 2026, and the World Bank scored a national digital database of civil registration records not operational at 31 May 2025.

How the record is made. On paper: in February 2026 the Interior ministry's security adviser called the system long manual and fragmented. In 2021 the World Bank found electronic records stored locally in civil registration centres of Brazzaville and Pointe-Noire, and rural areas largely paper-based.

Last twelve months. On 20 February 2026 a workshop at Kintélé validated 17 recommendations on SIFEC. On 7 August 2026 the Interior minister told the Senate its rollout was imminent. On 22 September 2026 ACSI handed the system's operating documents to the territorial administration directorate.

Local offices doing the digital entry. None. After the handover of 22 September 2026 seven steps remained, user training and deployment among them. In 2020 the World Bank counted 2 of Brazzaville's 10 civil status offices as digitised.

Not held. Whether the electronic records kept in some Brazzaville and Pointe-Noire centres in 2020 and 2021 are still kept. Who pays for SIFEC's deployment.

COM.short: In 2026 offices register on paper while a digital system is studied and costed; when its three-centre pilot starts is not known.
COM.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The Ministry of the Interior carries the modernisation project Comoros calls AMECC, with the French embassy and UNICEF. By 14 August 2026 the country held a costed modernisation plan and a national mapping of civil registration centres. France and UNICEF financed the work to that date, and national institutions validated a residual financing need of EUR 9,009,900.

Events registered digitally. None. Births, marriages and deaths are registered in paper registers, and the digital system, an eCRVS, is only proposed, by a preliminary study validated on 25 March 2026.

How the record is made. In August 2026 the system was still largely dependent on old paper registers. In January 2026 the Minister of the Interior said acts are made on secured printed forms produced abroad, with recurring shortages.

Last twelve months. The study preceding digitalisation was launched in Moroni on 2 October 2025 and validated there on 25 March 2026. On 11 March 2026 the Council of Ministers did not adopt the draft decree for a national civil status agency. A UNICEF-recruited consultant ran a resource-mobilisation mission from 30 July to 16 August 2026.

Local offices doing the digital entry. None. The preliminary study covered 37 civil status centres and proposes a pilot in three, at Moroni, Mutsamudu and Fomboni. Of the 37, fewer than half have stable electricity and one in five has internet access.

Not held. When the three-centre pilot starts, and the period the costed plan and the 2024 strategic plan cover. Whether any office keeps records other than on paper.

CPV.short: In 2017 offices in all 22 municipalities entered births and deaths digitally, in urban centres only; whether records reach the national register is not known.
CPV.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. UNICEF's profile, compiled to November 2017, names the Directorate of Registries, Notaries and Identification of the Ministry of Justice as the authority registering births and deaths. Decreto-Lei 43/2007 places the civil registry database in that directorate's ownership.

Events registered digitally. Births and deaths. UNICEF's profile, compiled to November 2017, states that all vital events are recorded directly in the computer. NOSi's catalogue of 2025 lists a Civilian ID System that collects and processes civil registry data on births, marriages, deaths and stillbirths.

How the record is made. In 2017 events were recorded in applications located in the civil registry conservatórias, with a certificate issued immediately. The Civil Registry Code of 2014 requires entries in electronic form, held in a national civil registry database, and allows paper only when the system is unavailable.

Last twelve months. NOSi's catalogue of 2025 describes the Civilian ID System as a stream linking the civil registries to other government systems.

Local offices doing the digital entry. UNICEF's profile, compiled to November 2017, puts the applications in the conservatórias of all 22 municipalities, 22 of 22. Registration stations exist only in the urban centres of those municipalities; mobile teams reached rural communities during the birth registration project.

Not held. Whether the entry made at the conservatória is held in the national register in practice. Any share of offices, or rural share, newer than 2017; any fact on ownership, plan or finance from the last three years, and any event in the last twelve months.

DJI.short: Nine civil-status sites in Djibouti-Ville have entered births and deaths digitally since 2011, as stated in 2024; digital entry outside the capital is not known.
DJI.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The Ville de Djibouti states that it has held the civil-status service since the Ministry of the Interior transferred the competence in 2008, and that its communes have exercised it since 2011 through SIGEC, as the city names its computerised civil-status system. Terms of reference of February 2024 place a diagnostic of SIGEC and a budgeted action plan under PROGOUV, a EUR 8 million governance support project for the city.

Events registered digitally. The city stated on 28 April 2024 that the registration of births, marriages, divorces and deaths in Djibouti-Ville has rested since 2011 on software for entering, transmitting and using civil-status data. The February 2024 terms of reference state that maternity antennas enter birth declarations in the system and the central centre draws up death and marriage acts.

How the record is made. By the city's account of 2024, civil-status agents have fed its database continuously since 2011 as they make new entries. The terms of reference place the data on a central server in a room of the Hôtel de Ville.

Last twelve months. The city reported on 28 April 2024 a diagnostic of SIGEC by an international expert, commissioned under PROGOUV.

Local offices doing the digital entry. The February 2024 terms of reference list nine civil-status sites, all in Djibouti-Ville: the Mairie's central centre, three commune centres and five antennas in maternities.

Not held. Nothing dated 2025 or 2026 says any office outside Djibouti-Ville enters digitally, and no national count of offices, no plan and no event of the last twelve months is held. A 2025 ESCWA survey, held only in summary, says local offices hold no electronic records of births or deaths, which disagrees with the city's 2024 account.

DZA.short: Births are registered in a national digital register across 1,541 communes, a 2019 count; the share of local offices entering digitally is not known.
DZA.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. Law 14-08 of 9 August 2014 creates the national automated civil-status register under the Ministry of the Interior and Local Authorities. A university article published on 10 October 2025 places the register within the e-municipality programme of the national e-Algeria strategy, which it dates 2008 to 2028. The ministry's presentation of July 2026 lists the availability of financing among the levers of the digitalisation.

Events registered digitally. The same presentation states that since 2018 each newborn has a birth act and a national identification number at the end of its registration, the number generated automatically from the register. The ministry's deck of 19 June 2019 shows the register holding three databases, of births, deaths and marriages.

How the record is made. The 2019 deck places entry, control and update at commune level, with 48 wilaya databases for error correction and a national database at the ministry. Under the 2014 law each commune still inscribes acts on three paper registers kept in duplicate and transmits a digitised copy of every act to the national register.

Last twelve months. In July 2026 the ministry presented the register as its own, created in 2014, with unified national governance of civil-status data.

Local offices doing the digital entry. The 2019 deck shows 1,541 commune databases where entry, control and update are done. The 2025 article states that paper documentation persists alongside the digital services.

Not held. The 1,541 is a 2019 count of commune databases with no total of local offices, communes and their annexes together, and nothing held says the entry is made at the commune office when the event is registered. No event of the last twelve months and no rural figure is held.

EGY.short: Births and deaths are entered digitally at 4,571 health offices, as stated in 2026; the share of all offices is not known.
EGY.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The development plan for fiscal year 2026/27, as Youm7 reported it on 2 August 2026, credits the Ministry of Health and Population and the bodies concerned with developing the electronic birth and death registration system and names it within the digital-transformation axis of the national family development project. Law 143 of 1994 gives the Civil Status Organization of the Ministry of Interior the registration of births and deaths.

Events registered digitally. Egypt's presentation to the 2026 APAI-CRVS registrars-general meeting states that a central database for births and deaths runs on a secure platform and directly updates the statistics office's population clock.

How the record is made. A conference paper on the system implemented in 2017 states that data entry is done at the health office, which prints the birth or death certificate once entry is complete, with the offices linked online to a central database. The 2026 presentation describes automated health offices feeding the central database.

Last twelve months. An article of 20 January 2026 reports that the health ministry instructed all health affairs directorates to unify and improve the quality of data entered on the automated births and deaths registration system at health offices.

Local offices doing the digital entry. The 2026 presentation gives full nationwide automation of 4,571 health offices across the 27 governorates. The planning ministry's report of 2 August 2025 says 4,666 health offices are electronically linked.

Not held. No total of health offices is held against the 4,571 or the 4,666, and no rural share is published. Egypt's undated answers to a WHO questionnaire published in 2025 describe paper at registration points and electronic entry at the governorate centre, which disagrees with the 2026 account.

ERI.short: Births and deaths were handwritten at local offices and entered in regional electronic registers one level up in 2017; current practice is not known.
ERI.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. Eritrea has developed a five-year Strategic Civil Registration and Vital Statistics Plan for 2024-2028, recorded by the African Committee of Experts on the Rights and Welfare of the Child in observations adopted in April 2026.

Events registered digitally. Births and deaths are both registered in the sub-zoba's digital database after entry in the kebabi's handwritten register, according to a Dutch foreign ministry report of February 2017 cited by the Danish National ID Centre, which adds that death registration has no fixed or automatic routine.

How the record is made. A birth is first entered in the handwritten family register at the local kebabi office, which issues a transfer letter that the parents take to the sub-zoba office, where the data is entered into the database and the hard copies are archived (2017). A death goes the same way, by a "death letter" from the kebabi to the sub-zoba.

Last twelve months. The death certificate issued by the local municipality is computerised and carries a registration number, the US State Department said in 2025.

Local offices doing the digital entry. Each of the six zobas keeps an electronic population register, first introduced in zoba Maekel in 2003 and updated by the 54 sub-zoba administrations, while each of about 2,000 kebabi administrations keeps a handwritten family register, the Danish National ID Centre states, citing the European Asylum Support Office in May 2015.

Not held. How a birth is entered today, how many offices do the digital entry, who owns and pays for the registers, and whether the 2024-2028 plan names a digital system. The record-making facts date from 2015 and 2017, and nothing is held for the last twelve months.

ETH.short: Digital registration of births and deaths is in pilot, in Addis Ababa and 1,300 of 19,202 kebeles in 2025; use beyond pilots is not known.
ETH.summary:
Governance, planning, finance. The Immigration and Citizenship Service is the registration organ, with structures from federal to the lowest administrative level, under Proclamation No. 1370/2025 of 18 March 2025. The national eCRVS, which Ethiopia calls the Civil & Family Registration System, is homegrown, driven by the Prime Minister's Office and carries a three-phase rollout plan (July 2026).

Events registered digitally. The national eCRVS lists birth and death registration and certificates among its services, alongside marriage, divorce and adoption (July 2026).

How the record is made. The eCRVS is a decentralised, multi-tenant system on a shared architecture in which city administrations and regions provide all services, with offline access, rural connectivity, power and tablets listed as gaps (July 2026). Civil registration is mainly paper-based and manual, three copies of the form passing from kebele to woreda to the Service (July 2025).

Last twelve months. On 5 December 2025 the mayor of Addis Ababa launched the Integrated Civil Registration and Residency Service Technology and announced full implementation in 50 woredas from 8 December.
